# INTRODUCTION.

The **Tantrarâja** <note>literally "The King of Tantras"</note>, as its name implies, is an important work of its class. One of its parts is published here for the first time with a commentary called **Manoramâ** <note>"That which pleases the mind"</note> by Subhagânandanâtha. He belonged to the Kashmir school, as noted by the scholar Bhâskararâya in his commentary on the *Nityâshodashikârnava* <note>A significant Tantric text concerning the goddess Tripurasundarî</note>.

There are three sections of this <term>Tantra</term> <note>A category of esoteric Indian scriptures focusing on ritual, meditation, and philosophy</term>, each dealing with a separate <term>Mata</term> <note>A specific school or "way" of regarding and worshipping a deity</note>, namely **Kâdi**, **Hâdi**, and **Kahâdi**. These terms were mentioned in my work "Shakti and Shâkta" and will be explained later. I am told the final portion is also called *Shaktisanggama*, which consists of four parts. The first part is published here: the **Kâdimata** portion of the *Tantrarâja*, comprising 36 chapters of 100 verses each.

The manuscripts used to prepare this edition belong to the **Asiatic Society of Bengal**, the **Sanskrit College**, and **Pandit Yajnapurusha**, respectively. I am indebted to the latter for his assistance in preparing this and other works. **Ha** is the <term>Bîja</term> <note>A "seed-syllable," or a single-syllable mantra that contains the essence of a deity</note> of the god **Shiva**. **Ka** is the first letter of the seed-mantra of the goddess **Kâlî**, which is *Krîṅg*. In the *Bîjâbhidânam* <note>A dictionary of seed-syllables</note>, quoted on page 321 of Pandit Jaganmohana Tarkâlaṅkâra's edition of the *Mahânirvâṇa Tantra*, it is said:

> <note>original: "Ka Kâlî Brahma ra proktam mahâmâyârthakashcha Î / Vishvamâtrarthako nâdo bindur duḥkhapahârakah / Tenaiva kâlikâṅg devîṅg pûjayed duḥkhashântaye"</note>
> **Ka** is Kâlî; **Ra** is said to be Brahmâ; the long **Î** signifies the Great Illusion (Mahâmâyâ). 
> The **Nâda** <note>The subtle sound or resonance represented by a crescent</note> signifies the Mother of the Universe, and the **Bindu** <note>The point or dot above a letter representing concentrated power</note> is the remover of sorrow. 
> With this [mantra] alone, one should worship the Goddess Kâlikâ for the cessation of suffering.

When the <term>Devî</term> <note>The Goddess</note> asks in verses 7 and 8, "What is Kâdi?", Shiva replies that Kâlî and Kâdi are **Shakti** <note>The divine feminine power</note> and that "Thy form is the meaning of Kâdi" <note>original: "Kâdisangjnâ bhavadrûpâ"</note>. This signifies that the **triangle** is the form of the Goddess. The letter **Ka** written in the Bengali script ( ক ) and generally in earlier Devanâgara forms shows a triangle on the left side. According to the *Varṇoddhâra* and *Kâmadhenu Tantras* (as cited in the encyclopedia *Shabdakalpadruma*), the left line of this triangle represents the red **Brahmâ** <note>the Creator</note>, the right line represents the white **Vishnu** <note>the Preserver</note>, and the bottom line represents the dark green **Rudra** <note>the Destroyer</note>. The **Mâtrâ** <note>The horizontal top line of the letter</note> is the white goddess **Sarasvatî** herself. The crooked portion on the right, resembling a goad, is the lightning-like **Kuṇḍalinî** <note>The spiritual energy coiled at the base of the spine</note>. The empty space within the triangle is the white **Sudarshana** <note>a divine disk or vision</note> shining like millions of moons; with Him is **Kâlî**, the giver of **Kaivalya** <note>Final liberation or absolute independence</note>. In the three corners are the powers known as **Jyeshṭhâ**, **Vâmâ**, and **Raudrî**. This <term>Trikoṇa</term> <note>Triangle</note> is—

<summary>This introduction establishes the Tantrarâja as a major work of the Kâdi school of Tantra, explaining the esoteric symbolism of the Sanskrit letter 'Ka' as a representation of the Divine Mother and the cosmic trinity.</summary>

# INTRODUCTION.

known as the **Yonimandala** <note>The "Circle of the Source," a sacred geometric representation of the creative power of the Goddess</note> which is the seat (*Âsana*) of **Tripurâ Devî** <note>The "Goddess of the Three Cities," representing the supreme divinity presiding over the three states of consciousness</note>. She is the essence of knowledge (**Jnânâtmâ**) in whom are the four **Kalâs** <note>Divine aspects or powers</note> and as the collectivity of Knowledge (**Jnâna**), Will (**Ichchhâ**), and Action (**Kriyâ**), She is **Mûrtimân Prakriti** <note>Primal Nature personified</note>. From the letter **Ka** (**Kakâra**) comes **Kâma** <note>Desire, the primordial urge to create</note>. It is the Root-Nature (**Mûlaprakriti**) of all letters (**Varnas**) and the imperishable Power of Blossom (**Sphuradavyaya**), the Mother of all Deities (**Devas**) and the Giver of Liberation. In the *Chhândogya Upanishad* (4-10-5) it is said "Ka is the Absolute" <note>original: "Kang Brahma"</note>; "**Ka** is **Brahma**." It is that Power (**Shakti**) Which, being spread by means of the nine **Nâthas** <note>The "masters" or openings of the body through which experience flows: 2 ears, 1 mouth, 2 eyes, 2 nostrils, the genitals, and the anus</note>, manifests throughout the earth cycle after cycle (**Kalpa** after **Kalpa**), and at the end of the Great Cycle they and She return to him <note>original: "Sâ taiḥ sârddham brajechchamâm"</note>. **Shiva** and **Shakti** are one, and where one is worshipped, the other is worshipped. The *Sammohana Tantra* (Chapter I) says the **Kâdimata** is that school (**Mata**) in which the mantras begin with **Ka**. In **Hâdi**, they begin with **Ha**. It is also called the King of Swans (**Hangsarâja**) <note>A reference to the breath or the soul</note>. **Kahâdi** is formed by the union of **Kâdi** and **Hâdi**, which is within the scope of the Northern Tradition (**Uttarâmnâyagochara**). The *Kulârnava*, which belongs to the Upper Tradition (**Ûrddhvâmnâya**), is, I have been told, the highest Tantra in the **Kahâdi** school.

The Tantras of the **Kâdi** class are, according to the present Text, nine in number and are according to the *Manoramâ*: **Sundarîhridaya** <note>Heart of the Beautiful One</note>, **Nityâshodashikârnava** <note>Ocean of the Sixteen Eternal Ones; published in Vol. 56 of the Anandashrama Sanskrit Texts</note>, **Chandrajnâna** <note>Moon-Knowledge</note>, **Mâtrikâ** <note>The Mother-Letters</note>, **Sammohana** <note>The Enchanter</note>, **Vâmakeshvara** <note>Lord of the Left-hand Path</note>, **Bahurûpâshtaka** <note>Eight-fold Many-Forms</note>, **Prastârachintâmani** <note>Wish-fulfilling Gem of Expansion</note>, and **Meruprastâra** <note>Expansion of Mount Meru</note>.

**Bhâskararâya**, the learned Commentator on various **Tântrik** and **Upanishadic** <note>original: "Aupanishâdic"</note> texts, questions the accuracy of the *Manoramâ* on this point in his *Setubandha* <note>The "Bridge," his commentary on the Nityâshodashikârnava</note>. He there says that the *Nityâshodashikâ* is part of the *Vâmakeshvara Tantra* and the *Sundarî* or *Yoginîhridaya* is a part of the former. The three, therefore, make one Tantra. He also says in the same Commentary that the *Bahurûpâshtaka* is not one Tantra but eight, named after the seven Divine Mothers (**Mâtris**) beginning with **Brâhmî** and including **Shivadûtî**. I may here observe that if the *Sammohana Tantra* be counted as one of the nine, it cannot be the Tantra of that name published by **Rasika Mohana Chattopâdhyâya**, for that is a **Vaishnava** <note>Pertaining to the worship of Vishnu</note> Tantra and a fragment of a work consisting of 40,000 verses. A copy of another work of the same name was supplied to me from the collection of the great scholar (**Mahâmahopâdhyâya**) **Vindhyeshvarîprasâda Divedî**, and copies are said to be available in Nepal of this Tantra which is a **Kâdi** Tantra; therefore, it must be to this and not to the published *Sammohana* that the *Manoramâ* refers.

It also includes a scholarly critique by Bhāskararāya regarding the classification and numbering of these foundational texts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical introduction to the Tantrarāja Tantra, specifically explaining the Kadi school's approach to the worship of the Goddess Tripurasundari. It bridges the gap between external ritual and the internal realization of non-duality.</meta>

# INTRODUCTION.

The <term>Kâdi Tantras<note>A specific school of Tantric tradition that emphasizes the worship of the Goddess through lineages beginning with the letter 'Ka'.</note></term> give detailed injunctions touching the worship of <term>Shakti<note>The divine feminine power or cosmic energy.</note></term> in Her various forms: such worship being either **gross** (*Sthûla*), **subtle** (*Sûkshma*), or **supreme** (*Para*). Naturally, the <term>Sâdhaka<note>A spiritual practitioner or seeker.</note></term> begins with the first, and the ritual takes the practitioner up to the highest. The aim and object is the practical realization of the truths of <term>Advaita Vedânta<note>The philosophical system of non-duality, teaching that the individual soul and the absolute reality are one.</note></term>.

**Tripurasundarî** or **Lalitâ** <note>Names for the Supreme Goddess, meaning "The Beautiful One of the Three Cities" or "The Playful One"</note> has three aspects (*Rûpa*): **Gross**, **Subtle**, and **Supreme**. The ritual of Her worship is also of three kinds: **Physical** (*Kâyika*) by the body, **Vocal** (*Vâchika*) by speech, and **Mental** (*Mânasa*) by the mind—also called **External Ritual** (*Bâhyayâga*), **Internal Ritual** (*Antaryâga*), and **Contemplative Visualization** (*Bhâvanâ*).

This Tantra gives all the three forms whereby the practitioner is led by his <term>Guru<note>Spiritual teacher</note></term> through ascending stages to the **Success of Non-duality** (*Advaita Siddhi*). The Guru is one with the **Primal Power** (*Âdyâ Shakti*), who is the **essence of reflection** (*Vimarshamayî*), the cause of all. The ninefold nature of his body is seen in the nine apertures <note>The nine openings of the human body: two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, mouth, and the two organs of excretion/reproduction.</note>.

> The Guru is the Primal Power; she is known as the essence of reflective consciousness. The ninefold nature of his body appears in the form of the bodily openings.
> <note>original: "Gururâdyâ bhavechchhaktiḥ sâ vimarshamayî matâ / Navatvang tasya dehasya randhratvenâvabhâsate"</note>

The nine Gurus are in the form of the nine apertures. The body of the practitioner is the **Shrîchakra** <note>The "Sacred Wheel," a complex geometric diagram representing the Goddess and the cosmos.</note>, which consists of nine sub-chakras. The object of worship of the **Shrîchakra** is the realization of the **contemplation of non-separateness** (*Abhedabhâvanâ*) of the **Knower** (*Jnâtâ*), who is the **Priest** (*Hotâ*); of **Knowledge** (*Jnâna*), which is the **Libation** (*Arghya*); and of the **Known** (*Jneya*), which is the **Sacrificial Offering** (*Havih*).

> The Knower is one's own self; Knowledge is the libation; the Known remains as the sacrificial offering. The worship of the **Shrîchakra** is declared to be the unification of these three.
> <note>original: "Jnâtâ svâtmâ bhavejjnânam arghyang jneyang haviḥ sthitam / Shrîchakrapûjanang teshâm ekîkaranam îritam."</note>

The scheme of spiritual practice (*Sâdhanâ*) and the different parts of the **Shrîchakra** are explained in the **Chapter on Symbolic Interpretations** (*Vâsanâ Patala*, Ch. XXXV) of this work. The *Tripurâtâpinî Upanishad* deals with **Physical** and **Vocal** Action (*Karma*), and the *Bhâvanopanishad* with **Contemplation** or **Mental** Action. This last Upanishad summarizes in the main the "Chapter on Symbolic Interpretations" of the *Tantrarâja* and begins with the teaching: "The Holy Guru is the Power that is the cause of all" <note>original: "Shrîguruḥ sarvakâranabhûtâ shaktiḥ"</note> and ends with: "One who is devoted to this contemplation becomes liberated while still living" <note>original: "Bhâvanâparo jîvanmukto bhavati"</note>.

In order to follow the ritual of this work, it is necessary to understand the **Shrîyantra** <note>Another name for the Shrîchakra diagram.</note> figured on the cover of this volume. This celebrated diagram represents the human body and the whole universe and man (for what is in the former is in the latter and *vice versa*), as also the **Essential Nature of Shiva-Shakti** or the **Self** (*Âtmâ*). It is thus the symbol of the **Goddess** (*Devî*) as She is in Her own true form (*Svarûpa*) and as She is in the form of the universe.

<summary>This page explains that the Tantric path leads a practitioner from physical rituals to a mental realization of non-duality, where the knower, the knowledge, and the object known become one. It identifies the human body and the universe as identical manifestations of the Goddess, both represented by the sacred Shri Yantra.</summary>
<keywords>Kadi Tantra, Tripurasundari, Shri Chakra, Shri Yantra, Non-duality, Advaita Vedanta, Guru, Shakti, meditation, levels of worship, microcosm and macrocosm</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical introduction to the Kadi school of Tantra, shifting focus from the spiritual teacher to the geometric and metaphysical structure of the Shri Yantra—the primary sacred diagram used in this tradition.</meta>

# INTRODUCTION.

**The Soul of the Universe** <note>original: "Vishvâtmâ"</note>. The account here given is taken from the Text, which account agrees with that given in other **Tantras of the "Ka" Lineage** <note>original: "Kâdi Tantras"; a specific school of tradition starting with the letter 'Ka'</note> such as the **Heart of the Yogini** <note>original: "Yoginîhridaya"</note> and the **Ocean of the Sixteen Eternals** <note>original: "Nityâshodashikârnava"</note> and with the **Upanishad of Meditative Visualization** <note>original: "Bhâvanopanishad"</note> which is an Upanishad of the **Kadi Tradition** <note>original: "Kâdimata"</note>.

The **Sacred Diagram** <note>original: "Yantra"</note> is composed of nine triangles and **Circles** <note>original: "Chakras"</note> one within the other until the central point or **Seed-Point** <note>original: "Bindu"</note> is reached. In each of the nine Chakras the **Goddess** <note>original: "Devî"</note> is worshipped in its centre under one of Her nine names united with the **Mantra of the Sacred Sandals** <note>original: "Pâdukâ Mantra"</note> of seven letters. The nine triangles are four with points upwards—that is the **Forms of Shiva** <note>original: "Shrîkanthas"</note> or the masculine element—and the five downward pointed triangles or **Shiva’s Young Maidens** <note>original: "Shivayuvatîs"</note>, the feminine power or **Shakti** element. All are formed by the **Primordial Root-Nature** <note>original: "Mûlaprakriti"</note> of the **Shiva-Point** <note>original: "Shivabindu"</note>, the ninth being the Primordial Root-Nature, and the eight the **Transformed Evolutes** <note>original: "Vikritis"</note> which in relation to their productions are **Nature** <note>original: "Prakriti"</note>. The nine Chakras also represent **Creation** <note>original: "Srishti"</note>, **Maintenance** <note>original: "Sthiti"</note> and **Absorption** <note>original: "Sang-hâra"</note>, each set of three being formed of the combinations:
*   Creation-Creation
*   Creation-Maintenance
*   Creation-Absorption
*   Maintenance-Creation
*   Maintenance-Maintenance
*   Maintenance-Absorption
*   Absorption-Creation
*   Absorption-Maintenance
*   Absorption-Absorption.

The object of the worship is, as the **Upanishad of Meditative Visualization** says (Verse 10), the realization of the unity of the **Knower**, **Knowledge**, and the **Object of Knowledge** <note>original: "Jnâtâ, Jnâna, Jneya"</note>. This is summarized as **"the meditation on the non-difference between the knower, knowledge, and the known"** <note>original: "Jnâtrijnânajneyânâmabhedabhâvanam"</note>, which is the aim and object of every **Non-dualist** <note>original: "Advaitin"</note>. The nine Chakras are:
1.  The **Earth-City** <note>original: "Bhûpura"</note>
2.  Sixteen petals
3.  Eight petals
4.  First set of fourteen angles
5.  Second set of ten inner angles
6.  Third set of ten angles within these
7.  Fourth set of eight angles within these
8.  Three angles within these
9.  The point or **Seed-Point** <note>original: "Bindu"</note>.

These are called (commencing with the first above named or outermost): **Enchanter of the Three Worlds** <note>original: "Trailokyamohana"</note>, **Fulfiller of All Desires** <note>original: "Sarvâshâparipûraka"</note>, **Agitator of All** <note>original: "Sarvasangkshobhana"</note>, **Giver of All Good Fortune** <note>original: "Sarvasaubhâgyadâyaka"</note>, **Accomplisher of All Objects** <note>original: "Sarvârthasâdhaka"</note>, **Destroyer of All Disease** <note>original: "Sarvarogahara"</note>, **Protector of All** <note>original: "Sarvarakshâkara"</note>, **Bestower of All Success** <note>original: "Sarvasiddhiprada"</note> and **Full of All Bliss** <note>original: "Sarvânandamaya"</note>.

There are two ways in which the **Auspicious Diagram** <note>original: "Shrîyantra"</note> may be described. We may start from the outer Chakra and work inwards, which is called the **Order of Dissolution** <note>original: "Layakrama"</note>, or commence with the Bindu and work outwards. The latter, which is called the **Order of Creation** <note>original: "Srishtikrama"</note>, is here adopted. The central Seed-Point, or the Supreme united **Lord of Desire** <note>original: "Kâmeshvara"</note> and **Lady of Desire** <note>original: "Kâmeshvarî"</note>, is the Goddess **Tripurâ** or **Lalitâ** Who is the **Self** <note>original: "Âtmâ"</note>, whether as the **Individual Soul** <note>original: "Jîvâtmâ"</note> in bodies or as the bodiless **Supreme Soul** <note>original: "Paramâtmâ"</note>. For the Lord of Desire is the Supreme **Pure Consciousness** <note>original: "Samvit"</note> without **Limiting Adjuncts** <note>original: "Upâdhi"</note> and the Lady of Desire is His **Power** <note>original: "Shakti"</note>. This Seed-Point is in the innermost triangle or **All-blissful** <note>original: "Sarvânandamaya"</note> Chakra. The word **Source** <note>original: "Yoni"</note> in this worship does not mean the generative organ of a woman but means **Cause** <note>original: "Kâranam"</note>, the **Womb of the Universe**. This Seed-Point is threefold...

# INTRODUCTION.

...the triad <note>original: "traya"</note>, one above being the face of the **Goddess** <note>original: "Devî"</note> and the two below being Her Breasts. This is symbolism of worship in which in India, as elsewhere, human-like forms are employed, those forms being those seen by the worshippers of the culture. More abstractly, the three **Points** <note>original: "Bindus"</note> are Sun, Moon, and Fire; not the physical luminaries or elements so called, but names given to the **Illumination** <note>original: "Prakâsha"</note> and **Reflective Awareness** <note>original: "Vimarsha"</note> aspects of the **Supreme Point** <note>original: "Parabindu"</note> as it differentiates to create the Universe. Such aspects are again symbolized by the single and double **Points** <note>original: "Bindus"</note>, the **Nasalized Echo** <note>original: "Anusvâra"</note> and **Aspirate** <note>original: "Visarga"</note> breathings respectively. The worship of the Goddess **Lalita** is a part of **Auspicious Wisdom** <note>original: "Shrîvidyâ"</note>. Lalita is also called the **Primordial One** <note>original: "Adyâ"</note> or the **Eternal Deity of the Whole** <note>original: "Angginityâ Devatâ"</note> who is **Being** <note>original: "Sat"</note>, **Bliss** <note>original: "Ânanda"</note>, and **Fullness** <note>original: "Purnî"</note>. Around Her, as **Limb-Deities** <note>original: "Angga"</note> or **Encompassing Deities** <note>original: "Âvarana Devatâs"</note>, are the fifteen **Eternal Goddesses** <note>original: "Nityâ Devatâs"</note> representing the five **Elements** <note>original: "Bhûtas"</note> with their fifteen **Qualities** <note>original: "Gunas"</note> or (as one account goes) the three **Qualities** of **Goodness** <note>original: "Sattva"</note>, **Passion** <note>original: "Rajas"</note>, and **Inertia** <note>original: "Tamas"</note>.

The number ‘15’ is reached by dealing with each of the **Elements** from their aspects of **Goodness**, **Passion**, and **Inertia**, or by addition of the **Qualities** of the **Elements** themselves. In the triangle surrounding the Goddess are the nine **Lords** <note>original: "Nâthas"</note>. These correspond to the nine apertures which exist both in the cosmic and individual bodies, namely: the two Eyes and mouth (**The Divine Stream** <note>original: "Divyaugha"</note>), the two ears and the Penis (**The Perfected Stream** <note>original: "Siddhaugha"</note>), and the two Nostrils and Anus (**The Human Stream** <note>original: "Mânavaugha"</note>).

Lalita is the **Reflective Power** <note>original: "Vimarsha Shakti"</note> of the **Illuminating Shiva** <note>original: "Prakâsha Shiva"</note>. Lalita is red; for in the 28th Sutra of the **Upanishad of Meditative Visualization** <note>original: "Bhâvanopanishad"</note> it is said -> “Redness is the Reflective Awareness of all this <note>original: "Lauhityam etasya sarvasya vimarshah"</note>.” By “all this,” as the commentator **Bhaskararaya** <note>original: "Bhâskararâya"</note> says in his commentary on that Upanishad, is meant the **Lord of Desire** <note>original: "Kâmeshvara"</note>, Lalita, and the **Practitioner’s** <note>original: "Sâdhaka’s"</note> own self. **Passion** <note>original: "Râga"</note> and redness are one. It is said that -> “One’s **True Self** <note>original: "Âtmâ"</note> is the Goddess Lalita whose body is the universe <note>original: "Vishvavigrahâ"</note>. Redness is Her Reflective Awareness and worship is the meditation on this.” The **Central Point** <note>original: "Bindu"</note> is surrounded by a triangle, or the **Diagram that Grants Success** <note>original: "Siddhiprada Chakra"</note>. At the corners of this triangle, which is the Second Chakra, are the **Powers** <note>original: "Shaktis"</note> (distinct from the Eternals of that name): **The Lady of Desire** <note>original: "Kâmeshvarî"</note> (to be distinguished both from the Supreme Lady and the Eternal of that name), **The Lady of the Thunderbolt** <note>original: "Vajreshvarî"</note>, and **The Lady of the Garland of the Womb** <note>original: "Bhagamâlinî"</note>. These represent the **Unmanifest** <note>original: "Avyakta"</note> or **Nature** <note>original: "Prakriti"</note>, the **Great One** <note>original: "Mahat"</note> or Cosmic **Intellect** <note>original: "Buddhi"</note>, and the **Ego-sense** <note>original: "Ahangkâra"</note>. The three corners are the **Sacred Seats** <note>original: "Pîthas"</note> of **Kamarupa** <note>The Form of Desire</note>, **Purnagiri** <note>The Full Mountain</note>, and **Jalandhara** <note>The Water-Holder</note>. In the centre is the **Seat of Flight** <note>original: "Auddîyâna Pîtha"</note>, with the **Mantra of the Sacred Sandals** <note>original: "Shrîpâdukâ Mantra"</note> being -> “*Hung, Shring, I worship the Sacred Sandals of the Great Goddess Tripura Sundari, the Root Knowledge in its entirety, at the Seat of Oddiyana. Salutations!* <note>original: "Hûng, Shrîng, Samastâm Mûlavidyâm, Auddîyânapîthe Shrîmahîtripurasundarî-Devî Shrîpâdukâm pûjayâmi Namah."</note>” In the spaces outside this triangle are the five **Subtle Elements** <note>original: "Tanmâtras"</note> which are the five arrows of...

# INTRODUCTION.

**Desire** <note>original: "Kâma"</note>, **Mind** <note>original: "Manas"</note>, the sugar-cane bow of the **King of Desire** <note>original: "Kâma Râga"</note> which is his noose, and **Aversion** <note>original: "Dvesha"</note> which is his goad.

The third **Wheel** <note>original: "Chakra"</note>, known as the **Giver of All Protection** <note>original: "Sarvarakshâkara"</note>, is composed of eight angles. These are the first eight angles formed by the intersection of the triangles other than the central one already described. These angles are inhabited by the eight **Deities of Speech** <note>original: "Vashinî, Kâmeshvarî, Mohinî, Vimalâ, Arunâ, Jayinî, Sarveshvarî, and Kaulinî"</note> who are the **Presiding Deities** <note>original: "Devatâs"</note> of **Cold** <note>original: "Shîta"</note>, **Heat** <note>original: "Ushna"</note>, **Happiness** <note>original: "Sukha"</note>, **Pain** <note>original: "Duhkha"</note>, **Desire** <note>original: "Ichchhâ"</note>, and the three fundamental qualities of nature: **Harmony** <note>original: "Sattva"</note>, **Passion** <note>original: "Rajas"</note>, and **Inertia** <note>original: "Tamas"</note>. At this stage, the **spiritual practitioner** <note>original: "Sâdhaka"</note> strives to control these **qualities** <note>original: "Gunas"</note> and to remain unaffected by the **pairs of opposites** <note>original: "Dvandvas"</note> like pleasure and pain.

The fourth **Wheel**, the **Destroyer of All Disease** <note>original: "Sarvarogahara Chakra"</note>, is composed of ten angles presided over by the ten **Divine Energies** <note>original: "Shaktis"</note>: **The All-Knower**, **The Giver of All Power**, **The Giver of All Sovereignty**, **The One Composed of All Knowledge**, **The Destroyer of All Sickness**, **The Support of All**, **The Remover of All Sins**, **The One Composed of All Bliss**, **The Protectress of All**, and **The Giver of the Fruit of All Desires** <note>original: "Sarvajnâ, Sarvashaktipradâ, Sarvaishvaryyapradâ, Sarvajnânamayî, Sarvavyâdhivinâshinî, Sarvâdhârâ, Sarvapâpaharâ, Sarvânandamayî, Sarvarakshâ, Sarvepsitaphalapradâ"</note>. These are the **Deities** <note>original: "Devatâs"</note> of the various functions of the **vital fire** <note>original: "Vahnikalâ"</note> which are: **Exhalation** <note>original: "Rechaka"</note> or elimination, **Digestion** <note>original: "Pâchaka"</note>, **Absorption** <note>original: "Shoshaka"</note> which removes the imbalances of the **digestive fire** <note>original: "Jatharâgni"</note>, **Burning** <note>original: "Dâhaka"</note>, **Circulation** <note>original: "Plâvaka"</note> or the spreading of digestive fluids, **Secretion** <note>original: "Kshâraka"</note> such as bile, **Belching** <note>original: "Udgâraka"</note>, **Churning** <note>original: "Kshobhaka"</note> of the food, **Yawning** <note>original: "Jrimbhaka"</note>, and **Stupefaction** <note>original: "Mohaka"</note> which causes pain and fainting.

The fifth outer **Wheel**, the **Accomplisher of All Objects** <note>original: "Sarvârthasâdhaka"</note>, consists of ten angles and is presided over by the **Goddesses** <note>original: "Devîs"</note>: **The Giver of All Success**, **The Giver of All Wealth**, **The One Who is Dear to All**, **The Maker of All Auspiciousness**, **The Giver of All Desires**, **The Remover of All Sorrows**, **The Queller of All Death**, **The Remover of All Obstacles**, **The One Who is Beautiful in Every Limb**, and **The Giver of All Good Fortune** <note>original: "Sarvasiddhipradâ, Sarvasampatpradâ, Sarvapriyangkarî, Sarvamangalâkârinî, Sarvakâmapradâ, Sarvadukkhavimochanî, Sarvamrityuprashamanî, Sarvavighnanivârinî, Sarvângasundarî, Sarvasaubhâgyydâyinî"</note>. These are the Goddesses of the ten **vital breaths** <note>original: "Prânas"</note> which are controlled through their worship.

The sixth **Wheel**, the **Giver of All Good Fortune** <note>original: "Sarvasaubhâgyadâyaka"</note>, has fourteen angles in which reside the **Energies** <note>original: "Shaktis"</note>: **The All-Agitating**, **The All-Expelling**, **The All-Attracting**, **The All-Gladdening**, **The All-Deluding**, **The All-Paralyzing**, **The All-Crushing**, **The All-Subjugating**, **The All-Charming**, **The All-Intoxicating**, **The Accomplisher of All Objects**, **The Filler of All Wealth**, **The One Composed of All Mantras**, and **The Destroyer of All Dualities** <note>original: "Sarvasangkshobhinî, Sarvavidrâvinî, Sarvâkarshinî, Sarâhlâdinî, Sarvasammohanî, Sarvastambhinî, Sarvajambhinî, Sarvavashangkarî, Sarvaranjanî, Sarvonmâdinî, Sarvârthasâdhanî, Sarvasampattipûranî, Sarvamantramayî, Sarvadvandvakshayangkarî"</note>. These are the **Presiding Deities** <note>original: "Âdhidevatâs"</note> of the fourteen principal **energy channels** <note>original: "Nâdîs"</note>, namely: Alambushâ, Kuhû, Vishvodarâ, Vâranâ, Hastijihvâ, Yashovatî, Payasvinî, Gândhârî, Pûshâ, Shangkhinî, Sarasvatî, Îdâ, Pinggalâ, and Sushumnâ.

The seventh **Wheel** is the eight-petalled **All-Agitating Wheel** <note>original: "Sarvasangshobhana Chakra"</note> which surrounds the circle in which the other [parts of the diagram rest].

# INTRODUCTION. 7

The triangles mentioned are placed here. The **Goddesses** <note>original: "Devîs"</note> in this section are **Flower of the Bodiless**, **Girdle of the Bodiless**, **Intoxication of the Bodiless**, **Lust of the Bodiless**, **Line of the Bodiless**, **Force of the Bodiless**, **Goad of the Bodiless**, and **Garland of the Bodiless** <note>original: "Ananggakusumâ, Ananggamekhalâ, Ananggamadanâ, Ananggamadanâturâ, Ananggarekhâ, Ananggaveginî, Ananggamadanângkushâ, and Ananggamâlinî"</note>. These are the **Presiding Deities** <note>original: "Devatâs"</note> of the **Intellect** <note>original: "Buddhi"</note> regarding **Speech** <note>original: "Vachana"</note>, **Grasping** <note>original: "Âdâna"</note>, **Movement** <note>original: "Gamana"</note>, **Excretion** <note>original: "Visarga"</note>, **Blissful Feeling** <note>original: "Ânanda"</note>, **Relinquishment** <note>original: "Hâna"</note>, **Concentration** <note>original: "Upâdâna"</note>, and **Detachment** <note>original: "Upekshâ"</note>.

Outside this again is a **lotus of sixteen petals**, which is known as the **Wheel that Fulfills All Hopes** <note>original: "Sarvâshâparipûraka Chakra"</note>. Here are sixteen **Powers** <note>original: "Shaktis"</note>, namely: the **Attracter of Desire**, **Attracter of Intellect**, **Attracter of Ego**, **Attracter of Sound**, **Attracter of Touch**, **Attracter of Form**, **Attracter of Taste**, **Attracter of Smell**, **Attracter of Mind**, **Attracter of Fortitude**, **Attracter of Memory**, **Attracter of Name**, **Attracter of Seed**, **Attracter of Self**, **Attracter of Immortality**, and the **Attracter of the Body** <note>original: "Kâmâkarshanî, Buddhyâkarshanî, Ahangkârâkarshanî, Shabdâkarshanî, Sparshâkarshanî, Rûpâkarshanî, Rasâkarshanî, Gandhâkarshanî, Chittâkarshanî, Dhairyâkarshanî, Smrityâkarshanî, Nâmâkarshanî, Bîjâkarshanî, Âtmâkarshanî, Amritâkarshanî, and Sharîrâkarshanî"</note>. These are the deities governing the attainment of one's desires—specifically through the acquisition and strengthening of one's own faculties and the control over the powers of others. These powers include the intellect, the ego, sound (such as the ability to hear at a distance), touch, form, taste, smell, the mind, steadfastness, and memory; as well as the power of names (attraction through speech), growth, the subtle body, revivification, and the physical body. These **spiritual accomplishments** <note>original: "Siddhis"</note> are acquired through worship within this specific **Wheel** <note>original: "Chakra"</note>.

Outside the sixteen petals, in the surrounding space of the **Earth-Square** <note>original: "Bhûpura"</note>, are the ten **Powers of the Ritual Gestures** <note>original: "Mudrâshaktis"</note> (as referenced in the *Bhavana Upanishad*, verse 12). These are: the **Agitator of All**, **Chaser of All**, **Attracter of All**, **Possessor of All**, **Maddener of All**, the **Great Goad**, the **Sky-Walker**, the **Seed-Gesture**, the **Great Yoni**, and the **Three-Fold Gesture** <note>original: "Sarvasangshobhinî, Sarvavidrâvinî, Sarvâkarshanî, Sarvâveshakârinî, Sarvonmâdinî, Mahângkushâ, Khecharî, Bîjamudrâ, Mahâyoni, and Trikhandikâ"</note>. The first nine **Gestures** <note>original: "Mudrâs"</note> belong respectively to the nine component wheels of the **Holy Diagram** <note>original: "Shrî-Yantra"</note>, while the tenth is above all others. These nine powers represent—and are shaped into the form of—the nine **Foundational Centers** <note>original: "Âdhâras"</note>, except for the last which is transcendent. The scholar **Bhaskararaya** explains that these nine foundational centers consist of the six primary energy centers (the **Root Center** <note>original: "Mûlâdhâra"</note> and the others), the two **Thousand-Petalled Lotuses**, and the **Upper Palate Center** <note>original: "Lambikâgra"</note>—a center located approximately below the eyes and behind the nose.

Outside the sixteen petals are four circular lines containing three circular spaces. The outermost circle is on the same level as the sixteen-petalled, eight-petalled, and the first outer fourteen-angled wheels, and it is connected with these. The middle circle is on the level of, and connected with, the two sets of ten angles and the eight-angled wheel. The innermost circle is on the same level and connected with the inner wheel consisting of three angles.

# INTRODUCTION.

### 8

Outside these and on the outermost line of the **Earth Square** <note>original: "Bhûpura"</note> are worshipped the **ten Supernatural Powers** <note>original: "Siddhis"</note>, **Minuteness** <note>original: "Animâ"</note> and the rest. These in the **Manoramâ** <note>A famous commentary on the Tantrarâja Tantra</note> are said to be not different from (**Oneness**) <note>original: "Abheda"</note> **Destiny** <note>original: "Niyati"</note> and the **nine Sentiments** <note>original: "Rasas," referring to the fundamental human emotions in Indian aesthetics</note>. Four are at the doors, one at each; four at the corners, one at each, and one is above and one below. At the middle line the **eight Mother-Powers** <note>original: "Mâtrikâs"</note> are worshipped, four at the doors and four at the corners. These are **The Creative Power** <note>original: "Brâhmî"</note>, **The Great Lordship** <note>original: "Mâheshvarî"</note>, **The Youthful Power** <note>original: "Kaumârî"</note>, **The Pervasive Power** <note>original: "Vaishnavî"</note>, **The Boar-Headed Power** <note>original: "Vârâhî"</note>, **The Royal Power** <note>original: "Indrânî"</note>, **The Slayer of Passion and Malice** <note>original: "Châmundâ"</note>, and **Great Good Fortune** <note>original: "Mahâlakshmî"</note>, considered as constituted of **Desire** <note>original: "Kâma" or "Kâmamaya"</note>, **Anger** <note>original: "Krodha"</note>, **Greed** <note>original: "Lobha"</note>, **Delusion** <note>original: "Moha"</note>, **Pride** <note>original: "Mada"</note>, **Envy** <note>original: "Mâtsaryya"</note>, **Sin** <note>original: "Pâpa"</note>, and **Virtue** <note>original: "Pûnya"</note>.

**The Creative Power** is conjoined with **Desire** because She creates, **The Great Lordship** with **Anger** because She "destroys," **The Youthful Power** with **Greed** because, being youthful, She is full of longing, **The Pervasive Power** with **Delusion** because She fascinates the Universe by Her **Delusion** <note>original: "Moha"</note>, **The Boar-Headed Power** with **Pride** because the boar is an obstinate and proud animal ("pigheaded"), **The Royal Power** with **Envy** because **The King of Heaven** <note>original: "Indra"</note> Her consort is a jealous **Deity** <note>original: "Devatâ"</note>, **The Slayer of Passion** with **Sin** because by and through Her mediation injury is done, **Good Fortune** <note>original: "Lakshmî"</note> with **Virtue** because She is benign and leads the **Practitioner** <note>original: "Sâdhaka"</note> to all virtuous acts. On the inner line of the **Earth Square** the **ten Guardians of the Directions** <note>original: "Dikpâlas"</note> are worshipped, placed in the same way as the **Supernatural Powers**. These **Powers of the Seals** <note>original: "Mudrâ Shaktis"</note>, **Guardians of the Directions**, **Mother-Powers**, and **Supernatural Powers** constitute the ninth **Wheel** <note>original: "Chakra"</note> called **Enchanting the Three Worlds** <note>original: "Trailokyamohana"</note>.

The **Supernatural Powers** are first worshipped for self-protection during **Spiritual Practice** <note>original: "Sâdhanâ"</note>. The **Mother-Powers** are worshipped to suppress all evil inclinations associated with each of their names and to gain virtue, and the **Guardians of the Directions** for protection of the **Practitioner** and his **Practice**. The **Earth Square** is that in which the whole **Sacred Diagram** <note>original: "Yantra"</note> is placed. The **King of Tantras** <note>original: "Tantrarâja"</note> says that after worship in manner enjoined let the **Practitioner** <note>original: "Sâdhoka"</note> consider himself as like unto **The Goddess** <note>original: "Devî"</note> <note>original Latin/Sanskrit phrase: "Svâtmânang tatsamang smaret" - One should remember the self as equal to Her</note> and one with **The Goddess** <note>original: "Devyâtmâ"</note>. He is then happy.

Let us then consider the principle involved in this worship. **Tantric Practice** <note>original: "Tântrik Sâdhana"</note> is based on a very profound knowledge of the principles of psychology. The object here is the realization of the unity of the **Individual Soul** <note>original: "Jîvâtmâ"</note> with the **Mother** or **Goddess**. Now one may tell a **Student** <note>original: "Chela"</note> that this is the fact without anything more following from such mere instruction. The truth is not realised by mere oral instruction but by action following it. If the **Student** were to call the statement in question the answer of the **Teacher** <note>original: "Guru"</note> would not be a mere philosophical argument though reasoning has its place, but a direction to do certain things with the statement that the achievement of them will produce both capacity for the actual knowledge required. How? No one can really know any spiritual truth except he personally

What is sought is not a mere statement of fact however true it may be but that actual experience which it indicates and to which it leads. The mind must then be first prepared to fully receive and then realise the truth taught. Such preparation consists in placing before it successively and continuously the idea that every thing which exists in nature and therefore in the human body is, from the <term>Divine</term> <note>original: "Devatâ"</note> aspect, a <term>Divine Power</term> <note>original: "Shaktî"</note>. The universe is the body of the Mother as the Lord of all. But all is <term>Power</term> <note>original: "Shaktî"</note> whether as the Mother in Her <term>True Essential Nature</term> <note>original: "Svarûpa"</note> or in the form of every object in the universe. Matter is not something wholly apart from Spirit or God. It is an aspect assumed by Spirit. Further as "all this is <term>the Absolute</term> <note>original: "Brahman"</note>" every single thing or person is <term>the Absolute</term> <note>original: "Brahman"</note> in that particular form. The <term>Absolute</term> <note>original: "Brahman"</note> <term>Essential Nature</term> <note>original: "Svarûpa"</note> is pure Spirit and its Power or <term>Energy</term> <note>original: "Shaktî"</note> which manifests as the Universe is that same Spirit in material forms. But the matter also of these forms is <term>Power</term> <note>original: "Shakti"</note> for there is nothing but <term>Power</term> <note>original: "Shakti"</note> anywhere in anything which is apparent to us. Therefore Mind and Senses in their varying forms are each in their <term>Divine</term> <note>original: "Devatâ"</note> aspect particular <term>Powers</term> <note>original: "Shaktis"</note>, that is the whole Universe is informed by, and is the manifestation of, Spirit, but a particularly named <term>Deity</term> <note>original: "Devatâ"</note> is that Spirit in the particular manifestation to which the name is given. Thus the <term>Absolute</term> <note>original: "Brahman"</note> or <term>Consciousness-Power</term> <note>original: "Shiva-Shakti"</note> is the name of the Universal Spirit. But <term>Power</term> <note>original: "Shakti"</note> in that aspect in which It exists at rest in the <term>root energy center</term> <note>original: "Mûlâdhâra"</note> as the static centre round which all the bodily forces revolve is called <term>the Coiled Goddess</term> <note>original: "Kundalinî Devî," the dormant spiritual energy located at the base of the spine</note>. <term>Power</term> <note>original: "Shakti"</note> as the source of, and manifesting as, the vital functions is <term>life-force power</term> <note>original: "Prânashakti"</note> and each again of these functions is a separate <term>Power</term> <note>original: "Shakti"</note>, that is the general <term>Power</term> <note>original: "Shakti"</note> manifesting Herself in that particular way. The <term>practitioner</term> <note>original: "Sâdhaka"</note> is taught to realise this in his worship. He looks upon each part of and function of his body as a <term>Power</term> <note>original: "Shakti"</note> or <term>Deity</term> <note>original: "Devatâ"</note>, or more simply in earlier stages as presided over by a <term>Presiding Deity</term> <note>original: "Adhishthâtrî Devatâ"</note>. An elementary view is to regard, say, the Mind as something apart, over and governing which is a <term>Deity</term> <note>original: "Devatâ"</note> or <term>Power</term> <note>original: "Shakti"</note>. The more experienced and correct view is that the Mind is <term>Power</term> <note>original: "Shakti"</note>, that is a particular manifestation of It. By continual and repeated practice in <term>energy center</term> <note>original: "Chakra"</note> after <term>energy center</term> <note>original: "Chakra"</note> everything thus become divinised. It is seen not as gross and so-called inert matter but as what it is, namely <term>the Absolute</term> <note>original: "Brahman"</note> or <term>Power</term> <note>original: "Shakti"</note> in that form It is so seen because the Mind by constant and earnest association of the Divine with the Universe familiarises itself with, and then realises, the fact. Everything is thus a particular <term>Power</term> <note>original: "Shakti"</note>. The next step is to realise that all these

### 10

Specific <term>Divine Powers</term> <note>original: "Shaktis"</note> are, as it were, fragments of the one Power which is the <term>Primordial Divine Power</term> <note>original: "Âdyâ Shakti"</note>; and thirdly that the <term>spiritual practitioner</term> <note>original: "Sâdhaka"</note> himself, both in his essential nature (<term>Spirit</term> <note>original: "Âtmâ"</note>) and in his mind and body (which are particular aspects of <term>Divine Power</term> <note>original: "Shakti"</note>), is one with that <term>Supreme Power</term> <note>original: "Supreme Shakti"</note> which is the goal of all <term>Non-dualistic Vedântic teaching</term> <note>original: "Advaitavâda"</note>: <note>original: "Sâ, ham"</note> "She I am." The <term>practitioner</term> <note>original: "Sâdhaka"</note> worships all forms as specific <term>Divine Powers</term> <note>original: "Shaktis"</note>. He is then led up from lower to higher forms of <term>Power</term> <note>original: "Shakti"</note> until he places before himself for worship the Supreme Power Who is both the Mother of all these specific <term>Powers</term> <note>original: "Shaktis"</note> and Who appears in, and as, them. For there is nothing but the one Mother. As the human father is reborn in his son, so the Mother Who creates the Universe Herself enters into it. She makes and is the form in which She, in Her formless aspect, abides. 

Thus, to take the particular example under discussion, the <term>practitioner</term> <note>original: "Sâdhaka"</note> in the outermost <term>Circle</term> <note>original: "Chakra"</note> meditates (in connection with the <term>Deity</term> <note>original: "Devatâ"</note>) upon forms of sin and virtue, the emotions, and then desire, the mind and senses, the <term>vital channels</term> <note>original: "Nâdîs"</note>, the vital airs and fires, the <term>sensory mind</term> <note>original: "Manas"</note>, <term>subtle elements</term> <note>original: "Tanmâtra"</note>, <term>attachment</term> <note>original: "Râga"</note>, <term>aversion</term> <note>original: "Dvesha"</note>, <term>ego</term> <note>original: "Ahangkâra"</note>, <term>intellect</term> <note>original: "Buddhi"</note>, <term>primal nature</term> <note>original: "Prakriti"</note>, and the <term>gross elements</term> <note>original: "Bhûtas"</note>, of which the <term>Goddesses</term> <note>original: "Devîs"</note> are the fifteen <term>Eternal Ones</term> <note>original: "Nityâs"</note>. These are parts of the body (as indeed are all the rest) of the <term>Supreme Power</term> <note>original: "Supreme Shakti"</note> <term>Beautiful One of the Three Cities</term> <note>original: "Tripurasundarî"</note> or <term>The Playful Goddess</term> <note>original: "Lalitâ Devî"</note> from Whom they emanate. 

The Goddess, as the <term>Mistress of Desire</term> <note>original: "Kâmeshvarî"</note>, is one with the <term>Lord of Desire</term> <note>original: "Kâmeshvara"</note>, and the <term>practitioner</term> <note>original: "Sâdhaka"</note> thinks of himself as one with the Goddess. The <term>Chhândogya Upanishad</term> <note>One of the oldest and most authoritative philosophical texts of ancient India.</note> says that as one thinks, so he becomes. Practice of the ritual transforms the mind itself, and what is at first seen merely as an external <term>Sacred Diagram</term> <note>original: "Yantra"</note> with lines, curves and petals becomes a pure mental state in the <term>practitioner</term> <note>original: "Sâdhaka"</note> himself. He too is an <term>Auspicious Diagram</term> <note>original: "Shrî-Yantra"</note>, and he realizes himself as such. This realization is not to be had by mere <term>intellectual discussion</term> <note>original: "Vichâra"</note> but by the practical methods of the spiritual discipline enjoined. 

In the same way (for the <term>Tantric</term> <note>system of ritual and yoga</note> methods are everywhere substantially the same though the forms vary), the <term>practitioner</term> <note>original: "Sâdhaka"</note> in the Buddhist <term>Supreme Bliss</term> <note>original: "Demchog (Mahâsukha)"</note> <term>Scripture</term> <note>original: "Tantra"</note>, which I am about to publish, meditates on the <term>Sacred Circle</term> <note>original: "Mandala"</note> of the <term>Deity</term> <note>original: "Devatâ"</note>. He, the Deity as <term>Method</term> <note>original: "Thabs or Upâya"</note> which is <term>Compassion</term> <note>original: "Karunâ"</note>, is united with His spouse the <term>Great Female Practitioner</term> <note>original: "Mahâyoginî"</note> Who is <term>Wisdom</term> <note>original: "Shesrab or Jnâna"</note> which is the <term>Void</term> <note>original: "Shûnyatâ"</note>. Around these "two in one" are <term>Encompassing Deities</term> <note>original: "Âvarana Devatâs"</note> which form part of the Body of the Supreme Deity in whom by meditation they are merged, and the <term>practitioner</term> <note>original: "Sâdhaka"</note> unites himself with them and Him according to the doctrines of the "<term>not two</term>" <note>original: "Nyismed yeshes"</note> wisdom—that is, <term>Non-duality</term> <note>original: "Advaita"</note>. So also the object of worship of the Indian <term>Auspicious Circle</term> <note>original: "Shrî-Chakra"</note> is the realization of the inseparateness of the <term>Knower</term> <note>original: "Jnâtâ"</note> (who is the <term>Sacrificer</term> <note>original: "Hotâ"</note>), of <term>Knowledge</term> <note>original: "Jnâna"</note> (which is the <term>Offering Water</term> <note>original: "Arghya"</note>), and of the <term>Known</term> <note>original: "Jneya"</note> (which is the <term>Oblation</term> <note>original: "Havih"</note>).

->INTRODUCTION.<-

The following is a short analysis of the Chapters of the work here published.

### Chapter I. 

This begins with a prayer followed by a request made by the <term>Goddess</term> <note>original: "Devi"</note> of the <term>Auspicious One</term> <note>original: "Shiva"</note> that He should declare to Her an independent <term>Ritual Scripture</term> <note>original: "Tantra"</note> of the sixteen <term>Eternal Deities</term> <note>original: "Nityâ Devatâs"</note>, because the nine then existing <term>Ritual Scriptures</term> <note>original: "Tantras"</note>, through their interdependence, were the cause of confusion. That is, none of these scriptures were complete and the <term>Goddess</term> <note>original: "Devî"</note> wished to have a <term>Ritual Scripture</term> <note>original: "Tantra"</note> which should be all-inclusive. There would then be no necessity to have recourse to any other. 

The <term>Auspicious One</term> <note>original: "Shiva"</note> in reply gives the meaning of the <term>Ka-initial system</term> <note>original: "Kâdi," a specific lineage or tradition of mantras</note>, a summary of the contents of the scripture, the marks of the right <term>Spiritual Teacher</term> <note>original: "Guru"</note> and <term>Disciple</term> <note>original: "Shishya"</note>, the mode of worshipping the <term>Teacher</term> <note>original: "Guru"</note> and the manner of selection of a <term>Sacred Sound-invocation</term> <note>original: "Mantra"</note>, though He adds that this is not necessary in the case of the <term>Sacred Sound-invocations</term> <note>original: "Mantras"</note> of the <term>Eternal Deities</term> <note>original: "Nityâs"</note>. 

Verses 68-71 speak of the men who are qualified to gain <term>Spiritual Attainment</term> <note>original: "Siddhi"</note>. Verse 72 defines the terms <term>Sprout-union</term> <note>original: "Yoga Pallava"</note>, <term>Enclosure</term> <note>original: "Sampuṭa"</note>, <term>Intertwining</term> <note>original: "Grathana"</note> and <term>Interlacing</term> <note>original: "Vidarbha"</note> as applied to the <term>Ritual Recitation</term> <note>original: "Jap"</note> of a <term>Sacred Sound-invocation</term> <note>original: "Mantra"</note>. This is followed by nine verses enumerating twenty-five <term>defects</term> <note>original: "Dosha"</note> of <term>Sacred Sound-invocations</term> <note>original: "Mantras"</note> which it is the duty of the <term>Teacher</term> <note>original: "Guru"</note> to remove before giving the <term>Sacred Sound-invocation</term> <note>original: "Mantra"</note> to the disciple. 

Verses 82 and 83 state the duty of the <term>Teacher</term> <note>original: "Guru"</note> to be to teach the disciple the making of the <term>Womb-gesture</term> <note>original: "Yonimudrâ"</note> and to give him the <term>imparting of potency</term> <note>original: "Vîryyayojanî"</note> of the <term>Sacred Sound-invocation</term> <note>original: "Mantra"</note>. This means imparting to the disciple the <term>potency</term> <note>original: "Vîryya"</note> of the invocation: a process which is given in some detail in Chapter XXXV but can be only fully learnt from the <term>Teacher</term> <note>original: "Guru"</note>. The latter should (the verses continue) protect the disciple and teach him the meaning of the first and last letters of the <term>Mother-letters</term> <note>original: "Mâtrikâs," the sacred alphabet</note>. Without this the letters are like the autumn clouds which come and go without fruit of useful rain. 

Verse 84 says that the knowledge of this is <term>I-realization</term> <note>original: "Ahangkṛiti"</note>, from which <term>Ego-consciousness</term> <note>original: "Ahangkâra"</note> man becomes like unto the <term>Auspicious One</term> <note>original: "Shiva"</note> (<note>original: "Matsamo jāyate naraḥ"</note>: "The man becomes equal to Me"). <term>I-realization</term> <note>original: "Ahangkṛiti"</note> or <term>Ego-consciousness</term> <note>original: "Ahangkâra"</note> literally means the making of or realization of "I". The union of 'A' (the first letter) and 'Ha' (the last letter) makes the word <term>I</term> <note>original: "Aham"</note>, which contains within it all the letters of the alphabet and is therefore, in the terms of <term>Sacred Sound-invocations</term> <note>original: "Mantra"</note>, the full expression of the Self. The union of the first and last letters of the <term>Mother-letters</term> <note>original: "Mâtrikâ"</note> is the <term>Perfection of Identity</term> <note>original: "Tâdâtmya-siddhi"</note>, the receptacle of the sense of all <term>Sacred Sound-invocations</term> <note>original: "Mantras"</note>. Through it is realized the identity of the <term>Spiritual Practitioner</term> <note>original: "Sâdhaka"</note> with the <term>Mother-letters</term> <note>original: "Mâtrikâ"</note> and the <term>Deities</term> who are the <term>Meaning</term> <note>original: "Artha"</note> thereof. Verses 96-100 contain the following:—

*Chapter II.* This deals with the <term>Sacred Circle</term> <note>original: "Maṇḍala"</note> of the nine <term>Lords</term> <note>original: "Nâthas"</note> who are enumerated in verses 2-5. The <term>Divine Stream</term> <note>original: "Divyaugh," associated here with the two ears and mouth</note> consists of <note>The following are the names of the masters translated from Sanskrit:</note> the Bliss of Radiance, the Bliss of Reflection, and the Bliss of Bliss. The <term>Stream of Perfected Beings</term> <note>original: "Siddhaugha," associated with the eyes and penis</note> consists of the Sacred Bliss of Knowledge, the Sacred Bliss of Truth, and the Sacred Bliss of Fullness. The <term>Human Stream</term> <note>original: "Mânavaugha," associated with the two nostrils and anus</note> consists of Self-nature, Intuition, and the Fortunate One. The first class ever abide with the <term>Auspicious One</term> <note>original: "Shiva"</note> ("ever in My presence"), the second both near Him and on earth ("and also here on the ground"), and the third on earth ("they constantly dwell only on the ground"). They are all the <term>Auspicious One</term> <note>original: "Shiva"</note> ("of My own nature") in varying aspects. By their help the <term>Power of the Ka-lineage</term> <note>original: "Kâdishakti"</note>, Who is inseparable from the <term>Auspicious One</term> <note>original: "Shiva"</note>, revealed the fullness of the <term>Ritual Scripture</term> <note>original: "Tantrashâstra"</note> on earth in the <term>Golden Age</term> <note>original: "Krita Yuga"</note>. They are described as beautiful forms having two arms, two eyes, smiling and of gracious mien, making with their hands the <term>sacred gestures</term> <note>original: "Mudrâ"</note> of granting favours and dispelling fear. So they should be worshipped in their respective <term>Sacred Circles</term> <note>original: "Maṇḍalas"</note> (v. 8).

3

Verses 12-16 give the <term>Mantra of the Sandals</term> <note>original: "Pâdukâ mantra"</note> of seven letters. Then follow the names of sixteen letters of the nine <term>Masters</term> <note>original: "Nâthas"</note> who are one with the sixteen <term>Eternal Deities</term> <note>original: "Nityâ Devatâs"</note> (<term>The One who is the essence of the Sixteen Eternals</term> <note>original: "Shodashanityâtmâ"</note>). Instructions follow for the drawing of the <term>Sacred Circle</term> <note>original: "Mandala"</note> and worship of the <term>Spiritual Teacher</term> <note>original: "Guru"</note>. Verses 37-38 state the length of time a disciple should be tested before initiation is given to him. Verses 39-43 speak of the three modes of <term>Consecration</term> <note>original: "Pratishthâ"</note> (placing of the Goddess) which may be in the <term>Sacred Wheel</term> <note>original: "Chakra"</note> (that is, the <term>Wheel for the Worship of the Playful Mother</term> <note>original: "Lalitârchâchakra"</note>), in the disciple, or in the image of the Goddess: as also of the time when this should be done. It is the <term>Perfected Soul</term> <note>original: "Siddhâtmâ," that is, the "Knower of Truth" or Tattvavit</note> and not the man proud of his knowledge (<term>Arrogant Knower</term> <note>original: "Jnânagarbita"</note>) who should do this. He who performs it without the permission of his Spiritual Teacher, either in ignorance or prompted by hope of gain, goes with wife and child to Hell. Verses 44-51 speak of the Consecration of the <term>Auspicious Sacred Wheel</term> <note>original: "Shrîchakra"</note> and other connected rites. (The above are followed by 25 verses which occur in one of the Texts but are not noticed or commented upon by the <term>Delight of the Mind</term> <note>original: "Manoramâ," a famous commentary</note>. These have not been numbered). Verses 52-57 lay down the rules for instructing a good disciple. Fifteen verses beginning with verse 58 describe two kinds of <term>Ritual Bathing</term> <note>original: "Abhisheka"</note> and their respective merits. In these, nine gems are put into medicated water of one <term>measure</term> <note>original: "Khâri," approximately 4096 palas</note> namely: ruby (<term>lotus-hued</term> <note>original: "Padmarâga"</note>), pearl (<term>the pure</term> <note>original: "Muktâ"</note>), coral (<term>the budding</term> <note>original: "Pravâla"</note>), cat’s-eye (<term>the beryl</term> <note>original: "Vaiduryya"</note>), topaz (<term>king of flowers</term> <note>original: "Pushparâja"</note>), diamond (<term>the thunderbolt</term> <note>original: "Vajra"</note>), sapphire (<term>the blue</term> <note>original: "Nîla"</note>), the cow’s fat stone called <term>cinnamon stone</term> <note>original: "Gomeda"</note>, and emerald (<term>the green gem</term> <note>original: "Marakata"</note>). These gems represent the nine component parts of the human body, namely: chyle (<term>vital fluid</term> <note>original: "Rasa"</note>), flesh (<term>muscle</term> <note>original: "Mângsa"</note>), skin (<term>outer covering</term> <note>original: "Tvak"</note>), blood (<term>life-stream</term> <note>original: "Rudhira"</note>), semen (<term>vital seed</term> <note>original: "Shukra"</note>), marrow (<term>inner essence</term> <note>original: "Majjâ"</note>), bone (<term>the structure</term> <note>original: "Asthi"</note>), and fat (<term>adipose</term> <note>original: "Meda"</note>). Verses 73-74 enjoin that daily worship be performed thrice (<term>Worship at the three junctions of the day</term> <note>original: "Sandhyâtraya-bhajana"</note>) and speak of the <term>Rule for ritual placement for specific desires</term> <note>original: "Kâmya-nyâsavidhi"</note>. Verses 75-79 prescribe the auspicious periods for Ritual Bathing, and the following four verses the worship of the Spiritual Teacher and other rites. Verses 84-85 give the articles to be used in the making of the Sacred Circle of the Spiritual Teacher. Verses 88-98 contain a <term>Hymn of Praise</term> <note>original: "Stotra"</note> of the <term>Goddess of the Mother-Letters</term> <note>original: "Mâtrikâ Devî"</note> which also occurs in Chapter I of the <term>Ocean of the Sixteen Eternals</term> <note>original: "Nityâ-shodashikârnava"</note>. In its interpretation of this Hymn, the *Delight of the Mind* commentary follows the Kashmir School. Bhâskararâya <note>A celebrated 18th-century scholar and initiate into these mysteries</note> differs from it in some particulars.

*Chapter III.* From the <term>Practitioner's</term> <note>original: "Sâdhaka"</note> standpoint this is of great importance, for it gives the Mantras of the sixteen Eternal Deities. These are the <term>First</term> <note>original: "Âdyâ"</note> or <term>Primary Eternal Deity</term> <note>original: "Angginityâ Devatâ"</note>, and the other fifteen—or <term>Limbs</term> <note>original: "Anggas"</note>—are described by Bhâskararâya as being like unto, and rays of, the First Eternal Herself. She alone is united with the <term>Lord of Desire</term> <note>original: "Kâm-eshvara"</note>, in this differing from the remaining Eternal Deities, who in other respects resemble Her (see page 25 of the *Ocean of the Sixteen Eternals*). The Lord of Desire is defined in the 26th <term>Aphorism</term> <note>original: "Sûtra"</note> of the <term>Upanishad of Meditation</term> <note>original: "Bhâvanopanishad"</note>.

# INTRODUCTION.

as <term>the Lord of Desire is pure Awareness without limiting attributes</term> <note>original: "Nirupādhika-sangvideva Kāmeshvaraḥ"</note>, that is <term>Pure Awareness</term> <note>original: "Samvit"</note> without <term>limiting attributes</term> <note>original: "Upādhis"</note>; and <term>Lalita</term> <note>The "Playful One," the supreme goddess</note> as the supreme <term>Mistress of Desire</term> <note>original: "Kāmeshvarī"</note> is <term>the supreme deity Lalita is one’s own very Self, full of eternal bliss</term> <note>original: "Sadānandapūrṇaḥ svātmaiva paradevatā Lalitā"</note>, that is one's self is <term>Fullness</term> <note>original: "Pūrṇa"</note>, <term>Existence</term> <note>original: "Sat"</note> and <term>Bliss</term> <note>original: "Ānanda"</note> (ib 27). She is in the centre of the <term>Sacred Diagram of Fortune</term> <note>original: "Shrī Yantra"</note> which is <term>composed of all bliss</term> <note>original: "Sarvānandamaya"</note>. The <term>Sacred Utterance</term> <note>original: "Mantra"</note> of the <term>Primordial Eternal Goddess</term> <note>original: "Ādyā Nityā"</note> is (verses 3-5) <term>Heart</term> <note>original: "Hṛit," corresponding to the letter S</note>, <term>Life-force</term> <note>original: "Prāṇa," corresponding to K</note>, <term>Earth</term> <note>original: "Ilā," corresponding to L</note>, <term>Swan of Breath</term> <note>original: "Hangsa," corresponding to H</note>, <term>Burning</term> <note>original: "Dāha," corresponding to R</note>, <term>Fire</term> <note>original: "Vahni," corresponding to Ī</note>, and <term>Space</term> <note>original: "Khang," corresponding to the Bindu or nasal point</note>. H can be placed in the beginning, middle or end. By changing its position the other Mantras are obtained. H at the end is appropriate for <term>Liberation</term> <note>original: "Mukti"</note> and elsewhere for <term>prosperity</term> <note>original: "Sampat"</note>. The Mantras of the other <term>Eternal Goddesses</term> <note>original: "Nityās"</note> are given in verses 6-72.

The <term>Primordial Eternal Goddess</term> <note>original: "Ādyā Nityā"</note> is the <term>Power of Reflective Awareness</term> <note>original: "Vimarsha Shakti"</note> that is the Power of <term>Shiva as Pure Illumination</term> <note>original: "Prakāsha Shiva"</note>. Shiva is Illumination and the Reflective Power is, in the language of the <term>The Play of the Art of Desire</term> <note>original: "Kāmakalāvilāsa," a key Tantric text</note>, "the pure mirror in which He reflects Himself." (<term>He reflects Himself in the clear mirror of awareness</term> <note>original: "Pratiphālati vimarshadarpaṇe vishade"</note>). It is in this mirror, which is another aspect of Himself, that He knows Himself as the universe. It is this supreme <term>"I-ness"</term> <note>original: "Parāhantā"</note> which is the seed of all multiple world experience. According to this <term>Sacred Treatise</term> <note>original: "Tantra"</note>, the Primordial Eternal or Reflective Power becomes fivefold in the <term>Elements</term> <note>original: "Bhūtas"</note>: ether, air, fire, water, and earth; and by association of each of these with the three <term>Qualities of Nature</term> <note>original: "Guṇas"</note>, there are the fifteen Eternal Goddesses who are rayed forth from Her (<term>By the increase of qualities one by one, the number of the fifteen lunar days is reached</term> <note>original: "Ekaikaguṇabṛiddhyā tu tithisangkhyātvamāgatā"</note>). The number 15 is also obtained in another way, which is by <term>mathematical distribution</term> <note>original: "Vyavakarana"</note> or arithmetical progression of the number of the qualities of the five elements: <term>Ether</term> <note>original: "Ākāsha"</note> having one quality, <term>Air</term> <note>original: "Vāyu"</note> having two, and so on until we get to <term>Earth</term> <note>original: "Pṛithivī"</note> which has five. The addition of these qualities (1+2+3+4+5) makes fifteen. In the <term>The Dawn of Prosperity</term> <note>original: "Subhagodaya"</note> it is said that the fifteen minor Eternal Goddesses are the <term>Digits</term> <note>original: "Kalās"</note> of the fifteen <term>Lunar Days</term> <note>original: "Tithis"</note> beginning with <term>the first day</term> <note>original: "Pratipat"</note> of the light half of the lunar month and ending with the <term>Full Moon</term> <note>original: "Pūrṇimā"</note>; and the sixteenth, who is the Primordial One, <term>is She whose form is Being, Consciousness, and Bliss</term> <note>original: "Sachchidānandarūpiṇī"</note>. The 33rd Sūtra of the <term>Upanishad of Meditation</term> <note>original: "Bhāvanopanishad"</note> says "<term>Contemplating the transformation of time through the form of the fifteen lunar days</term> <note>original: "Panchadashatithirūpena kālasya pariṇāmāvalokanam"</note>." <term>Bhaskararaya</term> <note>A famous 18th-century commentator</note> in his commentary on this Sūtra says that the <term>Manifested Universe</term> <note>original: "Prapancha"</note> is of three kinds: <term>Time</term> <note>original: "Kāla"</note>, <term>Space</term> <note>original: "Desha"</note>, and that which is the union of both. "Realising the evolution of time through the fifteen letters" is thus the dissolution of the external world in one's own <term>Self</term> <note>original: "Ātmā"</note>, as is shown in Chapter 35 of the present work.

-><term>Contemplating the transformation of time through the form of the fifteen lunar days</term> <note>original: "Tithirūpena kālasya pariṇāmāvalokanam"</note><-
-><term>These fifteen are the Eternal Goddesses, and thus their inner meanings are declared</term> <note>original: "Nityāḥ panchadashaitāḥ syur iti proktāshcha vāsanāḥ"</note><-

Verses 73-87 give the Mantras of <term>Varahi</term> <note>The Boar-headed goddess, a form of the divine mother</note> and verse 88 gives the five names of Varahi, which are <term>Varahi</term>, <term>The Fifth One</term> <note>original: "Panchamī"</note>, and <term>Conqueror of the Universe</term> <note>original: "Vishvavijayā"</note>.

# INTRODUCTION.

*Bhadrakaumadi* <note>The "Auspicious Moonlight" goddess</note> and *Vartali* <note>A name for the goddess Varahi</note>. In verses 89-93 is found the <term>Sacred Utterance</term> <note>original: "Mantra"</note> of *Kurukulla* <note>A goddess associated with enchantment and the motherhood aspect of the internal spirit</note>.

*Varahi* is <term>Fatherhood</term> <note>original: "Pitrirûpâ," meaning 'in the form of the father'</note> and *Kurukulla* is motherhood. They are outside the <term>Eternal Moon-Phase Goddesses</term> <note>original: "Nityâs"</note> and a Chapter is devoted to them.

The *Upanishad of Contemplation* <note>original: "Bhâvanopanishad"</note> says (5):—

“<term>Varahi is of the form of the father; the lady Kurukulla is the mother deity</term>” <note>original: "Vârâhî pitrirûpâ kurukullâvalî devatâ mâtâ"</note>; and this <term>Tantra</term> <note>Ritual scripture</note> says:

-><term>The deities of the offering are one's own creative powers; the Fifth Goddess is the nature of the father;</term><-
-><term>Kurukulla is the mother; and the goals of human life are the oceans.</term><-
<note>original: "Balidevyah svamâyâh syuh panchamî janakâtmikâ / Kurukullâ bhaven mâtâ purushârthâstu sâgarâh"</note>

The <term>Fifth Goddess</term> <note>original: "Panchamî"</note> mentioned here is *Varahi* who is <term>of the nature of the father</term> <note>original: "Janakâtmikâ"</note> and *Kurukulla* is mother. Though *Varahi* is female she is yet <term>in the form of the father</term> <note>original: "Pitrirûpâ"</note>, her aspect being male <note>original: "Pungrûpâ"</note>. She is the <term>Deity</term> <note>original: "Devatâ"</note> of <term>Bone</term> <note>original: "Asthi"</note> which a child gets from its father, and *Kurukulla* is the <term>Deity</term> of <term>flesh</term> <note>original: "Mângsa"</note> which it receives from its mother.

Verses 94-95 give the <term>Sacred Utterance of the Sacrifice of the Phenomenal World</term> <note>original: "Prapanchayâga Mantra"</note> and verse 96 the <term>Sacred Utterances</term> of each of the five <term>Elements</term> <note>original: "Bhûta"</note>.

**Chapter IV.** This and the two following Chapters deal with the rites relating to the <term>Primordial Eternal Lalita</term> <note>original: "Âdyâ Nityâ Lalitâ"</note>. The Compiler of the Catalogue of Manuscripts in Nepal seems to have been insufficiently acquainted with the manuscripts he described. Thus he incorrectly says that the third Chapter is devoted to this subject. In his summary of the sixteen <term>Eternal Goddesses</term> <note>original: "Nityâs"</note> he leaves out three of them (namely *Vahnivasini*, *Sarvamangala*, and *Jvalamalini*) and wrongly includes *Varahi* and *Kurukulla* amongst the <term>Eternal Goddesses</term> and repeats the name of *Nitya* twice as the first and eleventh. He makes no mention of the <term>Sacred Wheel</term> <note>original: "Shrîchakra"</note>, the important part of this work, nor deals with the 35th Chapter which gives its philosophy. He states, in some cases incorrectly, the names of the nine <term>Masters</term> <note>original: "Nâthas"</note> on the authority of the late Librarian, Nepal Darbar, though the names are correctly given in the manuscript described. He confuses the nine <term>Masters</term> here described with *Adinatha*, *Kanthanatha* and other recognised <term>Incarnations</term> <note>original: "Avatâras"</note> of Shiva.

The fourth Chapter begins with the <term>Rite of Purifying the Hands</term> <note>original: "Karashuddhividyâ"</note>, the <term>Rite of Placing the Six Limbs</term> <note>original: "Shadangganyâsavidyâ"</note>, the <term>Rite of the Seat of the Goddess's Self</term> <note>original: "Devyâtmâsanavidyâ"</note>, the <term>Rite of the Seat of the Wheel</term> <note>original: "Chakrâsanavidyâ"</note>, the <term>Rite of the Seat of All Mantras</term> <note>original: "Sarvamantrâsanavidyâ"</note>, the <term>Rite of the Seat of Accomplishment and Attainment</term> <note>original: "Sâdhyasiddhâsanavidyâ"</note>, and the <term>Rite of Invocation</term> <note>original: "Âvâhanavidyâ"</note>.

# INTRODUCTION.

Some of the rites, such as the <term>Ritual Placement of the Six Limbs</term> <note>original: "Shadangganyâsa"</note>, are common to all the <term>Eternal Moon-Phase Goddesses</term> <note>original: "Nityâs"</note>. Verses 14-20 give the names of eight <term>Goddess-Powers</term> <note>original: "Shaktis"</note>, namely: the <term>Controller</term> <note>original: "Vashinî"</note>, the <term>Mistress of Desire</term> <note>original: "Kâmeshvarî"</note>, the <term>Enchantress</term> <note>original: "Mohinî"</note>, the <term>Pure One</term> <note>original: "Vimalâ"</note>, the <term>Rosy One</term> <note>original: "Arunâ"</note>, the <term>Victorious One</term> <note>original: "Jayinî"</note>, the <term>Mistress of All</term> <note>original: "Sarveshvarî"</note>, and the <term>Noble One</term> <note>original: "Kaulinî"</note>. It also provides their <term>Sacred Utterances</term> <note>original: "Mantras"</note> and the <term>Sequence of Placement</term> <note>original: "Nyâsakrama"</note>, the performance of which makes the <term>Practitioner</term> <note>original: "Sâdhaka"</note> possess the <term>nature of the Goddess</term> <note>original: "Devyâtmaka"</note>. These eight <term>Goddess-Powers</term> represent cold <note>original: "Shîta"</note>, heat <note>original: "Ushna"</note>, pleasure <note>original: "Sukha"</note>, pain <note>original: "Duhkha"</note>, desire <note>original: "Ichchhâ"</note>, and the three <term>Qualities of Existence</term> <note>original: "Gunas"</note> known as <term>Harmony</term> <note>original: "Sattva"</note>, <term>Passion</term> <note>original: "Rajas"</note>, and <term>Inertia</term> <note>original: "Tamas"</note>. The places on the body where <term>Placement</term> <note>original: "Nyâsa"</note> is performed with these powers are given in verse 21. See also the *Upanishad of Contemplation* <note>original: "Bhâvanopanishad"</note>, Verse 20. Verses 22-25 give the <term>Seed Syllables</term> <note>original: "Bîja Mantras"</note> of the nine <term>Ritual Gestures</term> <note>original: "Mudrâs"</note>. Compare the phrase "<term>The nine foundations are the powers of the gestures</term>" <note>original: "Âdhâranavakam mudrâshaktayah"</note> in the *Upanishad of Contemplation*, verse 12. Verses 30 and 31 list twenty <term>Ritual Gestures</term>. They are: <term>Invoking</term> <note>original: "Âvâhanî"</note>, <term>Establishing</term> <note>original: "Sthâpanî"</term>, <term>Restraining</term> <note>original: "Sannirodhanî"</note>, <term>Veiling</term> <note>original: "Avagunthanî"</note>, <term>Settling Near</term> <note>original: "Sannidhâpanî"</note> (that is, the four gestures of the <term>Arrow</term> <note>original: "Vâna"</note>, <term>Bow</term> <note>original: "Dhanuh"</note>, <term>Noose</term> <note>original: "Pâsha"</note>, and <term>Goad</term> <note>original: "Angkusha"</note>), <term>Salutation</term> <note>original: "Namaskriyâ"</note>, <term>Agitating</term> <note>original: "Sangkshobhanî"</note>, <term>Liquefying</term> <note>original: "Drâvinî"</note>, <term>Attracting</term> <note>original: "Âkarshanî"</note>, <term>Subduing</term> <note>original: "Vashyâ"</note>, <term>Intoxicating</term> <note>original: "Unmâdanî"</note>, <term>The Great Goad</term> <note>original: "Mahângkushâ"</note>, <term>Moving in the Void</term> <note>original: "Khecharî"</note>, <term>Seed</term> <note>original: "Bîja"</note>, <term>Source</term> <note>original: "Yoni"</note>, and <term>Arising of Power</term> <note>original: "Shaktyutthâpanî"</note>, which is also called the <term>Three-Sectioned</term> <note>original: "Trikhandâ"</note>. The <term>Weapon</term> <note>original: "Heti"</note> described above is fourfold, consisting of the <term>Five Arrows</term>, <term>Bow</term>, <term>Noose</term>, and <term>Goad</term>. The five arrows are the <term>five subtle elements</term> <note>original: "Tanmâtras"</note>. The mind as the <term>thinking faculty</term> <note>original: "Manas"</note> is the Sugarcane Bow. Attachment to objects is the bondage or the <term>noose</term> <note>original: "Râgâh pâshâh"</note>, and aversion to objects is the <term>goad</term> <note>original: "Dvesho’ngkushah"</note>. See the *Upanishad of Contemplation*, verses 21-24. Verses 34-54 describe the Gestures which, in verses 55-59, are said to be of three kinds: <term>Gross</term> <note>original: "Sthûla"</note>, <term>Subtle</term> <note>original: "Sûkshma"</note>, and <term>Supreme</term> <note>original: "Para"</note>, depending on whether they are made with the hands or body, contemplated within Sacred Utterances, or understood as they really are <note>original: "Tattvarûpena"</note>. The last ten Gestures are alluded to in the cited verse. The <term>Three-Sectioned Gesture</term> or <term>Arising of Power</term> is so called because it cuts the three—<term>the Knower, the act of Knowing, and the Known</term> <note>original: "Jnâtâ, Jnâna, Jneya"</note>—away from the <term>cycle of worldly existence</term> <note>original: "Sangsâra"</note> <note>original: "Tribhih jnâtrijnânajneyâtmabhih sangsârakhandanât"</note>. This is the Gesture by which the Goddess <term>Lalitâ is invoked</term> <note>original: "Lalitâvahâ"</note>. Verse 58 defines the term <term>Ritual Gesture</term> <note>original: "Mudrâ"</note> <note>original: "Mudang râtîti Mudrâ"</note> as that which gives pleasure to the deity. The text says that even the slightest mistake might produce displeasure where pleasure was intended. The meaning of the verse in the *Upanishad of Contemplation* is that the last ten Gestures are associated with <term>non-difference</term> <note>original: "Abheda"</note> from the nine <term>Foundations</term> <note>original: "Âdhâras"</note>, namely: the six <term>Energy Centers</term> <note>original: "Chakras"</note> beginning with the <term>Root Center</term> <note>original: "Mûlâdhâra"</note>, the <term>Tip of the Soft Palate</term> <note>original: "Lambikâgra"</note>, and two lotuses of a thousand petals—one of which is in the head and the other below the Root Center—the tenth being the totality of all these.

Verses 60 and 61 speak of the five kinds of <term>Offering Vessel</term> <note>original: "Arghyapâtra"</note>.

Lalitâ should be meditated upon as being red in colour. In the 28th verse of the *Upanishad of Contemplation*, it is said:
> "Redness is the <term>Reflective Awareness</term> <note>original: "Vimarsha"</note> of all this" <note>original: "Lauhityametasya sarvasya vimarshah"</note>.
The commentator Bhâskararâya says that by "of all" is meant Desire—
