# INTRODUCTION. 17

The <term>Lord</term> <note>original: "Ishvara"</note>, the Goddess <term>Lalitâ</term> <note>the "Playful One," the supreme form of the Mother Goddess</note>, and the <term>Practitioner's</term> <note>original: "Sâdhaka"</note> own self are fundamentally one. The <term>Reflective Awareness</term> <note>original: "Vimarsha"; the dynamic, self-aware aspect of consciousness</note> of these three is the redness of the <term>Goddess</term> <note>original: "Devî"</note> who is the object of worship. This is so because of the "welding" <note>original: "Âtmanyanurâgât"; literally, through attachment to the Self</note> of these three into one, and this attachment <note>original: "Râga"</note> or welding and Redness <note>original: "Lauhitya"</note> are considered one and the same (see also Chapter XXXV). Compare this with the saying: "One’s own <term>Soul</term> <note>original: "Âtmâ"</note> is the Goddess Lalitâ, whose body is the universe <note>original: "Vishvavigrahâ"</note>. Redness is Her Reflective Awareness—as mere <term>Radiance</term> <note>original: "Prakâsha"; the static, white light of pure consciousness</note> She is white, and redness indicates <term>Will</term> <note>original: "Ichchhâ"</note> and <term>Passion</term> <note>original: "Rajas"</note>—and worship is the Meditation on this identity." She possesses a blissful appearance and carries in Her hands arrows, a bow, a noose, and a goad. She is seated and united with the <term>King of Desire</term> <note>original: "Kâmarâja"; the male counterpart representing the primordial desire to create</note> and is surrounded by <term>Goddess-Powers</term> <note>original: "Shaktis"</note>. These powers are the same color as her, are decked in the same ornaments, and carry the same weapons, but they are not (as Lalitâ is) united with a consort.

Verses 66-71 enumerate the eighteen <term>Goddess-Powers</term> who should be worshipped in the first <term>Energy Circle</term> <note>original: "Chakra"</note>, known as the <term>Enchanter of the Three Worlds</term> <note>original: "Trailokyamohana"</note>. These are again divided into two groups. The first group of ten begins with the power of <term>Minuteness</term> <note>original: "Animâ"; the ability to become as small as an atom</note>, and the second group of eight begins with the <term>Creative Power</term> <note>original: "Brâhmî"</note>. The specific places for this worship are given in Chapters I and VIII of <italic>The Ocean of the Sixteen Eternals</italic> <note>original: "Nityâshodashikârnava"</note> (See also the <italic>Upanishad of Contemplation</italic> <note>original: "Bhâvanopanishad"</note> section 11 and Chapter XXV of this book). The first group of ten is associated with <term>Destiny</term> <note>original: "Niyati"</note> and the nine <term>Aesthetic Sentiments</term> <note>original: "Rasa"</note> beginning with <term>Erotic Love</term> <note>original: "Shringgâra"</note>. The second group of eight represents <term>Desire</term> <note>original: "Kâma"</note>, <term>Anger</term> <note>original: "Krodha"</note>, <term>Greed</term> <note>original: "Lobha"</note>, <term>Delusion</term> <note>original: "Moha"</note>, <term>Pride</term> <note>original: "Mada"</note>, <term>Envy</term> <note>original: "Mâtsaryya"</note>, <term>Merit</term> <note>original: "Pûnya"</note>, and <term>Sin</term> <note>original: "Pâpa"</note> (See <italic>Upanishad of Contemplation</italic> section 11).

Verses 72 and 73 name the <term>Goddess-Powers</term> to be worshipped on the sixteen-petalled lotus. These include the <term>Attractress of Desire</term> <note>original: "Kâmâkarshinî"</note> and others. These powers are the <term>Presiding Deities</term> <note>original: "Adhidevatâs"</note> of Earth <note>original: "Prithivî"</note>, Water <note>original: "Ap"</note>, Fire <note>original: "Tejas"</note>, Air <note>original: "Vâyu"</note>, Ether <note>original: "Âkâsha"</note>, Hearing <note>original: "Shrotra"</note>, Touch <note>original: "Tvak"</note>, Sight <note>original: "Chakshu"</note>, Taste <note>original: "Jihvâ"</note>, Smell <note>original: "Ghrâna"</note>, Speech <note>original: "Vâk"</note>, the Feet <note>original: "Pâda"</note>, the Hands <note>original: "Pâni"</note>, the Anus <note>original: "Pâyu"</note>, and the Genitals <note>original: "Upastha"</note>. There is then the <term>Mental Modification</term> <note>original: "Manovikâra"</note>, which some interpret as applying to all sixteen and others to the <term>Mind</term> <note>original: "Manas"</note> alone. These sixteen powers (See <italic>Upanishad of Contemplation</italic>) are enumerated not only in the <italic>King of Tantras</italic> <note>original: "Tantrarâja"</note> but also in the <italic>Ocean of the Sixteen Eternals</italic>, the <italic>Heart of the Yogini</italic> <note>original: "Yoginîhridaya"</note>, and other works.

Verses 75 and 76 give the names of the eight <term>Goddess-Powers</term> to be worshipped on the petals of the eight-petalled lotus (the third <term>Energy Circle</term>). They include the <term>Flower of the Bodiless One</term> <note>original: "Ananggakusumâ"</note> and others. These represent the <term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "Buddhi"</note> or conscious awareness of Speech <note>original: "Vachana"</note>, Taking <note>original: "Âdâna"</note>, Motion <note>original: "Gamana"</note>, Elimination <note>original: "Visarga"</note>, Bliss <note>original: "Ânanda"</note>, Relinquishment <note>original: "Hâna"</note>, Concentration <note>original: "Upâdâna"</note>, and Detachment <note>original: "Upekshâ"</note> (See Chapter XXXV; <italic>Upanishad of Contemplation</italic> 14; <italic>Ocean of the Sixteen Eternals</italic> I. 177-178 and VIII. 140-143).

<summary>This page explores the metaphysical identity of the Goddess Lalitâ as a manifestation of the practitioner's own consciousness and details the specific Goddess-Powers inhabiting the outer layers of the Sri Yantra. These deities represent the elements of the physical world, sensory organs, and psychological states that the practitioner must integrate during ritual.</summary>

-># INTRODUCTION.<-

The fourteen <term>Powers</term> <note>original: "Shaktis"; female personifications of divine energy</note> to be worshipped in the <term>Circle of the Bestower of Good Fortune</term> <note>original: "Saubhâgyadîyaka Chakra"</note> of fourteen angles are given in verses 77-79. They are "The Agitator of All" and others. They are the <term>Goddesses</term> <note>original: "Devîs"</note> of the fourteen <term>subtle energy channels</term> <note>original: "Nâdis"; the pathways through which life-force flows in the subtle body</note> (See Chapter XXXV of the *Bhiranda Upanishad* 15).

Verses 80-83 give the ten <term>Powers</term>, "The Giver of All Success" and others, to be worshipped in the ten-angled circle called the <term>Circle of the Accomplishment of All Goals</term> <note>original: "Sarvârthasâdhana"</note>. These are the deities of the ten "vital airs" or breaths in the body, the <term>Life-breath</term> <note>original: "Prâna"</note> and the rest (Chapter XXXV *Bhavana Upanishad* 16-18; *Nityâshodashikârnava* I. 184-186, VIII 151-155). The first five belong to the group of five commencing with the <term>Life-breath</term> and the second to the group commencing with the <term>Serpent-breath</term> <note>original: "Nâga"; one of the minor vital airs responsible for functions like belching or alertness</note>.

Verses 84-86 name ten <term>Powers</term> to be worshipped in the inner ten-angled circle called the <term>Circle that Removes All Disease</term> <note>original: "Sarvarogahara"</note>. These are the "All-Knowing One" and others, and the <term>Portions</term> <note>original: "Kalâs"</note> of fire. These are the [forces of] <term>Expelling</term> <note>original: "Rechaka"</note>, <term>Cooking</term> <note>original: "Pâchaka"; digestion</note>, <term>Drying</term> <note>original: "Shoshaka"</note>, <term>Burning</term> <note>original: "Dâhaka"</note>, <term>Flooding</term> <note>original: "Plâvaka"</note>, <term>Corroding</term> <note>original: "Kshâraka"</note>, <term>Belching</term> <note>original: "Udgâraka"</note>, <term>Agitating</term> <note>original: "Kshobhaka"</note>, <term>Yawning</term> <note>original: "Jrimbhaka"</note>, and <term>Deluding</term> <note>original: "Mohaka"</note>. Some say that the vital fire is tenfold because it resides in the seven <term>bodily tissues</term> <note>original: "Dhâtus"; such as blood, muscle, and bone</note> and the three <term>humors</term> <note>original: "Dosha"; the biological energies of Wind, Bile, and Phlegm in Ayurvedic medicine</note>. (See Introduction to the *Prapanchasâra Tantra* volume III of the *Tantrik Texts* edited by Arthur Avalon); but this is not apparently so according to the *Tantrarâja* (See Chapter XXXV also *Bhiranda Upanishad* 19; *Nityâshodashikârnava* 187-190, VIII 156-159; *Yoginîhridaya* III).

Verse 87 gives the <term>Sacred Sound Formula</term> <note>original: "Mantra"</note> and rules of worship of the eight <term>Powers</term>, the "Ruler" and others, to be worshipped in the eight angles (<term>Eight-Angled Circle</term> <note>original: "Ashtâra"</note>) or <term>Circle that Affords All Protection</term> <note>original: "Sarvarakshâkara Chakra"</note>. These, though not named in this Chapter, are the <term>Ruler</term> <note>original: "Vashinî"</note>, <term>Mistress of Desire</term> <note>original: "Kâmeshî"</note>, <term>Gladdener</term> <note>original: "Modinî"</note>, <term>Pure One</term> <note>original: "Vimalâ"</note>, <term>Tawny One</term> <note>original: "Arunî"</note>, <term>Victress</term> <note>original: "Jayinî"</note>, <term>Mistress of All</term> <note>original: "Sarveshî"</note>, and <term>Mistress of the Clan</term> <note>original: "Kaulinî"</note> (vv. 14-20). Between this circle and the next, which is a triangle called the <term>Circle Made of All Perfection</term> <note>original: "Sarvasiddhimaya"</note>, are worshipped the arrows, the bow, the noose, and the goad representing the <term>subtle elements</term> <note>original: "Tanmâtras"</note>, the <term>Mind</term> <note>original: "Manas"</note>, <term>Attachment</term> <note>original: "Râga"</note>, and <term>Aversion</term> <note>original: "Dvesha"</note>. The second line of verse 89 gives the place of worship of the nine <term>Masters</term> <note>original: "Nâthas"; the founding gurus of the tradition</note> <note>original: "Devyâḥ prishthataḥ"; literally, "at the back of the Goddess"</note> in the inner triangle. Verse 90 says that inasmuch as the Goddess in the center manifests Herself in sixteen different forms <note>original: "Shodashâkârataḥ sthitâ"</note>, the other fifteen should be worshipped in Her body <note>original: "Tasyâḥ tanau"</note>. The three <term>Powers</term>, the "Mistress of Desire," the "Mistress of the Thunderbolt," and the "She Who Wears a Garland of Wombs," are to be worshipped in the three corners beginning with the western (that is, lower) angle and going round to the right. That is, wherever the <term>Practitioner</term> <note>original: "Sâdhaka"</note> faces is regarded as the east. Therefore, the lower point of the triangle is the west. These are not the "Eternal Ones" <note>original: "Nityâs"</note> usually so called, but <term>Encompassing Deities</term> <note>original: "Âvarana Devatâs"</note> bearing the same names. These three corners are the <term>Sacred Seats</term> <note>original: "Pîthas"</note> of Kâmrûpa, Pûrnagiri, and Jâlandhara. These <term>Powers</term> are the <term>Unmanifest</term> <note>original: "Avyakta"</note>, the <term>Great Intellect</term> <note>original: "Mahat"</note>, and the <term>Ego</term> <note>original: "Ahangkâra"</note>—that is, <term>Primordial Nature</term> <note>original: "Prakriti"</note>, the cosmic...

-># INTRODUCTION.<-

<term>Intellect</term> <note>original: "Buddhi"</note> and <term>Ego</term> <note>original: "Ahangkâra"</note> (See *Bhâvanopanishad* 25). Then the <term>Goddess</term> <note>original: "Devî"</note> should be worshipped in the middle—that is, in the middle of the ninth <term>Circle</term> <note>original: "Chakra"</note> which is the <term>Seat of Uddiyana</term> <note>original: "Auddyânapîtha"; one of the primary sacred centers of power in the tantric tradition</note>. This is the <term>Physical Worship</term> <note>original: "Sthûlapûja"</note>. Her <term>Sandal Mantra</term> <note>original: "Pâdukâ Mantra"; a formula used to invoke the presence of the deity or guru, metaphorically represented by their sandals</note> is "Hrîng Shrîng, I worship the sacred sandals of the Great Goddess Tripura Sundari at the seat of Uddiyana with the entire root-knowledge." <note>original: "Hrîng Shrîng Samastâm mûlavidyâm auddyânapîthe shrîmahâtripurasundarî-devîshrî-pâdukâm pûjayâmi"</note> In each of the nine circles, the Goddess is worshipped in the center under one of Her nine names (given in the following Chapter verses 14-15) united with the seven-lettered Sandal Mantra.

Her worship again is of three kinds:—<term>Gross</term> <note>original: "Sthûla"; where She is thought of as red</note>, <term>Subtle</term> <note>original: "Sûkshma"; in the mantra-body or "mantra-tanu"</note>, and <term>Supreme</term> <note>original: "Para"</note> when the worship and its fruits are offered to Her. The Gross worship is the <term>Universal Knowledge</term> <note>original: "Samastavidyâ"</note>, the Subtle worship in the form of letters is the <term>Knowledge of Name and Form</term> <note>original: "Nâmarûpavidyâ"</note>, and the Supreme worship is the <term>Knowledge of Dedication</term> <note>original: "Arpana vidyâ"</note>.

Verses 98-100 speak of meditation on the identity of the <term>Teacher</term> <note>original: "Guru"</note>, the <term>Deity</term> <note>original: "Devatâ"</note>, and the <term>Sacred Sound</term> <note>original: "Mantra"</note> which (says the commentary *Manoramâ*) is very secret <note>original: "Rahasya"</note> and should not be disclosed, only to be learned from the teacher. The highest <note>original: "Turîya"; the fourth state of consciousness</note> form of the Goddess consists of the <term>Three Points</term> <note>original: "Bindutraya"</note> which are also the form of the fourth vowel. This circle has one point above and two below. The former is the face and the two below are the breasts, and the lines of the fourth vowel (I) are Her lower limbs. By meditation on these, the <term>Practitioner</term> <note>original: "Sâdhaka"</note> becomes <term>of the same nature</term> <note>original: "Tadâtmaka"</note> as the Goddess.

*Chapter V.* This continues the worship of <term>Lalitâ</term> <note>The "Playful One," a major form of the Goddess in this tradition</note>. After worshipping Her in the manner enjoined, the practitioner considers himself as the Goddess <note>original: "Svâtmânang tatsamang smaret"</note> and one with the Goddess <note>original: "Devyâtmâ"</note>. He is then happy (v. 5).

There are nine circles which the commentator <term>Bhâskararâya</term> (p. 40) says fall under three heads: <term>Creation</term>, <term>Maintenance</term>, and <term>Withdrawal</term> <note>original: "Srishti, Sthiti, and Sanghâra"</note>. The first three (1, 2, 3) are the group of **Creation**, of which the first is the **Creation of Creation**, the second is the **Maintenance of Creation**, and the third is the **Withdrawal of Creation**. The second group of three (4, 5, 6) of the nine are **Maintenance**, of which the first is the **Creation of Maintenance**, the second is the **Maintenance of Maintenance**, and the third is the **Withdrawal of Maintenance**. The last group of three (7, 8, 9) of the nine are **Withdrawal**, of which the first is the **Creation of Withdrawal**, the second is the **Maintenance of Withdrawal**, and the third is the **Withdrawal of Withdrawal**. In the *Tantrântara Tantra*, these three primary groups are called **Moon** <note>original: "Soma" or Creation</note>, **Sun** <note>original: "Sûryya" or Maintenance</note>, and **Fire** <note>original: "Anala" or Withdrawal</note>. It also introduces the classification of the nine circles into cycles of creation, maintenance, and destruction associated with the Moon, Sun, and Fire.</summary>

...the Fulfiller of all Desires <note>original: "shâ-paripûraka," likely "Sarvâshâparipûraka"; the second circle of the Shri Yantra</note> (Creation-Preservation), (3) the All-Agitating <note>original: "Sarvasangkshobhana"; the third circle</note> (Creation-Dissolution), (4) the Bestower of All Good Fortune <note>original: "Sarvasaubhâgyadâyaka"; the fourth circle</note> (Preservation-Creation), (5) the Accomplisher of All Aims <note>original: "Sarvârthasâdhaka"; the fifth circle</note> (Preservation-Preservation), (6) the Remover of All Diseases <note>original: "Sarvarogahara"; the sixth circle</note> (Preservation-Dissolution), (7) the Protector of All <note>original: "Sarvarakshâ-kara"; the seventh circle</note> (Dissolution-Creation), (8) the Giver of All Perfections <note>original: "Sarvasiddhiprada"; the eighth circle</note> (Dissolution-Preservation), and (9) the Consisting of All Bliss <note>original: "Sarvânandamaya"; the ninth and innermost circle</note> (Dissolution-Dissolution). This last is the place of the <term>Central Point</term> <note>original: "Bindu"</note> and is of the <term>Nature of Shiva</term> <note>original: "Shivâtmaka"</note> (verses 9 and 10). The <term>Female Deities</term> <note>original: "Yoginîs"</note> in these <term>Circles</term> <note>original: "Chakras"</note> are (1) the Manifest One <note>original: "Prakatâ"</note>, (2) the Hidden One <note>original: "Guptâ"</note>, (3) the More Hidden One <note>original: "Guptatarâ"</note>, (4) the Traditional One <note>original: "Sampradâyâ"</note>, (5) the One of the Lineage <note>original: "Kulakaulâ"</note>, (6) the One in the Womb <note>original: "Nigarbhâ"</note>, (7) the Secret One <note>original: "Rahasyâ"</note>, (8) the Most Secret One <note>original: "Parâpararahasyâ"</note>, and (9) the Highly Secret One <note>original: "Atirahasyâ"</note>. These are in the Middle of the Circles and are <term>Gross Forms</term> <note>original: "Sthûlavigrahâ"</note> being the <term>Veil</term> <note>original: "Âvarana"</note> of the <term>Subtle</term> <note>original: "Sûkshma"</note> or <term>Sacred Sound</term> <note>original: "Mantra"</note> form. The <term>Supreme Form</term> <note>original: "Para"</note> is unconditioned by time or space and is immanent in the last. The nine names of the <term>Goddess</term> <note>original: "Devî"</note> are Three-Cities <note>original: "Tripurâ"</note>, Ruler of the Three Cities <note>original: "Tripureshî"</note>, Beautiful One of the Three Cities <note>original: "Tripurasundarî"</note>, Dweller in the Three Cities <note>original: "Tripuravâsinî"</note>, Prosperity of the Three Cities <note>original: "Tripurashrî"</note>, Garlanded One of the Three Cities <note>original: "Tripuramâlinî"</note>, Perfected One of the Three Cities <note>original: "Tripurasiddhâ"</note>, Mother of the Three Cities <note>original: "Tripurâmbâ"</note>, and Great Beautiful One of the Three Cities <note>original: "Mahâtripurasundarî"</note> (verse 14). In each of these nine forms the Goddess is worshipped in the nine different Circles with the prescribed Sacred Sound <note>original: "Mantra"</note> (verse 15). Verses 17 and 18 say that as soon as the <term>Practitioner</term> <note>original: "Sâdhaka"</note> rises from his sleep in the early morning he should think of himself as the Goddess <note>original: "Tripurâtmânam"</note> and meditate on Her <term>Lustrous Light form</term> <note>original: "Jyotîrûpa"</note> in the head.

Verses 19-21 enjoin that during worship the Practitioner should wear a red cloth, smear himself with red sandalwood, and wear red garlands and red ornaments. He should be in a pleasant frame of mind, scented with camphor. He should sit in the <term>Lotus Posture</term> <note>original: "Padmâsana"</note> facing East and keep himself and his <term>Vital Breaths</term> <note>original: "Prânâh"</note> under control.

Verses 23-25 enjoin the worship of the nine gems, the garden of <term>Wish-fulfilling Trees</term> <note>original: "Kalpakodyâna"</note>, the six seasons, and the senses, which are compared to horses, and the objects of the senses, which are likened to elephants. Verse 26 also refers to the nine gems. In this connection may be noted the *Bhâvanopanishad* (verses 6-8) which says that <insert>the body is the island of nine gems</insert> <note>original: "Deho navaratnadvîpah"</note> which are Topaz <note>original: "Pushparâga"</note>, Sapphire <note>original: "Nîla"</note>, Cat’s Eye <note>original: "Vaidûrya"</note>, Coral <note>original: "Vidruma"</note>, Pearl <note>original: "Mauktika"</note>, Emerald <note>original: "Marakata"</note>, Diamond <note>original: "Vajra"</note>, Hessonite <note>original: "Gomeda"</note>, and Ruby <note>original: "Padmarâga"</note>. <insert>They are joined with the seven elements of the body and the hair</insert> <note>original: "Tvagâdisaptadhaturomasangyuktah"</note>. These gems in the body are the skin <note>original: "Tvak"</note> and the seven <term>Tissues</term> <note>original: "Dhâtus"</note>, namely Chyle/Plasma <note>original: "Rasa"</note>, Flesh <note>original: "Mângsa"</note>, Blood <note>original: "Rudhira"</note>, Reproductive Fluid <note>original: "Shukra"</note>, Marrow <note>original: "Majjâ"</note>, Bone <note>original: "Asthi"</note>, and Fat <note>original: "Meda"</note>, together with the Hair <note>original: "Roma"</note>. Time is divided into nine parts, namely: a <term>Ghatikâ</term> <note>24 minutes</note>, a <term>Yâma</term> <note>3 hours</note>, a <term>Day and Night</term> <note>original: "Ahorâtra"</note>, a <term>Day of the Week</term> <note>original: "Vâra"</note>, a <term>Lunar Day</term> <note>original: "Tithi"</note>, a <term>Lunar Fortnight</term> <note>original: "Paksha"</note>, a <term>Solar Month</term> <note>original: "Mâsa"</note>, a <term>Season</term> <note>original: "Ritu"; two months</note>, and a <term>Year</term> <note>original: "Abda"</note>.

-># INTRODUCTION. 21<-
->4<-

The principal <term>Hand Gestures</term> <note>original: "Mudrâs"</note> beginning with the <term>Agitating One</term> <note>original: "Sangkshobhinî"</note> are nine. The <term>Mother Letters</term> <note>original: "Mâtrikâs"; the phonemes of the Sanskrit alphabet</note> are divided into nine groups. There are nine <term>Lineage Teachers</term> <note>original: "Gurus"</note>. The <term>Essential Principles</term> <note>original: "Tattvas"</note> are nine (obtained by combinations of the <term>Knower</term> <note>original: "Jnâtri"</note>, <term>Knowledge</term> <note>original: "Jnâna"</note>, and the <term>Known</term> <note>original: "Jneya"</note>). The planets are nine, as are also the <term>Bodily Tissues</term> <note>original: "Dhâtus"</note> (Skin <note>original: "Tvak"</note>, Blood <note>original: "Asrik"</note>, etc.). Verse 47 speaks of the worship of the <term>arrows</term> (*Vâna*), <term>bow</term> (*Châpa*), <term>noose</term> (*Pâsha*), and <term>goad</term> (*Angkusha*). These ritual implements are categorized as <term>Gross</term> <note>original: "Sthûla"</note>, <term>Subtle</term> <note>original: "Sûkshma"</note>, or <term>Supreme</term> <note>original: "Para"</note>. As the first (Gross), the arrows are made of flowers; as the second (Subtle), they exist in the form of <term>Sacred Chants</term> <note>original: "Mantra"</note> (*Mantrâtmânah*); and as the Supreme, they are the five <term>Subtle Elements</term> <note>original: "Tanmâtras"</note> (as described in the Chapter dealing with <term>Latent Impressions</term> <note>original: "Vâsanâ"</note>). As Gross objects, they consist of the following flowers: the Lotus (*Kamala*), the Red Night-Lotus (*Rakta kairava*), the Water Lily (*Kalhâra*), the Blue Lotus (*Indîvara*), and the Mango Flower (*Sahakâraja*). The Bow, Noose, and Goad are similarly categorized as Gross, Subtle, and Supreme.

The bow is Sugarcane in its Gross form, made of Mantra in its Subtle form, and the <term>Mind</term> <note>original: "Manas"</note> in its Supreme form. The noose and the goad are of material or Mantra form, and their Supreme form represents <term>Desire</term> <note>original: "Râga," symbolized by the noose</note> and <term>Hostility</term> <note>original: "Dvesha," symbolized by the goad</note>.

Then follows the description of the <term>Daily Worship</term> <note>original: "Nityapûjâ"</note>.

Verses 78–79 direct that when performing <term>Preparatory Rites</term> <note>original: "Purashchârana"</note>, the company of an <term>unbeliever</term> <note>original: "Nâstika"</note> should be avoided. Verses 79–80 enjoin the avoidance of desire for, or criticizing, the land, house, and wife of another, and prohibit being angry with or beating women, even if they are perceived as wicked.

In verse 81, it is said that in the chapter on <term>Latent Impressions</term> <note>original: "Vâsanâ"</note> (Chapter 35), the signs which indicate the attainment of the state of an <term>Accomplished Master</term> <note>original: "Siddha"</note> are given; the following indicate that a man is moving toward that state: dreams of association with women, or of riding on an elephant, of enjoyment in a palatial house or on a mountain top, the seeing of kings, a procession of elephants, the singing and dancing of women in a dream, the seeing of festivals in a dream, and the seeing and taking of wine and meat in a dream. Some other signs are mentioned which indicate that a man is straying from the path of <term>Perfection</term> <note>original: "Siddhi,"</note> namely: seeing black soldiers, being beaten, the smearing of oil (which is not done by <term>Celibate Students</term> <note>original: "Brahmachârîs"</note>), sexual connection with others' wives, a state of anarchy, fear of fire, air, or water, the death of a friend, slighting a <term>Teacher</term> <note>original: "Guru"</note>, the accumulation of wealth, disease, and worshipping with other chants than the <term>Practitioner's</term> <note>original: "Sâdhaka's"</note> own.

Verse 88 states that he who performs <term>Mantra-Recitation</term> <note>original: "Japa"</note> without knowing the <term>Position of the Tortoise</term> <note>original: "Kûrmasthiti"</note> not only fails to obtain the fruit of his practice but meets with destruction. Therefore, the <term>Tortoise</term> <note>original: "Kûrma"</note> should first be known. The Tortoise is of four...

(6) One should meditate upon the supreme form, radiant and established in the heart, which is the very essence of the <term>Seed-Syllable</term> <note>original: "Bîja"</note>. Through this, the practitioner attains the highest state of consciousness and the mastery of the senses.

(7) If one focuses the mind on the central point of the <term>Sacred Diagram</term> <note>original: "Yantra"</note>, the movement of the breath becomes steady. By this practice, the "dust" of worldly existence is washed away, and the light of truth shines forth.

(8) The practitioner should then establish the <term>Mantra</term> <note>sacred sound formula</note> within the heart. By placing the syllables in the proper order—left, right, and center—the power of the <term>Goddess</term> <note>original: "Shakti"</note> is awakened within the body.

(9) The grouping of the letters is explained thus: the vowels and the consonants must be placed within the petals of the lotus, following the sequence of the <term>Lunar Days</term> <note>original: "Tithis"</note>.

(10) For the one who knows the secret of the sounds, the nectar of immortality flows from the crown of the head. This knowledge is the highest gift, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and final liberation.

(11) In the various directions, starting from the East, the practitioner should worship the <term>Protective Deities</term> <note>original: "Âvarana Devatâs"</note>. Through their grace, the diagram becomes a fortress of spiritual energy.

(12) This ritual produces a form as radiant as the moon. The seeker who remains steadfast in this practice attains the state of the <term>Creator</term> <note>original: "Brahmâ"</note> and resides in the eternal abode.

(13) By placing the syllables on the petals of the lotus, one becomes a master of speech and wealth. The divine energy flows through the channels of the subtle body, purifying the mind of all limitations.

(14) The meditation on the form of the Goddess, seated upon the lotus, brings about the union of the self with the Supreme. This is the path of the ancient masters, leading to the realization of the <term>Absolute Principles</term> <note>original: "Tattvas"</note>.

(15) Whether one is a seeker of power or a seeker of truth, this method provides the necessary foundation. Through the repeated recitation of the mantra, the boundaries of the individual self are dissolved into the infinite.

(16) For the one who is dedicated to the service of the teacher and the Goddess, there is nothing in the three worlds that is difficult to attain. The light of the self shines clearly, like a lamp in a windless place.

(17) In this way, the secret of the <term>Eternities</term> <note>original: "Nityâs"</note> is revealed. Let the practitioner approach this knowledge with devotion, for it is the key to the mystery of existence and the source of all joy.

There is no mention here or in the rest of the volume of <term>Maithuna</term> <note>ritual sexual union</note>. It states that the <term>Siddha</term> <note>an accomplished practitioner or spiritual adept</note> should never drink wine unless it has been first offered as <term>Arghya</term> <note>a ritual libation or offering</note> to the <term>Devî</term> <note>the Goddess</note> on whom as the object of worship the Mind must be kept. Wine should be drunk until the Mind is wholly absorbed in the Goddess. To drink more than that is sin. He, who drinks without offering and for the satisfaction of his desire, is a sinner, a worshipper of ignorance and should be punished by the King. The following verses, of which the above is a translation, should be noted by those who criticise this <term>Shâstra</term> <note>sacred scripture or authoritative manual</note>:

> The adept should never drink what has not been offered as a ritual libation to the Goddess. <note>original Sanskrit: "Na kadâchit pivet siddho devyarghyamaniveditam."</note>
> One should drink only so much as leads to the absorption of the mind in the Divine. <note>original Sanskrit: "Pânancha tâvat kurvîta yâvatâ syân manolayah."</note>
> If one drinks beyond that, they certainly become a sinner immediately. <note>original Sanskrit: "Tatah karoti chet sadyah pâtakî bhavati dhruvam."</note>
> Drinking wine for any reason other than the service of the Deity and the Guru, out of a craving for spirits, <note>original Sanskrit: "Devatâgurusevânyat pîvannâsavamâshayâ."</note>
> makes one a sinner, liable to punishment by the King, and a worshipper of ignorance. <note>original Sanskrit: "Pâtakî râjadandyashchâvîdyopâsaka eva cha."</note>

Verse 91 and following describe the <term>Yantra</term> <note>sacred geometric diagram used in meditation</note> called <term>Yonyarnava</term> <note>"The Ocean of the Source," a specific symbolic configuration</note>, the worship thereof and the fruits gained thereby.

She is red with red raiment and smeared with red sandal-paste. She smiles. Three eyes enhance the beauty of Her face. On Her forehead are beads of sweat shining like pearls. Above it is the half-moon. In Her four hands She holds the noose, goad, drinking cup, and with the last hand makes the gesture dispelling fear. She is seated in the middle of the **Lotus**, listless with desire (<term>Madâlasâ</term> <note>appearing languid or intoxicated by divine passion</note>) (vv. 7-9). She should be worshipped with all Her <term>Shaktîs</term> <note>attendant female deities representing specific energies</note>. In the corner of the triangle are **Kshobhinî** <note>the Agitator</note>, **Mohinî** <note>the Deluder</note>, **Lîlâ** <note>the Playful One</note> (v. 10). # INTRODUCTION.

The Goddesses of Action <note>original: "Kriyâ"</note> are to be worshipped in the corners of the triangle. In the middle is to be worshipped the eighth Eternal Goddess <note>original: "Nityâ," referring here to Shivaduti</note> who has assumed a supreme form <note>original: "Parâ tanu"</note> for the saving of Her devotees.

Directions are given for the drawing of the Sacred Diagram <note>original: "Yantra"</note> (verses 62-68); the Ritual for Infusing Life <note>original: "Prânapratishthâ Vidyâ"</note> is given (verses 62-68); as also a Meditation Image <note>original: "Dhyâna"</note> of the Life-force Power <note>original: "Prânashakti"</note> (which may be compared with that set out in the *Essence of the Manifested Universe Tantra* <note>original: "Prapanchasâra Tantra"</note> in the third volume of this series) and her ten Attendant Powers <note>original: "Parivârashaktis"</note> are stated. These are the ten vital airs **Out-breath** <note>original: "Prâna"</note>, **In-breath** <note>original: "Apâna"</note>, and so forth. In praise of this Eternal Goddess it is said (III. 46) that her Sacred Mantra <note>original: "Vidyâ"</note> is the Savior from All Calamities <note>original: "Samastâpattârinî"</note>. According to the *Heart-Pleasing Commentary* <note>original: "Manoramâ"</note>, "Calamity" <note>original: "Âpat"</note> refers to Lack of Discernment <note>original: "Aviveka"</note>. It destroys this and therefore all evils, makes the Spiritual Practitioner <note>original: "Sâdhaka"</note> pleasing to all (The Universal Delighter <note>original: "Vishvaranjanî"</note>), gives him prosperity (The Maker of Wealth <note>original: "Shrîkârî"</note>) and, granting all Spiritual Attainments <note>original: "Siddhis"</note>, leads the practitioner to the State of the Divine <note>original: "Shivatâvâptikârinî," literally "making one attain the state of Shiva"</note>.

*Chapter XIV.* This deals with The Swift One <note>original: "Tvaritâ"</note> or Totalâ Goddess, the ninth Eternal Goddess, so called because (verse 12) She is quick <note>original: "Tvarita"</note> to grant fruit to the practitioner and whose Meditation Image <note>original: "Dhyâna"</note> is given as follows (verses 6-10):—

She is of auspicious form in the first flush of youth and dark of colour. She has three eyes and four hands and Her beautiful lotus-like face smiles gently. She is clad in new leaves. She is adorned with eight fierce and great serpents, of four kinds, and with a waist chain and anklets. They represent the four social classes: **Priest** <note>original: "Vipra"</note>, **Warrior** <note>original: "Kshatriya"</note>, **Merchant** <note>original: "Vit" or "Vaishya"</note> and **Laborer** <note>original: "Shûdra"</note>. (The *Heart-Pleasing Commentary* says that there are two of each class and the ornaments should be understood as following the origination of each class). On Her head is a crystal crown with a crest of peacock's feather. Her arms are adorned with bangles made of beautiful peacock's tail feathers. These are also made up into an umbrella and banner. Strings of *gunjâ* berries <note>Small red and black seeds often used in forest-dweller iconography</note> are round and on Her throat and breasts which are smeared with red sandal. Smiling gently She holds in Her four hands a noose and a goad and makes the hand gestures <note>original: "Mudrâ"</note> of granting boons and dispelling fear.

Verses 13-16 give the names of Her attendants who are as follows:—

Her Powers <note>original: "Shaktis"</note> are The Sounding One <note>original: "Hungkârî"</note>, The Sky-Walker <note>original: "Khecharî"</note>, **The Fierce One** <note>original: "Chandî"</note>, The Cutter <note>original: "Chhedinî"</note>, The Thrower <note>original: "Kshepanî"</note>, The Woman-Maker <note>original: "Strîkârî"</note>, The Sounding One <note>original: "Hungkârî"</note> (?), and The Peace-Maker <note>original: "Kshemakârî"</note>. These, which are like the Guardians of the Directions <note>original: "Lokapâlas"</note> and are the Powers of the Mantra-letters, should be worshipped in the eight petals. The rest of the Chapter gives rules of **Worship** <note>original: "Pûjâ"</note>, directions for the drawing of the **Sacred Diagram** <note>original: "Yantra"</note>, lists of worship articles and the benefits to be gained by these various acts of worship. Chapter III, verse 47 says that the **Perfected One** <note>original: "Siddha"</note> in this <term>Sacred Knowledge (Vidyâ)</term> gains prosperity, beauty, fame, learning, wealth, health, long life and whatever he desires. He is affected neither by poverty nor poison.

*Chapter XV.* This deals with the tenth **Eternal Goddess** <note>original: "Nityâ"</note> called **Kulasundarî** ("The Beautiful One of the Lineage"), whose **Practitioner** <note>original: "Sâdhaka"</note> (III. 52) becomes **all-knowing** <note>original: "Sarvajna"</note>. Her **Meditation Image** <note>original: "Dhyâna"</note> is given (verses 3-11) as follows:—

She is propitious, supremely kind, and blissful, with twelve arms and six lotus-like faces which smile sweetly and three eyes in each face. She is red, seated on a red lotus, and is smeared with blood. Her raiment and ornaments are red and She is surrounded by **Powers** <note>original: "Shaktis"</note> who are also red. Her crown is bright with gems beyond all price and rubies; earrings, neck-chains, armlets, waist chains and anklets heighten Her own brightness. On Her beauteous breasts are clusters of red gems. In Her are all the words of the **Sacred Texts** <note>original: "Vedas"</note>. In Her right hands She carries a rosary of coral beads, a lotus, a <term>Water-pot (Kamandalu/Kandkâ)</term> made of gems, a <term>Drinking Cup (Chashaka)</term> made of gems full of wealth, a <term>Citron or Lemon (Mâtulungga)</term>, and with one hand She makes the <term>Gesture of Explanation (Vyâkhyânamudrâ)</term>. In the left hands are a book, a red lotus, a golden pen, a garland of gems, and a conch shell. She makes the <term>Gesture of Granting Boons (Varamudrâ)</term>. She is surrounded by <term>Gods (Devas)</term>, <term>Celestial Musicians (Gandharvas)</term>, and <term>Heavenly Beings (Kinnaras)</term> who sing Her praises, as also by <term>Nature Spirits (Yakshas)</term>, <term>Demonic Beings (Râkshasas)</term>, and the like. So should She be meditated upon for the attainment of learning, wealth, and beauty. When worshipped for the attainment of learning She is thought of as white, and when wealth is sought of Her, She is meditated upon as being of a golden colour.

Her eleven **Attendant Powers** <note>original: "Parivâra Shaktis"</note> are (verses 17-20) as follows:—

**Language** (Bhâshâ), **Wisdom** (Sarasvatî), **Speech** (Vânî), **Refined/Sanskrit** (Sangskritâ), **Natural/Prakrit** (Prâkritâ), **Supreme** (Parâ), **Sword-form** (Khadgarûpâ), **Wealth-form** (Vittarûpâ), **Beautiful** (Ramyâ), **Blissful** (Ânandâ), and **Curiosity** (Kautukâ), who should be worshipped in the <term>Nine Triangles (Navayonis)</term>. In the eight petals of the outer lotus should be worshipped (the eight <term>Mother Goddesses (Mâtrikâs)</term>) **Brâhmî** and others. In the square, the <term>World-Guardians (Lokapâlas)</term> and their **Powers** <note>original: "Shaktis"</note> (or in their feminine form) should be worshipped.

# INTRODUCTION.

The four following verses give directions for drawing Her **Sacred Diagram for Daily Worship** <note>original: "Nityapûjâ Chakra"</note> and as to the scents to be used in the worship of this **Goddess** <note>original: "Devî"</note> (17-24).

The Tantra then deals with the three **Syllables** <note>original: "Kûtas"</note> or parts of or divisions of the **Mantra** <note>original: "Aing, Klīng, Hsauh"</note>. The **Sacred Knowledge** <note>original: "Vidyâ"</note> of *Kulasundarî* <note>The Beautiful One of the Lineage</note> is **composed of the three Vedas** <note>original: "Trayîmayî"</note> or **made of the Vedas** <note>original: "Vedamayî"</note> and is, when its vowels are united with the consonants, the cause of the **Manifested Universe** <note>original: "Prapancha"</note> which is composed of both **Sound** <note>original: "Shabdamaya"</note> and **Meaning** <note>original: "Arthamaya"</note> (**The form of the Signifier and the Signified** <note>original: "Vâchya-Vâchakarûpa"</note>). The **Sâmaveda** <note>Veda of Chants</note> **begins with the letter A** <note>original: "Akârâdi"</note> and so does the **Rigveda** <note>Veda of Verses</note>. The **Yajurveda** <note>Veda of Ritual</note> **begins with the letter I** <note>original: "Ikârâdi"</note>. By the union of these, the **sound AI** <note>original: "Aikâra"</note> is produced (a + i = e and a + e = ai). The **sound AI** <note>original: "Aikâra"</note> or **The Pure** <note>original: "Shuchi"</note> is therefore **composed of the three Vedas** <note>original: "Trayîmaya"</note> (vv. 33-38). This is the meaning of *Aing*, the first **Syllable** <note>original: "Kûta"</note>. The meaning of the second **Syllable** <note>original: "Kûtas"</note> "*Klīng*" is given in vv. 39 & 40. This **Mantra** <note>sacred utterance</note> denotes Her as the cause of the **Universe in the form of the Signifier and the Signified** <note>original: "Vâchya-vâchakarûpa Prapancha"</note>. The consonants between *Ka* and *Ha* signify the five **Elements** <note>original: "Bhûtas"</note> and as such they are the **Object of Knowledge** <note>original: "Jneya"</note>, just as vowels are **Knowledge** <note>original: "Jnâna"</note> (the **Veda**). *Hsauh*, the last **Syllable** <note>original: "Kûta"</note>, is the **form of the Knower** <note>original: "Jnâtrirūpa"</note> (v. 41). The first **Syllable** <note>original: "Kûta"</note> is the **essence of Speech** <note>original: "Vâk-svarûpa"</note>; the second is **Fire** <note>original: "Vahni"</note>, which is the union of the **Divine Masculine** <note>original: "Shiva"</note> and **Divine Feminine** <note>original: "Shakti"</note>, for in it is the fourth vowel (î) and the **Sacred Point** <note>original: "Bindu"</note> and the **Emission** <note>original: "Visarjanîya"</note>, the origin of all the **Letters of the Alphabet** <note>original: "Mâtrikâs"</note>. By the last **Seed-Syllable** <note>original: "Bîja"</note>, She is the **Soul of the Universe** <note>original: "Vishvâtmarûpâ"</note>, whether united with the **Point** <note>original: "Bindu"</note> (**Space** <note>original: "Kha"</note>) or the **Emission** <note>original: "Visarga"</note> (**Creative Illusion** <note>original: "Mâyâ"</note>). This is the **Root of the Three Cities** <note>original: "Tripurâkanda"</note>, which is the united state of the **Knower, Knowledge, and the Known** <note>original: "Jnâtri, Jnâna, Jneya"</note>, the three humors of **Wind, Bile, and Phlegm** <note>original: "Vâta, Pitta, Shleshmâ"</note>, and the three lights of **Fire, Sun, and Moon** <note>original: "Agni, Sûryya, Soma"</note>. Therefore She pervades the whole Universe.

Vv. 45-55 speak of the effects of the **Mantra** <note>sacred utterance</note> according as it is united with other **Seed-Syllables** <note>original: "Bîjas"</note>. V. 68 speaks of the making of **Clarified Butter of Vishnu** <note>original: "Vishnu Ghrita"</note> which gives powers of speech.

*Chapter XVI.* This Chapter speaks of the Eleventh **Eternal Goddess** <note>original: "Nityâ"</note> called **The Eternal of Eternals** <note>original: "Nityâ Nityâ"</note>. All moving bodies are controlled by Her and by Her all **Individual Souls** <note>original: "Jîvas"</note> dwell in their respective bodies. According to Her **Meditation Image** <note>original: "Dhyâna"</note> (vv. 6-10) She is beneficent and pervades all beings (**The Soul of All** <note>original: "Sarvâtmikâ"</note>) for She is the **Pure Consciousness** <note>original: "Chaitanya"</note> in all. According to the **Manoramâ** <note>a specific commentary</note> She is the presiding **Deity** <note>original: "Devatâ"</note> over the **Yoginis** <note>original: "Dâkinî and others"</note> who are the **Powers** <note>original: "Shaktis"</note> of the bodily **Tissues** <note>original: "Dhātus"</note>. Coloured like the rising sun She bears on Her head a luminous crown. Her face is lit by a soft smile. She is dressed in red raiment and adorned with rubies. She has three eyes and twelve hands. With her right hands She carries the noose, the white lotus, sugar-cane bow, shield and trident and makes the **gesture of granting favours** <note>original: "Varamudrâ"</note>; and in the left hands she carries the goad, book, flowery arrows, sword, skull and makes the **gesture of dispelling fear** <note>original: "Abhayamudrâ"</note>. Her **Powers** <note>original: "Shaktis"</note> are countless and form a complete circle. Chapter XXV speaks of

# Chapter XVII. 

This Chapter deals with the twelfth **Eternal Goddess** <note>original: "Nityâ"</note> called **The Blue Banner** <note>original: "Nîlapatâkâ"</note>. After describing the **Ritual Consecration** <note>original: "Nyâsa"</note> of Her **Sacred Chant** <note>original: "Mantra"</note> (vv. 5-7) Her **Meditation Visualization** <note>original: "Dhyâna"</note> is given (vv. 8-12) as follows. *Chapter XVIII.* The last Chapter in this volume deals with the thirteenth *<term>Eternal Goddess</term>* <note>original: "Nityâ"</note> called the *<term>Eternal Goddess of Victory</term>* <note>original: "Vijayâ Nityâ"</note> whose *<term>Meditation Visualization</term>* <note>original: "Dhyâna"</note> (vv. 5-10) is given as follows:—Her body is lustrous red like that of the rising sun. She has five smiling faces in each of which are three eyes and She has ten hands. Her raiment is yellow. She bears a brilliant crown and on Her forehead a crescent moon. She is decked with all kinds of ornaments. In Her left hands She carries conch, noose, shield, bow, and white lily (*<term>White Water-Lily</term>* <note>original: "Kahlâra"</note>) and in Her right hands discus (*<term>Sacred Wheel</term>* <note>original: "Chakra"</note>), goad (*<term>Elephant Goad</term>* <note>original: "Angkusha"</note>), arrows (*<term>Arrows</term>* <note>original: "Sâyaka"</note>) and a citron (*<term>Citron</term>* <note>original: "Mâtulunga"</note>) fruit. According to the *<term>Ritual Application</term>* <note>original: "Prayoga"</note> when She is invoked for the purpose of victory in war and the like She is of terrific aspect but in daily worship Her aspect is benignant. In the *<term>Ritual for Battle</term>* <note>original: "Samaraprayoga"</note> She is meditated upon as seated on a lion and surrounded by *<term>Female Powers</term>* <note>original: "Shaktis"</note> who are mounted on Tigers. In other kinds of *<term>Ritual Application</term>* <note>original: "Prayoga"</note> She is to be meditated upon as seated at her ease (*<term>Comfortable Posture</term>* <note>original: "Sukhâsana"</note>) surrounded by *<term>Female Powers</term>* <note>original: "Shaktis"</note> similarly seated. # INTRODUCTION.

The text describes (in verses 26-27) the rules for *<term>preparatory ritual <note>A series of rites, including repetition of a sacred formula and offerings, performed to "awaken" or master a mantra.</note></term>* <note>original: "Purashcharana"</note> and the following verses give details of the worship: then in verses 55-58 is described the ritual involving a *<term>sacred sound-formula <note>A word or sound repeated to aid concentration in meditation.</note></term>* <note>original: "Mantra"</note> consisting of eighty letters. The fifteen verses which follow describe the drawing of a *<term>mystical diagram <note>A geometric design used as an aid to meditation or ritual worship.</note></term>* <note>original: "Yantra"</note> of nine chambers and the mode of worship therein. Verses 74 to the end of the Chapter give an account of the *<term>Diamond Diagram</term>* <note>original: "Vajra Yantra"</note> with a sacred sound-formula of eighty-one letters and its worship.

The author of the *<term>Beautiful One <note>A famous commentary on Tantric texts.</note></term>* <note>original: "Manoramā"</note> whilst commenting on the passage in the *King of Tantras* <note>original: "Tantrarāja"</note> "Concerning the sixteen *<term>Eternal Goddesses <note>A group of sixteen goddesses representing different lunar phases.</note></term>* <note>original: "Nityās"</note> there are nine complete scriptures," counts the *Ocean of the Sixteen Eternals Scripture* <note>original: "Nityāshodashikārnava Tantra," published as Volume 56 of the Ānandāshrama Series, Poona</note>, the *Heart of the Beautiful Goddess* <note>original: "Sundarīhridaya," the name given by some to the Second Part of the Ocean of the Sixteen Eternals</note> and the *Lord of the Left-Hand Path Scripture* <note>original: "Vāmakeshvara Tantras"</note>, separately. Bhāskararāya <note>A renowned 18th-century scholar and practitioner of the Shakta tradition.</note> contests this view, citing a passage from the *Heart of the Yogini* <note>original: "Yoginīhridaya"</note> itself: "In this *Lord of the Left-Hand Path* scripture are many matters the meaning of which is unknown" <note>original: "Vāmakeshvaratantre’sminnajnātārthāstvanekashah"</note> and the *Straight Reflection* <note>original: "Riju-vimarshinī"</note> which says: "The scripture named the Holy *Lord of the Left-Hand Path* scripture is revealed. In it is the *Ocean of the Sixteen Eternals* and in this latter are two parts of 400 verses each."

He also discusses the question whether the *Lord of the Left-Hand Path* scripture with its parts, or the *King of Tantras*, is the 65th independent scripture <note>original: "Svatantra"</note> referred to in the 31st verse of the *Wave of Bliss* <note>original: "Ānandalahari," see "Wave of Bliss" by Arthur Avalon</note>. "The *Lord of Creatures* <note>original: "Pashupati," an epithet of Shiva.</note> who knows all things in the universe, promulgated by means of the 64 scriptures the special *<term>supernatural powers <note>Success or perfection in spiritual or worldly goals achieved through ritual.</note></term>* <note>original: "Siddhis"</note> mentioned therein. Thereafter at Your entreaty He brought down to this world Your independent scripture <note>original: "Svatantra"</note> which contains the means of accomplishment of all the *<term>aims of human life <note>The four goals of human existence: righteousness (dharma), prosperity (artha), pleasure (kama), and liberation (moksha).</note></term>* <note>original: "Purushārthas"</note>." Those who support the claim of the *King of Tantras* <note>original: "Tantrarāja"</note> to be the independent scripture here referred to, say that it does show in fact independence. They cite the passage (1-3) in the *King of Tantras*: "the interdependence" <note>original: "Anyonyasāpekshya"</note> "of the scriptures produces confusion. Therefore Oh Lord speak to me that scripture relating to the sixteen Eternal Goddesses which is independent" <note>original: "Nirapeksha" or "Svatantra"</note> "of all other scriptures." According to the Commentator Gaurīkānta, by independent scripture in the verse cited is meant the *Ocean of Knowledge Scripture* <note>original: "Jnānārnava Tantra," Vol. 69 Ānandāshrama series</note>. Bhāskararāya supports the claim of the *Lord of the Left-Hand Path* scripture. He says that the *Beautiful Goddess* <note>original: "Sundarī"</note> scriptures such as the *Ocean of the Clan* <note>original: "Kulārnava"</note>, *Ocean of Knowledge* <note>original: "Jnānārnava"</note>, *Independent* <note>original: "Svachchhanda"</note>, *Supreme Bliss* <note>original: "Parānanda"</note>, *The Terrible Goddess* <note>original: "Bhairavī"</note>, *South-facing Form* <note>original: "Dakshināmūrti"</note> and other scriptures are full of *<term>external worship <note>Rituals involving physical offerings and outward actions.</note></term>* <note>original: "Bahiryāga"</note> rites and contain but little of *<term>internal worship <note>Meditative rituals performed within the mind and soul of the practitioner.</note></term>* <note>original: "Antaryāga"</note>, whilst the reverse is the case as regards the *Lord of the Left-Hand Path*. He claims that it is the most excellent of scriptures since its characteristic is inner worship.

It is true, he says, that the *<term>King of Tantras <note>original: "Tantrarâja"</note></term>* takes no notice of other scriptures regarding <term>external rites <note>original: "Bahiryâga"; physical rituals involving offerings, fire, and icons.</note></term> for the attainment of <term>Liberation <note>original: "Moksha"</note></term>; yet he maintains that it is the *Ocean of the Sixteen Eternals* (part of the *Vâmakeshvara*) which possesses independence regarding <term>Internal Ritual <note>original: "Antaryâga"</note></term>.

Bhâskararâya <note>A famous 18th-century scholar and commentator on Tantric literature.</note> also relies on the statement in the *King of Tantras* that the "<term>Heart of the Eternals <note>original: "Nityâhridaya"</note></term>" is another name for the *<term>Heart of the Female Practitioners <note>original: "Yoginîhridaya"</note></term>*; this latter work is the second part of the *Ocean of the Sixteen Eternals*, which itself is a portion of the *Vâmakeshvara Tantra*. Regarding this contention, however, it should be noted that when the *King of Tantras* says "Heart of the Eternals" is another name for the "Heart of the Female Practitioners," it is not referring to a specific scripture at all, but rather providing a synonymous name for the "Heart of the Female Practitioners." Bhâskararâya admits that there is not much said regarding <term>External Worship <note>original: "Bâhyayâga"</note></term> in the *Ocean of the Sixteen Eternals*. He addresses this, however, by quoting the religious precept: “He has accomplished all things who has acted according to the true intention of the <term>Scripture <note>original: "Shâstra"</note></term>, performing that which he is commanded to do by his own <term>Domestic Rules <note>original: "Grihya"; manuals guiding household religious duties</note></term>, whether it be much or little.” As a matter of fact, the *King of Tantras* contains both external and internal ritual instructions, whereas the *Ocean of the Sixteen Eternals* is, for the most part, a selection of internal ritual. Moreover, it should be noted that Bhâskararâya himself, when commenting on the *<term>Upanishad of Meditation <note>original: "Bhâvanopanishad"</note></term>* of the *<term>Kâdi School <note>original: "Kâdimata"; a specific lineage of the Shri Vidya tradition</note></term>*, quotes more extensively from the *King of Tantras*, and he begins that commentary by stating that the *Upanishad of Meditation* deals with internal ritual. To the statement in the *King of Tantras* ‘that all other scriptures are interdependent,’ he replies that the texts which speak of interdependence (<term>Statement on Interdependence <note>original: "Sâpekshyavachana"</note></term>) merely suggest that those who are <term>initiated <note>original: "Dîkshâ"</note></term> according to some other scripture will, by performing the rites prescribed in those texts to the best of their ability, attain great spiritual fruit; whereas those who are initiated according to the rites prescribed in the *King of Tantras* will, by that initiation alone—that is, without reference to rites prescribed in other scriptures—gain abundant fruit. Moreover, if indispensable rites are missing in this or any other scripture, they ought to be sought in the *<term>Ritual Manuals <note>original: "Kalpasûtras"</note></term>*—it being an established fact that these manuals were composed with the sole object of supplying what was lacking in any particular case (<term>With the purpose of providing the meaning required by each specific branch [of scripture] <note>original: "Tattachchhâkhâpekshitârtha samarpannârthatvena"</note></term>). Therefore, he says, the objection against the <term>Independence <note>original: "Svâtantrya"</note></term> of these two parts making up the *Sixteen Eternals*—on the grounds that nothing is said therein about Initiation, <term>Preparatory Ritual <note>original: "Purashcharana"</note></term>, and the like—cannot be maintained. His argument, however, concerning the Ritual Manuals...

# THE SACRED DIAGRAM

## The Auspicious Instrument of the Goddess

->[A visual representation of the cosmos]<-

The central figure on this page is the **<term>Auspicious Diagram <note>original: "Shri Yantra"; a complex mystical drawing used in the Śrī Vidyā tradition to represent the Goddess and the universe.</note></term>**, an intricate map of spiritual energy. 

At the very heart of the composition lies a **<term>central point <note>original: "Bindu"; the infinitesimal seed from which all creation emerges and to which it returns.</note></term>**. This point is surrounded by **nine interlocking triangles** of varying sizes:
*   **Four triangles** point upwards, signifying the masculine principle.
*   **Five triangles** point downwards, signifying the feminine principle.

The intersection of these nine primary shapes creates a complex web of **forty-three smaller triangles**, each representing a specific aspect of the divine hierarchy.

This central triangular complex is protected by two concentric circles of stylized lotus petals:
1.  An inner ring containing **eight petals**.
2.  An outer ring containing **sixteen petals**.

The entire <term>sacred circle <note>original: "mandala"</note></term> is enclosed within three simple concentric circles and finally framed by a square outer border. This border is characterized by four T-shaped **<term>earth-gates <note>original: "Bhupura"; the "city of earth" that acts as a boundary between the mundane world and the sacred space within.</note></term>**, located at the center of each side to invite the practitioner into the sacred geometry.

<summary>This page illustrates the Shri Yantra, a foundational geometric symbol in Tantra representing the union of masculine and feminine energies through interlocking triangles and lotus petals.</summary>

# THE KING OF TANTRAS
<note>original: "Tantrarājaḥ"; This text is a primary source for the Kadi branch of the Shri Vidya tradition, focusing on the worship of the Goddess in the form of the fifteen "Nityas" or lunar deities.</note>

## Accompanied by the Manoramā Commentary
<note>original: "Manoramā-ṭīkā"; The name Manoramā means "that which delights the mind." This commentary provides the philosophical and ritual depth necessary to understand the condensed verses of the original Tantra.</note>

---

### Chapter One
<note>original: "Prathamaḥ Paṭalaḥ"; A 'Paṭala' is a division or chapter within a Tantric text.</note>

**Without beginning or end, independent, having the three worlds under his own control,**
**Victorious is the ceaseless, all-pervading Time, who is the Great Leader (Vinayaka). (1)**
<note>original: "Anādyanto’parādhīnaḥ svādhīna-bhuvana-trayaḥ... kallo vināyakaḥ"; This verse establishes Time (Kāla) as the ultimate reality. In this school, Time is not merely a measurement but the dynamic aspect of the Divine. "Vinayaka" usually refers to Ganesha, but here it is interpreted as the "Supreme Leader" or "One without a leader above Him."</note>

---

->The Manoramā Commentary Begins.<-

->Salutation to the Holy Ganesha.<-

With this first verse, a hymn of praise to <term>Vinayaka (the Great Leader)</term> is offered, which contains within it the essential meaning of the entire treatise. In this context, he is **"without beginning or end"** because Time is devoid of any starting point or conclusion. He is **"independent"** — meaning he is free from being impelled or driven by any other force. He is the one **"having the three worlds under his own control"** — which means that the three "worlds" of the Knower, the Knowledge, and the Known are entirely within his own power.

**"Victorious"** (1) means that he is superior to the entire universe. He is **"ceaseless"** because of the continuous, unbroken nature of Time. He is **"all-pervading the universe"** because he is not limited by the constraints of space or form. **"Time"** (Kāla) is the specific name of the subject being described. **"Vinayaka"** is both the Lord of Obstacles and "one who is devoid of a leader" (meaning no one is superior to him).

This is the meaning: the Great Leader in the form of Time, described in this way, is the most excellent of all; likewise, Time, being without any master, is superior to the whole world. By this, the revered teacher <note>The commentator is referring to the author or the spiritual lineage</note> indicates that the ultimate reality of Time—which is identical to the <term>Nitya Lalita</term> <note>The "Eternal Red One," the supreme Goddess of this tradition</note>—is the very essence of the universe, and that the seekers of truth are ultimately identical with this reality. This is the central theme of the entire work. (1)

---

<margin>(1) The original manuscript text contains a variation: "Victorious is he who has ceased [all worldly activity]" (jayatyuparata).</margin>
<margin>(2) Some versions read: "He is indeed without beginning or end" (anādyantastu).</margin>
<margin>(3) Note: The phrase "meaning" (ityartha) is absent in the first manuscript edition.</margin>

<summary>This opening page introduces the Tantraraja Tantra with a hymn to "Time" (Kāla) personified as the deity Vinayaka. The commentary explains that Time is the independent, all-pervading reality that governs the "three worlds" of subject, object, and the process of knowing.</summary>

# THE KING OF TANTRAS
## Accompanied by the Delight of the Mind Commentary
<note>original: "Manoramā-khyā-ṭīkā-sahite Tantrarāje"</note>

In the twenty-first chapter and those following, the **Fire Offerings for Desired Results** (<term>Kāmya-homāḥ; rituals performed to achieve specific worldly or spiritual goals</term>) lead to great success. (16)

In the thirty-third chapter, the **Sacred Diagrams** (<term>Yantras; geometric symbols used for meditation and ritual</term>) are described according to their various fruits. In the thirty-fourth, the **Names**; in the thirty-fifth, their **Inner Realization**. (17)
<note>original: "Vāsanā"; In this context, Vasana refers to the deeper esoteric meaning or the meditative state produced by the ritual.</note>

In the thirty-sixth, the **Description of the Self**. The chapters are the **Embodiments of the Principles of Reality**. Each chapter consists of one hundred verses; such is this Collection of Tantra. (18)
<note>original: "Tattva-vigrahāḥ"; The 36 chapters of this text correspond to the 36 Tattvas (fundamental principles) of the Shaiva-Shakta philosophy, suggesting the text itself is a manifestation of reality.</note>

**Beautiful, pleasant-faced, pure, accessible, and learned in many Tantras;**
**Free from doubt, having severed all uncertainty, and impartial—such is the Guru.** (19)

**"Beauty"** is flawlessness in form; **"Pleasant-facedness"** is the quality of speaking with a smile. **"Purity"** is an honest and straightforward way of living. (20)

**"Accessibility"** is a lack of arrogance; being **"Content"** and **"Learned in many Tantras."** He is **"Without Doubt"** because he has realized the truth through the demonstration of its power. (21)

**"Impartiality"** is the absence of greed; **"Mastery"** (<term>Gurutvam</term>) is speaking for the benefit of others. Such a one is known as a **Guru**; any other kind only brings suffering to the disciple. (22)

One who is joined with the four prose-formulas, who is full of faith, and has a steady mind...

---

### The Commentary
<note>The following section provides the scholastic expansion on the verses above.</note>

...in another set of fifteen. Then—in the seventeenth. Further—in the nineteenth. Therefore—in the twentieth.
After that—in the twenty-second. Following that—in the twenty-fourth. In the one after—in the twenty-ninth. Above that—in the twentieth <note>The commentator here is clarifying specific chapter counts or verse groupings which may vary in different manuscript traditions</note>. Above that—in the twenty-second. Of this—referring to the worship and so on. **"Embodiments of the Principles"**—referring to the fact that they are characterized by the number thirty-six. [Numbers 8 through 18].

With the verses beginning with **"Beautiful"** and ending with **"Brings suffering,"** the author teaches the **Characteristics of the Teacher** (<term>Deśika-lakṣaṇam</term>).
In that context, **"Contentment"** means a sense of **Fullness**. **"Through demonstration"** means the demonstration of the Truth. **"Other"** refers to a teacher who lacks the aforementioned characteristics.
**"Brings suffering to the disciple"**—this means by the **theft of the disciple's wealth**, causing **physical exhaustion**, or causing **delusion and confusion of the intellect**. [Numbers 19 through 22].

(3) *Alternative reading:* "Demonstration of the Truth" (Pratipādanāt-tvasya) in the So. and Va. manuscripts.

# CHAPTER 1
## Determining the Characteristics of Teacher and Disciple

->**Free from greed, steady in body, acting with foresight, and with senses mastered,** (23)<-
->**A believer, with firm devotion to the Teacher, the Sacred Formula, and the Deity.**<-
->**Such a person should be a disciple; any other brings only grief to the Teacher.** (24)<-
->**When the Teacher speaks, the disciple should always respond in this way:**<-
->**"Be gracious, O Lord! O Divine One!" and "So be it," with great respect.** (25)<-
->**Having bowed, he should sit by the Teacher's side; likewise, he should depart only with permission.**<-
->**Watching the Teacher's face for instruction, he should serve and execute what is commanded with care.** (26)<-
->**He must not speak an untruth in the Teacher's presence, nor chatter excessively.**<-
->**Lust, anger, greed, pride, mockery, and praise,** (27)<-
->**Fickleness, crookedness, joking, and lamenting,**<-
->**Taking loans, or engaging in the buying and selling of goods—** (28)<-
->**A disciple who seeks to prosper should never do these things with the Teacher.**<-
->**Since the Teacher is Shiva himself in visible form, one should worship him by praising, bowing, and serving him.** (29)<-
->**As toward the Deity, so toward the Mantra; as toward the Mantra, so toward the Guru.**<-

---

With the two verses beginning with "By the four" and ending with "the teacher's [grief]," the author teaches the characteristics of the disciple. Among these, he is "endowed with the first four"—referring to the four qualities mentioned as characteristics of the Guru, such as beauty and the rest. "The other" refers to one who lacks these stated qualities <note>original: "ukta-guṇa-vihīnaḥ"</note> and "brings grief to the Teacher"—this grief includes loss of reputation, misfortune, and distress of the mind and body. (22, 23, 24)

With the five verses beginning with "When the Teacher speaks" and ending with "should worship by bowing," the author teaches the proper sequence of conduct for a disciple. In this context: **"Praise"** <note>original: "stutiḥ"</note> refers to the praise of oneself or others. **"Crookedness"** <note>original: "jihvāni"</note> means deceptive behavior. **"Lamenting"** <note>original: "paridevanaṃ"</note> refers to excessive wailing or idle chatter. **"One who seeks to prosper"** <note>original: "bhūṣṇuḥ"</note> means one who wishes to be victorious or successful. **"Worship"** means to serve. (25, 26, 27, 28)

With the ten verses beginning with "As toward the Deity" and ending with "endowed with devotion," the venerable author [explains the spiritual equivalence of the three...]

# THE TANTRARĀJA TANTRA
## With the Commentary named Manoramā

->**O Dear One, the sequence of devotion should be practiced toward one’s own self just as it is toward the Guru.** (30)<-

->**On the Guru's birthday, one should perform a festival with great care,**<-
->**including special worship, the feeding of practitioners, and the adoration of the Guru’s feet.** (31)<-

->**If the Guru has become all-pervasive <note>original: "vyāpte" – a respectful way to say deceased</note> or has gone far away, one should worship him through his elder brother and others.**<-
->**If staying in the same location, daily service is required; if he is far away, the distance is measured in leagues.** (32)<-

->**Depending on the length of time—from one season up to a year—the distance is considered up to six leagues.** <note>A <term>yojana</term> (league) is an ancient Indian measure of distance, roughly 8 to 9 miles.</note><-
->**Beyond that, if he is not too far, one serves by obeying his commands.** (33)<-

->**His seat, bed, clothing, ornaments, and sandals,**<-
->**as well as his shadow, his spouse, and anything else dear to him, should be honored.** (34)<-

->**In the same village, one should not perform separate worship without the Guru's permission.**<-
->**If the Guru arrives while one is in the middle of a ritual, one should bow and explain the situation.** (35)<-

->**If told "Finish the remainder," he should do so; otherwise, he acts by the Guru's command.**<-
->**Following that command, he should complete the rest of the rite with a steady mind.** (36)<-

->**If the Guru—or others worthy of respect—arrive during a ritual,**<-
->**this is the prescribed duty: one should not maintain a vow of silence with them.** (37)<-

->**One should never think of the Guru as a mere mortal; if one does...**<-

---

The author now teaches the "sequence of devotion" (<term>bhakti-krama</term>). In the text, "all-pervasive" means he has departed to another world <note>original: "lokāntaraṃ gate" – deceased</note>. "Gone far away" refers to traveling to a place beyond the six leagues mentioned later. "Through his elder brother and others" refers to the Guru's elder brother and those others who will be specified in the following verses. 

"In the same location" means when the Guru and disciple are residing in the same village, city, district, hamlet, or town. "According to the distance in leagues" connects to the phrase "if he is far away."

The phrase "in the same village" serves as a general term for the cities and other settlements mentioned previously. "Separate worship" refers to performing rituals for others without including or prioritizing the Guru...

# CHAPTER 1 | Defining the Disciple's Conduct and Mantra Components

->...success will never be achieved through mantras or the worship of deities [if the Guru is neglected]. (38)<-

->One should certainly perform his [the Guru's] worship with the mantra as prescribed. Having understood this well in that specific chapter, one should proceed with full devotion. (39)<-

->Regarding the *Nityās* <note>The fifteen lunar goddesses central to this Tantric system.</note> and the ancient traditions, the fractional components <term>aṃśaka</term> <note>Divisions of zodiac signs used to determine the strength and relationship of a mantra.</note> of the stars are discussed. Some instructions are also given here for the success of magical rites <term>abhicāra</term> <note>Rites intended to influence, subdue, or protect against enemies.</note>. (40)<-

->In the stars beginning with Aries <note>original: "aśvinyādiṣu" — the lunar mansion Aśvinī corresponds to the start of the sign Aries.</note>, excluding the nasal dot <term>bindu</term>, the aspiration <term>visarga</term>, and the final letter <note>The letter "Kṣa," which is considered a conjunct consonant ending the Sanskrit alphabet.</note>, one should apply the first four vowels. The nasal and the aspirate are universal. (41)<-

->Using that group of mantra-letters and the first letter of the practitioner's name, one should calculate whether it falls on the sixth, eighth, or twelfth position. (42)<-

->If the mantra-group belongs to the "enemy," it will bring him harm. Among the zodiac signs and stars here, one calculates using the combinations of seven, five, and three. (43)<-

->The fractional portions for the grace of the goals to be achieved <term>sādhya</term> should also be understood.<-

***

**[Commentary]**
"Or the worship of deities..." means one should not perform the worship themselves [without the Guru’s presence or permission]. If others worthy of worship are present, or those who have attained knowledge, they should be placed in front. "In that chapter" refers to the Second Chapter. (Verses 29–39)

From the words "Regarding the Nityās" until the word "everywhere," the author teaches the components of mantras through twenty-two verses. Here, the word "fractional components" <term>aṃśaka</term> refers to the zodiac signs and similar divisions. The word "etc." refers to the calculation of the Wheel of Success <note>original: "siddhādi-cakra"</note> and the calculation of "Debts and Credits" <note>original: "ṛṇāṛṇi" — a method used to see if a practitioner's name matches the mantra's energy.</note>.

"In the stars beginning with Aries" means in the signs of the zodiac starting with Aries. "Excluding the nasal dot, the aspiration, and the final" means without the nasal <term>anusvāra</term>, the aspirate <term>visarga</term>, and the letter *Kṣa*. "The four" refers to the first four letters [vowels]. "The nasal and the aspirate are universal" means they represent the nature of Shiva and Shakti <note>The masculine and feminine cosmic principles.</note>, and thus they are present in all things.

"Through that..." refers to the sequence of letters applied to the signs. The meaning is this: for every letter, there are thirty-three time-units <term>ghaṭikā</term> <note>A traditional unit of time equal to 24 minutes.</note>. Through these units, one should determine the fractional compatibility between the person performing the rite and the goal they wish to achieve.

# THE TANTRARĀJA WITH THE MANORAMĀ COMMENTARY

...Because those who are devoid of the realization of the Truth <note>original: *tattva-vijñāna-rahitāḥ*</note> are not so commanded [to act without these rules]. (44)

->**The Construction of the Sixteen-Square Grid**<-

By using five lines drawn from East to West and five lines from South to North, sixteen squares are created here. In these, one should write the groups of letters <term>varga</term> <note>The Sanskrit alphabet is organized into groups (vargas) based on where the sound is produced in the mouth.</note> in their proper order. (45)

One should arrange them in order by dividing them into four groups of four. In the first square of the first group, place the first [letter/group]; likewise, in the first square of the second group... (46)

...place the second; then another in another square, and similarly arrange the rest. In those respective squares, one should write each fifth letter [of the groups]. (47)

Thus, in the four sets of squares, one should write everything up to the letter 'Kṣa' <note>The final letter of the Sanskrit alphabet.</note>.

So it is said. One should calculate: starting from the zodiac sign corresponding to the first letter of the enemy's name and counting to the zodiac sign of the first letter of the mantra—if the count lands on the sixth, eighth, or twelfth sign, one should use such mantras for rites of subjugation <term>abhicāra</term> <note>Rites intended to influence or paralyze an opponent.</note> and the like. This is the meaning. This applies to what was said regarding the zodiac signs <term>rāśi</term>. Regarding the "stars"—this refers to the lunar mansions <term>nakṣatra</term> beginning with *Aśvinī*. By counting from the constellation of the enemy's first letter to the constellation of the mantra's first letter, if it falls on the seventh, fifth, or third position, one should perform subjugation rites with those mantras.

Regarding "the targets" <note>original: *sādhyānām*</note> and so on: among the three types of practitioners—the Target, the Practitioner, and the Perfected—the first type lacks the knowledge of Reality. Therefore, for them, the previously mentioned fractional components <term>aṃśaka</term> <note>Mathematical divisions of the zodiac signs.</note> must be examined during the initiation <note>original: *anugraha*</note>. (44-45)

When it says "one should write the groups in order," the meaning of the word "order" <term>krama</term> is shown: having divided the sixteen squares into four groups of four, moving clockwise <term>prādakṣiṇyena</term>, and assigning them to the groups of the Target <term>sādhya</term>, the Perfected <term>siddha</term>, the Highly Successful <term>susiddha</term>, and the Enemy <term>ari</term>.

**In the first of the first**—this means one should write the first letter in the first square of the first set of four. **In the first of the second**—this means in the first square of the second set of four, following the stated order. **Likewise**—this means that just as the first square was designated for the first set of four, one should do the same here. **The second**—write the letter 'Ā'. **From another**—in the first square of the third set of four. **Another**—write the third letter, 'I'. **And thus should the rest be arranged**—"thus" refers to the previous three sets of four. **Another**—the fourth set of four. The word **"and"** implies inclusion. **Should be arranged**—one should write. In the fourth set of four, one should write the fourth letter, 'Ī'...

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for constructing the sixteen-square grid (Siddha-Chakra) used to determine if a mantra is compatible with a practitioner's name.
