# CHAPTER 1 | DESCRIPTION OF THE RESULTS OF THE SIXTEEN-SQUARE LETTERS

> Wherever the first letter of one's own name is found in a square, from that point... (48)
> ...one should count through the categories starting with "Successful" until reaching the square where the first letter of the mantra appears.
> "Successful-Successful" is mastered through chanting; "Successful-To-be-Accomplished" <note>original: *siddha-sādhya*</note> is mastered by doubling the amount of chanting. (49)

This means one should write in the first square of each set. In those respective squares—the second squares of the four sets mentioned—one should write the "fifth" letters. This means one should write the fifth letters relative to the letters written in each of the first squares <note>In this system, letters are arranged not alphabetically, but by jumping five positions ahead to create a randomized grid</note>. Thus, as before, one should write the fifth letters of the letters in the second squares into the third squares. Then, one should write the fifth letters of the letters in the third squares into the fourth squares. In the four sets of four squares mentioned, by repeatedly writing the fifth letters in each square, one should fill all sixteen squares up to the letter *Kṣa* <note>The final letter of the Sanskrit alphabet</note>.

When written this way, the first square of the first set contains the four letters: *a, ka, ca, ha*. In the second square: *u, ṅa, pa*. In the third: *lṛ, bha, ma*. In the fourth: *o, ḍa, va*.
In the first square of the second set, there are four letters: *ā, kha, cha, la*. In the second: *ū, ña, pha*. In the third: *e, ba, ya*. In the fourth: *au, ḍha, śa*.
In the first square of the third set: *i, ga, dha, ña*. In the second: *ṛ, chha, va*. In the third: *ai, ṭa, ra*. In the fourth: *aṃ, ṇa, ṣa*.
In the first square of the fourth set: *ī, gha, na*. In the second: *ṝ, ja, bha*. In the third: *o, ṭha, la*. In the fourth: *aḥ, ta, sa*.

Once written this way, the letters situated above the letters of the first set of squares are seen in the second set of squares in due order. The meaning of the phrase "prescribed order" used earlier is that these fifty-one letters, from *A* to *Kṣa*, are seen in a scrambled arrangement <note>original: *vyākula-krama*</note> within these sixteen squares. (46, 47, 48, 49)

With the six verses beginning with "Successful-Successful" and ending with "well-determined," the author teaches the results of the letters in these sixteen squares. Here, the phrase "otherwise than this" refers to the "Highly Successful" <term>susiddha</term> category which follows "Successful-To-be-Accomplished." 

Regarding rites of subjugation <term>abhicāra</term> <note>Magic rituals intended to harm or paralyze an enemy</note>: if a mantra is "Enemy" <term>ripu</term> to the practitioner, it leads to their own downfall. This means that at the time of performing a rite against an enemy, if the practitioner uses a mantra that is "Highly Successful" for that enemy, the mantra will actually cause the death of the practitioner themselves.

->Especially in the combinations of "Debt-Success" <note>Calculating if the practitioner "owes" a spiritual debt to the mantra or vice versa</note>, specifically regarding the initiation into a mantra.<-

# CHAPTER 1 | THE RESULTS OF THE SIXTEEN-SQUARE RELATIONSHIPS

> Within the **Successful** category, a **Very Successful** result brings wealth; an **Enemy** result kills one's kin. Mastery of a **Successful** result within the **To-be-Accomplished** category comes only with great pain; a **To-be-Accomplished** result within the **To-be-Accomplished** category causes extreme suffering. (50)

> A **Very Successful** result in the **To-be-Accomplished** category is mastered through devotion; an **Enemy** in the **To-be-Accomplished** category steals one's prosperity. A **Successful** result in the **Very Successful** category gives the desired fruit through study. (51)

> A **To-be-Accomplished** result in the **Very Successful** category leads to perfection through chanting and rituals <note>original: *jāpa-ādyaiḥ*</note>; otherwise, it is not attained. A **Very Successful** result in the **Very Successful** category is famous as the result of effort made in a previous life. (52)

> Therefore, one who chants the mantra <term>Manu</term> for the attainment of all perfections <note>original: *siddhi*</note> should avoid certain combinations. If used in malevolent magic <term>Abhicāra</term> against an enemy, it may lead to one's own ruin. (53)

> An **Enemy** in the **Very Successful** category will surely destroy one's entire family. An **Enemy** in the **Successful** category kills the son; an **Enemy** in the **To-be-Accomplished** category kills the wife. (54)

> An **Enemy** mantra in the **Very Successful** category slowly uproots the family. An **Enemy** in the **Enemy** category is a mantra that kills the self; this is certain upon obtaining it. (55)

> Starting from the first letter of one's name and counting to the first letter of the mantra, one should triple the number and divide by the vowels. For the other way, one does the reverse. (56)

->One should take the name by which a person is famously known and by which they wake when sleeping. <-

With the six verses beginning with "Starting from the first letter of one's name" and ending with "from all sides," the author teaches the relationship of "Creditor and Debtor" <term>Uttamārṇa-Adhamarṇa</term> between the practitioner and the mantra, and the results thereof. 

In that context, **up to the first letter of the mantra** means: one should count from the first letter of one's own name to the first letter of the mantra according to the order of the alphabet <note>original: *mātṛkā-akṣara-krama*</note>. 

**Triple the number** means: multiply that count by three. 

**Vowels** <note>original: *svaraiḥ*</note>: The word "vowels" usually refers to the numbers sixteen or seventy-six. However, by tradition <note>original: *sampradāyāt*</note>, the number seven is accepted here. 

**Divide** means: one should divide the total by that number (seven). 

**The other way** means: counting the letters of the alphabet starting from the first letter of the mantra up to the first letter of one's own name. 

**Reverse** means: in this case, one should multiply by seven and divide by three. 

The meaning is this: this is the method to know the creditor-debtor relationship for all primary mantras <note>original: *vidyā-mantra*</note> and all their auxiliary parts. One starts from the first letter of the name according to the order of the alphabet...

# CHAPTER 1 | THE RESULTS OF THE DEBTOR-CREDITOR RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN THE PRACTITIONER AND THE MANTRA. 11

> Having performed the calculation, the one with the higher number is known as the **Debtor** <term>Adhamarna—the one who owes</term>; if the mantra is the debtor, it is considered the best result. If the practitioner himself is the debtor, he should abandon that mantra, because he is already in debt from a previous state. (57)

> Tell me, how can there be a state of "debt" for mantras and practitioners? Because of the habits formed in a previous life <margin>The original manuscript reads "from practice" <note>original: *abhyāsāt*</note>.</margin> or due to sin, a mantra may fail to yield its results. (58)

> When sin is destroyed, the results are obtained. If one's body perishes while still a debtor, the mantra from that previous life will return with great speed in the next life to bring success <term>Siddhi</term>. (59)

> A mantra received from an excellent <gloss>ra</gloss> teacher becomes a vessel for success. Even one who, out of the pride of wealth, disregards the mantra, still obtains enjoyment through it. <margin>The original manuscript reads "may obtain" <note>original: *mavāpnuyāt*</note>.</margin> (60)

> One is known as a debtor to a good mantra <margin>The original manuscript reads "of that mantra" <note>original: *sa mantrasya*</note>.</margin> if its worship was performed in the past. Therefore, the purification of debt must be performed by everyone in every way. (61)

> One should perform the practice using rosaries made of **Rudraksha** seeds, **Lotus** seeds <note>original: *padmākhyaiḥ*</note>, **Putrajiva** seeds <note>A seed traditionally used for the protection of children and in spiritual practice</note>, **Red Sandalwood** <note>original: *kucandanaiḥ*</note>, **Crystal**, **Coral**, **Pearls**, or those fashioned from **Gold**. (62)

---

Count the letters of the alphabet preceding the first letter of your name; multiply that number by three, divide by seven, and determine the remainder. Then, count from the first letter of the mantra to the first letter of your own name; increase that number by seven, divide by three, and determine the remainder. 

By the verse starting "Having performed," this is what is meant: Between the two remainders calculated from the previous instructions, the one associated with the higher number is the **Debtor** <term>Adhamarna</term>, and the one with the lower number is the **Creditor** <term>Uttamarna</term>. 

In this context, if the **mantra** is the debtor, there is an abundance of fruit <note>Meaning the mantra "owes" the practitioner success</note>. If the **practitioner** is the debtor, the practice will be fruitless <note>Meaning the practitioner is merely paying off a karmic debt to the mantra</note>. Therefore, one should abandon those sciences <term>Vidya</term> where one is the creditor and instead accept those where the mantra is the debtor. "By all" refers to all practitioners and the goals to be achieved. "In every way" means regarding both mantras and feminine knowledge-systems <term>Vidya</term>. (56, 57, 58, 59, 60, 61, 62)

Through the four verses beginning with "Rudraksha" and ending with "chanting" <note>original: *japa*</note>, the text instructs on the types of rosaries <term>Akshamala</term>. In this context, **"bad sandalwood"** <note>original: *kucandana*</note> refers specifically to **red sandalwood**. (63, 64, 65)

# THE TANTRARĀJA WITH THE COMMENTARY NAMED MANORAMĀ
## CHAPTER 1 | ROSARIES, ATONEMENT, AND THE CONDUCT OF THE PRACTITIONER. 12

->**The Composition of the Rosary**<-

A rosary for chanting <term>Japamālā—a string of prayer beads</term> made of silver is progressively more fruitful. A true "rosary of letters" <term>Akṣamālā—literally a 'garland of letters' from A to Kṣa</term> is formed by the characters of the alphabet from *A* to *Kṣa*. (63)

One should chant the mantra interspersed with these "mother-letters" <term>Mātṛkā—the letters of the Sanskrit alphabet viewed as divine energies</term> in both forward and reverse order. In this way, one becomes endowed with every good quality and attains all success. (64)

One should perform the act of chanting <term>Japa</term> using the tips of the fingers, excluding the index finger <note>In many Tantric traditions, the index finger is associated with the ego and is often avoided during sacred recitation</note>. Alternatively, one may count the repetitions by touching the joints of the fingers. (65)

->**Atonement for Errors**<-

If a forbidden act is committed unintentionally, one should quickly chant the mantra <term>Vidyā—the feminine form of a mantra</term> one hundred times; by this, he is certainly freed from that sin. (66)

To pacify the faults arising from the omission of daily duties <term>Nitya-karma</term>, one should chant the mantra a hundred times. If occasional or special duties <term>Naimittika-karma</term> are omitted, one should then chant it a thousand times. (67)

->**The Conduct of the Practitioner**<-

The practitioner should possess a pure heart and a pleasant face, wear white garments, and remain ritually clean. He should turn away from criticizing others, their deities, or their philosophical systems. (68)

He should be free from desire for the wealth, women, or land of others. He should be compassionate toward all people, circumspect in his actions, and free from worldly attachment. (69)

One who is a believer <term>Āstika</term>, devoted to his Guru, and constantly observant of the rules—such a person, endowed with all virtues, shall attain success in the mantra. (70)

Otherwise, for one who behaves differently yet persists in worshiping the mantra for a long time, there is no success for him anywhere, at any time, or in any manner. (71)

***

**The Commentary named Manoramā**

With the two verses beginning with "unintentionally" (66) and ending with "then" (67), the author teaches the methods of atonement <term>Prāyaścitta—ritual acts to neutralize errors</term>.

With the four verses starting from "pure" (68) and ending with "in any manner" (71), he teaches the proper conduct of the practitioner <term>Sādhaka-samācāra</term>.

Regarding the phrase "visions of deities" <note>original: *devatā-darśaneṣu*</note>—this means one should avoid criticizing both the deities themselves and the philosophical systems or "visions" through which they are viewed. These "visions" <note>original: *darśaneṣu*</note> refer to the Vedic, Vaishnava, and other such established traditions. (68, 70, 71, 72)

***

# CHAPTER 1 | DESCRIPTION OF JOINING AUXILIARY ACTS TO MANTRAS. 13

->**The Methods of Mantra Composition**<-

->Joining at the beginning is *Yoga*; at the end, it is *Pallava*; and on both sides, it is *Sampuṭa* <note>original: "sampuṭo(1)dvayoḥ"</note>.<-
->Alternating character by character is *Grathana*, while *Vidarbha* is formed by placing characters in between. (72)<-
->Having recognized the faults of a mantra, a Guru should remove them instantly.<-
->Otherwise, that Guru certainly destroys the disciple in no time. (73)<-

With the verse starting with "At the beginning, Yoga," the author teaches the method of joining auxiliary acts <term>Sāṅga-karma—the "limbs" or auxiliary parts of a ritual, such as the practitioner's name or a specific goal</term> with mantras. 

In this regard, the following is explained: 
1. **Yoga** <term>Yoga—literally 'joining'</term>: This is the name for joining the auxiliary acts at the beginning of the mantras or <term>Vidyās—feminine mantras</term>. 
2. **Pallava** <term>Pallava—literally 'sprout' or 'leaf'</term>: This is the name for joining them at the end of the mantra. 
3. **Sampuṭa** <term>Sampuṭa—literally 'casket' or 'enclosure'</term>: This is the name for joining them at both the beginning and the end. 
4. **Grathana** <term>Grathana—literally 'weaving'</term>: This is the name for the mutual intermingling of the mantra letters and the auxiliary letters, one by one. 
5. **Vidarbha** <term>Vidarbha—literally 'interweaving'</term>: This is the name for joining two letters of each alternately. 

This *Vidarbha* is of three types: 
*   One may join one auxiliary letter between every two mantra letters. 
*   One may join one mantra letter between every two auxiliary letters. 
*   One may join two auxiliary letters between every two mantra letters. 
These are the three varieties. (73)

Through the nine verses beginning with "the faults of mantras," the author teaches the defects that can affect a mantra's efficacy. Regarding the phrase "that Guru" <note>The commentator notes that "sa guruḥ" (that Guru) here actually refers to the mantra itself</note>, the word "that" refers to the mantra. 

The faults include: 
*   **Six-eared** <term>Ṣaṭkarṇa</term>: When the mantra is overheard by two people other than the Guru and disciple during recitation. 
*   **Chanting with excessive power**: When a minor deity's mantra is chanted alongside a powerful deity's mantra, causing the minor one to be "terrified." 
*   **Proud** <term>Garvita</term>: When the mantra is not favorable toward the practitioner. 
*   **Obtained without rule**: When a mantra is received without the proper initiation <term>Dīkṣā</term>. 
*   **Enemy-housed**: When the mantra falls into an "enemy square" according to the practitioner's astrological chart. 
*   **Conquered**: Mantras that have been defeated or rendered powerless. 
*   **Burdened by past actions**: When the practitioner’s own past sins prevent the mantra from working. 
*   **Without 'Ha' or 'Sa'**: Mantras lacking these vital seed-syllables. 
*   **Devoid of essence**: Weak mantras. 
*   **Incomplete form**: Mantras missing essential letters. 
*   **Distressed**: When only a fragment of a mantra is used. 
*   **Obstructed**: When the mantra is blocked from providing the practitioner's desired result. 
*   **Nasalized**: Over-reliance on nasal consonants. 
*   **Applied at the wrong time**: Using a mantra during its "sleeping" phase.

The characteristics of the "sleep" and "waking" of mantras are now described: 
Mantras primarily containing the sounds *Om*, *ca*, *ra*, and *ha* are **Fiery** <term>Āgneya</term>. Mantras primarily containing "cool" or lunar letters are **Gentle** <term>Saumya</term>. When the practitioner's breath flows fully through the right nostril, it is a Fiery state...

# PAGE 14 | TANTRARĀJA WITH THE MANORAMĀ COMMENTARY

->Therefore, listen with concentration, O Goddess, to the remedy for these faults!<-
->I shall truly describe the method of remedy within the various applications. (74)<-
->A mantra overheard by a third party is "burned"; it becomes "terrified" by excessive chanting.<-
->It is "haughty" if obtained without proper ritual, and "enemies" are those placed in the enemy’s square. (75)<-
->Mantras consisting mostly of short syllables are "young"; those with long syllables are "old."<-
->Those whose essence is lost through excessive ritual labor are "defeated" and "powerless." (76)<-

---

This section explains the waking state <term>Prabodha-kāla—the time when a mantra is spiritually active</term> for various classes of mantras. For others, such as the "gentle" or lunar mantras, this is their time of sleep. When the breath flows through the left nostril <note>associated with the lunar Ida channel</note>, it is the waking time for lunar mantras; conversely, it is the sleeping time for "fiery" or solar mantras. 

The practitioner <term>Sādhaka—a spiritual seeker or ritualist</term> who employs mantras for desired goals without knowing these nuances only causes trouble and exhaustion for themselves. The text then defines specific defective states:

**Fainted** <note>original: "mūrcchitāḥ"</note>: These are inactive mantras. They are incapable of bringing about the success envisioned by the practitioner.

**Sleeping** <note>original: "svāpagāḥ"</note>: Like a person in deep slumber, these mantras are indifferent and do not face or respond to the practitioner.

**Neglect of Chanting** <note>original: "ajapāt"</note>: This refers to the failure to follow the prescribed daily worship and sequence taught by the Guru from the very day of initiation. <note>The commentator notes that the grammatical joining (sandhi) here is archaic or "rishi-like" and should not be over-analyzed.</note>

**Intoxicated** <note>original: "mattāḥ"</note>: These mantras produce both desired and undesired results indiscriminately, even for a practitioner who is otherwise diligent.

**Reading from Pages**: This refers to the fault of chanting a mantra after merely seeing it written down somewhere, without receiving it properly from the mouth of a Guru.

**Other Letters**: This occurs when letters outside the specific mantra are included, either due to the practitioner’s inattention or accidental insertion.

**Nailed/Locked** <note>original: "kīlitāḥ"</note>: Just as a name might be fixed or "nailed" to a wall, a mantra becomes locked and immobile due to the practitioner's carelessness or confusion with similar-sounding names.

**Obstructed**: These are mantras that are blocked or prevented from manifesting.

**Lacking Union** <note>original: "visandhikāḥ"</note>: These are mantras where the rules of Sanskrit grammar—such as *Guṇa*, *Vṛddhi*, or *Yaṇ* <note>vowel blending rules</note>—have not been applied where they were required.

**Suffering**: Mantras that have become troubled or distressed.

**Possessed of Enmity**: These are mantras worshiped alongside "enemy mantras." The specific characteristics of how mantras become "enemies" to one another will be explained later in the *Vāsanā-paṭala* <note>the chapter on inner realization/symbolism</note>, so it is not detailed here.

**Fragmented**: Mantras with a broken or incomplete form.

**Partial Chanting**: Chanting only a portion of the complete sacred knowledge <term>Vidyā—specifically a female deity's mantra</term>.

**Lacking Limbs**: Chanting without the necessary ritual gestures and placements <term>Nyāsa—the practice of "installing" parts of the mantra onto the body</term>.

**Exposed**: Mantras that are not kept secret. Secrecy provides weight and power to a ritual, while public exposure leads to fruitlessness.

---

(1) The variant "Yogantu" is found in the So. manuscript.
(2) The variant "Mantrastrastāditi" is found in the So. manuscript.

# PAGE 15 | CHAPTER 1: DESCRIPTION OF MANTRA FAULTS

->The twenty-five defects that hinder the power of a sacred sound.<-

Mantras that are incomplete in form, severed, paralyzed, or overly nasalized; those used at the wrong time, or recited when they are in a state of "waking" or "sleeping" (77);

Those that are "intoxicated" from being recited during specific lunar phases <note>original: "parveṣu"</note>, or "locked" by different classes of sounds; those that are obstructed, lack proper phonetic joining, are distressed, or joined with "enemies" <note>referring to sounds that are astrologically incompatible with the practitioner</note> (78);

Those that are fragmented, lacking the necessary ancillary rituals, or unprotected; those taught by an uninitiated teacher are considered to be "devoid of power" (79);

Constant use leads to "bluntness"; they are "afflicted" by excessive slowness in recitation. They become "diseased" by babbling during chanting, and "muddled" when combined with other mantras (80);

They are "dishonored" through an attitude of neglect, instability in practice, or irregularity. These are the twenty-five faults described; the Guru should pacify them through the proper remedies. (81)

---

The commentary explains this for all deities and all mantras. 

**Taught by the incomplete** <note>original: "apūrṇena"</note>: This refers to a mantra obtained during a ceremony of grace by one who lacks the <term>Pūrṇābhiṣeka—the "Full Consecration" or highest level of initiation</term>, or one who acts without the Guru's specific command.

**Devoid of power** <note>original: "hīnavīryāḥ"</note>: These have a diminished strength. Because they were transmitted without the prescribed rituals, their inherent energy <note>original: "śakti"</note> was never awakened. For such a disciple, practicing these is not only useless but can lead to misfortune.

**Bluntness** <note>original: "kuṇṭhatvam"</note>: This means they are ineffective. Even mantras that have been "perfected" <note>original: "susiddhā"</note> can become like a blunt weapon—lacking a sharp edge—if the practitioner uses them constantly for worldly applications without pause.

**Afflicted** <note>original: "kliṣṭā"</note>: This describes a state of distress caused by **excessive slowness** <note>original: "ativilambanāt"</note>. This occurs when one lingers too long on the individual letters of the mantra beyond the time prescribed by the tradition.

**Diseased** <note>original: "rugṇāḥ"</note>: Afflicted or pained. This results from **babbling during recitation**—that is, engaging in improper or mundane conversation while trying to maintain the count of the mantra.

**Muddled** <note>original: "āvilāḥ"</note>: Confused or disturbed. When one mixes the current mantra with other mantras—inserting bits of different chants in the middle—both mantras become confused. This leads to fruitlessness and spiritual danger.

**Neglect** <note>original: "upekṣā"</note>: To abandon or disregard the practice.

**Instability in practice** <note>original: "anavasthayā"</note>: This refers to reciting the mantra while ignoring the sequence taught by the Guru or the traditional scriptures, and instead following one’s own invented path.

**Irregularity** <note>original: "vaiṣamyāt"</note>: A lack of balance or consistency in the chanting, worship, or fire-oblations. This implies doing too much or too little, or failing to maintain a steady devotional state.

**Dishonored** <note>original: "avamānitāḥ"</note>: To treat the mantra with contempt or disrespect. 

**The Guru should pacify them** <note>original: "śamayed guruḥ"</note>: This means the teacher should resolve these defects using the methods that will be described in the following sections.

---

# PAGE 16 | TANTRARĀJA TANTRA WITH THE MANORAMĀ COMMENTARY

Binding the <term>Yonimudrā—the ritual gesture representing the source</term> and joining the "potency" <note>original: "vīrya"</note> of the mantras; the self-possessed Guru should protect the disciple by awakening both of these in him. (82)

The definition of a Guru is simply this: he should make known the "Beginning and the End" <note>original: "ādimāntyam"</note>. Letters <note>the individual sounds of a mantra</note> devoid of the "Beginning and the End" are as empty as autumn clouds. (83)

Therefore, from the very beginning, he <note>the practitioner</note> should perform that specific "I-consciousness" <note>original: "ahaṅkṛti"</note>; through the realization of this "I-consciousness," a man becomes equal to Me <note>the Goddess or the Supreme Self</note>. (84)

By joining the first and last letters of the <term>Mātṛkā—the phonetic matrix or "Little Mothers" of the alphabet</term> which is established in an eternal sequence, know that to be the "attainment of identity" <note>original: "tādātmya-siddhi"</note>, which is the embodied form of the meaning of all mantras. (85)

For the twice-born <note>those initiated into the traditional Vedic path</note>, the sacraments are declared according to the Vedas. Yet even for them, in every such instance, one should perform the ritual according to the rules of this Wisdom <note>referring to the Tantric Vidya</note>. (86)

He should maintain the remembrance of the Wisdom and perform the actions prescribed everywhere; by this, the attainment of "becoming one with That" truly occurs in all things. (87)

---

Through the four verses beginning with "Binding" and ending with "embodied form," the author instructs the teacher <note>original: "deśika"</note> on his duties.

In this context, **Binding** means focused contemplation. **Yonimudrā**—as will be explained later in the Chapter on Fire Offerings <note>original: "Homa-paṭala"</note>—is the movement of the life-breath and the mind through the central channel <note>original: "suṣumṇā"</note>, traveling between the root-center <note>original: "mūlādhāra"</note> and the opening of the crown <note>original: "brahmarandhra"</note>. The "binding" of the Yonimudrā means the contemplation of that movement.

**Joining the Potency** means the union of the "Mantra-Potency" (described later in the Chapter on Contemplation) with the specific mantra and the practitioner. This should be understood clearly from the mouth of one's teacher.

**The Beginning and the End** refers to the first and last elements. **Devoid of the Beginning and the End** means lacking the knowledge and connection to the "Beginning and the End." **Letters** here means mantras that are merely physical forms of syllables. **That specific I-consciousness** refers to the nature of the first and last letters of the phonetic matrix. (83-86)

The verse beginning with "Eternal" explains the following: The word **"Aham"** <note>the Sanskrit word for "I"</note> is formed by joining the first letter 'A' and the last letter 'Ha' of the letters whose sequence is eternally established. By the logic of <term>Pratyāhāra—a grammatical method where the first and last letters represent the entire series</term>, one realizes that their own self is the essence of the alphabet, the nature of all speech, and the soul of all deities. (87)

<summary>This page defines the true Guru as one who can transmit the internal "potency" of a mantra by teaching the "I-consciousness" (Aham), which synthetically links the first and last letters of the alphabet to represent the totality of creation.</summary>

# PAGE 17 | THE DUTIES OF THE MASTER (NATHA)

For the other castes as well, one should perform rituals with the <term>Vidya—the sacred mantra-wisdom</term>. At death, cremation is performed with the Vidya, and every other ritual should be carried out with the Vidya. (88)

According to one's means, one should worship and feed one or many <term>Yogis—practitioners of yoga</term> who have attained success through the Vidya and who have been invited in advance. (89)

After honoring him with rings, garments, and other gifts, and having bowed to him, the practitioner <note>original: "mantrī," one who possesses the mantra</note> should dismiss him with the Vidya for the sake of the success of his own wisdom, O <note>Addressing the Goddess as the auspicious one</note> Shiva! (90)

The Guru's birthday, the day one received the Wisdom <note>the day of initiation</note>, one's own birthday, and the day of the <term>Natha-vyapti—the pervasive presence of the Lineage Masters</term>; (91)

The day of the "Intersection of the Three Letters," and the Day of Fullness—these are the six distinguished festival days; including the seventh, they form the "Seven Festivals." (92)

One should perform worship on these occasions either every month or every year. While the Guru is alive <margin>A variant reading suggests: "While the Guru is alive but at a distance"</margin>, if he is pervasive, his son and others (93)

Should be worshiped as his equal; one should attend to them with bows and other honors. In their absence, one should worship a member of his lineage or his devotee. (94)

---

Through the five verses beginning with "For the twice-born" <note>referring to verse 86 on the previous page</note> and ending with "O Shiva," he teaches the <term>Natha-krtya—the ritual duties of the Master</term>.
In that context: "twice-born" refers to the Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas. "Sacraments" refers to rites such as the birth-ceremony.
"Other castes" refers to the Shudras and those born of various mixed social unions <note>original: "anuloma-pratiloma-saṅkara"</note>. (86–90)

Through the five verses beginning with "Of the Guru," he teaches the festivals and other occasions. In that context:
"The Day of the Intersection of the Three Letters" refers to the days associated with specific letters that will be described later in the <term>Matrka-patala—the Chapter on the Phonetic Matrix</term>. On whichever day two letters of a phonetic group and the letter representing the <term>Ghatika—a unit of time (24 minutes)</term> coincide—these three letters together constitute the "Intersection of the Three Letters." Because the method for this will be explained much more clearly in that specific section, it is not elaborated upon here. (91–95)

# THE TANTRARAJA WITH THE COMMENTARY CALLED MANORAMA

One should offer praise with these five verses daily for the attainment of all success. By reciting them at the time of waking in the morning, the day becomes auspicious <note>original: "bhavet"; a variant reading is "vrajeet," meaning the day "proceeds" well</note>. (95)

Salutations to you, O Master! O Blessed Lord! To Shiva, appearing in the form of the auspicious one <note>original: "Shivaya"; a variant reading is "Gururupine," meaning "in the form of the Guru"</note>! To you who have assumed many physical forms for the sake of the realization and descent of <term>Vidya—sacred mantra-wisdom</term>! (96)

To the ever-new one, who possesses nine forms <note>likely referring to the nine traditional masters or "Nathas" of the lineage</note>, yet whose sole essence is the Ultimate Reality. To you, the mass of pure consciousness, the sun that shatters the darkness of all ignorance. (97)

To the independent one, whose form is fashioned out of compassion, whose soul is Shiva. To the one who becomes dependent upon his noble devotees, appearing in the form of worldly existence for their sake. (98)

To the discernment of those who discern, and the <term>Vimarsha—reflective self-awareness</term> of those who reflect. To the light of all lights, the very form of knowledge for the knowers. (99)

One should bow to the front, at the sides, at the back, above, and below. [Praying:] "Always establish your seat within me in the form of my own consciousness." (100)

The "Pervasive Presence of the Earth Element" <note>the first and densest of the thirty-six elements in this system's cosmology</note> has thus been correctly described.

---

With the five verses beginning with "Salutations" and ending with "seat," the text teaches the <term>Natha-stotra—the Hymn to the Master</term>. Therein:

**To the new:** This refers to the one who is eternally desirable because he is forever fresh and new. 

**To the one of nine forms:** To the one whose physical manifestation is distinguished by the number nine.

**To the one whose sole form is the Ultimate Reality:** This means his single essential form is that of Shiva himself. He is capable of the true knowledge of the reality of "Discernment" and "Reflective Awareness," which are the states of <term>Idanta—"this-ness"</term> (objective world) and <term>Ahanta—"I-ness"</term> (subjective self). 

**Of lights:** This refers to those who possess the nature of the perceiver or the knower of mantras. (96, 97, 98, 99, 100)

By the verse beginning with "In front," this is what is expressed: "Establish my identity with yourself across all space, time, and forms." This refers to Shiva. (101)

The commentary clarifies the Master's role as both the universal Ultimate Reality and a compassionate form assumed for the devotee.</summary>

### [ CHAPTER 1 ] THE CONCLUDING STATEMENT

Through the contemplation of this in the heart, that Reality is assimilated into one’s own self <gloss>1</gloss>. (101)

Thus ends the first chapter <gloss>2</gloss> of the **Kadi school** <note>The "Kadi" (beginning with the letter 'Ka') is one of the two primary philosophical traditions of the Shri Vidya lineage</note> of the **Shodashanitya Tantra** <note>The "Tantra of the Sixteen Eternals," referring to the sixteen lunar phases or Nitya goddesses</note>.

# Now, the Second Chapter.

Now I shall describe the <term>Masters</term><note>Sanskrit: *Nathas*. These are the semi-divine and human teachers who form the lineage of the tradition</note>, who share my own form and possess eternal bodies. They serve as the staircase for the <term>Descent of Knowledge</term><note>Sanskrit: *Vidyavatara*. This refers to the process by which transcendent wisdom is brought down to the human level</note>, and I shall also describe their worship. (1)

Taking the names **Illumination**, **Reflection**, and **Bliss**, I manifest myself in the world through these divine forms. (2)
<note>In this philosophy, "Illumination" (*Prakasha*) represents pure consciousness, while "Reflection" (*Vimarsha*) is the self-awareness of that consciousness</note>

From these three, the Radiant ones were born, and there are likewise three <term>Perfected Ones</term><note>Sanskrit: *Siddhas*. Beings who have achieved spiritual perfection and supernatural powers</note>. They are spoken of by my auspicious mouth as **Knowledge**, **Truth**, and **Fullness**. (3)

The Divine Masters always reside near me, while the Perfected Masters dwell here upon the Earth. From them, three others were then produced. (4)

(1) These are named **Natural State**, **Intuition**, and **The Fortunate One**. They constantly dwell upon the Earth and share my very essence. (5)

In this way, through these nine Masters, the <term>Tantra</term><note>A body of sacred texts and practices</note>—whose majesty is renowned in the world—was fashioned by the **Power of the Ka-lineage** <note>Sanskrit: *Kadi-shakti*. The primordial energy associated with the specific school of thought this text belongs to</note>, who is inseparable from you, during the **Golden Age**. (6)

These Masters have two eyes and two arms, and they possess beautiful and graceful forms. They have peaceful, smiling faces, and their hands are held in the gestures of **granting boons** and **dispelling fear**. (7)

The four aims of human life: virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation</note> and facilitate the transmission of the Tantra.

# Chapter 2: Discourse on the manifestation of the Nine Masters, their tasks, the spreading of knowledge, and their mantras.

They are worthy of worship in their respective <term>sacred circles</term><note>Sanskrit: *Mandalas*. Ritual spaces or diagrams used to focus spiritual energy</note>. By His command, the goddesses residing in the <term>Auspicious Wheel</term><note>Sanskrit: *Sri Chakra*. A complex geometric symbol representing the union of the Divine Masculine and Feminine</note> <gloss>(1)</gloss> take on the forms of gods. (8)

<gloss>(2)</gloss> They bear names composed of beloved syllables and are all filled with bliss. In their own circles, their names end with the word **Master** (*Natha*); however, O Goddess, in the Great Circle, their names end with the word **Power** (*Shakti*). (9)

Likewise, they may begin with names like **Illusion** (*Maya*) or **Prosperity** (*Lakshmi*), and are known by nine-lettered names. For the worship of these nine powers and deities— (10)

Which is the <term>sacred formula</term><note>Sanskrit: *Vidya*. In this context, it refers to a mantra that embodies a specific goddess or power</note> that brings complete satisfaction and grants all success? With that seven-syllable formula, O Goddess, <gloss>(3)</gloss> one should perform worship preceded by the specific name. (11)

"Tell me that formula which is beloved by all." [Shiva replies:] "Listen, O Goddess! It brings great success and makes all things dear." (12)

---

The second chapter consists of one hundred verses, beginning with "Now the Masters." Through the first eleven verses, ending with "preceded by the name," the text explains the sequence of the nine Masters' manifestation, their roles, how they spread knowledge, and their mantras.

In that context, the phrase "sharing my form" indicates they possess eternal bodies. The word "likewise" is used here as a conjunction. "Auspicious-faced" refers to names that begin with the word *Sri*. They are "of my essence," meaning they take the form of Shiva. These masters have unique <gloss>(4)</gloss> three-syllable names. There are nine such general three-syllable designations. One should understand them in three distinct categories: **Divine**, **Perfected**, and **Human**. 

Through the explanation of the meaning of the unique three-syllable names of these nine Masters, one should understand from the mouth of the worshiped teacher that they are forms of the undifferentiated Shiva. Regarding "in their respective circles," the specific circles will be described later. The word "etcetera" refers to matters such as one's own head (where the master is meditated upon). "Filled with bliss" means their names include the word "Bliss" (*Ananda*). This refers to the nine Masters. "Preceded by the name" means using each of their specific names during the ritual. (1-11)

Through the five verses beginning with "In copper" and ending with "standing in reverence," the text teaches the seven-syllable mantra common to all systems of the Goddess (*Shakti-tantra*). In that context, "which" refers to the seven-syllable formula. "Javi" refers to the method. "Marut" refers to...

<margin>
**Javi** refers to the letter *Va*. **Marut** refers to the vowel *ā*. **Gotrā** is the letter *Da*. **Dharā** is the vowel *u*. **Prāṇa** is the letter *Ka*. **Marut** is as before (*ā*). **Nabhaḥ** is the letter *Ma*, meaning the nasal dot (*bindu*). **Tritīyakam** (the third) indicates the syllable. **Javi** is as before (*Va*). **Kṣmā** is the vowel *u*. **Jyā** is the letter *Ja*. **Vāta** is the sound *a*. **Vyāpta** is the letter *Ya*. **Marut** is as before, the vowel *ā*. **Nabhaḥ** is as before (*Ma*). **Agni** is the vowel *ī*. The mention of "deities" refers to male subjects. (12–16)
</margin>

Through the passage beginning with "The Nine" and ending with "the names," consisting of three and a quarter verses, the author teaches the sixteen-syllable names of the nine Masters, who are essentially the sixteen forms of the **Eternal Goddess** (*Nityā*). In this context, "sixteen-syllable" refers to the full mantra name. (17–18)

Through the passage beginning with "Circle-making" and ending with "otherwise," consisting of a verse and a quarter, he teaches the continuity of the **Tradition** (*Paramparā*). In this context, **Circle-making** (*Maṇḍalīkaraṇa*) refers to the connection between the beginning and the end. **Attainment** (*Āpti*) means authority or validity. **Succession** (*Anvaya*) refers to the lineage or continuity. (19)

### [ In the 2nd Chapter ]
->**Description of the sequence of writing the letters of the Three Names, and so forth**<-

The practitioner’s names are derived from the sequence of the day, or from the letters belonging to that day. They are also "without illusion" <note>Sanskrit: *amāyah*; a technical term meaning the name is written without the <term>Visarga</term> (the ':' aspiration sound)</note> and without the final letter. <note>(1)</note> (20)
One name is obtained through the lineage sequence; the second is obtained through the calculation of time; and the third is the one that is well-known externally. O Seeker! A practitioner possesses these three names. (21)
Therefore, a practitioner who has received the sacred knowledge should be honored with these three. One should perform worship through verses and hymns to ensure the preservation of the **Tradition**. (22)
One should perform the **Worship of the Circle of Teachers** <note>Sanskrit: *Guru-maṇḍala-pūjā*</note> on the seven sacred festivals. On the Full Moon, one should write out the sixteen-syllable names and worship them. (23)
On the other six festivals, one should write only the nine-syllable names. In all these instances, O Goddess! one should perform the worship while reciting the seven-syllable mantra. (24)
In the worship of the Teachers’ Circle, nine offerings are prescribed in all places. Now, listen to those offerings with which one should worship them. (25)

---

Regarding the verses beginning with "The practitioners' names" and ending with "for the sake of the tradition": the text teaches the three names that must be known for mortals. In this context, the word "or" indicates a combination—meaning that there are two names [of a specific ritual type]. "Letters of the day" refers to those which will be explained in the <term>Twenty-fifth Chapter</term>. Furthermore, there are two types. "Without illusion" (*amāyaḥ*) means without the <term>Visarga</term>. "Without the final" (*anantyaḥ*) refers to a form lacking the final letter 'cha'.

This is what is being said: regarding the "hour-syllables" <note>Sanskrit: *ghaṭikākṣara*; syllables associated with specific units of time</note> to be discussed later, by accepting the identity of the *Visarga* and the letter 'cha' and setting one aside, fifty letters are produced. "Obtained through sequence" (*paryāyataḥ prāptam*) means a name received from the alternative names of one's own Guru. "Obtained through time" (*kālāvāptam*) refers to the name derived from the number remaining when the total days from the start of the <term>Yuga</term> <note>An immense cosmic age</note> until the day the sacred knowledge was received are divided by nine. "Established externally" (*bāhyataḥ siddham*) is the name given by one's mother and father. With "those three"—referring to the names. In the phrase "worship through verses and hymns," it implies that one should perform the worship in the ritual circles using specifically the name obtained through the lineage sequence. (20, 21, 22)

Regarding the verses beginning with "The worship of the Teachers' Circle" and ending with "duly declared": these four verses teach the sequence for writing the letters of the names within the worship circle. There, the "seven festivals" are those mentioned in the first chapter. In that context, "to you also"...

### [ In the 2nd Chapter ] — Description of the Circle of Teachers, the Examination of Students, and Timing.

Having divided them into sixteen parts, one should indeed write those names within them in this manner. (32)

Thus, worship is performed while the Guru is living; but when he has **attained Me** <note>original Sanskrit: *māmupete*. The commentary clarifies this refers to the Guru's death or spiritual liberation—merging with the Divine.</note>, you should draw these locations in the form of a circle <note>Sanskrit: *maṇḍalīkṛtya*</note>. (33)

O Shiva! <note>The text addresses the Goddess, the consort of Shiva.</note> He who worships the Masters thus, remaining focused during the sacred festivals, becomes a supreme teacher <term>Deshika</term> <note>A consecrated initiator or spiritual guide.</note> and a perfected soul. From that worship, the **highest attainment of knowledge** <gloss>(1) The original manuscript variant reads: "Knowledge that is unsurpassed."</gloss> is achieved. (34)

Otherwise, if this is not done, the outcome for both the teacher and the student will certainly lead to calamity: disease, injury by weapons or fire, mental derangement, or death by drowning. (35)

One may suffer such misfortunes <gloss>(2) The original manuscript variant reads: "The King's influence."</gloss> as death by the decree of a king or by a strike of lightning. Therefore, one should perform the ritual exactly in the stated sequence for the fulfillment of all goals. (36)

(37)

Afterward, with a focused mind, the teacher should impart the knowledge according to the prescribed sequence. If he speaks it otherwise, the Guru, along with the student, shall meet with destruction. (38)

---

The commentator explains the section starting with the syllable *Sha*:
In the phrase "one should write thus," the word **thus** means according to the sequence of the tradition received through the lineage. To explain: starting from the square located at the bottom-left of the central four squares, one should move clockwise around that central group of four, and then proceed similarly around the outer squares.

**Attained Me** means liberated <note>Sanskrit: *mukte*</note>. **Having made a circle** means having drawn a circular shape. **Otherwise** means being devoid of the ritual worship of the Teacher’s Circle. In the phrase "and so forth," the word "forth" <note>Sanskrit: *ādi*</note> is a technical shorthand indicating the prevention of all possible calamities. (31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36)

With the two verses beginning with "One, two..." and ending with "the Guru attains," the author teaches the period for **examining the student** based on their social class. In this context, **fitness** refers to the purity of the student’s conduct as previously described. (37, 38)

## In the Tantrarāja with the Commentary named Manoramā

The various types of **consecration** <term>Pratiṣṭhā</term> <note>The ritual process of "establishing" or infusing life/power into a sacred object or person.</note> regarding the **Sacred Wheel** <term>Chakra</term>, the Goddess, and the disciple are now described. This should be performed by one who knows the essential truths and follows the established tradition. (39)

A wise man should have this performed during a "fixed" zodiac sign, when auspicious planets are present, at a favorable and virtuous **auspicious moment** <term>Muhūrta</term>, or during the Full Moon at an auspicious rising. (40)

On the day of the **coincidence of the three letters** <term>Akṣara-traya-sampāta</term> <note>A complex calculation involving the astrological alignment of specific syllables associated with the day, the lunar deity (Nitya), and the hour.</note>, or during the three "full" days, or during the five sacred junctions previously mentioned, or whenever there is an auspicious rising. (41)

One whose soul is perfected <gloss>(1) A variant reading suggests "a pure soul."</gloss> should perform the consecration, and not another who is merely arrogant in his knowledge <gloss>(2) A variant reading suggests "one devoid of knowledge."</gloss>. If one performs it out of delusion or greed without the permission of the Guru— (42)

He shall meet his end along with his wife and children and go to a place of suffering <note>original: *niraya*, often translated as hell or a state of spiritual bondage.</note>. Therefore, one should only practice this after receiving permission through the **Full Initiation** <term>Pūrṇābhiṣeka</term> <note>The highest level of consecration in this tradition, granting the student the authority to act as a teacher.</note>. (43)

First with honey, clarified butter, and milk, then with coconut water...

***

With the five verses beginning with "In the Chakra, the Goddess..." and ending with "one should practice," the author teaches the various methods of consecration. 

In that context: **In the Chakra** refers to the *Lalitā-chakra* (the Sri Chakra). **In the Goddess** refers to the physical image or statue of the Goddess. **Follows the tradition** means even if one knows the essential truths, they must be dedicated to the regular and occasional rites of worship. **Fixed** refers to the fixed signs of the zodiac. **Favorable** refers to the specific day and related factors. **Virtuous** is an adjective describing the *Muhūrta* (the chosen moment). 

Alternatively, if those conditions are not met: **Or** is used for emphasis. **During the Full Moon**—specifically when the **breath** <note>original: *shvāsa*. This refers to the yogic practice of timing rituals based on which nostril the breath is flowing through (Svara Yoga).</note> is in an auspicious state. In any other case, it should not be done. 

**On the day of the coincidence of the three letters**—this refers to the sequence of letters described in the twenty-fifth chapter, where one observes the meeting of the letters of the day, the *Nityā* deities, and the hours <gloss>(3) A variant reading is noted here regarding the calculation of the letters.</gloss>. **The three full days** refers to the 5th, 10th, and 15th lunar days. **The five sacred junctions** refers to the seven festivals mentioned previously, excluding two of them, thus leaving five. 

**Or whenever there is an auspicious rising**—this is another option. This means that if one ignores all the previously mentioned rules regarding the lunar day, the day of the week, the yoga, and the lunar mansion, one may perform the rite solely based on the auspicious state of one's own breath; this is a tradition followed by those who have attained spiritual perfection. 

**Perfected soul** means a knower of truth. **Delusion** means ignorance. **Greed** means the desire for wealth. **Place of suffering** means a state of distress. (39–43)

With the eight verses beginning with "With honey..." and ending with "equality of the future," the author teaches the consecration of the Sri Chakra and related matters.

->Having bathed [the Śrīcakra] with water and the "imperishable herbs" <note>original: *acarauṣadhaiḥ*</note> as previously described; (44)<-

->Having invoked and worshiped, and having established the deity in the Chakra at the [auspicious] moment, one should worship. One should worship them in sequence with the **Sacred Mantra** <term>Vidyā</term> arising from the time of attaining the Nityā-essentials <note>referring to the specific lunar goddesses or *Nityās* governing that specific time</note>; (45)<-

->While touching the **Sacred Wheel** <term>Śrīcakra</term> with the tips of the fingers, one should recite the mantra and also worship the Chakra. Having done this for three days, one should then adopt the daily ritual sequence; (46)<-

->With scents, flowers, fresh incense, lamps, food offerings, and **libations** <term>Tarpaṇa</term> <note>Ritual offerings of liquid, usually water or nectar, to satisfy the deities</note>, one should worship the Goddess (2) <gloss>A variant reading specifies "the Goddess" specifically</gloss> for three nights along with the male and female practitioners <term>Yogis and Yoginis</term>; (47)<-

->This is the sequence for the Consecration of the Goddess that brings about her Presence. One should then give the ritual fee <term>Dakṣiṇā</term> to the Guru, who is the visible Manifestation of Shiva himself; (48)<-

->Either one's entire possessions, or half of it, or half of that, according to his command. If not, how will the **transmission of power** <term>Śakti-saṅkrānti</term> <note>The vital spiritual moment where the Guru's energy passes to the disciple or the ritual object</note> happen for him? (49)<-

->[Giving] elephants, horses, buffaloes, rams, cattle, servants, and land; gold, ornaments, clothing, a house, or anything else desired. (50)<-

---

In this context, "with the mentioned imperishable herbs" refers to the fifty imperishable herbs mentioned in the twenty-fifth chapter. "With the mantra arising from the time of attaining the Nityā-essentials" refers to the specific mantra of the Nityā deity of the day, called forth according to the time as explained in the twenty-fifth chapter. "Them in sequence" refers to the twenty-one thousand seven hundred and twenty-six Nityā mantras mentioned in that chapter.

The word "also" <note>original: *api*</note> indicates a different order; it means one should either touch it while reciting, or recite after touching. The meaning is this: after the invocation, one should worship three times each with the daily Nityā mantra, the third section of the Root Mantra <note>the *Mūla-vidyā* or primary mantra of the tradition</note>, and the Root Mantra itself, and then perform the rest of the sequence with them. Or, having touched the Chakra, one should recite those specific time-Nityā mantras in the specified numbers. 

"With libations" <note>original: *tarpaṇaiḥ*</note> means with nectar-like substances that grant satisfaction. "This [is the sequence] for the Goddess" refers back to the previously mentioned sequence. "According to his command" means by the will of the Guru. In the phrase "or a house," the word "or" indicates an inclusion of all such items. "According to one's power" <note>implied in the commentary</note> means according to one's wealth. "Under his control" means that all of one's activities should be done only with his [the Guru's] permission. || 44 || 45 || 46 || 47 || 48 || 49 || 50 || 51 ||

## Chapter 2 | Description of Deities and Correspondences

->**Sacred Trees and Animal Forms**<-

The sacred trees are proclaimed in their specific order: the **Varala**, the **Sarala** <note>a type of pine tree</note>, the **Sarja** <note>the Sal tree</note>, and the **Bakula** <note>Spanish cherry</note>; likewise the **Panasa** <note>Jackfruit</note>, the **Arka** <note>Crown flower</note>, the **Shamī** <note>Sponge tree</note>, the **Kadamba**, the **Ābhūta**, the **Nimba** <note>Neem</note>, the **Atima**, and the **Madhūka** <note>the Butter tree, used for its oil and flowers</note>. 

Next, the animal forms <term>Yonis</term> associated with the lunar mansions are listed: the **Horse**, the **Elephant in rut**, the **Goat**, the **Serpent**, the **Female Serpent**, and the **Cat**. Then the **Goat-faced**, the **Cat-faced**, the **Mouse**, the **Bull**, and the **She-buffalo**. Then the **Tiger**, the **Buffalo**, the **Tigress**, the **Deer**, the **Bitch**, and the **Monkey**. Finally, the **Cow**, the **Donkey**, the **Ram**, the **Monkey**, the **Woman**, the **Mare**, the **Goat**, and the **Female Elephant**. 

When suffering from diseases or other miseries arises, the wise practitioner <note>original: *Dhi*</note> should perform rituals for peace <term>Shanti</term> by doubling the count of the specific auspicious hours <term>Muhurta</term> as previously instructed for his disciples.

### The Internal Centers of Meditation

One should contemplate the following number of mystical diagrams <term>Yantras</term> within the energy centers of the body:
*   In the **Root Center** <term>Ādhāra</term>: Five circles <term>Chakras</term>.
*   In the **Self-supported Center** <term>Svādhiṣṭhāna</term>: Four circles.
*   In the **City of Jewels** <term>Maṇipūraka</term>: The same number as the previous two combined <note>Nine circles</note>.
*   In the **Unstruck Center** <term>Anāhata</term>: One should contemplate five mystical diagrams.
*   In the **Pure Center** <term>Viśuddha</term>: Four diagrams.
*   In the **Command Center** <term>Ājñā</term>: Five diagrams, in that sequence.

On the days corresponding to the lunar calendar, one should contemplate the Auspicious Goddess **Shodashi** <note>The "Sixteen-Year-Old" Goddess, a primary deity in this system</note> in this manner. One should worship the Goddess residing in each specific center to attain all forms of prosperity. These centers should be visualized starting from the Root center through the application of Yoga. 

Indeed, one should never attempt to contemplate all of them everywhere at once. For those who are unable to perform these internal contemplations, they may perform the ritual outside of the specific diagrams by constructing the "Root Lotuses" as described and worshiping according to the rules.

In this way, one should worship the Auspicious Goddess residing in the circles on the specific lunar days and weekdays. By worshiping the Goddess, one obtains desired fruits within the stated timeframes. Ritual offerings <term>Bali</term> should also be given on those very days according to the established procedure. There are fifty couples <term>Mithunas</term> <note>Representing the union of Shiva and Shakti or vowel/consonant pairs</note> in the aforementioned primary and secondary circles. The Goddess remains the sovereign of all those residing in the centers during the dawn and dusk transitions <term>Sandhyā</term>.

With the six verses beginning with "It is said" and ending with "the sound," the author teaches the sequence for instructing a worthy disciple, an alternative method of instruction, and the duties of the disciple. 

In that context: **"Purified over many days"** refers to the purification performed over a long period to ascertain the stability of the disciple's faith, worship, and devotion. 

**"With pots"** means using nine, four, or even just one consecrated vessel. 

**"In the center"** refers to the middle of the three **Shri Chakras**. 

**"From his own heart"** <note>original: *svāntāt*</note> means from the teacher's <term>Deshika</term> own inner self. The specific ritual meaning of this section is not elaborated here because it is to be obtained directly from the mouth of the teacher at the time of the preceptor’s consecration <term>Acharya-Abhisheka</term>.

**"Whose soul is the Goddess and whose mind is fulfilled"** means visualizing his own form as the form of the Goddess and knowing his self to be identical with Her. This implies that the teacher, existing solely as the form of the deity, should provide instruction with a heart full of compassion, focused only on the benefit of the student, and seeing the instruction as the form of the entire universe. 

**"Oneness of the Deity, Teacher, Mantra, and Self"** refers to the essential identity of the Deity, the Teacher, and the Mantras with one's own self, in the manner described in the concluding verse of the fourth chapter. **"Moving..."**

## In the 2nd Chapter ] The Statement of the Authors of Consecration Tantras

Otherwise, the wandering power <term>Shakti</term> returns to the Teacher <term>Guru</term> without doubt.
Therefore, in his presence, one should perform worship and follow his commands. <note>The "wandering power" refers to the spiritual energy or attention of the disciple; if it is not properly anchored through the Guru, the connection to the lineage is lost.</note> (56)
Since the realization of one's own identity is obtained from the Teacher, who is the very soul of the mantra <term>Manvatman</term>,

one should perform acts of grace and other rituals for the sake of spiritual success <term>Siddhi</term>; otherwise, it will not be attained. (58)
Having constructed a ritual diagram <term>Chakra</term>, and placing a ceremonial pot <term>Kumbha</term> in its center within the central "womb" triangle <term>Yoni</term>,
filling it with water boiled with medicinal herbs <term>Kwathodaka</term>, one should recite the sacred mantra while performing the sprinkling ritual. (59)
For a powerful seeker who is devoted to the traditional conduct passed down through the lineage,
the second consecration should be performed for the satisfaction and success of the deity. (60)
Having created a vast ritual diagram <term>Chakra</term>, making sixteen small triangles within each "womb" triangle <term>Yoni</term>,
one should place the ceremonial pot in the center there. (61)

**Commentary:**
"Wandering" <note>original: *chanchala*</note> means fickle or moving. "Soul of the Mantra" <note>original: *manvatmanah*</note> is defined according to the method mentioned at the end of the fourth chapter. In the phrase "with wealth and so forth," the word "so forth" <note>original: *adi*</note> refers to houses, fields, and other such possessions. (52–57)

From "Then, the two-fold consecration..." until the verse ending in "should practice," these fifteen verses teach the two types of consecration for practitioners and the methods for performing them. Here, in the phrase "acts of grace etc.," the word "etc." refers to specific ritual applications <term>Prayoga</term>. 

"Having constructed a ritual diagram" refers to the worship diagram <term>Puja-yantra</term> described in the thirty-third chapter. "Water boiled with medicinal herbs" refers to water that was boiled with the milky barks of trees <term>Kshira-oshadhi</term> and then cooled. "Lineage" <note>original: *kramo*</note> refers to the daily traditional practice. 

"Second" refers to the **Full Consecration** <term>Purna-abhisheka</term>. "A vast ritual diagram" refers to the previously mentioned ritual wheel of the Goddess Lalita, constructed to a size suitable for placing the ceremonial pot, as will be described later. We will explain its exact proportions in that section. "Making sixteen triangles in each womb" means that within each triangle, one should draw nine horizontal lines according to tradition, following the proportions that will be described in the thirty-third chapter. By this, sixteen triangles are formed...

# Chapter 2 ] Description of the Method of Consecration. 33

On the day of one's birth star, having risen early in the morning, one should worship their own <term>Nityā</term> <note>original: "Nityā"; one of the fifteen eternal lunar goddesses who represent the phases of the moon and aspects of time</note> deity. One should then recite the mantra a thousand times and perform the <term>Homa</term> <note>Fire sacrifice</note> ritual in all directions. (67)

With the sounds of horns, the <term>Kāhala</term> <note>A large, straight trumpet used in temple rituals</note>, conch shells, and other instruments, accompanied by music and dancing, and amidst the joyous bands of yoginis who each embody the deity... (68)

...the Guru himself should personally perform the consecration, accompanied by those who have been purified through the sacred circles. From that moment on, the Guru should explain the <term>Krama</term> <note>The "sequence" or specific oral lineage of the mantra and practice</note> to the disciple. (69)

The disciple should then carry out the ritual cycle without interruption for the duration of his renown. Along with the consecration, he should recite the sacred knowledge (<term>Vidyā</term>) a thousand times. (70)

Alternatively, one may arrange ninety-six jars in that place. Having summoned the <term>Shaktis</term> <note>Divine feminine energies or powers</note> into them and worshipped them, one should perform the consecration. (71)

Or, one may perform the consecration on the birthday using just a single jar. In this way, one should regularly perform both the daily and the occasional rites without interruption. (72)

---

Having drawn three triangles at the three corners of the "All-Auspicious Triangle" (<term>Sarvamaṅgalā-trikoṇa</term>) using three slanted lines, and having made sixteen sub-triangles within them, one draws a circle in the space between them. In the center of that, one should draw sixteen <term>Yoni-Vajras</term> <note>original: "yoni-ṣoḍaśa-vajra-garbhāṇi"; "womb-thunderbolt" shapes representing the union of creative power and indestructible reality</note> shaped like thunderbolts, facing one another. 

The mantras for the <term>Nityā</term> goddesses, who are the nature of Time, will be described in the twenty-fifth chapter; these are the mantras for the deity of that specific day. 

The meaning of the text is as follows: In all consecrations, on the preceding day, one should perform the preparatory rite of "indwelling" (<term>Adhivāsana</term>), and on the next day, the consecration. Or, one may perform the preparation and the consecration together immediately. 

"On the birth star" (<term>Janmarkṣe</term>)—this means the "Full Consecration" (*Pūrṇābhiṣeka*) should be performed on the disciple's birthday. "One should perform the <term>Homa</term>"—this refers to the sequence described for the daily fire sacrifice. "In all directions" (*Samantataḥ*) connects to the following instructions. 

"By the circles" (*Vṛttaiḥ*)—this refers to those who have been previously empowered by the deity's presence. "His own Krama" (*Sva-krama*)—this refers to the specific order of the letters of the mantra. "Uninterrupted cycle" (*Avicchinna-paryāyam*)—the word <term>Paryāya</term> <note>Cycle</note> here refers to a period of thirty-six days. 

The meaning is this: If the cycle is broken without the Guru's permission, a penance is prescribed, consisting of the consecration ceremony accompanied by a thousand recitations. For every day that was missed, one must perform sixty <term>Ghaṭikās</term> <note>A unit of time approximately 24 minutes long; 60 Ghaṭikās constitute a full 24-hour day</note> of recitation during the three junctions of the day (dawn, noon, and dusk)...

# Chapter 2 ] Description of the Method of Consecration. 34
### Commentary titled "Manoramā" on the Tantrarāja

->By means of the Masters, the Principles, and the Eternal Lunar Divinities, and through the Knowledge of the <term>Kālanityā</term> <note>original: "Kālanityā"; the "Eternals of Time," specifically the fifteen goddesses representing the phases of the moon</note>...<-
->...at the base Foundation, the Heart, the Head, the Mouth, the Sun, and the Moon. (73)<-
->Meditating during the three junctions of the day, one should chant the vowels and the groups of consonants.<-
->One should perform the placement of the "Mothers" <note>the Sanskrit alphabet sounds</note> at their specific sites for the perfection of the divine body. (74)<-
->When the planets are in unfavorable alignment, on the day of one's birth star, or during an eclipse of both the Sun and Moon...<-
->...on the New Moon, or when suffering from the troubles caused by enemies, one should perform the divine consecration. (75)<-
->By the power of that rite, no faults ever touch him.<-
->Small malicious acts, cruel deeds, and magical sorceries devised by enemies are neutralized. (76)<-

***

Having performed the atonement a hundred times, one should worship starting from that day. In that context—this applies only to the <term>Śrīcakra</term> <note>The "Great Wheel," a complex sacred geometric diagram representing the cosmos and the goddess</note>. 

The option of using "one jar" <note>mentioned in the previous page's final verse</note> is intended for those seeking specific desires. (58–72)

With the verses starting with "By means of the Masters..." and ending with "...perfection of the body," the text teaches the worship during the three junctions of the day (<term>Sandhyā</term>) and the specific placements (<term>Nyāsa</term>) for fulfilling desires. This is what is meant: 

1. **Morning Junction:** Because the knowledge of the Self begins with the Guru, one worships the **Masters** (<term>Nāthas</term>).
2. **Midday Junction:** Because the entire universe exists in the form of the thirty-six principles, one worships the **Principles** (<term>Tattvas</term>).
3. **Evening Junction:** By reflecting on the form of the Eternal Lunar Knowledge, which represents completeness, one performs the worship of the **Eternals** (<term>Nityās</term>).

The meaning of "all groups of consonants and vowels" will be explained in the twenty-fifth chapter, so it is not elaborated upon here. Regarding "placement at the sites of the Mothers"—one should place the <term>Śrīvidyā</term> <note>The sacred mantra of the Goddess</note> along with the specific <term>Nityā</term> of that day at all the locations of the "Mother-letter" placements, which will be described in the fifteenth chapter. This is the traditional instruction. (73–74)

With the five verses starting with "When the planets..." and ending with "...the consecration," the text teaches the specific times for the consecration (<term>Abhiṣeka</term>) and its power. "Eclipse of both" refers to the Sun and the Moon. "Small acts" refers to magical rites meant to cause hatred or to drive someone away. "Troubles" refers to spiritual, divine, or physical sufferings. "The end of all sorrow" refers to the ending of the sorrow caused by the "constriction of the heart" <note>a technical term for the soul's limited state before liberation</note>. (75–79)

# Chapter 2 ] Description of the Materials and Construction of the Guru’s Mandala. 35

"O Supreme Lord, how does the power of that consecration arise? Tell me of that power by which all afflictions are destroyed without remainder. (77)"

"Through water that takes the form of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire, the mere touch of it destroys all defects without remainder; therefore, there is nothing equal to consecration. (78)"
<note>In this tradition, ritual water is mentally transformed into a synthesis of three cosmic energies: the Moon (cooling/nurturing), the Sun (illuminating), and Fire (purifying).</note>

"The nature of water as the Moon, Sun, and Fire has been proclaimed above. Therefore, for the calming of all sorrows and pains, one should perform this sacred sprinkling. (79)"

"During the seven sacred holidays <note>original: "parvas"; specific junctions in the lunar calendar</note>, or at other auspicious times with great care, or even every year, one should perform the worship of the Guru with ritual offerings. (80)"

"When natural portents <note>original: "utpāta"; refers to ominous events like earthquakes or comets</note> arise, one should worship using 'flowers of heaven' <note>likely high-quality or rare ritual flowers</note>. Once consecrated according to the traditional rules, the seeker should provide an offering to the Guru. (81)"

"To the Guru, to those who received knowledge before him, to his younger spiritual brothers, to the Guru's Guru, and to his Guru—honoring those from whom one has gained knowledge... (82)"

"...through prostrations, worship, hymns of praise, and acts of service, one should satisfy them. Otherwise, one's own spiritual power will flow back to them. (83)"
<note>This warns that failing to honor the lineage causes the merit of one's practice to return to the source rather than staying with the student.</note>

"With pastes made of camphor, sandalwood, saffron, and fine musk mixed together, one should everywhere construct the sacred circle <term>Mandala</term> of the Guru. (84)"

***

### The "Manoramā" Commentary

With the four verses beginning with "During the seven..." (Verse 80) and ending with "...to them" (Verse 83), the text instructs on the worship of the Guru and related matters. In that context, in the phrase "or even every year" (80), the word "even" (*eva*) is used to emphasize that this is a mandatory duty, while the word "or" (*vā*) indicates this is the "lowest" or minimum option for a practitioner.

Worshiping every month with wealth and offerings is the "medium" path. Worshiping with wealth and devotion during the seven sacred holidays and other holy times is the "highest" path.

Regarding "natural portents" (81): these refer to the three types of disturbances—divine (astrological), atmospheric (weather-based), and terrestrial (earthquakes). 

"Attendance" <note>original: "upāsana"</note> refers to the "following with one's mind" or mental devotion. "One's own" (83) refers to the power residing in the disciple. "Flowing back to them" means the power returns to the Guru.

With the two verses beginning with "Camphor..." (84) and ending with "...O Supreme Goddess" (85), the text instructs on the materials for constructing the Guru's Mandala. In this context:
- "Moon" (*Candra*) refers to camphor.
- "Light" (*Laghu*) refers to eaglewood <note>original: "aguru"; a fragrant wood used in incense</note>.

In the section beginning with "On the forehead..." (85), the text describes things that must be worn. "Everywhere" means it brings success in all circumstances.

# 36 THE TANTRARAJA WITH THE COMMENTARY CALLED MANORAMA

->After the worship, having wiped the ritual remnants, one should place that offering on the chest and the two shoulders;<-
->the Supreme Goddess shall then provide prosperity in every way. (85)<-
->In the previously mentioned Mandalas <note>sacred geometric diagrams</note>, in all those places where worship was prescribed,<-
->one should visualize all of them as lotuses. (1) (86)<-
->At the beginning and end of the worship, one should then recite five verses.<-
->Having attained the state of being one with the Goddess from the Guru, one should recite the twelve verses. (87)<-
->I bow to the Goddess who takes the form of Ganesha, the Planets, the Stars, the Yoginis, and the Zodiac signs;<-
->who is composed of Mantra, the Mother of the world, and the form of the sacred seats. (88)<-
->I bow to the Great Goddess, the Mother of the alphabet, the Supreme Sovereign,<-
->who brings an end to the restless, swirling agitation of the currents of Time. (89)<-

---

Through the verse beginning with "Previously mentioned," the author teaches the specific rules for the Guru-Mandala <note>the sacred circle dedicated to the lineage of teachers</note> described earlier. This is what is meant: Having correctly constructed an eight-petaled lotus with a central pericarp <note>the seed-head of the lotus</note> within a grid of nine-by-nine squares, one should write the letters of the names [of the Gurus] in sequential order. We shall clearly explain its measurements and the method of construction in the Chapter on Yantras <note>the *Yantra-patala*</note>. (86)

Through the verse beginning with "At the beginning," the author teaches the timing for reciting the two hymns of praise for the Master <note>the Guru</note> and the Deity. In that context, the phrase "having attained... from the Guru" means having understood the ultimate truth that the Master truly appears in the form of the Deity. (87)

Henceforth, regarding the twelve verses of the hymn to the Goddess: since they have already been explained by the Great Souls of Kashmir in the *Nitya-shodasharnava* <note>The 'Ocean of the Sixteen Nityas', a foundational scripture of this tradition</note>, that same explanation of those twelve verses is written here:

**Ganesha**, etc.: Ganesha is Vinayaka <note>the elephant-headed remover of obstacles</note>. He is described here as having the nature of Time. **Planets**: The Sun and the others. **Stars**: Ashvini and the other lunar mansions. Their mantras and names will be discussed later. **Yoginis**: Vashini and the other attendant deities. **Zodiac signs**: Aries and the others. **In the form of**: Because She is the ultimate cause of all these. **Goddess**: This refers to the act of worship. **Composed of Mantra**: Because She consists of the letters of the alphabet. **I bow**: The act of bowing signifies the realization of oneness between the worshiper and the Goddess. **Mother** <note>original: "Matrika"</note>: She is the Mother-power who gives birth to the entire universe. **The form of the sacred seats**: This means She is the foundation of everything through the modes mentioned above. 

This is what is meant: when the meditative feeling—that the entire collection of sounds and the progression of Time are identical to one's own Self—becomes stable, that is <term>Jivanmukti: the state of being spiritually liberated while still alive</term>. 

**I bow**: [To the one] who brings an end to the restless, swirling agitation of the currents of Time—of Time...
