<meta>This page continues the fourth chapter of the Tantrarāja Tantra, specifically focusing on the construction of the fifth and sixth mantras associated with ritual "seats" (āsanas) and the seventh mantra used for the "invitation" (āvāhana) of the goddess into the ritual space.</meta>

# [ Tantrarāja Tantra ]
## [ Chapter Four ]
### Accompanied by the Manoramā Commentary

->Then "water," joined with "juice," and that combined with "chara" and its own;<-
->That which stands between it and the Power is declared the sixth. (10)<-
->One should offer the "Seat of Accomplishment for Seekers" by worshipping the Goddess with that [mantra].<-
->With the seventh, one should perform the "Invitation" using the "three-fold" gesture and the word of obeisance. (11)<-

**Hsr... Klīṃ Hsauḥ...** <note>These are "Bīja" or seed-syllables, condensed phonetic sounds used in meditation</note> is the fifth, the knowledge of the **Seat of All Mantras** <note>original: "sarvamantrāsana-vidyā"</note>. "Seat of All Mantras" refers to the description of the **Śrī Cakra** <note>The sacred geometric diagram of the Goddess</note>. Since it is composed of the Mother-letters <note>The Sanskrit alphabet</note> beginning with A, Ka, Tha, and so on, and because the lines of the triangle will be described later, the meaning is that this is the place where all mantras are found. (9)

With the half-verse starting with "Then" and ending with "worship," the author teaches the knowledge of the **Seat of Accomplishment for Seekers** <note>original: "sādhya-siddhāsana-vidyā"</note>. There, "water" refers to the letter **Va**. The word "and" is for addition. "Juice" refers to the letter **La**. "Chara" refers to the letter **E**. "Its own" refers to the **Bindu** <note>The nasalized dot or "m" sound that completes a seed-syllable</note>; it is joined with those two. The word "and" is for addition. The word "that" refers to the specific form. 

This is what is meant: joined with the letters Va, La, and the Bindu, the compound syllable **Vlṛm** <note>The text specifies "Vlṛm" though the phonetic components described usually form "Vleṃ"</note> is formed. "That which stands between it and the Power is declared the sixth"—"that" refers to the spoken syllable **Vlṛm**. "Power" refers to the syllable **Hsrīṃ**. "Standing between" means placed in the middle of these two. 

This is what is meant: for the goddess **Bālā** <note>A young form of the Supreme Goddess Tripurasundarī</note>, there are three seed-syllables. They should begin with **Hrīṃ** and end with **Vlṛṃ**. The form is: **Hrīṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ Vlṛṃ**. This form of Bālā is the knowledge of the **Seat of Accomplishment for Seekers**. (10)

Regarding the "Seat of Accomplishment for Seekers": it means the place where all desired accomplishments <term>siddhis</term> of the seekers <term>sādhyas</term> are found, the realization of the indivisible nature <note>Footnote 1: A variant reading in some manuscripts is "Through the realization of accomplishment" (vimarśāt siddheriti)</note>. Here, the phrase "by worship of the Goddess" applies to all four seats. The method of applying the mantras for these four seats will be explained in the fifth chapter.

With the verse and a half starting with "Seventh" and ending with "is declared," he teaches the seventh, the **Knowledge of the Invitation** <note>original: "āvāhana-vidyā"</note>. There, "with the seventh"—"knowledge" is implied. "With obeisance"—joined with the word *Namaḥ* (salutation). "With the three-fold"—"gesture" <term>mudrā</term> is implied. Although it will be described later, the author calls it "excellent" everywhere. 

"Joined with the 'Heart and Vehicle of Haṃsa,' that is considered the seventh"—the meaning is: the **Kulasundarī** mantra joined with the letters Ha, Sa, and Ra in each of the three seed-syllables is the Invitation Mantra. "But in the middle, the connection of fire..."—this means one should join Ha and Sa before the middle seed-syllable and place Ra after the consonant La. Thus, with Ha, Sa, Ka, La, Ra, Ī, and the Bindu, the middle seed-syllable is formed, ending in the **Māyā** seed <note>The syllable Hrīṃ</note>. In the other...

<meta>This page continues the fourth chapter of the Tantrarāja Tantra, transitioning from the mantras for ritual seats to the specific phonetic construction of the mantras for the attendant goddesses (Śaktis) of the Śrī Cakra, such as Vaśinī and Kāmeśvarī.</meta>

# [ Tantrarāja Tantra ]
## [ Chapter Four ]
### Description of the Knowledge of Lalitā, Vaśinī, Kāmeśvarī, Mohinī, and Vimalā

->Joined with the "Swan," the "Heart," and "Burning," that indeed is considered the seventh.<-
->The union with "Burning" occurs in the middle, and by the "Wind" at the end of the consonant. (12)<-

->The "Sky" with "Burning," "Fire," and "Power" at the beginning, shall be itself.<-
->Beginning with those, one should recite the names of all the Powers stationed in the Circle by their names. (13)<-

->By "Burning," "Earth," "Juice," "Stone," and "Self," the seed-syllable of Vaśinī is uttered.<-
->Joined with "Breath," "Juice," and "Power," is the great syllable of Kāmeśvarī. (14)<-

->From the union of "Void," "Water," "Juice," and "Fire," comes the mantra of Mohinī.<-
->The "Pervasive" joined with "Juice," "Stone," and "Voice" is declared the seed-syllable of Vimalā. (15)<-

->By the union of "Jya," "Space," "Fire," "Burning," and "Self," is the mantra of Aruṇā.<-

The meaning is that one should place the letter **Repha** <note>The "R" sound, often called "Burning" or "Fire" in tantric code</note> between the letter **Sa** and the vowel. By using the letters **Ha**, **Sa**, **Ra**, **Au**, and the **Visarga** <note>The aspiration sound written as two dots</note>, the final seed-syllable ending in **Māyā** is formed: **Hsrauḥ, Hsklūṃ, Hstraiḥ Namah**. (12)

With the verse beginning "The Sky," the author teaches the two seed-syllables which serve as the "Pranava" <note>A foundational or primordial sound, like Om</note> for the worship-mantras of the Powers <note>The Śaktis or attendant goddesses</note> stationed within the **Śrī Cakra** <note>The supreme sacred geometric diagram of the Goddess Lalitā</note>.

In that context:
**Sky** <note>original: "Viyat"</note> refers to the letter **Sa**.
**With Burning, Fire, and the Dot** <note>original: "sadāha-vahni-sra"</note> refers to the letters **Ra** and **Ī** along with the **Bindu** <note>The nasalized dot representing the union of Shiva and Shakti</note>, forming **Śrīṃ**.
**Power at the beginning** <note>original: "śaktyādyaṃ"</note> refers to the syllable **Hlṛkhkhā**.
This is what is meant: One should worship all the Powers using their respective worship-names and mantras, preceded by the seed-syllables **Hlṛkhkhā** and **Śrīṃ**. (13)

With the verse beginning "Burning, Earth," the author teaches the <term>Kūṭākṣara</term> <note>A "peak" or "complex" syllable formed by stacking multiple consonants</note> formulas for **Vaśinī** and **Kāmeśvarī**.

**Burning, Earth, Juice, Stone, and Self** <note>original: "dāha-bhūmī-rasā-cmā-svaiḥ"</note> refers to the letters **Ra, Va, La, Ū**, and the **Bindu**, forming the syllable **Vlūṃ**.
**Joined with Breath, Juice, and Power:**
**Breath** <note>original: "Prāṇa"</note> refers to the letter **Ka**.
**Juice** <note>original: "Rasā"</note> refers to the letter **La**.
**Power** <note>original: "Śakti"</note> refers to **Hlṛkhkhā**.
Joined together, the complex syllable formed by **Ka, La,** and **Hlṛkhkhā** is **Klṛhlūṃ**. (14)

With the verse beginning "Void," the author teaches the two complex-syllable formulas for **Mohinī** and **Vimalā**.
There, **Void** <note>original: "Śūnya"</note> refers to the letter **Na**.
**From the union of Water, Juice, and Fire** refers to the union of **Va, La, Ī**, and the **Bindu**; thus, the syllable is **Nlūṃ**.
**Pervasive** <note>original: "Vyāpta"</note> refers to the letter **Ya**.
**Joined with Juice, Stone, and Voice** refers to its union with **La, U**, and the **Bindu**, forming the syllable **Ylūṃ**. (15)

With the first half of the verse beginning "Jya, Space," the author teaches the complex-syllable formula for **Aruṇā**.

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for constructing the seed-syllables (bījas) of the Eight Speech-Deities (Vāg-devatās) within the Śrī Cakra. # Tantrarāja Tantra
## Chapter Four
### The Mantras of the Speech-Deities

->The "Swan" joined with the "Heart," "Juice," and "Water," pervaded by "Earth" and "Space," is the mantra.<-
->It is specified for Jayinī, providing victory in all places.<-
->In debates, legal disputes, and certainly in battles. (16-17)<-
->The letter "Ka" joined with "Space" and "Burning," pervaded by "Earth" and "Space," is the mantra<-
->Declared as Sarveśvarī, the one who always grants all success. (18)<-
->The "Swallower" joined with "Space," "Burning," "Fire," and "Self," is the mantra of Kaulinī.<-
->With these eight mantras, joined with the Powers and their phonetic classes,<-
->Ending with the Speech-Deities, a ritual placement is performed by which one becomes the Goddess herself.<-
->Even a mortal is then worshipped by all the gods, everywhere and at all times. (19-20)<-

---

In that context, the syllable for **Aruṇā** <note>Mentioned at the end of the previous page</note> is formed by the union of "Jya" with "Space," "Burning," "Fire," and "Self"—by the sequential combination of the letters **Ja**, **Ma**, **Ra**, **Ī**, and the **Bindu** <note>The nasal 'm' sound represented by a dot</note>, it becomes **Jmrī**. (16)

With the verse beginning "The Swan" and ending with "certainly," the author teaches the secret syllable-cluster <term>Kūṭākṣara; a complex, multi-consonant syllable used in tantric practice</term> for **Jayinī** and its power. 

There, "Swan" <note>original: "haṃsa"</note> refers to the letter **Ha**. "Joined with the heart, juice, and water" refers to being combined with the letters **Sa**, **La**, and **Va**. "Pervaded by earth and space" means joined with the letters **Ya**, **U**, and the **Bindu**. The result is this: the cluster formed by **Ha**, **Sa**, **La**, **Va**, **Ya**, **U**, and **Bindu** is **Hsrlvūṃ**. (17)

With the verse beginning "The letter Ka" and ending with "always," the author teaches the secret syllable-cluster for **Sarveśvarī** and its influence. 

There, "Ka" refers to the letter **La** <note>In the secret code of this lineage, 'Ka' can represent 'La'</note>. "Joined with space and burning" means joined with **Ma** and **Ra**. "Pervaded by earth and space" means joined with **Ya**, **U**, and the **Bindu**. The result is this: by the letters **La**, **Ma**, **Ra**, **Ya**, **U**, and **Bindu**, it is **Lmryūṃ**. (18) <margin>Other manuscripts read this as **Rmryūṃ** or **Imryūṃ**</margin>

With the first half of the verse beginning "The Swallower," he teaches the secret syllable-cluster for **Kaulinī**. 

There, "Swallower" <note>original: "grāsa"</note> refers to the letter **Kṣa**. "Space, burning, fire, and self" refers to the letters **Ma**, **Ra**, **Ī**, and the **Bindu**. This forms **Kṣmrī**. 

With the verse beginning "With these" and ending with "always," he teaches the sequence of ritual placement <term>Nyāsa; the practice of mentally "touching" or installing mantras into specific parts of the body to divinize the practitioner</term> for the goddesses beginning with Vaśinī, and the results thereof. 

There, "with the eight mantras" refers to the secret syllable-clusters just described. "With the Powers" refers to—

# Tantrarāja Tantra
## Chapter Four
### The Locations for Placement and the Mantras

-> One should perform the ritual placement at the crown-aperture, the forehead, the third-eye center, <-
-> the throat, the heart, the navel, the root-base, and on both feet from the base to the tips. (21) <-
-> "Go" joined with "Burning," "Wind," and "Self" is the first; the second is the same in reverse. <-
-> "Wind," "Foot," "Breath," and "Juice" joined with "Foot" and "Self" is the third. (22) <-
-> "Earth" joined with "Juice," "Earth," and "Space" is the fourth, followed by the "Power" and the "Heart." <-
-> With "Breath," "Burning," "Earth," and "Self"—the next is the seventh. (23) <-
-> The "Swan" with the "Heart" and "Lustre," and the two joined with "Burning," "Moving," and "Self." <-
-> The eighth is declared to be the "Swan," "Heart," "Breath," "Wind," and "Self." (24) <-
-> "Pure" joined with "Self"—likewise the ninth is proclaimed. <-
-> These nine single-syllable mantras, O Great Goddess, are the forms of the Ritual Seals (Mudrās). (25) <-

This refers to the previously mentioned eight Powers, beginning with Vaśinī <note>The "Subduer," the first of the eight Speech-Deities</note>, being joined with the remaining elements. The phrase **joined with the phonetic classes** means that each is joined with the groups of letters beginning with A, Ka, Ca, Ṭa, Ta, Pa, Ya, and Śa, ending with the name of the Speech-Deity. **The Speech-Deity** implies the ritual placement ends with the four-syllable name. **Consisting of the Goddess** means the body of the deity; because the deities are composed of letters, they possess a physical form.

The meaning is as follows: one should pronounce the sixteen vowels beginning with **A** and ending with the **Visarga** <note>the 'ḥ' sound</note>, each with a nasal dot (bindu), and then over that, pronounce the cluster-syllable <term>Kūṭākṣara; a complex, multi-consonant seed-syllable</term> **lhṛṃ**. Then, while saying "Salutations to the Speech-Deity Vaśinī," one should perform the placement. In the same way, one should perform the placement of the other mantras, ending with the class-seed, the name of the Speech-Deity, and "salutations" <note>original: "namas"</note>, thereby creating the aforementioned forms. The addition of the word "salutations" is specified here because of the rule stated previously that "in the subsequent worship, the word 'salutations' is used." (20)

With the verse beginning with **at the aperture**, the author teaches the locations for the ritual placement of the mantras of the eight Powers, Vaśinī and the others. In that context, **at the aperture** means the <term>Brahma-randhra; the "Aperture of Brahma" located at the top of the head</term>. **In the Ājñā** means in the middle of the eyebrows <note>the third-eye center</note>. **From the base to the tips** means that while reciting the mantra, one should stroke with both palms starting from the base of the feet up to the tips. After that, one should perform the **Pervasive Placement** <term>Vyāpaka-nyāsa; a ritual where the mantra is "spread" over the entire body</term> three times using both hands: with the first section of the Root-Knowledge <note>the Mūla-vidyā or primary mantra of the goddess</note> from the head to the heart, with the second section from the heart to the toes, and with the third section from the toes back to the heart, following the process shown by the teacher, ending at the hem of the garment. The inner contemplation <note>original: "vāsanā"</note> of this should be understood only from the mouth of a Guru. (21)

With the four verses beginning with **Go** and ending with **Great Goddess**, the author teaches in sequence the nine seed-mantras of the nine Ritual Seals (Mudrās). In that context, **Go** refers to the letter **Da**. **Burning, Wind, and Self** refer to the letters **Ra**, **A**, and the nasal dot (bindu). <note>Decoding the first bīja as "Draṃ"</note>

<margin>(2) Variant reading: "by the names of the Powers."</margin>

# Manoramā Commentary on the Tantrarāja Tantra
## Page 70

-> O Goddess! Hear now the Arrow-syllables that bestow good fortune. <-
-> Pervasion, Burning, Juice, Earth, and the Heart-Wind, each joined with the Self. (26) <-
-> The Mudrā-syllables are first; the Arrows are all-arousing. <-
-> Known as the Śākta <note>relating to the Goddess or Power</note> and Śaiva <note>relating to Śiva</note> arrows, they are spoken of in two sets of five. (27) <-
-> When Fire and Water are joined with the Self, they form the two Bow-syllables which enchant all. <-

**Drīṁ**: This is the "other"—the second. By reversing "Wind" and "Fire," the mantra **Drīṁ** is formed. The meaning is this: one should replace the "A" sound of the previous seed-syllable with the "Ī" sound. **With Breath, Juice, Foot, and the Self**: these are the letters *Ka*, *La*, *Ī*, and the *Bindu* <note>original: "vinda," the nasal dot representing consciousness</note>, forming **Klīṁ**. (22)

**On Earth**: the letter *Va*. **Joined with Juice, Earth, and the Self**: the letters *La*, *Ū*, and the *Bindu*, forming **Blūṁ**. **The Power-Heart**: the letter *Sa* joined with the *Visarga* <note>original: "visarjanīya," the two dots indicating a voiced breath</note>. This is the fifth syllable: **Saḥ**.

**With Breath**: the letter *Ka*. **With Burning-Earth**: the letter *Ra*, joined with the *O* sound and the *Bindu*. This is the sixth: **Krauṁ**. (23)

**The Swan with the Heart, Lustre, and Radiance, joined with Burning-Moving and the Self**: "The Swan" is the letter *Ha*. "The Heart" is *Sa*. "Lustre" is *Kha*. "Radiance" is *Pha*. "Joined with Burning-Moving and the Self" means these are joined with the letter *Ra*, the *E* sound, and the *Bindu*. The result is this: the letters *Ha*, *Sa*, *Kha*, *Pha*, and *Ra* are joined with *E* and the *Bindu* to form a complex conjoined syllable <term>Kūṭa-akṣara</term>, which is the seventh mantra: **Hskhphreṁ**. (24)

The eighth mantra is formed of the **Swan, Heart, Breath, Wind, and the Self**: the letters *Ha*, *Sa*, and the *Au* sound with the *Bindu*, forming **Hsauḥ**. (25)

**Pure joined with the Self**: the syllable **Aiṁ**. **Forms of the Seals**: the Ritual Seals <term>Mudrās</term> possess a triple nature—Gross, Subtle, and Supreme. The physical gestures are the "Gross" form; the syllables themselves are the "Subtle" form; and the inner meditative state <note>original: "vāsanā," the mental impression</note> is the "Supreme" form. (25)

With the two verses beginning with **Arrow-syllables** and ending with **spoken of**, the text teaches the ten varieties of Arrow-syllables and their two-fold nature.

Therein: **Pervasion, Burning, Juice, Earth, and the Heart-Wind, each joined with the Self**: the letters *Ya*, *Ra*, *La*, *Va*, and *Sa*, each joined with the long *Ā* sound and the *Bindu*, form the five Arrow-syllables of Power <note>Śakti</note>: **Yāṁ, Rāṁ, Lāṁ, Vāṁ, Sāṁ**. These are also the five Mudrā-syllables.

**The Mudrā-syllables mentioned first**: these are the five syllables **Drāṁ, Drīṁ, Klīṁ, Blūṁ, Saḥ**. These are the "All-Arousing" arrows of Śiva, who takes the form of Desire <term>Kāmatanu</term>, and they bring all women under one's influence. The two-fold nature of these arrows—Gross and Subtle—will be explained in the fifth chapter. (26-27)

# Manoramā Commentary on the Tantrarāja Tantra
## Page 71

### Chapter 4: On the Formation of Letter-Gestures and Named-Gestures

-> Joined with the "Swan-goers" and situated in the "Burning Fire," along with the "Self" and the "Wind." (28) <-
-> These are declared as the two Noose-syllables which subjugate all. A single syllable for the Goad-gesture paralyzes all; it is the sixth. (29) <-
-> Invocation, Establishing, Restraint, Veiling, and the gesture known as Placement Near; then the Weapon-gesture and the Salutation. (30) <-
-> Agitation, Liquefaction, Attraction, Subjugation, Intoxication, and the Great Goad; the Space-Moving, the Seed, the Source, and the Raising of Power. (31) <-
-> These twenty gestures are declared; now hear their formation. By performing these correctly, the mantras are mastered through effort. (32) <-
-> Placing the hands in a prayer position, cross the two ring fingers. When their nails are grasped by the index fingers, it becomes the "Triple-Section" gesture, which brings forth the Goddess Lalitā. (33) <-

---

**The Commentary:**

Regarding the letters *Ya* and *Dha* joined together with the *Bindu* <note>original: "vinda," the nasal dot of resonance</note>: these form **Yaṁ** and **Dhaṁ**, which are the two "Bow-syllables" of the Divine Couple (Śiva and Śakti). The author will explain the specific "Bow" syllables further in the fifth chapter.

With the verses beginning with **"Joined with the Swan..."** and ending with **"...the two Noose-syllables,"** the text teaches the two syllables for the Nooses. Here, **"Swan-goers situated in the Burning Fire with the Self"** refers to the syllable **Hrīṁ**. <note>original: "hrīṁ"; derived from H (Swan), R (Fire), and Ī (Self/Shakti) with the nasal resonance</note>. **"With the Self and Wind"** refers to **Āṁ**. These are the two Noose-syllables for both deities, as mentioned previously.

The second half of the verse, beginning with **"A single syllable for the Goad,"** describes the Goad-syllable common to both. In this context, the "Sixth Gesture" syllable is **Krauṁ**. (28-29)

In the three verses starting with **"Invocation"** and ending with **"through effort,"** the names of the twenty gestures to be formed are taught. Among them, **"Placement Near"** <note>original: "sannidhāpana"</note> is the name of a specific gesture. By the word **"Weapon"** <note>original: "heti"</note>, the Arrow, Bow, Noose, and Goad gestures are meant; thus, this single term represents four distinct mudrās. (30-32)

The verse starting with **"Placing the hands..."** teaches the method for forming the **Triple-Section** gesture <note>term: "Trikhaṇḍā mudrā"; a major ritual gesture in Shakta traditions symbolizing the three-fold nature of reality</note> for the purpose of invocation. It is so named because it has three sections, and because it "shatters" (*khaṇḍana*) the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) through the realization of the Knower, the Knowledge, and the Known. **"Brings forth Lalitā"** means it is used for her invocation. According to tradition, the "Invocation" of the all-pervading Goddess Lalitā refers to the act of perceiving her manifold creative variety as distinct from oneself. The rest of the text is easy to understand. (33)

<note>(1) A variant reading in the 'vaṃ.' manuscript reads: "The variety is partitioned."</note>

## Page 72

### With hands facing downward, joined together and with fingers extended, one should perform the Establishing gesture. This is considered the "Universal Stabilizer." (34)
### With the middle and little fingers formed into a fist, their nails joined to the tips of the thumbs, and the hands closely joined at the nails—this is the Restraint gesture. (35)
### With the index fingers held straight and the other fingers in a fist, starting from the sides, one should place the hands crosswise at the beginning of the movement. (36)
### This is the Veiling gesture. Furthermore, for the Presence gesture, the Salutation is understood to be either with hands open or in a bud-like shape. (37)
### The Arrow-and-Bow gesture is formed with the thumb and the fist. The Noose gesture is formed by that same position, but with the joining of the index finger and the thumb. (38)
### With the thumb placed on the back of the little and ring fingers, the index finger curved, and the middle finger held straight—this gesture is called the Goad. (39)

---

**The Commentary:**

With the two verses beginning with **"With hands facing downward..."** and ending with **"...the Restraint gesture,"** the author teaches the sequence for forming the two gestures of Establishing and Restraining, which are common to all deities. In this context, **"Restraint"** <note>original: "sannirodhana"</note> refers to the prayer for the deity to have "undivided attention" or to become fixed in the practitioner's presence.

With the two verses beginning with **"With the index fingers held straight..."** and ending with **"...either open or bud-like,"** the author teaches the sequence for forming the Veiling gesture <term>Avaguṇṭhana: a gesture used to "screen" or protect the ritual space from negative influences or the "improper gaze" of the uninitiated</term> and the Presence gesture. In this context, **"at the start"** means the resting of the left hand at the start of the right hand's movement, and the resting of the right hand at the start of the left hand's movement <note>this refers to the crossing of the wrists</note>. **"Veiling"** refers to making the ritual space invisible to the eyes of the unworthy. **"Presence"** refers to the prayer for the deity to face the practitioner and accept the ritual offerings.

With the verse beginning with **"The Arrow..."** the author teaches the sequence for forming the Arrow gesture and the Noose gesture. In this context, **"joining of the index finger and the thumb"** means the contact of the tips of these two fingers.

With the verse beginning with **"With the thumb placed..."** the author teaches the sequence for forming the Goad gesture <note>original: "aṅkuśa," the hook used by elephant drivers, symbolizing the power to pull or attract</note>. Here, the instruction implies that the middle finger is joined while held in a straight position. These four are known as the "Weapon-gestures" <term>heti-mudrās: gestures representing the symbolic weapons held by the deity</term> which represent the very nature of the deity...

# Chapter 4 | Description of the Salutation, Universal Agitator, and Universal Liquefier Gestures. 73

### Within the **Sky-moving** <term>Khecharī; a high-level gesture representing the movement of consciousness in the "sky" of the heart</term> gesture which will be described later, when the two index fingers are placed on the backs of the hands and joined straight together, it is called the **Salutation** gesture. (40)

### With the little, ring, and middle fingers joined at their nails, the thumbs placed upon the little fingers, and the index fingers held straight—this is the **Universal Agitator** gesture, which causes agitation throughout the three worlds. (41)

### O Goddess! In this same gesture, when the middle fingers are also made straight like the index fingers... (42)

---

**The Commentary:**

Regarding the previous verse [39], the practitioner should visualize the respective weapons of the deity as being held in their own hands. These gestures should be performed with the realization of one's own identity with the deity <note>original: "devatā-bhāvena"</note>. According to the oral tradition <term>Sampradāya; the lineage of teachers passing down secret knowledge</term>, when performing these with the mantra, one should combine the physical gesture with the recitation of the corresponding ritual formula. (39)

With the verse beginning **"Within the Sky-moving..."**, the author teaches the sequence for forming the **Salutation** <note>original: "Namaskāra"</note> gesture. Here, "Salutation" refers to a ritual performance <note>original: "abhinaya"</note> that demonstrates one's lack of separation from the object of worship. This is a very secret <note>original: "atyupahvara"</note> meaning within our tradition. It is through this gesture that the act of bowing everywhere becomes effective in attaining divine grace. The tradition holds that the display of these five gestures—starting from the **Establishing** gesture and ending with the **Salutation**—should be performed while reciting the third section of the Root-Vidyā <note>the primary mantra of the goddess</note>. (40)

With the verse beginning **"With the little..."** and ending with **"...causes agitation,"** the author teaches the sequence for the **Agitator** <note>original: "Saṃkṣobhaṇī"</note> gesture. In this context, "index fingers" means both index fingers. It is called the "Agitator of the Three Worlds" because it brings about joy <note>original: "sukha-kāriṇī"</note>. This means that by merely seeing this gesture, the hearts of all deities and all women experience a surge of blissful expansion. (41)

With the two half-verses beginning with **"In this same..."** and ending with **"...of women,"** the author teaches the sequence for the **Universal Liquefier** <note>original: "Sarvavidrāvaṇī"</note> gesture. In the phrase "In this same," it refers to the **Agitator** gesture just described. "In the middle" implies the fingers. The word "Goddess" is a form of address. "Made like the index fingers" means they should be held straight. "When this is done" is the implied conclusion of the instruction. (42) It is called "Universal Liquefier" because it subjugates all deities and causes the "liquefaction" <note>original: "vidrāvaṇa"; in Tantric psychology, this refers to a state of intense attraction or the "melting" of the ego into bliss</note> of the wombs of all women.

<margin>(2) "In the visualization" according to the So. manuscript; "And in the visualization" according to the Ti. manuscript.</margin>
<margin>(3) "Pankara" according to the So. manuscript.</margin>
<margin>(4) "The one who brings fame" according to the Ti. manuscript.</margin>

The commentary emphasizes that these gestures are not merely physical acts but methods to realize non-duality with the deity and invoke spiritual bliss.</summary>

# 74
->**Tantrarāja with the Manoramā Commentary**<-

> The **Universal Liquefier** <term>Sarvavidrāvaṇī; a gesture meant to "melt" or soften spiritual resistance</term> gesture melts <note>original: "vidrāvaṇī"</note> all women. When those two [fingers] are combined in the shape of a hook <note>original: "aṅkuśa"</note>, it is considered the **Attracting** <term>Ākarṣaṇī</term> gesture. (43)
> 
> Having turned the fingers around so the nails touch the palms, with the thumbs joined to the index fingers by the nails, this is the **Possession-inducing** <term>Āveśakāriṇī</term> gesture. (44)
> 
> Extending the tips of the hands, one should cross the little fingers. By joining their tips, the middle fingers are bent, while the ring fingers remain straight. (45)
> 
> With the index fingers placed on those nails, and the thumbs over the middle fingers—this is the **Intoxicating** <term>Unmādinī</term> gesture, which causes universal intoxication. (46)
> 
> In this same gesture, if the ring fingers are bent and the index fingers are shaped like hooks, this is the **Great Hook** <term>Mahāṅkuśā</term> gesture, which performs both immobilization and attraction. (47)
> 
> Properly crossing the left and right hands over the elbows, one should bind them at the wrists, [placing] the hollowed palms on the backs of the middle [fingers]... (48)

---

**The Commentary:**

With the words **"With those two..."** in the second half of the verse [43], the author teaches the sequence for forming the **Attracting** <note>original: "ākarṣaṇī"</note> gesture. In that context, "with those two in the shape of a hook" means using the middle and index fingers formed into hooks as previously described, while joined with the ring fingers (this last part is implied). The meaning is as follows: the previously mentioned "Liquefier" gesture becomes the "Attracting" gesture when the two ring fingers are joined with the middle and index fingers in a hook shape. "Attraction" <note>original: "ākarṣa"</note> means bringing something close; it signifies achieving stability in making one's own desires manifest. (43)

With the verse beginning **"Having turned..."**, the author teaches the sequence for forming the **Possession-inducing** gesture. Here, "turned fingers" means crossing the fingers. "Possession-inducing" <note>original: "āveśakāriṇī"</note> means that which causes the awakening of the state or "flavor" of the deity within the practitioner. (44)

With the two verses beginning **"Extending the tips..."** and ending with **"inducing,"** the author teaches the sequence for forming the **Intoxicating** gesture. Here, "Universal Intoxication" means it causes intoxication and "moistening" <note>original: "kledanakari"; refers to the flow of internal spiritual nectar or emotional softening</term> in all women. (46)

With the verse beginning **"In this..."**, the author teaches the sequence for forming the **Great Hook** gesture. Here, "In this" refers to the **Intoxicating** gesture. "Bent" <note>original: "bhugne"</note> refers to the contact with the tips of the thumbs. (47)

With the three verses beginning **"Left and right..."** and ending with "deities" [in the following verses], the author teaches the sequence for forming the **Sky-moving** <term>Khecharī</term> gesture. Here, "on the backs of the middle" means on the backs of the middle fingers. "Sky-moving" means it grants the attainment of the state of a "Sky-walker" <note>original: "khecaratva"; a high level of spiritual mastery or literal flight in yogic lore</note>. In this section regarding the formation of gestures, no further explanation is written because the text is easy to understand. (48-50)

### [In the 4th Chapter] Instruction on the Sequence of Forming the Seed, Great Yogini, and Power-Raising Gestures.

->75<-

Having bent the two index fingers, one should make the two thumbs straight. One should place the little and ring fingers crossed on the back of the hand. (49)

This is the **Sky-Moving** <term>Khecarī; literally "moving in the void," referring to a state of high spiritual consciousness</term> gesture, which brings joy to the Goddess Lalitā <note>The principal deity of this Tantra</note>. By the mere formation of this gesture, all deities are perfected. (50)

The middle fingers are placed below the sides of the middle [fingers], and the little fingers are at the tips in reverse order. The two ring fingers are crossed below, and the two index fingers are shaped like hooks. (51)

The others [fingers] are at the tips of those nails. This is called the **Seed** <term>Bīja; representing the core essential vibration or power</term> gesture. By joining the little fingers and thumbs, the **Three-Fold Great Womb** <term>Mahāyoni-trikhaṇḍikā; a gesture representing the creative source of the universe</term> is formed. (52)

The little, ring, and middle fingers are crossed on the back in sequence. By turning them upward <note>original: "ūrdhvayogena"</note> and straightening the index fingers on both hands... (53)

---

**The Commentary:**

**By the two verses beginning with "Middle..." and ending with "Three-Fold," the author teaches the sequence for forming the Seed gesture and the Great Womb gesture. In that context, "in reverse order" means they should be placed oppositely. It is called the Seed gesture because it is the cause of all spiritual success.** (52)

**By the two verses beginning with "Little..." and ending with "is called," he teaches the sequence for forming the Power-Raising <term>Śaktyutthāpana</term> gesture. In that context, "Concentration" <note>original: "samādhi"</note> means that which is perfectly established; it refers to the sense of identity with the deity within one's own self. "Embodiment" <note>original: "mūrtīkaraṇa"</note> means the visualization of one's own body as the form of the deity.** (54)

**With the five verses beginning with "Gesture" <note>original: "mudrā"</note> and ending with "Shiva," he teaches the threefold nature of gestures, their seats, the definition of the word "gesture," its logic, and so on. In that context, "Reality" <note>original: "tattvam"</note> means "that-ness" or the true state of things. "In sequence from the thumb" means starting from the thumb and following the sequence from the element of Ether to the element of Earth <note>Tantric practice often maps the five fingers to the five elements: thumb/ether, index/air, middle/fire, ring/water, pinky/earth</note>. "Illusion" <note>original: "māyā"</note> is the obscuration of the knowledge of the world and of one's own true self.** 

**Regarding the term "gesture" <note>original: "mudrā"</note>, the text notes it is derived from the root "rā" meaning "to give" <note>original: "dāne"</note>—because it "gives" the realization of one's own divine nature. Regarding the phrase "anger and joy arise from a slight difference"—here, while the fist itself takes the same form for both striking and saluting, the "slight difference" lies in the curvature or straightness of the wrist. This means that anger is the opposite of joy, and joy is the opposite of anger. Although the single form of the fist is the same for both striking and bowing—depending on whether it is curved or uncurved—it can manifest either anger or grace. The fist that signifies grace is called a "gesture" <note>mudrā</note>, whereas the fist signifying anger is just [an ordinary fist].** (58)

---

<margin>Variant reading: "The obstruction of knowledge of the world and the self" in the So. manuscript.</margin>

# In the Tantrarāja, accompanied by the commentary named Manoramā

This is the **Power-Raising** <term>Śaktyutthāpana; the gesture used to "wake up" the internal spiritual energy</term> gesture, used during chanting, worship, and meditative absorption. It is said that by the formation of this gesture, the manifestation of the deity is achieved. (54)

O Goddess! Gestures are of three types according to their construction, mantra, and essential nature. They are known as the **Gross**, **Subtle**, and **Supreme**. Hear now, my dear, about this threefold nature! (55)

The form of the construction and the mantra have just been told to you. The fingers represent the essential principles <term>tattvas; the building blocks of reality</term>, and the elements <term>bhūtas; earth, water, fire, air, and ether</term> are represented in order starting from the thumb. (56)

By observing the specific movements and formations of these gestures, one declares: "I am outside of your illusion <term>māyā; the creative power that can also delude</term> only by your grace." (57)

A "Mudrā" is so called because it **gives joy** <note>original: "mudam rāti"; a traditional etymology where 'muda' means joy and 'rā' means to give</note>. In another sense, it is simply a fist; through slight variations, it generates anger or joy in living beings. (58)

For this reason, the gestures of all the gods are considered to be givers of joy. Therefore, O Auspicious One <note>original: "Śive"</note>, these gestures should always be displayed at the time of worship. (59)

---

**The Commentary:**

**By the two verses beginning with "Three-metals" and ending with "O Auspicious One," the author teaches the five types of offering vessels <term>arghyapātra; a vessel used to hold consecrated water</term> and the method for preparing the offering. In this context, by the word "three-metals," gold, silver, and copper are meant.** <note>These metals are traditionally combined in ritual objects to balance planetary and elemental energies.</note> **In a single vessel. Regarding the preparation of the offering: in that offering-water, prepared according to the method to be described in the Fifth Chapter, one should show the Cow and Womb gestures.** 

**The binding of the Cow Gesture <term>Dhenu-mudrā; also called Surabhi-mudrā, representing the wish-fulfilling cow of plenty</term> is as follows: having formed a hollowed palm by interlacing the fingers in a specific order, one should join the two index fingers of the left and right hands to the right and left middle fingers respectively, like a staff. Similarly, one should join the two little fingers of the left and right to the right and left ring fingers respectively, like a staff.** <note>This creates a complex interlaced shape meant to resemble the udders of a cow.</note> **This is the Surabhi Gesture. One should learn the specific way of displaying it from the mouth of a Guru.** 

**After displaying that, one should chant the mantra of the "Six Limbs" <term>ṣaḍaṅga; a ritual where mantras are placed on the heart, head, hair-tuft, armor, eyes, and weapons</term> and the Nityā mantra ten times each.** <note>The Nityās are sixteen goddesses representing the lunar days.</note> **The order is either a single recitation of the Six-Limbed mantras and ten recitations of the third section of the Root Wisdom <term>mūla-vidyā</term>, or it refers to the act of worship itself. Following that, one should worship or chant three times with the Nityā-Wisdom of that day (which has three parts) and the Root Wisdom. This is the practical meaning. "In the form of the Wisdom"—this describes the offering-water according to the stated sequence. "By the Wisdom"—this means by the three-part mantra of the goddess Lalitā. Through this worship, the water attains the nature of the Wisdom itself.** (60-61)

---

(1) "By chanting" <note>original: "japeneti"</note> — this is the reading in manuscript 'Va'. "He should chant" <note>original: "japet"</note> — this is the reading in manuscript 'Sa'.

### [ In the 4th Chapter ] An Account of the Meditation on the Attendant Powers and Other Matters

One should prepare the offering water <term>arghya; a ritual libation offered to a deity</term> in a single vessel made of three-metals <note>typically a ritual alloy of gold, silver, and copper</note>, glass, or clay. By using the holy waters designated by the "six-limbs" <term>ṣaḍaṅga; a set of six mantras used to consecrate parts of the body or ritual items</term>, each ten times, (60)

and by chanting the Mantra <note>original: "vidyā-rūpeṇa"</note>, one should sprinkle that offering water. O Auspicious One <note>original: "Śive"</note>! One must sprinkle all the tools for one's own worship entirely with the mantra. (61)

One should meditate on the red-hued Goddess Lalitā, holding the arrows, bow, noose, and goad in her hands. She is joyful and seated upon the lap of the King of Desire <note>original: "Kāmarāja"; a name for the deity Kameshvara, the consort of Lalitā</note>. (62)

In all daily and occasional worship, she is described as being accompanied by her attendant powers, in the form mentioned in the "desire-focused meditations" <note>original: "kāmyadhyāna"; specific visualizations used to achieve particular worldly or spiritual goals</note>. (63)

Since they are the radiant manifestations of the central, primary Goddess, the visualization of the powers of the nine enclosures <term>navāvaraṇa-śakti; the groups of goddesses who inhabit the nine nested layers of the Sri Yantra</term> should be identical to that of the Goddess herself. (64)

Except for the union with the King of Desire, O Supreme Sovereign, all the ornaments and weapons of those goddesses stationed in the Cakra are entirely the same as hers. (65)

[The powers are:] First Aṇimā <gloss>The power to become as small as an atom</gloss>, then Laghimā <gloss>The power to become weightless</gloss>, and following that, Mahimā <gloss>The power to become immense</gloss>...

---

**The Commentary:**

By the two verses beginning with "The red-hued" and ending with "in worship," the author teaches the meditation on Lalitā for both daily and occasional rites. There, the "arrows, bow, noose, and goad in her hands" indicates the position of the weapons in her four hands, starting from the lower right hand and moving to the upper right hand in a counter-clockwise direction. The meaning of the phrase "connected with" <note>original: "yanvitām"</note> must be understood only from the mouth of one's teacher <term>guru</term>. She is "joyful" because her form consists of a hundred types of bliss.

Regarding "the form described for desire-focused meditations": this means she should be meditated upon in both daily and occasional worship as being endowed with anklets, waist-chains, bracelets, fine garments, the swastika mark, necklaces, throat-ornaments, armlets, rings, earrings, crowns, and so on. (62–63)

By the two verses beginning with "The central" and ending with "entirely," the author teaches the meditation on the multitude of attendant powers. There, "radiant manifestations" refers to the Goddess's urge to emanate, as in the scripture: "May I be many, may I bring forth progeny." The secret meaning of the phrase "except for the union with the King of Desire" <note>referring to the fact that the attendant goddesses do not sit on the lap of Shiva as the central Goddess does</note> must be understood only from the mouth of the teacher. (64–65)

Through the five verses beginning with "Aṇimā," which end with the first enclosure, the author describes the square <note>original: "caturaśre"; the outermost part of the Sri Yantra</note> of the first enclosure...

With the section beginning "Kusuma" and ending with "situated," consisting of two and a half verses, the author teaches the mantras of the eight powers of the eight-petaled lotus in the third enclosure and the sequence of their worship. In that context, by demonstrating one mantra, the other seven mantras should be applied accordingly: "Hrīm Shrīm <note>these are "seed" syllables representing the energy of the Goddess</note>, I worship the power-sandals of Ananga-Kusuma," and so forth. || 75 || 76 ||

With the section beginning "Inside" and ending with "names matching their meaning," consisting of three verses, the author teaches the mantras of the fourteen powers in the fourteen-spoke enclosure (the fourth enclosure), as well as the sequence of worship for the powers of the "Secret Ten-Spoke" enclosure. Here, the phrase "starting in the fourteen-spoke" and the word "and others" indicates that even in the "Secret Ten-Spoke" enclosure, one should worship moving counter-clockwise starting from the front of the Goddess. "Vashankari" means "The Subjugator." These powers begin with the word "All" <note>original: "Sarva"</note>; one should add the word "All" to the beginning of the fourteen names, following the two mentioned seed-syllables. 

Regarding the "Seven-Syllable Power Mantra," the tradition is that the two syllables of the word "Shakti" are taken as they are, rather than using the aspirated "Hrīm" sound. "In sequence" means in the order mentioned. One should worship each power in each corner, beginning from the corner directly in front of the Goddess. For example: "Hrīm Shrīm, I worship the power-sandals of the Shakti (Power) who Agitates All <note>original: "Sarva-saṃkṣobhiṇī"</note>." One should apply the other thirteen mantras in the same way. || 77 || 78 || 79 ||

<header>### In the 4th Chapter: Description of the sequence of worship mantras for the Powers, Weapons, and Other Elements</header>

The author now teaches the ten mantras. In that context, "Knowledge" <note>original: "jña"</note> means "All-knowing" <note>original: "sarvajñā"</note>. Following the previous method: "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ—I worship the sandals of the All-knowing Goddess." <note>original: "sarvajñā-devī-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi"</note> One should apply this to the other nine mantras as well. || 84 || 85 || 86 ||

With the verse beginning with **Likewise, in the inner**, he teaches the mantras and the worship sequence for the eight Powers to be worshipped in the seventh enclosure (the eight-spoked area). There, "from the west" means starting from the front and proceeding as before regarding the application of the group Seed-syllables; this is to be joined with the "seven-syllable" mantra. "In the place of Salutation" <note>original: "namaḥ-pade"</note> means one should discard the word "Salutation" <note>original: "namaḥ"</note> as prescribed in the sequence of ritual placement <note>term: "Nyasa" — the ritual "placing" of mantras on the body or the diagram</note> and instead join the seven-syllable mantra into those eight mantras.

[The mantra is:] "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ—A Ā I Ī U Ū Ṛ Ṝ Ḷ Ḹ E Ai O Au Aṃ Aḥ—Blūṃ—I worship the sandals of the Speech-Goddess Vashini." <note>original: "vaśinī-vāgdevatā-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi"</note> <margin>(2) In the same way, one should join the other seven mantras.</margin> Similarly, the other mantras are to be applied. Here too, the application of the two Seed-syllables <note>Hrīṃ and Śrīṃ</note> is done everywhere, because of the initial rule and the rule regarding the conclusion. || 87 ||

With the one and a half verses starting with **Around the central** and ending with **O Great Goddess**, he teaches the worship mantras and the sequence for the weapons. "Around the central triangle" means this: around the very central triangle where the Principal Deity resides, in the respective positions of the limbs, (3) one should worship the respective weapons starting from the Arrows and ending with the Goad. As for "The Seed-syllables have been stated," it means this:

At the end of the two previously specified Seed-syllables "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ," the mantra for the Arrows is: "Yāṃ Rāṃ Lāṃ Vāṃ Śāṃ Drāṃ Drīṃ Klīṃ Blūṃ Saḥ—Salutation to the Arrows that cause all to blossom/tremble." <note>original: "sarvajṛmbhaṇebhyo bāṇebhyo namaḥ"</note> 

Then, at the end of the stated two Seed-syllables "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ," the mantra for the Bow is: "Thaṃ Dhaṃ—Salutation to the Bow that causes all delusion." <note>original: "sarvamohanāya dhanuṣe namaḥ"</note> 

Following that, at the end of the stated two Seed-syllables "Hrīṃ Śrīṃ"...

**Hrīṃ (7) Ā (7) Salutation to the Noose for the subjugation of all.** <note>original: "sarvavaśīkaraṇāya pāśāya namaḥ"</note> This is the Noose-mantra. Then, **Hrīṃ (7) Hrīṃ (7)**—at the end of these two stated seed-syllables—**Salutation to the Goad for the immobilization of all.** <note>original: "sarvastambhanāya aṅkuśāyanamaḥ"</note> This is the Goad-mantra. Here too, the joining of the two seed-syllables is as described previously.

With the latter half of the verse beginning with **the Masters**, the author points out the place of worship for the nine Masters. || 88 ||

With the verse beginning with **The Goddess at the center**, he teaches that the Goddess consists of the sixteen Eternal Ones <note>term: "Nityās" — sixteen aspects of the lunar cycle personified as goddesses, with the sixteenth being the central deity herself</note> and, through that, the worship of the other fifteen Date-Eternal Ones <note>term: "Tithi-nityas" — the goddesses governing the lunar days</note> within her form. || 90 ||

With the two verses (including six extra syllables) beginning with **In the middle triangle** and ending with **one should worship**, he teaches the three Powers to be worshipped in the three corners of the middle triangle in the eighth enclosure, their mantras, and the sequence of worship. There, starting from the west—that is, the corner in front of the Goddess—one fragment <note>term: "khaṇḍa" — a section or division of a long mantra</note> of the Knowledge-mantra <note>term: "Vidyā" — the primary sacred mantra of the Goddess</note> belongs to each Power. The Seats <note>term: "Pīṭhas" — sacred centers of power, often associated with geography</note> are three: named Kamarupa, Purnagiri, and Jalandhara. The names of the Powers are three: Kameshvari, Vajreshvari, and Bhagamalini. **Joined with the seven-syllable Goddess-mantra**—this means that after the two syllables "De-vi," one should add the seven-syllable mantra preceded by "Shri." Thus: "Shri (7) Hrīṃ (7) [first fragment of the root mantra], in the Seat of Kamarupa, I worship the auspicious sandals of the Goddess Kameshvari." <note>original: "kāmarūpapīṭhe kāmeśvarīdevīśrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi"</note> The other two mantras should be constructed in the same way. The use of the word "Shri" here follows the tradition. || 92 ||

<header>### Instructions on Mantras for the Worship of the Goddess</header>
<meta>Within the 4th Chapter]</meta>

> One should worship her joined with the seven-syllable mantra and likewise offer honor.
> These two are declared to be the "Qualities" and also the "Yoginis" <note>Yoginis are semi-divine female spirits or aspects of the Goddess.</note> || 65 ||
> The names of the enclosures are stated; the sequence is "May they accept the worship."
> For the Goddess, it should be "May [she] accept" (1). Hear, my dear, of this threefold nature. || 66 ||

With the section beginning with "Afterward" and ending with "the worship," the author teaches the "gross" <note>term: *sthūla* (gross/physical form) – referring to the deity visualized with a body and attributes, as opposed to a subtle sound-form.</note> worship of the Goddess in the very center of the ninth enclosure using two half-verses of ten syllables. In that context, **the complete vidya** <note>term: *vidyā* – a female mantra.</note> refers to the "Fourth Wisdom" mentioned previously. **Joined with the names of the Seat and the Goddess**—this means the name of the sacred Seat and the name of the Goddess. The name of the Seat is "at the Seat of Odyana" <note>Odyana or Uddiyana is a legendary sacred site in Tantric geography.</note>. The name of the Goddess is "The Auspicious Great Beautiful One of the Three Cities" <note>original: *Śrī-Mahā-Tripura-Sundarī*</note>. **Joined with the seven-syllable Goddess [mantra]**—as before, this means one should utter the two syllables "Devi" and then the seven-syllable mantra preceded by "Shri." 

Thus the formula is: **Hrīṃ Śrīṃ** [The complete root-mantra] **I worship the holy sandals of the Goddess, the Auspicious Great Beautiful One of the Three Cities, at the Seat of Odyana.** <note>original: "hrīm śrīm samastāṃ mūlavidyāṃ oḍyāṇapīṭhe śrīmahātripurasundarīdevīśrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi"</note>. Here too, the use of the word "Shri" twice follows the established tradition. || 83 ||

With the verse starting "In each circle" and ending "should be," consisting of one and a half verses, the author teaches the nine worship-mantras and the nine offering-mantras for the Goddess in each of her nine enclosures, using nine specific names. Regarding those **nine names**: these are the names beginning with "Tripura" mentioned in the fourteenth and fifteenth verses of the fifth chapter, and they are to be worshipped using the methods of arrangement described there. 

The method of arrangement is as follows: **The Root-Mantra - Tripura - I worship the holy sandals.** (2) In this order, one should join the other eight names. According to tradition, the "joining of the two seed-syllables" <note>The syllables *Hrīṃ* and *Śrīṃ*.</note> should not occur in any of these nine mantras. However, by tradition, the word "Shri" should be used twice in the ninth mantra. 

**That** refers to the two types of worship. **Two** refers to the two seed-syllables. **Qualities** refers to those such as the "Manifest" ones <note>term: *prakaṭa* – the first level of Yoginis in the Sri Yantra.</note>. These are the qualities known as the "Auspicious Powers" <note>original: *śrī-śakti-saṃjñā-guṇān*</note>. These are also discussed in the twelfth and thirteenth verses of the fifth chapter. This connects to the phrase **declared to be the Yoginis**. They are so declared because of their divine nature. 

**The names of the enclosures** (3) refers to the titles of the nine enclosure-circles, such as "The Enchanter of the Triple World" <note>original: *Trailokya-mohana* – the outermost square of the Sri Yantra.</note>. These are declared in the ninth and tenth verses of the fifth chapter. They are used as follows: **Hrīṃ Śrīṃ, may these Manifest Yoginis in the Enchanter of the Triple World circle accept this worship.** One should follow this pattern for the other eight enclosures...

(2) *Note on manuscript variants:* The sequence for "joining the others" varies slightly in the So. and Vam. manuscripts.
(3) *Alternative reading:* Some manuscripts read "names of the nectar" or "end of the names."

---

One should join the mantras. In that context, the final phrase is—**Hrim Hrim! May this Most Secret Yogini <note>referring to the Goddess in the central point</note> in the Great Wheel of Universal Bliss accept the fruit of this great worship.** Here, the use of the word "Great" <note>original: "Mahā"</note> follows the oral tradition of the lineage. || 84 || 85 ||

Regarding the verse beginning with **The Vidya** and ending with **O Spouse of Shiva**, which spans more than a single line: the author teaches the threefold nature of the Goddess who resides in the center, categorized as Gross, Subtle, and Supreme.

In this context, the **Gross** <note>term: *sthūla* — the tangible or visualizable form</note> refers to the form described previously as "red-colored," etc. One should worship her with the **Complete** [Vidya]—meaning the "Fourth Vidya" <note>a specific high-level mantra</note>.

**With the Name**—this means one should worship the **Subtle** form with the Vidya that takes the form of her names.
**The Mantra-body**—this means the form composed of letters. This connects to the "Subtle form." The Subtle form of the Goddess is composed of the sacred sounds of the alphabet.

**The Supreme form** <note>term: *para-rūpa* — the ultimate, formless reality</note>—is that which is unconditioned by space, time, or other limitations.
**Through dedication**—one should worship her by the act of offering the worship itself. This means one should worship the Supreme form of the Goddess using the specific mantra for dedicating the ritual. Every auspicious thing should be offered to the Goddess. Therefore, according to the principle that "even that most auspicious worship should be offered back to Him [the Supreme]" <margin>original: "tasyaiva," as noted in manuscript version 'so'</margin>, one should everywhere offer the deities both the physical offerings and the act of worship itself. 

**Is known**—it follows that she "becomes worshiped." The meaning is "one should worship having known this." The gist of the matter is this: the practitioner should worship with the understanding: "I worship the Gross form of the Goddess with the complete Fourth Vidya; the Subtle form, which is composed of letters, with the Name-Vidya; and the Supreme form with the Offering-Vidya." One should understand this same logic applies to the other eight enclosures of the mandala as well. || 86 || 87 ||

With the three verses starting with **The Vidya** and ending with **one should meditate**, the author teaches the meditation on the essential unity of the Guru, the Mantra, the Deity, and one's own Self. Because this subject is extremely secret, it is not usually disclosed, but here it is explained in detail by the command of the Master <note>original: "Nātha" — the founding teacher of the tradition</note>.

**The Vidya consists of three seed-syllables**—the three sections <note>original: "khaṇḍa"</note> of the root-mantra. 
**Crowned by the fourth vowel**—ending in the fourth vowel, which is the long "I" <note>The Sanskrit vowel sequence is a, ā, i, ī. The "fourth" is *ī*.</note>. The letter "I"...

<meta>This page concludes the fourth chapter of the Shodasha Nityatantra, continuing the discussion on the symbolic visualization of the Goddess's mantra and her identification with the Guru and the practitioner's self. It specifically focuses on the esoteric geometry of the letter 'Ī' as a representation of the Goddess's body.</meta>

<page-num>85</page-num>
<header>In the 4th Chapter ] Explanation of the sequence of meditation on the union of Guru, Mantra, and Deity.</header>

> The upper part is a single point <note>original: "bindu"</note>, and the lower consists of two points.
> One should meditate on the form of the breasts through these, and the remaining limbs through the rest of the script. || 100 ||
> This pervasiveness, consisting of the element of Air <note>term: *Vayu-tattva* — the principle of movement and vital breath</note>, is thus correctly described.
> By internalizing this in the mind, that reality is made one with one's own self. || 101 ||

->Thus, in the Illustrious Tantra of the Sixteen Nityas, in the Kadi tradition, ends the fourth chapter named<-
->**The Worship of Lalita.**<-

The meaning is: "ending in the letter 'Rā'" <note>this refers to a specific phonetic structure in the mantra</note>. That refers to the "Fourth" nature; the nature of that "Fourth" form is the letter 'Ī'. By "nature" <note>original: "svarūpam"</note>, the written form of the script is meant. It is described as being like three points—in all scripts, the nature of this "Fourth" vowel exists as a cluster of three dots <note>note: in many ancient Indian scripts, the letter 'Ī' was written as three dots arranged in a triangle</note>. By this, the text establishes the identity of the Guru and the Deity for the practitioners. **Meditation on that**—meaning the meditation on being identical with that. **Granting great success**—because of attaining the nature of the unbroken Self. || 88 ||

With the verse beginning with **The upper part**, the author teaches the sequence of meditation for the Yoga that accomplishes the identity of the Guru, the Mantra, and the Deity with one's own self. In that context, **the upper part is a single point**: the meaning is that because the three sections of the Root-Mantra <note>term: *Mula-vidya* — the primary mantra of the Goddess</note> all end in the "Fourth vowel" <note>the vowel 'Ī'</note>, and its form consists of three dots, the upper dot is visualized as the Goddess's face, the two dots situated below are her two breasts, and the remaining lines of that letter represent the complete limbs of the Goddess. In this way, there is a single form for the Deity and the Mantra. By visualizing the nature of the Guru and one's own self as residing within that form while chanting this Wisdom-Mantra <note>term: *Vidya*</note>, the stated fruits will certainly be achieved through the accomplishment of identity <note>original: *tādātmya*</note>. The fact that the Guru is identical to the mantra should be understood directly from his own mouth <note>referring to oral transmission from teacher to student</note>. || 101 ||

->Thus, in the Illustrious Tantras of the Sixteen Nityas, in the commentary named **Manorama** (The Heart-Delighting)<-
->composed by **Subhanandanatha**, also known as King Prakashasimha of the Prapanchasara tradition,<-
->on the complete Tantra known as the **Sri Kadi-mata**,<-
->the fourth chapter, which is dedicated to revealing the sequence of daily and occasional worship<-
->of the eternal Goddess Lalita, is now fully concluded and reviewed.<-

# Now, the Fifth Chapter.

->With that very same meditation, one should chant the mantra, concentrated on the sacred knowledge.<-
->Thinking of your own union <note>original: "sāyujya"</note> with the Self, success will surely be attained, there is no doubt. || 1 ||<-
->With the third section of the mantra, one should perform the worshipful offerings:<-
->Water for the feet, the guest-offering, water for sipping, the bath, garments, and ornaments. || 2 ||<-
->Perfume and flowers, incense and lamps, the food offering and sipping water again,<-
->Betel leaf, the worship, the hymn of praise, the libation <note>original: "tarpaṇa"</note>, and the act of salutation. || 3 ||<-

->Scribal Note on Verse Count — In the fourth chapter, there is no diagram <note>original: "yantra"</note> included in the explanatory sequence.<-
->The total verse count is two hundred and seventy-eight.<-

## Now, the Fifth Chapter.

In the previous fourth chapter, the author taught the practice of meditation on the oneness of the Guru, the Mantra, the Deity, and one's own Self—which is the sacred knowledge of the eternal Goddess Lalitā <note>original: "Lalita-nityā-vidyā"</note>—and her daily worship. Now, in this fifth chapter, through verses beginning with **With that very meditation** and ending with **In that way**, he teaches the remaining sequence for the daily worship of that Goddess Lalitā, starting from the previously mentioned parts up to the division of the earth <note>term: *kūrma-vibhāga* — a ritual method of partitioning space or the ground, literally 'the division of the tortoise'</note>.

There, with the verse beginning **With that very meditation**, he teaches the method of chanting the mantra <note>original: "japa"</note> and the certainty of attaining success. In that context—**with that very same meditation**—means by using the meditation on the identity of the Guru, the Mantra, the Deity, and one's own Self, as described at the end of the previous chapter. **Union** <note>original: "sāyujya"</note> means identity or oneness. || 1 ||

With the first half of the verse beginning with **With the sacred knowledge**, he teaches the mantra for presenting the ritual offerings to the Deity. In that context, although it says **with the third section**, the tradition <note>original: "sampradāya"</note> holds that one should perform it using that section together with the specific eternal mantra <gloss>( 1 )</gloss>, according to the command of the Master. || 2 ||

With the three half-verses beginning with **Water for the feet** and ending with **salutation**, he teaches the sixteen offerings of hospitality <note>term: *ṣoḍaśopacāra* — the standard sixteen acts of service offered to a deity or honored guest</note> common to the Tantras <gloss>( 2 )</gloss>. Among these, the second instance of **sipping water** is not counted as a separate offering because it is considered a subsidiary part of the food offering. **Libation** <note>original: "tarpaṇa"</note> refers to the presentation of honey, milk, coconut water, fruit juice, or water for the guest-offering, according to what is available. **The act of salutation** refers to the hand gestures <note>original: "mudrā"</note> prescribed for that specific time. The connection of the verse is that one should perform the worshipful offerings, sixteen in number, in this manner. || 3 ||

---

<gloss>( 1 ) A variant reading in the commentary manuscript: "together with the eternal knowledge" <note>original: "nityā-vidyā-sametena"</note>.</gloss>
<gloss>( 2 ) A variant reading in the manuscript: "common to you" <note>original: "tava sādhāraṇān"</note>.</gloss>

It emphasizes that success in mantra-chanting comes from a sense of absolute identity between the practitioner, the teacher, and the divine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the instructions for the fifth chapter regarding the daily worship (pūjā) of the Goddess Lalitā. ### [From the 5th Chapter] Description of the Concluding Acts of Worship and Other Matters.

Having worshipped in this way, combined with the meditation mentioned before,
One should chant the mantra a thousand or a hundred times, or the count specified for that day. || 4 ||

Then, through the grace of the Goddess, one should think of oneself as identical to her.
Having performed the three types of ritual placement <term>nyāsa — the practice of mentally "placing" sacred syllables or deities onto specific parts of the body to transform the physical self into a divine vessel</term>, one should move about happily, embodying the Goddess herself. || 5 ||

The person who performs this daily routine, being devoted to their Guru,
No suffering will ever occur to them anywhere at any time. || 6 ||

For anyone who acts with malice, causes suffering, or shows neglect toward such a practitioner,
By our grace <note>the "our" refers to the deities or the lineage of teachers</note>, those very actions will become their defining mark <note>original: "lakṣaṇam hi tat"; this implies that the practitioner is protected, and any ill-will directed at them is redirected or serves as a sign of the aggressor's own nature</note>. || 7 ||

Listen now to the names of the Nine Enclosures <term>navāvaraṇa — the nine concentric circuits or layers of the Śrī Yantra</term> and the names of their respective powers,
Through whose worship in those specific chakras one attains incomparable success. || 8 ||

The "Deluder of the Three Worlds" <note>original: "Trailokyamohana"</note> is the outer circuit, then the "Fulfiller of all Hopes," <note>original: "Sarvāśāparipūraka"</note>
The "Agitator of All," <note>original: "Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa"</note> and the "Bestower of all Good Fortune." <note>original: "Sarvasaubhāgyapradāyaka"</note> || 9 ||

---

With the two verses starting with **Having worshipped thus** and ending with **happily**, the author teaches the concluding acts of worship. There:
**In front** means before the Goddess. **Born of that day** <note>original: "tad-dina-jam"</note> means the specific requirements for that day of worship. The word "or" is used for emphasis. The meaning is that one should chant the mantra 121 times <note>Sanskrit: "ekaviṃśatyadhika-śata-vāraṃ"</note>: nine times as prescribed for the morning twilight, twenty-six times for the midday, sixteen times for the evening twilight, and sixty times as specified for the sixty hours <term>ghaṭikās — a traditional unit of time equal to 24 minutes</term> of the day. || 4 ||

**Through grace** means by the power of the meditation on identity bestowed by the divine state. After the ritual placement <note>nyāsa</note> of the self as the Goddess, it means one should always move about with the awareness "I am the Deity." <note>A variation in the Tī manuscript reads: "one should perform it."</note> || 5 ||

With the two verses starting with **In this way** and ending with **that**, the author teaches the spiritual influence of one who practices the daily routine. There: **Devoted to the Guru** <note>original: "guru-paraḥ"</note> means one whose every action and movement is dependent on the Guru. || 6 || **That is the sign** refers to the daily practitioner. What is being said is this: For the daily practitioner, whether they encounter favor, hostility, or neglect <note>A note from the Mo manuscript explains: "neglect resulting from a lack of enthusiasm for the daily routine of the Nine Enclosures"</note>, our grace will manifest through these very occurrences. || 7 ||

With the verse starting with **Nine**, he introduces the Nine Enclosures and the names of their powers. There, **by which** refers to the names. || 8 ||

---

## Page 88
### In the Tantrarāja, accompanied by the commentary named Manoramā

...[The fifth enclosure is] the one that achieves all purposes <note>original: "sarvārthasādhana"</note>, and then the one that removes all diseases.
The one that provides all protection, and beyond that, the bestower of all success. || 10 ||

The one full of all bliss is the location of the central point <term>bindu — the infinitesimal seed-point at the center of the Yantra representing the source of all creation</term>, which is of the nature of Shiva.
Thus, O Parvati, these are the nine names that correspond to their specific qualities. || 11 ||

[The governing powers of these layers are:] the Manifest <note>original: "prakaṭā"</note> which are external, the Hidden <note>original: "guptā"</note>, then the More Hidden <note>original: "guptatarā"</note>,
Then the Traditional <note>original: "sampradāyā"</note> residing within, those Internalized in the Womb <note>original: "nigarbhikā"</note> of the Kula and Kaula traditions. || 12 ||

The Secret ones <note>original: "rahasyā"</note> follow those, then the Secret ones of the Beyond-and-Below <note>original: "parāpara-rahasyā"</note>.
Those preceded by the word "Highly" (the Highly Secret ones) reside in the center and possess gross forms. || 13 ||

[The presiding Goddesses of the nine layers are:] Tripurā, Tripureśī, Sundarī, Suravāsinī,
Śrīmālinī, Siddhāmbā, and Mahātripurasundarī. || 14 ||

---

With the three verses beginning with "Trailokya" and ending with "Parvati," the author teaches the nine meaningful names of the Nine Enclosure Chakras <term>navāvaraṇa-cakra — the nine distinct geometric levels of the Śrī Yantra</term>. Among them: "The Agitator of All" <note>original: "sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa"</note> refers to that which causes total agitation <note>of the creative forces</note>. "The Bringer of Great Fame" means the one who causes renown. 

In the word *paridāyakam* (bestower), the prefix *pari* is used merely to complete the meter of the verse. It means the "Bestower of All Good Fortune." || 8 || 

"Remover of all diseases": one should connect the word "Remover" <note>original: "hara"</note> after the word "all diseases." "Bestower of all success": the tradition holds that it is called "Bestower of all success" because it consists entirely of all success. || 10 ||

"Location of the point" <note>original: "vindusthāna"</note> refers to the middle-most point. "Full of all bliss" is connected to the phrase "of the nature of Shiva." The location of the point is the center of everything, just like the Absolute <term>brahman — the ultimate, formless reality in Hindu philosophy</term>. "Corresponding to their qualities" <note>original: "guṇayogīni"</note> means the names are meaningful based on their functions. "Parvati" is an address to the Goddess. || 11 ||

With the two verses starting with "Manifest" and ending with "forms," he teaches the nine meaningful names of the powers <term>yoginī — the goddesses who preside over each enclosure of the yantra</term> of the nine enclosures. In this context, the tradition states that their attributes represent their unconditioned nature. 

Regarding the names of the powers in the third and the final enclosures, the terms for their pervasive qualities are used, such as "More Hidden Yoginis" and "Highly Secret Yoginis." In the other enclosures, the terms for all qualities are used, such as "Hidden Yoginis." 

"Kula-Kaula" and "Beyond the Kula" <note>original: "kulottīrṇā"</note> are both used according to the tradition, meaning one should follow the instructions of the Lineage Masters <note>original: "nāthādeśa"</note>. "Internalized in the womb" <note>original: "nigarbhikā"</note> simply means "Those in the Womb." || 12 || 

"Secret of the Beyond-and-Below" <note>original: "parāpararahasyakā"</note> means the "Beyond-and-Below Secret" ones. "Preceded by 'Highly'" means the "Highly Secret" ones. "Residing in the center and possessing gross forms": these are the Highly Secret ones who possess forms. Here, the "gross form" <note>the visible deity or enclosure</note> is the outer covering of the "subtle form," which is the mantra itself...

### Chapter 5 | Description of the Sequence of Worship and Mantras

In the middle six names, one should worship by joining the word "Tripura" at the beginning, combined with the seven-syllable Vidya <term>Vidyā — a sacred mantra, specifically the feminine form of knowledge represented as a goddess</term> placed in the middle. || 15 ||

<note>original: "madhyaṣaṭke tu puratastripuretipadānvitaiḥ"</note>

I shall now describe the sequence of worship, its specific variations, the ritual practice for attaining the Vidya, the conduct and vows of the practitioner, and the signs of success. || 16 ||

One should meditate upon oneself as being of the same nature as Tripurā, located in the aperture of the crown of the head. One should also visualize the feet of the Guru <note>original: "nāthāṅghri"</note> in the form of light, having established his own body within that divine form. || 17 ||

<note>The "aperture" refers to the Brahmarandhra, the spiritual center at the top of the skull.</note>

The goddesses possess various colors, weapons, forms, vehicles, and ornaments. They are omnipresent and always bestow all success when provided with a ritual offering <term>bali — a ritual oblation or food offering given to deities or spirits</term>. || 18 ||

---

...controlled by... Although the gross and subtle forms lead one to the Supreme Form, because they are distinct and act as a sort of veil <note>original: "āvarakavat"</note>, they are traditionally termed "Enclosures" <term>āvaraṇa — literally 'covering' or 'veil'; here referring to the concentric layers of the sacred diagram</term>. This is the traditional meaning. || 13 ||

With the two verses beginning with "In the middle..." and ending with "...should worship," the author teaches the nine specific names for each of the nine enclosures of the Goddess, and the sequence for arranging the mantras for worship in those respective places. In this context, "Tripureśī" refers to "Tripureśvarī." "In the middle six" refers to the six names starting with Sundarī and ending with Ambā. In the case of "Puravāsinī," the meaning is "Tripuravāsinī." The tradition holds that one must join the word "Tri" to these. "Vidyā" refers to the Śrī Vidyā. The method for arranging the mantras was already explained by us in the previous chapter. || 14 || 15 ||

With the verse beginning "Sequence of worship," the author poses five questions. Among them, "specifics" <note>original: "tad-viśeṣān"</note> refers to the methods of contraction and expansion in the ritual. "Signs of success" refers to the physical or spiritual omens that the Vidya-practice is working. || 16 ||

With the two verses beginning "Nature of Tripurā" and ending with "offering," the author instructs what the practitioner should do at the time of waking in the morning. At the time of rising, after the meditation in the crown of the head, follows the ritual placement <term>nyāsa — the practice of 'charging' parts of the body with divine energy through touch and mantra</term>. "Nature of Tripurā" means one should meditate on the Goddess’s form as one’s own form, preceded by an investigation of the sacred traditions which will be described later. "Through the offering" implies using the sixteen-syllable mantra. An offering <note>original: "bali"</note> consists of flowers and other substances along with prepared food; by giving this, the goddesses become the bestowers of all success. Having meditated in this way, one should give the morning offering for the sake of attaining all perfections. || 17 || 18 ||
