Having drawn a hexagon and created a circle with an interval of one finger-breadth outside it, one should write the letters from *A* to *Cha* <note>the first six letters of the Sanskrit alphabet</note> in that path, as described previously. ### [ In the 7th Chapter ] Description of the extraordinary results of the thirty-two Yantras.

Through the sixteenth [diagram], by [offering] clarified butter into the fire <gloss>(1)</gloss>, one is never troubled by spirits <note>original: *bhūtādyaiḥ*, referring to ghosts, demons, or elemental entities</note> or similar beings. # Now begins the Eighth Chapter.

Now, O Goddess, I shall describe in order the third among the sixteen <term>Nityās: eternal lunar goddesses representing the phases of the moon</term>, who is Bhagamālinī, along with her ritual components and her retinue. || 1 ||

I will explain her limbs <note>original: *aṅgas*; the ritual divisions of her mantra</note>, her meditation visualization <note>original: *dhyāna*</note>, the deities of her retinue, the sequence of her worship, the fire sacrifice <note>original: *homa*</note>, and her various types of mystical diagrams <note>original: *yantras*</note>. || 2 ||

I have previously explained to you the extraction of her mantra. Her ritual limbs are formed by the syllables of that mantra; the "Heart" <note>the first of the six ritual placements</note> is said to be formed by the first syllable. || 3 ||

Then, the "Head" is formed by the next four syllables, and the "Crest" <note>original: *śikhā*</note> is said to be formed by the next three. The remaining limbs <note>Armor, Eyes, and Weapon</note> are formed by groups of four syllables each, in sequence. || 4 ||

She is the color of the dawn <note>original: *aruṇām*</note>, adorned with ruby-red ornaments, beautiful, with a face bearing a gentle smile. She is three-eyed, endowed with six arms, and seated upon a lotus. || 5 ||

In the previous seventh chapter, after teaching the ritual procedure for the second Nityā, Kāmeśvarī, the author now teaches the ritual procedure for the third, Bhagamālinī. "Previously" refers to the third chapter. "Limbs" implies that one should perform the six-fold placement. "By the first" refers to the first letter of the root mantra <note>original: *mūla-vidyā*</note>. || 3 ||

"By groups of four" <note>original: *catuṣṭayatayaiḥ*</note> means by sets of four syllables each. "The remaining limbs" refers to the Armor, the Eyes, and the Weapon. Here too, as before, one should join the appropriate ritual endings <note>original: *jāti*; such as Namaḥ, Svāhā, etc., used in Nyāsa</note>. || 4 ||

In that context, "seated upon a lotus" <note>original: *kamalāsanām*</note> means staying upon a lotus seat. With her left arms, starting from the upper one—

# Chapter 8 | Description of the Shaktis to be Worshipped

With arms holding a white water-lily <term>original: kalhāra</term>, a noose, a goad, and a sugar-cane bow, and with her right hands holding a lotus, a goad, and arrows made of flowers; || 6 ||

She is surrounded on all sides by praised groups of Shaktis <note>The female personifications of the Goddess's own powers</note> who are of a similar nature to her, and by others who arise from the syllables of her mantra, embodying the madness and intoxication of the God of Love. || 7 ||

With one hundred and twenty-five groups, and the five Shaktis of Form <term>original: rūpiṇī-śakti-pañcakam</term>, one should join the seven-syllable mantra and worship the Shaktis in that same number. || 8 ||

[The names of the twenty Shaktis are:]
1. Madanā <note>The Intoxicating One</note>
2. Mohinī <note>The Deluding One</note>
3. Lolā <note>The Trembling or Fickle One</note>
4. Jambhinī <note>The Crushing One</note>
5. Udyamā <note>The Exerting One</note>
6. Śubhā <note>The Auspicious One</note>
7. Lahalādinī <note>The Greatly Gladdening One</note>
8. Drāviṇī <note>The Liquefying One</note>
9. Prīti <note>Affection</note>
10. Rati <note>Erotic Pleasure</note>
11. Raktā <note>The Impassioned One</note>
12. Manoramā <note>The Captivating One</note> || 9 ||
13. Sarvonmādā <note>The All-Intoxicating One</note>
14. Sarvasukhā <note>The All-Blissful One</note>
15. Anaṅgā <note>The Bodiless One</note>
16. Abhitodyamā <note>The One who strives everywhere</note>
17. Analpā <note>The Great (Non-small) One</note>
18. Vyakta-vibhavā <note>She of Manifest Power</note>
—all of whom take the form of diverse agitations. || 10 ||

These Shaktis total two hundred and fifty-five. One should worship the Goddess surrounded by them to attain all desired goals. || 11 ||

---

**Commentary:**

This section follows the sequence. || 6 || The phrase "groups of Shaktis of a similar nature" is stated because of their independent nature. "By others" refers to those like Madanā and the rest, who are distinct from the Shaktis arising from the syllables of the mantra. "Embodying the madness and intoxication of the God of Love" is a description that applies generally to all the groups of Shaktis. || 7 ||

Through the verse beginning with "One hundred and twenty-five," the author teaches the one hundred and twenty-five Shaktis who form the Goddess's retinue, who are the essence of the mantra's syllables, as well as their corresponding mantras. The meaning is as follows:

One should pronounce the twelve vowels accompanied by the nasal dot <note>the *bindu*, creating sounds like Am̐, Ām̐, etc.</note>, then pronounce the one hundred and twenty-five syllables of the mantra in order, and finally say, "I worship the sandals <note>original: *pādukā*; a term of deep respect for a deity's presence</note> of the Shakti of Form." By this method, there arise as many mantras and Shaktis as there are syllables—one hundred and twenty-five. || 8 ||

With the three verses beginning with "Madanā" and ending with "attain all desired goals," the author teaches the two enclosures <term>original: āvaraṇa; the concentric layers of a mandala</term> consisting of the twenty Shaktis and the Shaktis of the mantra syllables. # In the Eighth Chapter ] Declaration of the Worship Sequence, its Fruits, and Other Matters.

In the center, having invoked that Bhagamālā, who possesses the form already described <note>original: *uktavarūpiṇīm*; referring to the visualization of the goddess provided in earlier verses</note>, and having performed the rites of installation and stabilization, one should worship her with the ritual offerings. || 17 ||

Having prepared the water offering <term>arghya; a respectful libation of water, flowers, and grains</term> with the "limb" mantras and the root mantra, and having sprinkled it using the root mantra, one should then worship the powers of Attachment and Aversion <note>original: *rāga* and *dveṣa*; here personified as gatekeeping Shaktis</note> on the two sides of the door. || 18 ||

Likewise, one should worship Sound, Touch, Form, Taste, and Smell <note>The five sensory perceptions personified</note> as before. In the space between the two inner circles, one should similarly worship the Six Limbs <note>the *ṣaḍaṅgāni*; ritual points associated with the heart, head, hair-tuft, armor, eyes, and weapons</note>. || 19 ||

Within that Bhagamālā circle, one should worship Madanā and the other attendants. In the center, around the Goddess, one should also worship the six weapons. || 20 ||

Then, one should worship the Goddess with the sixteen prescribed offerings <term>upacāra; traditional hospitality rites such as incense, lamps, and food offerings</term>. Using the first letter of the mantra, one should perform the two food offerings <note>original: *bali*; offerings left for the spirits or secondary powers</note>. || 21 ||

By rotating the three lines of a triangle to produce a circle, and then producing another circle within it with a radius measured as one-fifth of the tip, one should triple the measurement of the diameter plus a sixteenth part. Dividing that total measurement into ten parts, and marking each part around the heart ten times, one should draw twenty transverse lines in the "cow-urine" pattern <note>original: *gomūtrikā-krama*; a zig-zag movement resembling the path of a walking cow, used to create complex intersections</note> moving from the outside inward and then outward again. When this is done, there will be twenty triangles whose tips touch the outer circle and the inner circle. On the square path <term>vīthi</term> which is four inches wide and divided into inner and outer sections, one should worship the stated powers in the order described.
|| 13 || 14 || 15 || 16 || 17 ||

**Sprinkling**—refers to the self and other ritual objects. **From the root**—by means of the root mantra <note>the *mūla-vidyā*</note>. **As before**—the phrase "possessing the form" includes the three-syllable mantra. || 18 || **In the middle of those two circles**—in the path between the two circles of the pericarp of the five-petaled lotus. And so, in the sequence starting from the northwest, in the middle of the twenty-five triangles located between them, moving clockwise from the tip. || 19 || **Within that Bhagamālā**—in the middle of the twenty triangles located between the two circles. Then, **around the Goddess** means this: the six weapons of the Goddess are in the middle of that circular path. Dividing that circular path with six transverse lines into six parts, one should worship the weapons in order, clockwise from the tip, starting from the upper left hand and ending with the lower right hand. || 20 || **With the first letter**—this means along with the first syllable of the mantra. The first syllable of the root mantra, accompanied by the nasal dot <term>savinduka; the 'bindu' or 'm' sound indicating the resonance of consciousness</term>, should be used twelve times...

### In the final stage, one should worship the remainder with the Sixty of Nectar, O Goddess!
### The letters *Jyā*, *Kaṃ*, *Dāva*, *Ambu*, and *Hṛt* are combined with their own "Illusion" to form the fivefold Nectar. || 36 ||

### These five, when differentiated by the vowels, become eighty; likewise with the "Illusion."
### When those are deprived of the "impotent" letters, they become sixty; and likewise they become so with the "Illusion." || 37 ||

### Through this sixty, one hundred [and sixty] are specified as the "Nectar-form" among the groups of letters.
### Their application is prescribed everywhere within this Tantra. || 38 ||

The tradition is that one should write each individual letter of the mantra within the "Illusion" syllable <note>original: *māyā*; refers to the seed-syllable HRĪM</note>. || 33-34 || The remaining parts [of the mantra] are one hundred and twenty-five in number. || 35 ||

**In the final**—meaning in the fourteenth Yantra. **With the Sixty of Nectar**—which will be described by the phrase *jyā-kaṃ-dāvo-’mbu-hṛt-svena*.
**Jyā** is the letter *Ja*.
**Kaṃ** is the letter *Sa*.
**Dāva** is the letter *Tha*.
**Ambu** is the letter *Va*.
**Hṛt** is the letter *Sa*.
**With their own** <note>original: *svena*</note>—meaning with the *Bindu* <term>the nasalization dot representing concentrated consciousness</term>.
**With the Illusion**—meaning with the *Visarga* <term>the two dots representing the creative emission of the Goddess</term>. || 36 ||

**Likewise with the Illusion**: Among the "Nectar letters" which are counted as eighty when combined with the vowels and the *Bindu*, if one removes the *Bindu* and joins the *Visarga* everywhere, those same letters become eighty more. This is the meaning.
**Deprived of the impotent** <note>original: *ṣaṇṭha-hīnaiḥ*</note>—meaning deprived of the four vowels *Ṛ, Ṝ, Ḷ, Ḹ* <note>In Sanskrit grammar, these vowels are often called "neuter" or "impotent" as they do not initiate certain grammatical changes</note>.
**And likewise they become so with the Illusion**—this means that even when joined with the *Visarga* and deprived of the four "impotent" vowels, there are sixty letters. || 37 ||

The statement **"One hundred is specified through the sixty"** <note>This refers to 160 total</note> is due to the inclusion of the four "impotent" vowels.
**Among the groups**—in the *mātṛkā* <note>the alphabet conceived as a series of "Little Mothers" or divine powers</note>.
**Nectar-form**—the five-letter group is what remains. Here, without the fourteen <note>This may refer to a specific grouping of vowels</note> "impotent" ones, the count of Nectar-letters is exactly one hundred and twenty.

The sequence for constructing the fourteen Yantras containing these one hundred and sixty Nectar-letters is as follows:
Having drawn three circles with one-inch intervals between them, creating inner and outer divisions, one should draw a hexagon according to the measurements in the middle of the third innermost circle. In the center of that, one should draw a "source-triangle" <term>yoni; a downward-pointing triangle</term> with equal lines facing oneself. In the middle of that, one should write the syllable *Hṛllekhā* <note>the seed-syllable HRĪM</note> together with the name [of the person or object]. Within the "Illusion-part" <note>the space inside the syllable HRĪM</note>, one should write the first letter of the mantra.

In the outer triangles, one should write the second, third, and fourth letters of the mantra. In the six outer corners, one should write the letters from the fifth to the tenth, proceeding clockwise from the top. In the circular path outside of that, one should write the remaining one hundred and twenty-five letters of the mantra beginning from the eleventh letter, as before. In the circular path outside of that, one should likewise write the letters [of the alphabet] with the *Bindu*, as before. In the circular path outside of that, one should likewise write the letters from *A* to *Kṣa* with the *Bindu*. This is the first Yantra.

The second and remaining thirteen...

### [In the Tenth Chapter] The Description of Yantra Construction.

> **Hear, O Beloved, the application of the fourteen diagrams (yantras): subjugation, attraction, paralysis, health, victory, and prosperity. || 39 ||**
> 
> **By the prescribed method, one should achieve success regarding gems, elephants, horses, cows, sheep, and buffalo, in order; and likewise for men, women, and kings. || 40 ||**
> 
> **By means of the Nectar-letters <note>original: amṛtārṇaiḥ</note>, the letters of one’s own root-mantra <note>original: svamūlārṇaiḥ; the "root" is the primary mantra of the practitioner's deity</note>, those dedicated to the Goddess Lalitā, and the fourteen syllables of the Nityā deities—along with one hundred and sixty-one... || 41 ||**
> 
> **...totaling four hundred and fifty-six—hear now, O Beloved! the method of constructing the diagrams with these, and their respective fruits. || 42 ||**

In the final twelve of the [fourteen] diagrams, the ten letters written in the first diagram are placed above. In the second, the same; in the third, the third set of ten, and so on. Having written them sequentially in the twelve, one should encircle them with the remaining letters on the outside. To achieve the count of one hundred and twenty-five letters, one should start from the letter following the tenth letter written in the middle and write the mantra letters, ending with the letter preceding the middle *hṛllekhā* <term>the seed-syllable HRĪM, the "heart-streak"</term>. 

In the final fourteenth diagram, one should write five Nectar-letters with dots <note>original: savindukāni; referring to the bindu or nasalization dot representing concentrated power</note> in five of the corners of the hexagram <term>ṣaṭkoṇa</term>, starting from the second corner. On the outer path of the remaining mantra letters, one should place the sixth Nectar-letters with dots, interspersed in all directions with vowels and the letter *ṭha*, followed by those same letters with the creative emission <note>original: visarga; the two dots indicating the outward flow of energy</note>, and then the five Nectar-letters with the creative emission. In this way, one should write the one hundred and twenty-five letters. || 39 ||

Through the two verses beginning with **"Of the fourteen..."** and ending with **"...one should achieve success,"** the author teaches the fourteen results of those fourteen diagrams in their proper order. There, the phrase "one should achieve success by the prescribed method" refers to practices such as wearing the diagram on the body or placing it in a specific location. || 39-40 ||

Through the one and a half verses beginning with **"By means of the Nectar-letters..."** and ending with **"...it is stated,"** the author teaches the specific numbers of mantra letters for the construction of the thirty-three <note>The text mentions thirty-three here, possibly referring to a larger sub-set of diagrams or a specific ritual variation</note> diagrams, as well as the total sum. 

The meaning is as follows: 
- One hundred and six Nectar-letters.
- One hundred and twenty-five letters of the root-vidyā <term>primary sacred mantra</term>.
- The fourteen letters of the Nityā-vidyā (excluding those for Lalitā which are already counted without the root-vidyā).
- One hundred and sixty-one additional letters.
Summing these together, the total is stated to be **four hundred and fifty-six**. || 41 ||

Through the latter half of the verse beginning with **"With these..."**, he introduces the diagrams themselves and their fruits. There, "with these" means with the letters of the quantities just stated. || 42 ||

### [The Tenth Chapter Continued]
### The Construction of the Thirty-Third Yantra

> **Having fashioned a triangle and an eight-petaled lotus, with two outer circles, one should place the Syllable of Illusion <note>original: māyāstham; refers to the seed-syllable HRĪM</note> in the center, along with the name [of the person for whom the ritual is performed] written inside the triangle. || 43 ||**
> 
> **Between the two intervals... [and] on the outside, moving through the five and the eight, one should write the fourteen letters. In the middle of the circles, one should write the Mother-alphabet <term>Mātṛkā; the sacred sequence of Sanskrit letters from A to Kṣa</term>. || 44 ||**
> 
> **Having written these, one should employ them once they are perfected through worship, fire-offerings, recitation, and consecration. This thirty-third diagram is joined with the Power-syllable <note>original: śakti; the syllable HRĪM</note> and the five Nectar-syllables. || 45 ||**
> 
> **It is used in cases of severe fever, chills, and quartan fever <note>original: cāturthike gade; a fever that recurs every fourth day, historically associated with malaria</note>; likewise for pox, measles, and ailments arising in the eyes or the abdomen. || 46 ||**

---

With the three verses beginning with "The triangle..." and ending with "the five," the author teaches the method for constructing the thirty-third Yantra using the four hundred and fifty-six letters previously mentioned, comprised of the five Nectar-syllables and the Power-syllable known as the Heart-streak <term>Hṛllekhā; the primary seed-syllable HRĪM</term>.

Regarding this, the following is stated: With a compass set to a desired scale, one should create two circles—an inner and an outer—separated by a gap of one inch. Within the center of that, one should create a pericarp <note>original: karṇikā; the central seed-head of a lotus</note> using a circle with a one-inch interval. Outside of that, in a three-inch path, one should draw the eight petals. In the middle of the pericarp, one should draw a triangle with three equal lines <note>original: yoni; literally "womb," a common term for a downward-facing triangle in Tantra</note> whose three points touch the circle of the pericarp. 

In the middle of that triangle, one should write the Heart-streak syllable accompanied by the name, as described before. In the three corners [of the triangle], one writes the first three of the prescribed number of letters. In the two intervals between the pericarp-circle and the triangle, one writes three letters. In the eight petals on the outside, one writes eight letters, moving clockwise from the tip. Thus, one writes fourteen letters in total. In the path between the outer circles, one should likewise write the Mother-alphabet, starting with 'A' and ending with 'Ha'.

Among these letters, the first Yantra is made with the first fourteen letters. The second Yantra is made with the fourteen letters following those initial fourteen. In this same sequence, using fourteen letters at a time, one creates the other thirty Yantras. The final [thirty-third] Yantra is made with the eight letters remaining after the first thirty-two Yantras are assigned, combined with the five Nectar-syllables and the Heart-streak syllable, thus totaling fourteen letters. Having created these thirty-three Yantras, one should employ them through worship, fire-sacrifice, recitation, and consecration. Here, the worship and recitation are performed using the Mother-alphabet and the specific letters written in the diagram; this is the rule for all letter-based Yantras. || 45 ||

With the fourteen verses beginning with "In fever..." and ending with "ailments," the author teaches the thirty-three fruits of the thirty-three Yantras in their proper order. Regarding "quartan" <note>original: cāturthike</note>—it refers to the peace or relief from pain on the fourth days...

### [Chapter 8]
### The Description of the Construction of the Worship Chakra

**...in the case of affliction by Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, Piśācas, and serpents <note>original: uraga; refers here to divine or demonic serpent beings</note>; in the distress caused by child-seizing spirits <term>Bālagraha; supernatural entities believed in ancient Indian medicine to cause sudden illnesses in infants</term>, in misfortune, in barrenness, and in the distress caused by enemies. || 47 ||**

**In legal disputes, in cases of madness, in the face of the king’s anger, and likewise in the fear of thieves; in the event of being possessed by the six groups of Ḍākinīs <note>original: ḍākinyādi-gaṇaiḥ; a class of semi-divine, often fierce, female spirits</note> or by Brahma-rākṣasas <note>original: brahma-rākṣasaiḥ; the powerful and fierce spirit of a deceased learned person who misused their knowledge</note>. || 48 ||**

**In cases of urinary disorders, jaundice, and the various diseases arising from the three imbalances <term>Doṣas; the three fundamental energies of the body in Ayurveda—Vāta (air), Pitta (fire), and Kapha (water)</term>, one should apply the thirty-three diagrams in the order described, according to the prescribed method, O Goddess! || 49 ||**

->**The General Worship of the Nityā Goddesses**<-

**Listen, O Goddess! I shall now describe the general worship of the Nityā goddesses, beginning with Kāmeśvarī, according to the union of the principal deity and her subordinate parts. || 50 ||**

**One should draw twenty lines from East to West and twenty from South to North. By this, O Parvati, square cells are produced. || 52 ||**

---

On the paper... [Regarding verses] 46 and 47: The phrase "being possessed by the six" <note>original: ṣaḍbhirākrāntyām</note> refers to the six types of results or conditions mentioned. || 48 ||

With the verse beginning "Beginning with Kāmeśvarī," the author introduces the fifteen types of general worship for the fifteen Nityās, who are subordinate parts <note>original: aṅga; "limbs" or components</note> of the goddess Lalitā, by means of their mutual relationship as parts and whole. In this context, "of the Nityās beginning with Kāmeśvarī" implies the remaining fifteen. || 50 ||

With the verse beginning "Of those," the author instructs on the collection of mantra-syllables for the fifteen deities—Lalitā and the others—and introduces a general "Chakra for Desired Worship" <note>original: kāmya-pūjā-cakra</note> using those letters. In this context, "with those" refers to the syllables of the quantity previously stated [296]. || 51 ||

Through the twenty verses beginning with "East to West" and ending with "one should worship," the author teaches the construction of the complete worship chakra, the sequence of worship, and the specific materials for the ritual. Within those, the first eleven verses—beginning with "East to West"—describe the construction of that chakra and the sequence of worship for your fifteen Nityā goddesses...

# [Chapter 8] Determining the Worship Circle

> Having drawn two squares on the outside and doors in the four directions, one should worship twelve deities in order at the sides and the corners of the doors. || 60 ||
>
> Brahmi and Maheshvari <note>Two of the Eight Mother Goddesses (Matrikas)</note> are at the Western door, on the left and right sides. Kaumari and Vaishnavi are at the Northern door; Varahi and Indri are at the Eastern door. || 61 ||
>
> Chamunda and Mahalakshmi are at the Southern door. Those situated in the corners starting from the Northwest <note>original: vāyv-ādi-koṇagāḥ</note> are the powers of Space <term>Desha</term>, Time <term>Kala</term>, and Sound <term>Ākāśa-śabda; literally 'sky-sound'</term> in the stated order. || 62 ||
>
> One should worship them in their prescribed forms with ritual offerings: spirits, meats, and well-prepared fish. || 63 ||

---

This refers to the Fourteen Nityas <note>The Eternal Goddesses</note>. || 58 || 59 || 60 || "At the Eastern" — the word "door" is implied. || 61 || 62 ||

In summary, these eleven verses explain the following: Having created a square with an internal span of thirty-five <note>The text shows a correction from twenty-five to thirty-five</note> finger-widths <term>Aṅgula; a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to the width of a thumb</term>, one should draw another square two finger-widths inside it. Within that two-finger gallery <term>Vīthī; a ritual path or corridor within the diagram</term>, there are doors in the four directions.

Having established the square measurement with four primary lines, one should strike eighteen lines horizontally and eighteen lines vertically <note>original: sūtrāṇy-āsphālya; "striking the threads," a method of snapping a chalk line to create a grid</note> at intervals of one finger-width. In the very center, forty-nine squares are unified into a single space. There, one should produce two circles using a compass <term>Bhrama; a tool for drawing circles</term> so that they just touch the lines of the square. In the middle of that, one should construct a fourteen-petaled lotus with a pericarp <term>Karṇikā; the central seed-pod of the lotus</term>.

In the center of that pericarp, one should draw a triangle <term>Yoni; a symbol of the feminine creative power</term> that touches the three circles and has equal lines. In the middle of that, one should write the Heart-syllable <term>Hrllekhā; the sacred seed-syllable 'Hrīṃ'</term>. Outside of that, from the West to the Northwest <note>original: vāyv-antam</note>, one should write the Heart-syllable in each of the fourteen petals in a counter-clockwise direction <note>original: vāmāvartena</note>.

Outside the square of that lotus, in the four directions starting from the East, one should unify four squares from the inner and outer divisions. In those spaces, one should write the Heart-syllable containing the "desired objective" <note>A specific name or wish inscribed within the mantra</note> as previously described.

Starting from the thirty-six outer squares <note>Representing the 36 Tattvas or elements of reality</note> and moving inward in a clockwise direction, one should write the letters of the Vidyas <note>Sacred mantras</note> of the fifteen Nityas—from Kameshvari to Chitra—in order, filling the two hundred and fifty-five squares.

At the four outer doors of the square, from the West to the South, one should worship the eight powers—Brahmi and the others—on the left and right sides according to the directions. In the corners starting from the Southwest <note>original: nirṛty-anteṣu</note>, one should worship the powers of Space, Time, and Sky-Sound.

Inside those, in the previously mentioned squares, one should worship the letters of the fifteen Nityas in a clockwise direction, starting from the Northeast square. In the four Heart-syllables in the directions (starting from the West) which contain the "desired objective," one should worship the goddess Bhagamalini. Finally, in the very center of everything, one should worship her with her specific mantra.

With fried cakes, rice pudding, milk, plenty of ghee mixed with sugar, bananas, jackfruit, and other fruits, and also with honey. || 64 ||

One should please the Goddess with these food offerings, as well as with dance, song, and other arts. The ritual may last for one night, three nights, five, or seven. || 65 ||

It may also last for nine nights <term>Navarātra; a traditional nine-night festival period</term>, a fortnight, a full month, or even longer. It could last for a year, ending in the month of Phalguna <note>The last month of the Hindu lunar calendar, typically February-March</note>; such worship destroys all suffering. || 66 ||

In the event of unfavorable planetary alignments, chronic illnesses, or unnatural occurrences; when there are omens from the gods or various types of malevolent magic <term>Abhicāra; rituals intended to harm or influence others</term>. || 67 ||

In times of poverty, failure to achieve victory, famine, or oppression by enemies, and in other terrible hardships, this worship grants all desires. || 68 ||

Having prepared it on a pedestal, on level ground, or upon a ritual platform within a mandala <gloss>(1)</gloss>, one should worship using the prescribed forms and materials <gloss>(2)</gloss>. || 69 ||

"Prescribed forms" means that the fourteen Nityās located on the outer petals possess the same physical forms, ornaments, and weapons as the central Nityā. Here, the specific food offerings mentioned are to be offered in the fifteen circles described in the sequence for the "desire-driven" worship <term>Kāmya; rituals performed to achieve a specific result or benefit</term> of the primary and secondary deities. The author will state later that in all cases, for both "occasional" <term>Naimittika; rituals triggered by specific events like eclipses or illness</term> and "desire-driven" rites, one should perform the worship of all sixteen Nityās with these specific materials. || 63 || "With honey" refers to the product of bees. || 64 || 65 || 66 || "Chronic illnesses" refers to the eight major diseases, such as those caused by wind <note>referring to Vāta in Ayurvedic medicine</note>. "Occurrences" refers to the gods—because of the opposition of the deities, one performs...

### The Commentary named "Manoramā" on the Tantrarāja

Having made [the diagram] on a surface shaped like a **Yoni** <term>Yoni: a triangle representing the divine feminine source or vulva</term> with a measurement of twenty-six inches, one should place eleven lines at intervals of twelve inches. || 92 ||

Through this, there arise more than a hundred triangles—one hundred and forty-four, to be precise. Within these, one should write the **fourteen-syllable mantras** <note>original: *manvākṣarāṇi*; these refer to the specific syllables of the Goddess Bhagamālinī</note> continuously, entering in a clockwise direction. || 93 ||

In the remaining nine spaces in the center, which are endowed with the **nine groups of letters**, one should then write the names of the **Nine Masters** <note>original: *Nāthān*; the lineage of spiritual masters</note> joined with the name of the target and the specific ritual action. || 94 ||

One should write this repeatedly everywhere, following the rotation [of the diagram]. || 95 ||

At midnight, one should meditate on that target woman, imagining her consumed by the **fire of the God of Love** <note>original: *madanavahni*; the heat of intense desire</note>, her heart stolen away, and her hands placed over her head in a gesture of supplication. || 96 ||

[Visualize her] with disheveled hair, rolling eyes, glowing a deep red, her body trembling like a cloth banner tossed by the wind. || 97 ||

Devoid of discernment, intoxicated, and having transcended pride, shame, and fear—one should meditate on her thus. One should worship the **Chakra** <term>Chakra: the geometric ritual diagram</term> with the Goddess below, unclad <note>original: *digambarām*; literally "sky-clad"</note>. || 98 ||

One should worship using Japanese roses <note>original: *japā*; Hibiscus rosa-sinensis</note>, pomegranates, *Bandhuka*, *Kinshuka*, and other fragrant flowers. || 99 ||

After thrice-seven nights <note>21 days</note>, she arrives in the state described above, overcome by intoxication. Until her body falls <note>meaning: for the rest of her life</note>, she remains like his inseparable shadow. || 100 ||

---

The author now teaches the construction of the **Woman-Attracting Yantra**, its drawing, the method of its worship and recitation, and the nature of its result. In that context, "fourteen-syllable mantras" refers to the one hundred and thirty-five syllables of the secret knowledge of **Bhagamālinī** <note>original: *Bhagamālinī-vidyā*; Bhagamālinī is the "Goddess crowned with a garland of yonis"</note>. || 91–93 ||

Regarding the phrase "endowed with the nine groups": Having divided the sixteen vowels starting with 'A' into two groups, one should then divide the remaining letters from 'Ka' to 'Ksha' into groups of five. By doing so, the sequence begins with *ḷ, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, sa*...

The procedure <note>original: *vṛttāntaḥ*</note> involves creating a **Yoni** <term>Yoni: a triangle representing the divine feminine source</term> with two lines measuring twenty-six inches, facing oneself. One should divide one line of that triangle into twelve parts, making eleven marks. By doing the same on the other two lines and drawing lines from mark to mark in sequence, one should strike eleven lines across. When this is done, one hundred and forty-four chambers <note>original: *vastrāṇi*; literally "cloths," but here referring to the triangular divisions or cells of the grid</note> are produced. 

Within these, moving in a clockwise direction starting from the upper left, one should write the mantra <note>original: *vidyā*</note> of the Goddess **Bhagamālinī** one hundred and thirty-five times. In the remaining nine spaces in the center, one should write the nine specific syllables belonging to each of the Nine Masters of the nine letter-groups. Furthermore, in all one hundred and forty-four triangles, one should write the names of the "target" and the "practitioner" according to the previously described method. Having invoked the Goddess into the center, meditated upon her, and worshipped her as prescribed, one will obtain the stated results within the specified time. || 100 ||

### Commentary on the Ninth Chapter

In the previous eighth chapter, after teaching the ritual procedure for the third Nitya goddess, Bhagamālinī, the text now teaches the ritual for the fourth Nitya, **Nityaklinnā**. This occurs in the ninth chapter, which consists of approximately one hundred verses, starting with "Now, concerning the sixteen..." and ending with the physical form.

In this section, with the two and a half verses beginning with "Now, concerning the sixteen..." and ending with "...O Supreme Goddess," the author outlines the contents of this chapter. Regarding the phrase *the mantra has been uttered previously*—it should be understood that this refers to the **third chapter**. The phrase *with them*—should be understood as "along with the surrounding powers <note>original: *parivāra-śaktibhiḥ*</note>." The phrase *specified*—refers to the collection of topics to follow. || 2 ||

With the three verses (and a half) beginning with "With the first..." and ending with "...one should place," the sequence for the **six-limbed ritual projection** <term>Ṣaḍ-aṅga-nyāsa: the practice of "placing" syllables of a mantra onto specific parts of the body to divinize the practitioner</term> is taught. Here, the phrase "with two" refers to the two syllables of the knowledge-mantra <note>original: *vidyā-akṣarābhyām*</note>. The "remaining" refer to the five limbs in their proper order. || 3–4 || Regarding the six-limbed...

### [In the 8th Chapter] Description of the Preliminary Ritual of the Knowledge [Mantra], etc.

With food <term>andhasā: specifically cooked rice or grain offerings</term> sprinkled with ghee, or with fragrant flowers, one should perform the fire offering in the number stated previously, concluding the rite as before. || 21 ||

Having worshiped the Goddess, then having dissolved her into one's own self as before <note>original: *udvāsya*; the ritual act of withdrawing the deity from an external image or diagram back into one's own heart</note>, and having performed the ritual placement <term>nyāsa: the practice of "pinning" or installing parts of a mantra onto specific parts of the body</term> and recited the pair of hymns, one should conduct oneself as being one with Her. || 22 ||

Listen, O Goddess! I shall speak of the thorough spiritual practice <term>sādhana: a disciplined path of practice</term> of the Knowledge <gloss>1. variant: Now [I speak] of the Knowledge</gloss> which bestows desired fruits, whereby the practitioner becomes fit for the ritual applications. || 23 ||

With controlled senses and eating only sacrificial food <term>havis: pure food like milk, fruits, or unsalted grains offered to the fire</term>, one should recite the mantra during the three transitions of the day <note>the *sandhyās*: dawn, noon, and sunset</note>. As before, one should perform one hundred thousand recitations, and then one-tenth of that number for the fire offering and the water libation. || 24 ||

One should offer the libations with flowers of the Madhūka tree <note>the Honey Tree, *Madhuca longifolia*</note> soaked in the "three sweets" <note>honey, ghee, and sugar</note>, or with flowers of the Bakula tree, and with water scented with camphor, sandalwood, and musk. || 25 ||

Thereafter, one becomes fit for the ritual applications of the Nityā goddesses <gloss>2. variant: fit for the application by a Brahmin</gloss>, being likewise intent on their constant worship. A devotee who recites the mantra a thousand times daily should perform what is prescribed and not otherwise. || 26 ||

---

The meaning is that one should perform the food offering <note>original: *bali*</note> at the beginning and the end with the mantras of Cara and Kurukullā. || 18 || In the order stated. **As before** means having performed the ritual acts starting with the "Face of the Fire" <note>the preparation of the sacrificial fire</note>. || 20 || **With food** (*andhasā*) means with cooked rice. **As before** means following the sequence of the daily worship. **The number stated** means the number which is one-tenth of the total recitations. **That** refers to the fire offering (*havana*). || 21 || **Having worshiped** means using the Root Mantra. **As before** means the union within one's own heart in the form of pure light. **The pair of hymns** refers to the hymn consisting of five verses and the hymn consisting of twelve verses. This recitation of the pair of hymns is common to all the Nityā goddesses. **One with Her** (*tan-mayaḥ*) is as explained before. || 22 ||

With the four verses starting with **"of the Knowledge"** and ending with **"not otherwise,"** the author instructs the method for the preliminary ritual of the Knowledge <term>puraścaraṇa: a set of five activities (chanting, fire offering, libation, bathing the deity, and feeding priests) performed to "awaken" a mantra</term>. There, the word **whereby** means through the spiritual practice. || 23 || **During the three transitions** means being intent on worship in the same manner as the practice for the goddess Lalitā. **As before, one hundred thousand** means the number of recitations corresponds to the number of letters in the mantra, according to the age <note>meaning the specific requirements for the current world-age</note>. || 24 ||

With the verse starting with **"with Madhūka flowers,"** he describes the materials for the fire offering and libations of the preliminary ritual in their proper order. There, **soaked in sweets** refers to the Madhūka flowers being drenched in the "three sweets" and then offered in the fire—this is the implied meaning. || 25 || **The stated ritual applications**. With the phrase **"intent on constant worship,"** etc., the following is said: even after the preliminary ritual is complete, the practitioner—intent on constant worship, reciting the mantra a thousand times every day, devoted to the Teacher of the Knowledge, and skilled in the ritual applications—should not do otherwise. This rule applies to all the deities. || 26 ||

## [In the 8th Chapter] In the Tantra-Rāja, accompanied by the commentary named Manoramā

By offering red lotuses smeared with the "three sweets" <note>original: *trimadhvakta*; a ritual mixture of honey, ghee, and sugar</note> in the fire sacrifice, one attains prosperity <term>Lakshmi: the goddess of wealth and beauty</term>. Likewise, with red water lilies, one may bring women under one's influence. || 27 ||

By offering jasmine, malati, jati, and rose-lotus flowers <note>these refer to various species of fragrant jasmines and the "hundred-petaled" lotus or rose</note> boiled in the milk of a white cow that has a calf of the same color... || 28 ||

...one attains fame, knowledge, wealth, health, good fortune, and victory. By offering the blossoms of the Golden Shower tree <note>Sanskrit: *āragvadha*; the *Cassia fistula*, known for its bright yellow flowers</note> smeared with honey... || 29 ||

...one obtains gold, the paralysis of enemies, or even the calming of the anger of kings and others. By offering red oleander flowers <note>Sanskrit: *karavīra*</note> smeared with ghee... || 30 ||

...one obtains red garments, and the subjugation of women, kings, and fish <note>original: *matsya*; likely a symbolic reference or a specific class of beings in this context</note>, as well as success in jewelry, vehicles, and commerce as desired. || 31 ||

By offering salt and white or other <gloss>black</gloss> mustard seeds smeared with their respective oils at midnight, one may draw a desired woman to oneself. || 32 ||

One should offer <unclear>black-petaled</unclear> <gloss>1. variant: *yadānāda*</gloss> flowers smeared with oil in the middle of the night; within a month, the enemy will surely be afflicted with intense pain and fever. || 33 ||

By offering the seeds of the marking nut <note>Sanskrit: *āruṣkara*; the *Semecarpus anacardium*, which produces a caustic juice</note> smeared with ghee and food at night, incurable ulcers will appear on the enemy's body, defying the efforts of physicians. || 34 ||

With the body thus burning, the enemy goes to the abode of Death <note>original: *Yamālaya*</note>. The same result is achieved with the seeds of the *dvāraka* <gloss>3. variant: *raṅgolajaiḥ*: perhaps derived from the Indigo plant</gloss> soaked in their respective oils. || 35 ||

***

The six verses beginning with "By lotuses" and ending with "woman" teach the attainment of various fruits through different types of fire sacrifices. There, the phrase "with a calf of the same form" means a white calf. || 27 || 28 || 29 || 30 || 31 ||

"Other" means black [mustard seeds]. "Or" signifies an alternative. "Smeared with their oils" means smeared with the oil of the two types of mustard seeds mentioned. || 32 ||

Through the three verses beginning with "Smeared with oil" and ending with "by these," the author teaches the fire sacrifice for the subjugation and punishment of enemies. There, "by the seeds of those" refers to attaining the stated results through the offering of marking nut seeds. || 33 || 34 || 35 ||

### [In the 2nd Chapter] Description of Sacrifices for Desired Results

By offering black pepper <note>original: *marīca*</note> and mustard seeds smeared with ghee into the fire at night for a period of one month, one will certainly bring a desired woman who is afflicted with the "fever of love" <note>original: *kāma-jvara*; a poetic way of describing intense romantic longing or obsession</note>. || 36 ||

By offering black pepper combined with mustard seeds seven times each night, one can consistently bring even a bride who is otherwise difficult to attain due to her fortitude, pride, or high-born family. || 37 ||

One should offer food and ghee daily, or at least one hundred and eight times. By this practice, O Dear One! <note>Addressing the Goddess, a common feature in Tantric dialogues</note> one becomes an enjoyer of a world filled with abundance. || 38 ||

By sacrificing rice grains <note>original: *śālī*</note> mixed with ghee, one attains the state of "The Dark One" <note>original: *kālīm*; here likely referring to the power or prosperity associated with the goddess Kali</note>. By offering mung beans <note>original: *mudga*</note> into the fire, one's desires are fulfilled and misfortunes are averted. || 39 ||

One should perform a sacrifice at night using a doll <note>original: *puttalī*; an effigy used in ritual magic</note> made from the wood of a tree associated with the target’s birth star <term>Nakshatra: the 27 lunar mansions of Vedic astrology</term>, or made of dough mixed with dust from the target’s feet, or crafted from mustard, pepper, and salt. || 40 ||

The doll should be cut with a very sharp weapon into twelve parts: the two forefeet, the two shanks, the two knees, the two thighs, the section below the navel, the torso up to the throat... || 41 ||

...and the head. By offering these twelve parts in order into the fire, men, women, and even kings... || 42 ||

...come under one’s control <term>Vashya: the tantric art of subjugation or enchantment</term> within seven days; they become afflicted with a feverish longing for the practitioner, or may even meet their end through this singular focus of will. || 43 ||

---

#### [Commentary: The Manoramā]

With the two verses starting with "By pepper..." and ending with "...a bride," the text teaches the fire sacrifice for attracting women. The meaning there is easy to understand. || 36 || 37 ||

With the two verses starting with "With food and ghee..." and ending with "...shall be," the text teaches the attainment of results through the prescription of sacrificing substances like food. In that context, the meaning of the sentence is established. The word "and" indicates a conjunction of effects. || 38 || 39 ||

The "Target's Star Tree" <note>original: *sādhyarkṣa-vṛkṣa*</note>: The author will personally describe the trees corresponding to the twenty-seven stars, starting with Ashwini, later on. "Rajī" refers to mustard. "Lona" refers to salt. The meaning is as follows: one should sacrifice a doll made of the wood of the tree associated with the target's birth star, or a doll made of dough mixed with the dust of the target's feet, or one made of mustard, pepper, and salt ground into a fine paste, following the prescribed order. || 40 ||

"The two forefeet" refers to the front parts of the feet severed at the ankle joints. "The two shanks" refers to the legs severed below the knees...

# In the Tantraraja with the Commentary named Manorama

With dough <term>Pishta: flour mixed with water used to create ritual effigies</term> mixed with jaggery, black pepper, and cumin, one should fashion a doll. Then, one should place the name of the target <term>Sadhya: the person intended to be influenced or "subjugated" by the ritual</term> upon its heart. || 44 ||

One should cook that doll in the ghee <note>original: *ghṛta*; clarified butter</note> that remains from a sacrifice performed with the target's name <note>original: *sa-nāma-homa-saṃpāta-ghṛta*; the residual consecrated oil from a fire ritual where the target's name was invoked</note>. Then, without touching it with the tips of one's fingers, one should recite the mantra a thousand times. || 45 ||

Having worshiped that doll smeared with the residual ghee, one should eat it while reciting the mantra of that science <term>Vidya: specifically refers to the mantra or goddess-centered knowledge being practiced</term>. Men, women, and even kings shall remain under his influence until the end of their lives. || 46 ||

By making a round cake <note>original: *vṛttam*; a circular sacrificial bread or *apūpa*</note> from that same dough and clearly inscribing the target's name in the center, and then cooking and eating it as described before... || 47 ||

...they will be under his influence for a period of one year. By making it with the specific syllables of their name, and then cooking and eating it <note>See footnote 1</note>, one subjugates them for half that duration <note>six months</note>. || 48 ||

---

<note>The following is the Manorama commentary explaining the verses above and the conclusion of the previous section.</note>

**Regarding the ritual cutting described previously:** The doll is cut from the left thigh and above. From the pair of thighs to the joint of the waist, and below the navel—meaning, the piece cut from the region of the navel. The remaining piece is that which is divided up to the heart. **From the neck**—meaning, the piece cut from the throat. || 41 || **By the head**—meaning the part situated above the throat. **In sequence**—meaning one should offer these into the fire after cutting them in the order mentioned. || 42 || **Through undivided union** <note>original: *ananya-yogataḥ*</note>—meaning through the meditation on one's oneness with the Self. || 43 ||

With the three verses beginning with **"With dough"** and ending with **"until the end of their lives,"** the text teaches the subjugation of men, women, kings, and others through the eating of a doll. There, **the doll** should be of the measurements previously described. **In the heart**—meaning the name of the target is written on the heart of the doll, as previously instructed. || 44 || **In the ghee remaining from a sacrifice with the name**—this refers to the ghee left over from each offering of the mantra performed alongside the target's name. **That doll** [is what is cooked]. || 45 || **Having worshiped**—this is done using the ritual for "infusing life" <term>Prana-pratishtha: the ritual of breathing life into an image or object</term>. **Smeared with ghee**—smeared with the residual consecrated ghee. **The mantra of that science**—meaning, while maintaining the intent of consuming the target. || 46 ||

With the two verses beginning with **"from that same"** and ending with **"half that duration,"** the text teaches subjugation through the eating of a specific type of cake. **From that same**—meaning with the flour mixed with jaggery and other ingredients mentioned before. **Round**—meaning a circular cake. **As before**—referring to the cooking in residual ghee and other steps. || 47 || **They**—men and others. **A year**—the grammatical use of the second case indicates a continuous duration of time. **"They will be"**—due to the divine nature of the text, the specific form is used to imply "may they become" or "they shall certainly be." **With the syllables of their name**—meaning the dough is prepared and shaped into the form of the letters of the target's name.

---

(1) "By eating it, one subjugates them for half that time"—this is a variant reading found in the original manuscript. <note>original: *khādaṃstu vaśayettāṃ tadardhakam*</note>

### In the 9th Chapter | Description of Libations for Various Desired Outcomes | Page 168

Through libations <term>Tarpana: a ritual act of "satiating" or pleasing a deity or power by pouring out liquids, usually water</term> performed with the water of coconut fruits, women are brought under one's influence. By using waters scented with camphor, men shall remain under one's control. || 49 ||

Through libations with salt water, all shall become his servants <note>original: *kiṅkara*; one who carries out the bidding of another</note>. Likewise, with water mixed with salt, women are brought under control. || 50 ||

By performing libations while reciting someone's name using pure water for a month, or half that (a fortnight), or for seven nights, that person shall remain under his control day and night. || 51 ||

By performing libations with coconut water scented with <term>Ketaki: the fragrant screw-pine flower</term> and mixed with camphor <note>original: *indu*; literally "the moon," a poetic term for camphor due to its white color and cooling nature</note>, women become so captivated they would offer their very lives and their own wealth. || 52 ||

Through libations with waters scented with <term>Nameru: the Suraparni tree, often associated with divine qualities</term>, kings are brought under control. Libations with waters scented with <term>Champaka: a highly fragrant yellow flowering tree</term> are pleasing to everyone. || 53 ||

Through libations with waters scented with <term>Patala: the trumpet flower</term> and <term>Shatapatra: literally "the hundred-petaled," referring to the lotus or rose</term>, one becomes a constant source of wonder to the whole world. || 54 ||

Libations performed with waters scented with musk <note>original: *kastūrī*</note> grant all successes. Libations with water scented with the fragrance of camphor and sandalwood... || 55 ||

...certainly brings about the total accomplishment of one's desired goal within a <term>Mandala: a ritual cycle of forty-nine days</term>. One who uses water mixed with barley meal <note>original: *saktu*; roasted grain flour</note> becomes wealthy in riches and grain for a long time. || 56 ||

***

**Commentary**

"Having done" is the meaning. "Likewise" means as stated previously. "Sprinkled with the residual ghee" <note>This refers back to the *sam-pāta-ghṛta* or the consecrated oil mentioned on the previous page</note> refers to those being influenced, such as the men and others. "Half of that" means six months <note>Referencing verse 48</note>. As stated before, the second method achieves results in six months. || 48 ||

With the eight and a half verses beginning with "Coconut fruits" (49) and ending with "destroying obstacles," the text teaches the application of various libations for desired outcomes. In that context, "waters of the coconut fruit" means the liquid found inside the coconut. || 49-50 ||

|| 51-52 || *Nameru* is the *Suraparni* tree. || 53-54 || *Indu* refers to camphor. || 55 || "From a mandala"—a *Mandala* is a name for a period of forty-nine days. "Wealthy" means being filled with riches, grain, and so on. || 56 ||

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for constructing Yantras (mystical diagrams) from the previous page. While the preceding text introduced the basic geometry of the hexagon and circles, this section provides the specific mathematical and alphabetic permutations required to create a set of fifty-five distinct Yantras used for various magical and spiritual purposes.</meta>

-># Explanation of the Fifty-five Yantras and their Results<-
->[From the 9th Chapter]<-

Listen in order, O Supreme Goddess! to the five groups of five, totaling five hundred combinations <note>The text suggests a complex mathematical expansion of these diagrams</note> formed by the union of each of the Elemental Letters <note>original: *bhūtākṣarāṇāṃ*; these are specific seed-syllables representing Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Space</note>. || 65 ||

In all of these, draw a circle on the outside and write the Mother-Alphabet <term>Mātrikā: the "Little Mothers," referring to the Sanskrit alphabet from A to Kṣa, which is believed to embody the creative energy of the universe</term> around it. Afterward, the ritual application <note>original: *viniyoga*; the specific way a mantra or tool is put into practice to achieve a result</note> is described. || 66 ||

There are three diagrams for subduing <note>original: *vaśye*; the act of attracting or bringing others under one's influence</note>, two for drawing someone toward oneself <note>original: *ākarṣe*</note>, and two for pacification <note>original: *śāntyāṃ*</note>. The various types are conceived by changing the placement of the letters of the [target person's] name in the center. || 67 ||

Thus, the variation of their results becomes twenty-seven-fold. Listen to the remaining ones, O Goddess of the Gods, in the order of their ritual application. || 68 ||

[They are] immobilization <note>original: *stambhana*; to paralyze an enemy's speech or actions</note>, delusion <note>original: *mohana*; to cloud the mind</note>, then hatred and expulsion <note>original: *uccāṭana*; to force someone to leave their home or position</note>, as well as death, affliction through diseases, and that which causes the ruin of a family lineage. || 69 ||

***

**[Commentary]**

In the corners and directions of the center [referring to Verse 63]... the ten Elemental Letters in order—these are the ten letters mentioned in the coded instructions for extraction <note>original: *uddhāra-saṃketo*; the cryptic method used in Tantric texts to "extract" or reveal a hidden mantra</note>. || 64 ||

The four verses starting with "The hexagon..." [from the previous page] and ending with "Afterward..." [Verse 66] explain the following: Having drawn a circle of the desired size, draw a hexagon <note>original: *ṣaṭkoṇa*</note> in its center. Outside that circle, draw two more circles at a distance of one finger's width apart. In the path created by the outermost circle, write the fifty-one letters from 'A' to 'Kṣa' along with the nasal dot <note>original: *savindukāni*; specifically the *Anusvara* or 'ṃ' sound which empowers the letters</note>, starting from the top in a clockwise direction.

In the very center of everything, write the *Hṛllekhā* <term>Hṛllekhā: the seed-syllable "HRĪM," known as the "streak of the heart," representing the Goddess Bhuvaneshvari</term>, which is the beginning of the root-mantra <note>original: *mūlavidyā*</note>, along with the letters of the person's name as described before. Write the six letters from the second to the seventh syllable of the mantra in the six corners of the hexagon, starting from the top and moving clockwise.

Write the remaining four letters of the mantra in the four cardinal directions in the path outside the hexagon, clockwise. In that same path, but in the four intermediate corners (from Northwest to Southwest), write the ten Elemental Letters in groups of two or three as appropriate to the ritual. This is the **First Yantra**.

To make the **Second Yantra**: place the second letter of the mantra in the center, and write the remaining letters in order around it, ending with the first letter. By placing each of the eleven letters of the mantra in the center one by one in this manner, eleven yantras are produced.

Within each of these eleven, by varying the placement of the ten "Elemental Spoke" letters according to the prescribed order, fifty-five yantras are created <note>11 central mantra variations × 5 element groupings = 55 total yantras</note>.

Regarding the ritual application <note>original: *viniyoga*</note>: "Three for subduing"—meaning there are three types of yantras for the three categories of subduing: women, men, and kings.

**In attraction**—Regarding the attraction of women and men toward each other, there are two types of attraction. **In pacification**—regarding calamities and ill-omens, there are two types of pacification, and thus two Yantras. **The conception of their variations**—means the specific design of the Yantra variations. || 67 ||

**Thus**—in the manner stated. **The variation of their results**—the variation in the fruits of the Yantras. **Twenty-seven-fold**—this includes the three types for subduing, attracting, and pacifying, along with the twenty-four other types starting with immobilization <note>original: *stambhana*</note>. Through the five verses starting with "Subduing is threefold" and ending with "by that," the following is explained:

Among the fifty-five Yantras mentioned, there are three for the subject of subduing. There are two for the subject of attraction, and two for the subject of pacification. For the **others**—the twenty-four types of applications starting from immobilization and ending with the *Maṇḍalas*—there are two for each. Thus, for the fifty-five Yantras, there is a twenty-seven-fold purpose. In all of them, by the skill of arranging the letters of the name, various threefold conceptions are made. Because of this, each of these fifty-five Yantras is capable of granting twenty-seven types of results. || 68 || 69 || 70 || 71 ||

With the two and a half verses starting with **"In the *Vidyā*"** and ending with **"joining,"** the author teaches the sixteen Yantras formed by the letters of the Root *Vidyā* as modified by vowels. In that context, the **eleven** [letters] are: *Ha, Ra, Na, Ta, Ya, Ka, La, Ma, Da, Va, Sa*. <note>The text lists the specific consonants used in the mantra</note> Here, because there is an absence of conjunct vowels <note>original: *saṃyuktasvara*</note>, only the basic vowels are used. || 72 ||

**In the prescribed Yantras**—this refers to the linear arrangement of the fifty Yantras previously mentioned. **Using eleven divisions**—this means using the eleven letters as modified by the vowels. || 73 || This is what is being stated here...

# Chapter Ten

Now, hear the procedure for Bheruṇḍā, who is the fifth among the sixteen Nityās <term>Nityās: a group of sixteen goddesses representing the lunar days in the Śrī Vidyā tradition</term>, O wise one! I shall describe it to you according to the rules. || 1 ||

The extraction of the mantra <term>mantroddhāra: the coded process of revealing a secret mantra</term> was explained in the third chapter. [Here I shall describe] the ritual "limbs" <term>aṅgas: parts of the body correlated with mantra syllables</term>, the deities of the protective enclosures <term>āvaraṇa-devatās: subsidiary deities arranged in circles around the main goddess</term>, the sequence of worship, and the mystical diagrams <term>yantras</term>, as well as the method for the subjugation of enemies. || 2 ||

[I will also explain] the application of ritual pegs <term>kīla-prayoga: the use of consecrated stakes or "nails" in protective or aggressive magic</term>, victory for kings in battles, and the protection of cities, elephants, and horses, as well as the protection of the kingdom, in proper sequence. || 3 ||

One should perform the "six-limbed" placement <term>ṣaḍ-aṅga-nyāsa: a ritual where six parts of the mantra are assigned to six points on the body</term> using the six syllables found between the first syllable and the final two syllables of the mantra. [These are placed] at the cranial fissure <note>original: *randhra*; refers to the *Brahmarandhra* at the crown of the head</note>, the third-eye center <note>original: *ājñā*; the space between the eyebrows</note>, the mouth, the throat, the heart, the navel, and the two feet <note>original: *paṭṭadvaye*; literally "the two tablets," interpreted here as the feet</note>. || 4 ||

One should place the nine-syllable mantra preceded by the placement of the Mother-Letters <term>mātṛkā-nyāsa: the ritual installation of the Sanskrit alphabet on the body</term>. Then, O Pārvatī, hear the description of the Powers <term>śaktis</term> residing in the enclosures and the visualization <term>dhyāna</term>. || 5 ||

---

->**Now begins the Tenth Chapter.**<-

In the previous ninth chapter, after teaching the knowledge <note>original: *vidyā*; refers to the mantra and ritual system</note> of the fourth Nityā, Nityaklinnā, the author now teaches the procedure for the fifth, Bheruṇḍā Nityā. This is done through the hundred verses of the tenth chapter, beginning with "Now, among the sixteen..." and ending with "...consisting of that."

Within this, the subject matter of the chapter is outlined in the first three verses ending with "...in sequence."

In those verses, "the application of ritual pegs" <note>original: *kīla-prayogān*</note> refers to specific methods for the suppression of enemies by installing ritual stakes made of specific trees during certain lunar mansions <term>nakṣatras</term>. || 1 || 2 || 3 ||

With the two verses starting with "the first and last" and ending with "O Pārvatī," the author teaches the system of ritual placements <term>nyāsa</term> and related practices.

In that context, the phrase "by those located between the first and the last two" means that by setting aside the very first syllable and the final two syllables of the mantra, one should perform the six-limbed ritual with the remaining characters. "Fissure" refers to the *Brahmarandhra* <note>the spiritual opening at the top of the skull</note>. "Ajna" is the space between the eyebrows. "On the two tablets" refers to placing two syllables on the two feet. || 4 ||

"Preceded by the placement of the Mother-Letters" means this is performed after the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* which will be described later. || 5 ||

In the outer circuit, one should worship the eight goddesses led by Brāhmī <note>The Eight Mothers or Mātṛkās</note> as well as the Powers of the Ages <note>original: *yuga-śaktīḥ*; refers to the four cosmic eras: Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali</note>. || 6 ||

Having fashioned two squares <term>bhūpura: the earth-enclosure or "city of the ground" that forms the outer border of a yantra</term> provided with doors in the cardinal directions, [one should place] an eight-petalled lotus within it, with two circles in between. || 11 ||

### The Manoramā Commentary

With the five verses beginning with "In the outer" and ending with "eight-fold," the author teaches the goddesses of the protective enclosures <term>āvaraṇa-śakti: subsidiary deities who guard the central divinity</term>. Among these:
The **Powers of the Ages** (*Yuga-śaktis*) are the Power of the Kṛta Age, the Power of the Tretā Age, the Power of the Dvāpara Age, and the Power of the Kali Age.
Here, the eight powers led by Brāhmī are located in the doors situated in the West and other directions, positioned on the two sides (the right side of the deity and so on), and the Powers of the Ages are in the corners such as the Northwest, proceeding in a clockwise direction. || 6–7 ||

**According to the stated ritual method:** This refers to the method of joining the specific name of the deity between the two seed-syllables <term>bīja: "seed" sounds that concentrate divine power</term> and the seven-syllable mantra suffix, while proceeding in a clockwise direction. The tradition holds that when no specific instructions are given for surrounding deities, one should always place the two seed-syllables at the beginning and the seven-syllable sequence at the end. || 8 ||

Similarly, starting from the Southwest direction... || 9–10 ||

With the three verses starting with "Two squares," he teaches the "Daily Worship Circuit" <term>nityā-paryāya-cakra</term> of the Goddess. In this context, the eight-angled figure is within the two square enclosures. The meaning is as follows: Having drawn an east-west line, one should divide the measure of that line into ten parts. Having made a mark at the end of the third part from the eastern tip and from the western tip according to that measure, and having fixed the eastern tip of that line, with the measure of that western mark...

->### Chapter 10: On the Results of the Primary Diagram and Other Matters<-

With the first three seed-syllables starting from the second, and with the sixth, one performs acts of restraint. With the other three and the final two, one performs acts of grace. || 24 ||

Having drawn a six-pointed star <note>original: *ṣaṭkoṇa*; a hexagon formed by two intersecting triangles</note> and a pair of circles, one should write in the center the second syllable joined with the name of the target. One should write the other three syllables in the corners. || 25 ||

In the lower ones <margin>Some manuscripts read: "in the spaces"</margin>, those which have arrived should always be written. In the space between the two circles, [one should surround them] with the syllables of the wind <note>original: *pavanārṇakaiḥ*; refers to the syllable 'Ya' and its variations associated with the element of Air</note> combined with the name of the target. || 26 ||

Having enveloped these and chanted the mantra, one should place the diagram in a cremation ground <term>śmaśāna: a site for disposing of the dead, considered a site of great power for "fierce" or aggressive rituals</term> when the enemy’s astrological sign enters the eighth house. This results in causing discord <term>vidveṣaṇa: a ritual intended to create division or hatred between people</term>. || 27 ||

By grinding neem-leaf juice and writing with charcoal from a cremation ground on the skin of a spotted cat or mouse, it occurs two thousand times (?) <note>This likely refers to the number of mantra repetitions required for the ritual to take effect</note>. || 28 ||

One should write this diagram on the skin of a leopard’s face or on cowhide. Having written one’s own name first and then the enemy’s... || 29 ||

---

### The Manoramā Commentary

With the verse beginning "With the first three starting from the second," the author divides the syllables of the secret knowledge <note>original: *vidyā*; referring to the mantra of the goddess</note> into those used for restraint <note>original: *nigraha*</note> and those for grace <note>original: *anugraha*</note>.

In that context, the phrase "with the other three and the final two" implies: "one should perform peaceful rites" <note>original: *śāntika*</note>. || 24 ||

With the eleven verses starting with "A six-pointed star" and ending with "restraint," the author teaches the primary diagram of this knowledge, centered on the second syllable. Through this diagram, he teaches four types of applications: causing discord <note>original: *vidveṣaṇa*</note>, victory in debate <note>original: *vāda-vijaya*</note>, eradication <note>original: *uccāṭana*</note>, and killing <note>original: *māraṇa*</note>.

In this context, the "second syllable" is the sound *Kroṃ* <note>original: *kroṃkāra*</note>. The "other three" are the third, fourth, and sixth syllables of the mantra. || 25 ||

"In the lower ones" refers to the three downward-pointing triangles of the six-pointed star; in these, one should write those syllables along with the visarga <note>The ':' aspiration mark in Sanskrit</note>. By this, it is implied that the upper triangles should contain syllables marked with the bindu <note>The nasal 'm' dot</note>. After writing the ten digits of the wind-syllable in a clockwise direction, one should write the name of the target <note>original: *sādhya-akṣara*; the name of the person the ritual is intended to affect</note>. || 26 ||

"These" refers to the four syllables—the second, third, fourth, and sixth. "In that" refers to the time of the rising of the eighth astrological house. || 27 ||

"Spotted" <note>original: *pṛṣat*</note> refers to a cat. "Akhu" refers to a mouse. (This marks the end of the section on the application of causing discord...)

## The Tantrarāja with the Manoramā Commentary

### Chapter 10: Ritual Applications for Victory and Destruction

Having placed the upper skin over the lower one, one should join them beneath a heavy stone. After reciting the mantra the prescribed number of times, one will conquer that legal opponent. <note>original: *prativādin*; refers to an adversary in a debate, dispute, or lawsuit</note> || 30 ||

Just by looking at the face of the practitioner, the opponent's effort is paralyzed. He will flee, unable to answer, or he will simply say, "I am defeated." || 31 ||

With orpiment <term>haritāla: a bright yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used as a pigment and in alchemy</term> ground and mixed with the juice of turmeric <note>original: *niśā-rasa*; turmeric is often used in rituals to "paralyze" or "stain" an intention</note>, one should write the diagram for victory in debate in the manner previously described. || 32 ||

Written in blood on the skin of a Ruru deer <note>a species of deer often mentioned in ancient Indian zoology</note>, it should be buried in the house of the enemy at the prescribed time, accompanied by the stated sequence of worship and recitation. || 33 ||

Through the power of this diagram, one will certainly drive the enemy away <term>uccāṭana: the magical act of "uprooting" or forcing someone to flee their home or country</term> within a month. If it is written in blood on human skin and buried in a cremation ground... || 34 ||

...accompanied by the ritual sequence of worship and recitation at the stated time, within a month the enemy goes to the dwelling of Yama <note>the God of Death; this implies the enemy dies</note>, afflicted with a burning fever. || 35 ||

One should write the third [syllable] in the center and the others all around it. One should then press it into beeswax, having thought of the target's astrological sign <note>original: *sādhyarkṣa-yoni*; referring to the lunar mansion (nakshatra) and birth-origin of the target</note>. || 36 ||

Written with cremation ashes and thrown into a dry or abandoned well <note>original: *naṣṭa-kūpaka*</note> at the prescribed time, it will destroy the enemy in water. <note>original: *salile ripuṃ nāśayet*; this could mean death by drowning or a watery disease</note> || 37 ||

***

**The Commentary named Manoramā**

**On Verse 28:** "That diagram"—refers to the diagram previously mentioned for the purpose of creating discord (*vidveṣaṇa*). It is written on the skin of a leopard or a cow. The substance for writing is orpiment, which will be described further on. "In the former"—refers to the tiger-faced skin. || 28 ||

**On Verse 30-31:** "The upper and lower"—refers to the two skins joined together with their respective names: the upper skin contains the name of the opponent, and the lower skin is placed beneath it. "At the two junctions"—refers to the morning and evening twilights. || 30 || 31 ||

**On Verse 32-34:** For victory in debate, one should surround the diagram with the ten syllables of the Earth element <note>original: *pārthiva-daśākṣaraiḥ*</note> previously mentioned for the purpose of "stunning" or "paralyzing" (*stambhana*). || 31 || 33 || 34 ||

**On Verse 35:** "At the stated time"—this means on the eighth night, as previously explained. || 35 ||

**On Verse 36-37:** From "The third..." until "...through the power," there are eleven verses describing the third letter of the *Vidyā* <note>the sacred mantra of the goddess</note> and its applications.

### Chapter 10: Description of the Daily Worship, the Mandala, and the Offering of Oblations

->An octagon should be made within two enclosure-squares, combined with a circle;<-
->within that, one should create a hexagon <term>ṣaṭkoṇa: a six-pointed star or six-sided figure</term> of the same form.<- || 12 ||
->Within that, one should create a triangle <term>yoni: literally 'womb' or 'source,' representing the Goddess</term>; in its center, one should worship<-
->Bheruṇḍā, the fifth Nitya <note>one of the sixteen Lunar Goddesses in this tradition</note>, surrounded by the previously stated powers.<- || 13 ||
->Having prepared the ritual water <term>arghya: a libation offered to a deity</term> using the "six-limb" and "root" mantras, the practitioner should worship facing East.<-
->He should then offer the oblation <term>bali: a ritual offering of food or materials</term> with the "sixteen-limb" mantra, at the beginning and the end in the proper sequence.<- || 14 ||
->Now I shall describe the meditation <term>dhyāna: a guided visualization used to realize the deity's form</term> of the Goddess, which grants the perfection of all goals.<-
->O Parvati! Listen to the description of the powers residing in her surrounding circles, in their proper order.<- || 15 ||
->She has a body resembling molten gold, and is endowed with three eyes.<-
->Her face is adorned with a beautiful smile, and she is decorated with divine ornaments.<- || 16 ||

---

**Commentary (The Manoramā):**

Having fixed the center point and revolving from the previous markings, one produces two "fish" <note>original: *matsya*; a technical term in Sanskrit geometry for the almond-shaped intersection of two circles, used to draw a perfect perpendicular line</note> on the south and north sides. By fixing the thread between the centers of these two "fish," one strikes the north-south line. Then, starting from the central "swan-foot" <note>original: *haṃsapada*; likely a mark or intersection point used as a reference</note>, one makes marks on the four side-lines at the desired distance. Fixing the compass at those marks, one draws "fish" at the four corners using the distance from the central "swan-foot" as the measure. In those, from fish to fish, one should successively strike the four boundary lines. When this is done, a perfect square with four chambers is formed.

There, by fixing the center of the middle "swan-foot" and revolving the compass outward to the measure of the square's corner, one draws a circle. Then, extending the four ends of the two middle lines to the edge of that circle, one should strike four lines: from the eastern end to the southern end, from the southern to the western, from the western to the northern, and from the northern back to the eastern. When this is done, two overlapping squares will produce eight corners in the eight directions. This is the method for constructing an octagon <note>original: *aṣṭakoṇa*</note> in all such contexts. "Of the same form" means including a circle. || 11 || 12 ||

"Of the same form" (in verse 13) also means including a circle. The sequence of constructing the diagram is as follows: having made two squares with gates in the four directions according to the measurements, one should place a circle inside them. Inside that, draw an eight-petaled lotus. Inside that, an octagon according to the measurements. Inside that, a circle. Inside that, a hexagon as before. Inside that, a triangle <note>original: *yoni*</note> with its own circle and equal lines. There, one should worship the Goddess in the order prescribed. || 13 ||

With the verse beginning "Ritual water..." (verse 14), the text teaches the preparation of the *arghya* and the giving of the *bali* (oblation). The meaning is that the oblation should be given at both the beginning and the end using the sixteen-limb mantra. "In sequence" refers to the oblation material being accompanied by the ritual hand-gestures <term>mudrā: symbolic gestures used to seal or direct energy</term>. || 14 ||

With the five verses beginning "Now I shall describe the meditation..." and ending with "always," the meditation of the Goddess along with her retinue is described...
