**The Commentary (Manoramā):**

He describes the daily sequence. In that context, one should visualize the weapons starting from the upper left hand and ending with the lower right hand, moving in a sequence from left to right. || 15-17 || "At other times" means during specific ritual applications. || 18 || "In the same way" means as stated previously. || 19 ||

With the verse beginning with "Thus," he teaches the conclusion of the worship. There, the word "thus" <note>original: "tathā"</note> implies the clockwise direction <term>prādakṣiṇya</term> and the state of having the same number of syllables as the two root-mantras. "By the previously stated rule" refers here to the mention of vegetable offerings and other foods <note>original: "vyañjanādikaṃ"</note>. || 20 ||

With the three verses beginning with "Bathing" and ending with "destroys him," he teaches the method of mastering the knowledge-mantra <term>vidyā-sādhana</term>, the sequence of its application, and the transgression <note>spiritual fault or danger</note> incurred by performing the sequence incorrectly. There, "nine hundred thousand" <note>original: "navalakṣakam"</note> means, according to the special rule, a number of repetitions equal to the number of syllables in the mantra, taking a "lakh" <note>100,000</note> as the unit. || 21-22 || "Moreover" means it results not only in fruitlessness but even in one's own destruction. || 23 ||

### Instructions for the Primary Yantra and its Applications

### [Chapter 10]

->That same [yantra], written with ground lead <term>vahnimūla: literally "fire-root," traditionally referring to lead or plumbum in alchemical and tantric contexts</term> and human blood on cowhide, should be placed quickly above a hearth with fire.<- || 38 ||

->By the fire burning day and night, within a month the enemy will fall into the fire <note>original: "agnau pated ripuḥ," suggesting the enemy will be consumed by fever or literal disaster</note>. The yantra is constructed with the third seed-syllable in the center, surrounded by the others.<- || 39 ||

->Using the feathers of an owl and a crow [as pens], one should write with the first-mentioned substance <note>human blood and lead</note>. Having buried it on donkey-skin in the center of a sacrificial pit, and above that—<- || 40 ||

->On the bark of the target's tree <note>The specific tree associated with the enemy's birth star or nakṣatra</note>, one should perform fire offerings <term>homa: ritual fire sacrifice</term> with Datura seeds <term>unmatta: the Datura plant, known for its intoxicating and toxic properties</term> soaked in pungent oil. Through this, the enemy certainly goes mad or dies <margin>Variant: Through the fire offering, the enemy dies</margin>.<- || 41 ||

->A ritual stake <term>kīla: a wooden pin or stake used in magic to "pin down" an effect</term> made from the target’s birth-star tree, combined with the stated yantra and bound with donkey sinews, should be buried in the enemy's town at night.<- || 42 ||

->When the moon enters the eighth zodiac sign [from the enemy's sign], within a month that town becomes a cemetery <note>original: "pitṛkānanam," literally a forest of the ancestors/cremation ground</note>. Alternatively, one may write the stated yantras on the skin of the feet of a crow, owl, crane, hawk, heron, or partridge;<- || 43 ||

->Having bound it in a corpse’s shroud <term>preta-cīra: cloth taken from a dead body or a cemetery</term>, one should bury it on a Tuesday at the specified time at a crossroads <term>catuṣpatha: a site where four roads meet, considered a powerful location for spirits and magic</term>.<- || 44 ||

->Within twenty-one days, the enemy will flee, driven mad across the ten directions. Those same yantras, placed on the skins [of the animals mentioned] and buried in the grounds of his home—<- || 45 ||

->—will destroy elephants, humans, horses, cows, donkeys, camels, goats, and buffaloes <gloss>sairibhān: buffaloes</gloss>. This happens within a week or a month, certainly due to the power of the yantra.<- || 46 ||

---

**Commentary:**

The text teaches the procedure for the **Primary Yantra** and its thirteen specific applications. Regarding the phrase "the others," it means one should write the second, fourth, and sixth seed-syllables. The phrase "from the target's birth-star" follows the same logic as previously described. "Driven mad across the ten directions" indicates the result of the ritual. The term **buffaloes** is used to explain *sairibhān*. In this section, the construction of the yantra is considered easy to perform.

# THE TANTRARĀJA WITH THE MANORAMĀ COMMENTARY

->Listen, O Goddess of the Gods, to the pacification ritual for that [harmful magic], performed through meditation on the yantra and ritual bathing. This is achieved by placing the letters of the mantra within the yantra and through the power of the mantra's meaning and visualization.<- || 47 ||

->Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, one should write the first [letter of the mantra] in the center along with the name [of the person to be protected]. On the eight petals, one should write the set of four [other letters] twice.<- || 48 ||

->One should surround the outer circle with the letters of the alphabet <term>mātṛkā: the 'little mothers' or the Sanskrit alphabet from A to Ksha</term>. By worshipping this with the previously mentioned substances according to the application—<- || 49 ||

->Various afflictions will be destroyed through the power of the mantra. Now, listen to the method for the victory of kings in battle, following the destruction of their enemies.<- || 50 ||

->One should combine each letter of the mantra with the sixteen vowels. By this, the mantra letters will number one hundred and—<- || 51 ||

->—forty-four. Listen to the construction of the yantra with these, by which victory in battle becomes certain everywhere.<- || 52 ||

***

Regarding the verses beginning with "That pacification" and ending with "power": In these three verses (and two half-verses), the author teaches five yantras using the first, fifth, seventh, eighth, and ninth letters of the Vidya <note>Vidya: specifically the mantra of the Goddess being discussed</note> to provide a pacifying ritual <term>shānti-prayoga: a ritual meant to neutralize or heal</term> against the "cruel applications" previously mentioned.

In this context, the **meditation** will be described in the chapter on meditations. **Ritual bathing** <term>abhisheka</term> means placing the letters in the center of the yantra and performing the repetition <term>japa</term> of those five letters as before. || 47 || 48 ||

**The previously mentioned** [substances] refer to the materials for writing used in pacification rites, such as white sandalwood, camphor, etc., as well as white flowers. **According to the application** refers to the standard methods of sprinkling or pouring. 

The meaning is this: Having constructed an eight-petaled lotus of appropriate size and two circles outside it, one writes the first letter in the center of the pericarp <note>The central seed-pod of the lotus</note> along with the "target" <note>sādhya: the person for whom the ritual is being performed</note>. Then, moving clockwise from the top, one writes the fifth, seventh, eighth, and ninth letters twice on the eight petals. In the outer circular path, one writes the alphabet from 'A' to 'Ksha' clockwise. This is the **first yantra**. By placing each of the other four letters in the center [one by one] and surrounding them with the remaining letters, one creates five yantras in total that pacify the previously mentioned disturbances. || 49 ||

Regarding the verses beginning with "Victory" and ending with "becomes": In these thirteen verses, the author teaches the modification of the mantra letters with vowels, their total count, the construction of yantras with them, and their specific applications. In this context, by saying **each letter of the mantra**, it is not intended that one should only use non-repeating letters <note>The commentator is clarifying a technical point about how to count the 144 letters</note>. || 50 || 51 || 52 ||

### [Chapter 10] Description of the Application of the Count of Letters Modified by Vowels, and so on.

->One should draw thirteen lines from East to West and thirteen lines from South to North. By this, as many squares <term>koṣṭhāni: cells or compartments in a grid</term> are created throughout.<- || 53 ||

->Having formed an octagon, one should then draw two circles on the outside. Inscribe the letters in order, starting from the Northeast <note>original: 'Śiva', the deity of the Northeast</note> and ending in the Southwest <note>original: 'Nirṛti', the deity of the Southwest</note>.<- || 54 ||

->Within the nine squares belonging to the fourteenth letters <term>manvarṇa: syllables corresponding to the number fourteen</term>, one should write the name [of the person to be protected]. In the eight outer corners, one should write the letters starting from the second syllable.<- || 55 ||

->In the intermediate spaces, one should write the first letter between the two circles. One should then place those same letters intertwined <gloss>(1)</gloss> <term>vidarbhitam: a ritual method of interweaving the letters of a name with the letters of a mantra</term> with the letters of the alphabet <term>mātṛkā</term>.<- || 56 ||

->Having written this on a cloth and made it into a banner <term>dhvaja</term> for use in a military expedition <note>original: 'ranodyame'</note>, one should display it; by that, the enemies flee in the ten directions.<- || 57 ||

***

**As many** — This means the number of letters, which is one hundred and forty-four. **Throughout** — In the form of a perfect square. || 53 || **An octagon** — As described previously. || 54 || 55 || **Those** — The letters of the mantra <note>Vidya</note>. **With the letters of the alphabet** — With the letters of the alphabet combined with the "subject" <note>Sadhya: the person for whom the ritual is performed</note>. **Intertwined** — Interwoven as described in the next verse. One should write them.

By these four verses, starting with "East to West" and ending with "one should place," the following is stated: Having drawn thirteen horizontal and vertical lines at equal intervals to form a grid, one should draw a circle around it that just touches the corners. Outside of that, one should draw a square as before, and outside of that, draw two circles with a one-inch gap between them.

In those squares, one should write the letters modified by vowels, starting from the Northeast and ending in the Southwest, beginning each row at the top and ending at the bottom. There, in the nine squares designated for the fourteenth letters, one should write the name of the subject. Outside of that, in the eight corners moving clockwise, one should write the eight letters starting from the second letter of the mantra. The first letter should be written in the eight spaces between those corners. In the outer circular path, one should write the mantra letters interwoven with the letters of the alphabet and the name of the subject.

Whichever letter of the mantra, when joined with a vowel, becomes a "Manu" <note>the 14th syllable</note>, the name of the subject should be written in the square where that letter falls. This applies to the squares associated with the nine letters of the mantra. It is said here that in these nine squares, the second letter of the mantra is joined with the syllable **Om**, and the fourth letter of the mantra is joined with the syllable **Om**...

<header>Eleventh Chapter.</header>

Now, among the sixteen Nityas <term>Nitya: "Eternal" goddesses representing the sixteen phases of the moon</term>, she who is proclaimed as the sixth is the sacred knowledge of **Vahnivāsinī** <note>original: "Vahnivāsinyāḥ"; Vahnivāsinī translates to "She who dwells in fire," signifying her association with the transformative power of heat and light</note>. Her mantra is taught to you as having nine letters. || 1 ||

I shall now describe her ritual components: the placement of letters <term>Lipinyāsa: the ritual practice of "painting" or mentally projecting the letters of the alphabet onto the body</term>, the meditation, the worship with her associated powers, the method of her ritual practice, and the specific applications. || 2 ||

I will explain these through the different types of fire sacrifices and mystical diagrams. Listen, O Beloved! One should join the second seed-syllable of the mantra with the long vowels. || 3 ||

Ending with the syllable of Māyā <note>The syllable *Hrīṃ*</note>, one should perform the ritual placement on the six limbs using the hands. One should then place the nine letters of the sacred knowledge into the **nine orifices** of the body. || 4 ||

One should perform a pervasive placement <term>Vyāpaka: a ritual gesture where the hands move over the entire body to distribute the mantra's energy</term> with the complete mantra to achieve identity with the Goddess. This pervasive placement should be performed in the practice of all such sacred knowledges. || 5 ||

By doing so, the practitioner becomes one with Her; through this, successes <term>Siddhi: supernatural powers or spiritual accomplishments</term> quickly arise by the grace of the gods. || 6 ||

->Now begins the eleventh chapter.<-

In the previous tenth chapter, after teaching the ritual rules for the fifth Nitya, Bheruṇḍā, the text now teaches the rules for the sixth Nitya, Vahnivāsinī. This is covered in the eleventh chapter, which consists of one hundred verses ending with the word "on earth." With the two and a half verses starting with "Now, among the sixteen..." and ending with "O Beloved," the author outlines the contents of the chapter. With the five verses (and a half) starting with "Knowledge" and ending with "is proclaimed," the four types of ritual placements <term>Nyāsa: the rhythmic "touching" of body parts while reciting mantras to sanctify the physical form</term> are taught. In that context, "should join with long vowels" refers to the long vowels ending with the Māyā syllable—specifically the six long vowels: ā, ī, ū, ai, au, and aḥ <note>These are the vowels used to empower the seed syllables during the ritual</note>. || 3 || "In the nine orifices"—this refers to the two eyes, the two ears, and the two nostrils. The remaining three of the nine letters are placed in the mouth, the genitals, and the anus, in that order, within the nine openings. || 4 ||

# Instruction on Ritual Placement, Meditation, and Related Rituals

### Chapter 11 (Continued)

For all goddesses, one should first perform the six-limbed ritual placement of the Mother <term>Mātṛkā: the Sanskrit alphabet personified as the "Mother" of all mantras</term> as well as the placement of the Mother herself. Afterward, one should perform the specific placement prescribed for that particular deity. || 7 ||

In the case of **Lalitā** <note>The supreme form of the Goddess in this tradition</note>, however, this is said to be done specifically through the eight groups of letters. Therefore, for her, it is described as a letter-by-letter placement. || 8 ||

->**The Visualization of the Goddess**<-

One should meditate upon her as resembling molten gold, a beauty in the flower of her youth. Her face is like a lovely, smiling lotus, and her eyes are long like lotus fibers. || 9 ||

She is endowed with eight arms and is radiant with ruby ornaments. Her garments are tinged red by the shimmering rays of her ruby-encrusted crown. || 10 ||

She is dressed in yellow silk and wears a girdle with jeweled anklets. She shines with clusters of ornaments composed of a mixture of precious gems and pearls. || 11 ||

Her presence is like the orb of the full moon. She holds a red lotus, a conch shell, and a sugarcane bow. In her left hands, she carries a white water-lily <note>original: "kahlāra"</note> and a golden horn. || 12 ||

In her right hands, she holds arrows of flowers and a citron fruit. She is surrounded on all sides by her attendant powers <term>Shaktis: feminine personifications of divine energy</term> who appear exactly like herself. || 13 ||

Having meditated in this way, one should worship **Vahnivāsinī** <note>original: "Vahnivāsinī"; meaning "She who dwells in fire"</note>, whose body is the entire universe. Her attendants are **Jvālinī** <note>The Blazing One</note>, **Visphuliṅginī** <note>The Sparkling One</note>, **Maṅgalā** <note>The Auspicious One</note>, and **Sumanoharā** <note>The Very Beautiful One</note>. || 14 ||

---

**Commentary:**

One should place the nine letters of the mantra starting from the Southeast. The pervasive placement <term>Vyāpaka: a ritual gesture covering the whole body</term> is done as described previously.

Regarding the phrase "the six-limbed placement of the Mother": I [the commentator] do not elaborate on this here because the placement of the Mother and its six-limbed ritual will be explained in the fifteenth chapter concerning **Kulasundarī** <note>The eleventh Nitya goddess</note>. || 7–8 ||

Through the five verses beginning with "molten gold" and ending with "whose body is the entire universe," the text instructs the practitioner on the daily worship meditation of the Goddess along with her retinue. Regarding the weapons: one should visualize them in the left and right hands, proceeding from the top downwards. || 9–13 ||

# The Ritual Mandala and the Attendant Shaktis

### In the Tantrarāja, with the Commentary Named Manoramā

The various <term>Shaktis: feminine personifications of divine energy</term>, who are marked with gold, are to be worshipped in the eight corners of the diagram. Starting from the front, one should proceed in a clockwise direction. || 15 ||

# Chapter 11: On the Results of Special Worship and Desire-Oriented Fire Sacrifices

->One should worship the two deities in the east and the west respectively.<-
->When the specific ritual limbs are not mentioned, one should prepare the respectful water offering <term>arghya: a ritual reception offering usually consisting of water, milk, and herbs</term> using the "limb" and "root" mantras. || 24 ||<-
->If the substance for the fire-sacrifice <term>homa: the act of pouring offerings into a consecrated fire</term> is not specified, one should use clarified butter <note>original: "ghṛta"</note> or food.<-
->If the number of repetitions is not specified, it should be one thousand or one hundred as enjoined by the manual <note>original: "tantra"</note>. || 25 ||<-
->The completion of the worship, if not explicitly described, is stated to be as it was before.<-
->The method for mastering the mantra <term>vidyā: a female deity's specific melodic mantra</term> in this sacred manual, O Supreme Goddess, is also the same. || 26 ||<-
->Because it does not depend on other mantras, its completeness is not diminished by this.<-
->Now I shall describe the procedure for the desire-oriented fire-sacrifice which grants all that is wished for. Listen! || 27 ||<-
->Take one <term>prastha: an ancient measure of volume, approximately 750-800 grams</term> of unboiled rice and place it in a new vessel.<-
->Then take the milk of a red cow that has a calf of the same color. || 28 ||<-
->Add twice the amount of milk and cook it over a consecrated fire.<-
->Having formed a ball of the cooked rice <note>original: "siktha"</note> and moistening it with clarified butter, place it in the hand with white sugar. || 29 ||<-
->Holding it, recite the mantra one hundred and eight times, and then perform the fire-sacrifice.<-
->This sacrifice, if performed on the first day of the lunar month <term>pratipat: the first day of either the waxing or waning moon</term>, brings forth the Goddess of Fortune <note>original: "Mahālakṣmī"</note>. || 30 ||<-
->Likewise, if performed on Fridays for a year, one becomes equal to a king.<-
->On the fifth lunar day specifically, one should perform the sacrifice as described before. || 31 ||<-

The commentary explains the daily sequence of the ritual. The construction of the sacred diagram <note>original: "cakra"</note> there is easy to understand. Regarding the recitation and the fire-sacrifice:
|| 22 || || 23 || 24 || 25 || **"As before"** — this means like the conclusion of the worship of the goddess Lalitā. **"In that way"** — this means like the discipline for mastering Lalitā's mantra. This implies that for mantras ranging from one syllable to nine syllables, if the number of repetitions is not stated, the rule follows that of the nine-syllabled mantra of Lalitā, because this ritual also involves nine syllables. **"By this"** — refers to the practitioner who accepts the instructions previously and subsequently stated in this manual. || 26 ||

There, **"in a consecrated fire"** means a fire established according to the ritual injunctions for sacrifice. **"Sikthakam"** means a ball of cooked rice. **"With white"** means including sugar. || 27 || 28 || 29 ||

---

Regarding Verse 30: **Likewise** means as performed in the fire-sacrifice for the first lunar day <term>pratipat</term>. **Especially** is said because the fifth day is the unique lunar day <note>original: "asādhāraṇa-tithi"</note> of the goddess Vajravāsinī. **As before** refers to the fire-sacrifice of the first day. || 31 || Regarding Verse 32: **On that** refers to the fifth lunar day. **With white** implies with white flowers. || 33 || **One obtains all those things at all times from the fire-sacrifice of clarified butter**—the grammatical connection is that from the butter-offering, one obtains all desired objects. || 34 || **One who has taken a vow** means one who is accompanied by their own ritual resolution <term>saṅkalpa: a formal statement of intent made at the start of a ritual</term>.

Through the five verses beginning with "Starting from the first lunar day..." and ending with "...should perform," the author teaches that the fifteen Nityā goddesses <note>The Nityās are fifteen deities who represent the 15 days of the waxing and waning moon; the 16th is the Great Goddess herself</note> correspond respectively to the fifteen lunar days. He describes the attainment of their specific mantras and the particular modes of adoration on those days. In that context, **each embodied** means they take the form of each specific lunar day. **The resolution of the vow** is as explained previously. || 35-36 || **On which lunar day** means on those specific days. || 37-38 || **Everything** refers to the ritual applications <term>prayoga</term> and so on.

# Chapter 11 | Description of the Method for Attaining the Mantras
### Page 197

->One should perform every action only after attaining identity with the deity through the sacred mantra.<-
->O Lord! Tell me now, in full detail, the method for obtaining these fifteen mantras,<- || 39 ||

->so that they may become favorably disposed toward the practitioner.<-
->[Śiva replied:] Listen, O Goddess! I shall describe the auspicious method of obtaining the mantra,<- || 40 ||

->by which success is achieved through the yoga of union between the mantra and the deity.<-
->This is the very form of bliss—the unity of one’s own state of being with the creative power <term>māyā: the power that manifests the universe</term>,<- || 41 ||

->which many sages even today still strive to attain, O Mother!<-
->Using paste made of red sandalwood, or saffron, or vermilion, or auspicious red ochre,<- || 42 ||

->one should construct a large, clearly-drawn, and beautiful sacred diagram <term>cakra</term>.<-
->This should be the specific diagram declared for each goddess in the sequence of her daily worship.<- || 43 ||

->on that specific lunar day <term>tithi</term>, the practitioner, who is disciplined and possesses the required qualities, should face East.<- || 45 ||

->That water, if it flows toward the East, the North, or the center, bestows all success.<- || 46 ||

->burning by fire, death, disease, poverty, or exile from one's country.<- || 47 ||

->Then, the practitioner should put on two auspicious and pure garments.<- || 48 ||

Within that section, the phrase "by which method" refers to verses 39 through 43. # Chapter 11 | Description of Meditation, Diagrams, and Related Rites
### Page 188

<header>Description of Meditation, Diagrams, etc.</header>

->[ Within the 11th Chapter ]<-

One should perform the consecration and other rites in this manner, because these [goddesses] are identical to her. <note>original: "tanmayā"</note> O Supreme Goddess! In various worship rituals, these goddesses act as limbs <term>aṅga: subordinate parts of a ritual or deity</term> for one another. || 58 ||

When one goddess is established as the primary form, the others become her retinue <term>parivāra: the surrounding circle of attendant deities</term> in a similar fashion. At other times, they are considered in their previously described individual forms for the purpose of worshipping their specific principles. || 59 ||

The meditation for attaining the desired arts <term>kāmyakalā: specific powers or aesthetic perfections</term> related to them has been described in that [relevant] chapter. Thus, the entire general procedure has been fully explained. || 60 ||

"Lord! Tell me the difference between what are called *Vidyās* and *Mantras*."
[The Lord replied:] "Listen, O Goddess! to the specific distinction, whether in the context of the sacred arrangements or in general. || 61 ||

The differences between deities based on the letters of the alphabet are twofold in their entirety. The sacred formulas belonging to your [feminine] aspect are known as *Vidyās*, while those belonging to my [masculine] aspect are called *Mantras*." <note>This is a fundamental distinction in Tantra: feminine power formulas are Vidyās, masculine ones are Mantras.</note> || 62 ||

"Furthermore, O Beloved! listen to the diagrams <term>yantra: geometric focal points for meditation</term> and their respective fruits. Using the eight letters that do not repeat within the sacred formula <note>original: "vidyākṣaraiś-canādṛttāny-akṣarāṇy-aṣṭa"</note>, || 63 ||

along with the union of the vowels, one hundred and twenty-eight combinations are said to arise. Having drawn two circles, one should place an eight-pointed star between them..." || 64 ||

---

**Commentary:**

With the two and a half verses beginning with "Of these" <note>original: "āsām-ityādinā"</note> and ending with "procedure" <note>original: "vidhānakam-ityantena"</note>, the author summarizes the instructions for meditation on the fifteen Nityā goddesses—treating them as mutual limbs of one another—during daily, occasional, and desire-driven rituals. In that context, "in a similar fashion" means having a form equal to the primary goddess. "At other times" refers to when they are worshipped individually as their own primary forms. || 58 || 59 || "Described in that chapter" refers to the Chapter on Meditation. "Thus" refers to the manner previously stated. || 60 ||

With the verse and a half beginning with "Vidyā" <note>original: "vidyā ityādinā"</note> and ending with "Mantra" <note>original: "mantraka ityantena"</note>, the author teaches the difference between a *Vidyā* and a *Mantra* in response to a question. In this context, "Your deities" refers to feminine deities. "My deities" refers to masculine deities. || 61 || 62 ||

With the five and a half verses beginning with "Furthermore" <note>original: "punarityādibhir"</note> and ending with "entirety," the author teaches sixteen diagrams. In this context, "Of her" refers to the sacred formula of the Goddess Vahnivāsinī Nityā. <note>Vahnivāsinī is the "one who dwells in fire."</note> The "eight letters that do not repeat" refers to the letters beginning with *Oṃ*...

Having created them, one should place the eight letters, and eight in the middle. Having placed the **Māyā** syllable <term>Māyā: The seed-syllable "Hrīṃ," representing the power of the Goddess</term> along with the name [of the target], one should surround it with the **Tāra** syllable <term>Tāra: The sacred syllable "Om," also known as the Pranava</term>. || 65 ||

***

The letters **Ha**, **Ra**, **Va**, **Na**, **Sa**, **Pa**, and **Ma** are the eight non-repeated final letters. <note>The commentator is clarifying the specific phonetic components of the mantra being discussed</note> This involves the use of vowels combined with all [consonants]. The vowels are taken from the non-repeated groups, and the consonants follow them; this is the universal rule. || 63 || <note>This commentary refers back to the preceding verses on the previous page</note> Then, "the two"—this means having created two [circles] within the eight-pointed figure. || 64 ||

"By the **Tāra**"—this means by the **Pranava** (Om). || 65 || "Those"—as before. These are the letters modified by vowels, written in a clockwise direction. The sequence for constructing the diagram is as follows:

Using a compass <term>bhrama: a tool for drawing circles</term> at a desired scale, one should create two circles with a one-inch space between them. In the center, having made an eight-pointed figure <term>aṣṭakoṇa: an octagon or eight-pointed star</term> as before, and having placed two circles within that as well:

1. In those eight points, one should write the first eight letters starting from the top in a clockwise direction.
2. In the very center, one should write the **Hṛllekhā** <term>Hṛllekhā: The syllable "Hrīṃ"</term> accompanied by the name [of the person intended] as before, and surround it with the **Pranava** (Om).
3. In the space between the inner circles, one should write the letters of the five elements <term>pañcabhūtākṣarāṇi: seed-syllables representing Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Ether</term>, ten for each, according to the ritual action.
4. In the path between the outer circles, one should write the fifty-one letters starting from **A** and ending with **Kṣa** in a clockwise direction starting from the top.

This constitutes the first diagram. On the eight points of this very diagram, one should write the subsequent sets of eight letters derived from the vowels and modified letters of the previously written Vidyā. By doing this, sixteen diagrams are produced. Through them, one should accomplish whatever is desired. || 68 ||

***

<margin>(1) A variant reading in the manuscript suggests "inner circles of the ground" instead of "within the inner circles."</margin>
<margin>(2) A variant reading suggests "letters from A to Kṣa within the outer circles as before."</margin>

# 11th Chapter: The Description of Punishment, Favor, and Auspicious or Inauspicious Results

By simply installing it, the previously mentioned result occurs, O Goddess! <note>original: "oṣvari" — a vocative address to the Goddess, likely a variant of Ishvari</note> One should write the second [diagram] on a skull fragment and heat it at night. || 71 ||

---

### Commentary (Manoramā)

Through the thirty-three half-verses beginning with "The first" and ending with "on the earth," the author teaches sixteen diagrams. Among these, the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth (six total) are for punishment/restraint <term>Punishment: Nigraha, rituals intended to suppress or harm an opponent</term>. The eleventh is for both punishment and favor <term>Favor: Anugraha, rituals for blessing or helping</term>. The remaining ones describe auspicious and inauspicious results.

In this context, "in that juice" refers to the juice of the **red vajri** <note>original: "rakta-vajri", identified in the commentary as the Red Leadwort or Chitraka plant</note>. "Khadira charcoal" refers to the embers from the wood of the **Khadira** tree <note>original: "khadirendhanāṅgāra", Acacia catechu, known for its very hot and long-lasting coals</note>. By the word "by that," it refers to the two aforementioned [materials]. In this section, wherever a specific substance for heating is not mentioned, one should assume the use of Khadira charcoal. || 68-73 || "At the prescribed time" and "as before" refer to the previous instructions. || 74 || "On a dark garment" is connected to the preceding verse. || 75 || "As before" ...

# 11th Chapter: The Tantrarāja
## With the Commentary named Manoramā
### Page 202

Having written the name [of the target] on the **seventh** [diagram] upon a lead plate according to the rules, one should place it inside a human skull and bury it in a cremation ground <term>Cremation ground: śmaśāna, a site of powerful and often chaotic spiritual energy</term> at night. || 79 ||

At the time prescribed for the enemy, the enemy is seized <note>original: "grasyate" — meaning swallowed or possessed</note> by flesh-eating demons <term>Piśācas: a class of malevolent, flesh-eating spirits or ghosts</term>. Having prepared the **eighth** [diagram] on a clay potsherd, one should bury it at the enemy’s doorway at night. || 80 ||

Within seven days, the enemy is driven out <term>Uccāṭana: the magical act of expulsion or making someone flee their home</term> and departs from that house for elsewhere. Having prepared the **ninth** [diagram] on gold and fashioned it into a ring on an auspicious day, || 81 ||

During a successful astrological alignment <term>Siddhayoga: a favorable combination of weekday and lunar mansion</term>, at a propitious ascendant, or when Jupiter is rising, the person [wearing it] is liberated from the pains of sorcery <term>Kṛtyā: malevolent magic or a personified female deity sent to destroy an enemy</term>, untimely death, diseases, and other miseries. || 82 ||

Having prepared the **tenth** [diagram] on a silver plate and placed it somewhere within the dwelling, one should worship it to pacify the falling of stones <note>original: "aśmapāta" — a phenomenon where stones mysteriously fall on a house, often attributed to poltergeists or spirits</note> and similar disturbances. || 83 ||

Likewise, one protects those afflicted by spirits and seizures through the wearing of this [diagram]. On the **eleventh**, one should write it on a lotus [leaf or drawing] using a paste of sandalwood and camphor <note>original: "pāṭīrendu-dravaiḥ" — literally the fluids of sandalwood (pāṭīra) and the moon (indu, a poetic synonym for camphor)</note>. || 84 ||

Following the same order mentioned previously, after rolling it into a small pill, and placing it inside a phallic emblem <term>Liṅga: a symbol of the god Shiva</term> made of white wax, and having worshipped it again, || 85 ||

One should place it in the middle of honey and worship it daily at the twilights with very white, fragrant flowers according to the ritual rules. || 86 ||

Within a month, or half a month, or even seven days, enemies will certainly come under one's control. If they are diseased, they shall obtain health by [using] the clarified butter <term>Ghee: clarified butter used in rituals and medicine</term>. || 87 ||

Those afflicted by fevers, in particular, will become comfortable without any effort. [But if this diagram is] placed in the middle of sour fermented gruel <note>original: "sauvīra" — a sour liquid made from fermented grain, used here for "sour" or "bitter" magic</note>, it causes enmity between two rivals. || 88 ||

# The Tantrarāja with the Commentary named Manoramā
## [Chapter 11: Continued]

Successful delivery <note>original: "mukhaprasūtiḥ" — literally "easy birth" from the mouth of the womb</note> occurs for women through the worship and contemplation of this [sixteenth diagram]. By writing a person's name on the **sixteenth** diagram and wearing it, || 98 ||

By contemplating this essence within the heart, that very reality is made one's own.

# Chapter Twelve

Now, I shall describe the ritual procedures for the **seventh** of the sixteen Nityā goddesses <note>The Ṣoḍaśa-Nityās, or "Sixteen Eternals," are goddesses representing the sixteen phases of the moon in the Śrī Vidyā tradition</note> that I have mentioned. Listen to this teaching, which accomplishes all purposes. || 1 ||

Her secret mantra <term>Vidyā: specifically refers to a mantra of a female deity</term> has already been declared as being composed of twelve syllables. I will now explain its ritual limbs <term>Aṅgas: ritual divisions of a mantra used for protection or empowerment</term>, the placement of letters <term>Lipi-nyāsa: the practice of mentally "installing" the letters of the alphabet on different parts of the body</term>, the meditation, and the worship with the Power-Goddesses <term>Śaktis: the attendant female deities surrounding the primary goddess</term>. || 2 ||

I shall explain, in the prescribed order and according to the rules, the spiritual practice, the fire-offerings, and the various diagrams <term>Yantras: geometric diagrams used in meditation and ritual</term> according to their different results. || 3 ||

Take two [syllables], then one, then another one, then two, two, and two <note>The 12-syllable mantra is divided into six groups of 2, 1, 1, 2, 2, and 2 syllables respectively</note>. Enclosing them with the syllable of Māyā <gloss>Hrīṃ</gloss>, one should perform the six-fold ritual placement in sequence. || 4 ||

One should place the syllables of the mantra, each enclosed by the Śakti-syllables <gloss>Hrīṃ</gloss>, in groups of ten upon the eyes, ears, nose, the organ of speech, the mouth, the navel, and the secret region <gloss>the genitals</gloss> in order. || 5 ||

She is red in color, wearing red garments, and adorned with red perfumes and garlands. She has four arms, three eyes, and a crown blazing with rubies. || 6 ||

### Now Begins the Commentary on Chapter Twelve

In the previous eleventh chapter, after teaching the ritual procedure for the sixth Nityā, Vajri-vāsini, the author now teaches the procedure for the seventh Nityā, Mahāvajreśvarī. This is covered in the twelfth chapter, consisting of one hundred verses, ending with the attainment of [all goals]. Here, with the three verses beginning with "Now, of the sixteen..." the author outlines the contents of the chapter. The mantra itself was mentioned previously in the third chapter. || 1–3 ||

With the two verses beginning with "Two [syllables]," the author teaches the sequence of ritual placement (Nyāsa). Here, "one each" refers to the head and the crest <note>original: "śiras" and "śikhā"</note>. "By Māyā" means the syllable <gloss>Hrīṃ</gloss>. The "limbs" are the heart and the other ritual points. In sequence, and joined with their specific ritual gestures, they are enclosed by the Śakti syllables—that is, the <gloss>Hrīṃ</gloss> syllable—making ten in total. Excluding the two <gloss>Hrīṃ</gloss> syllables, they are placed on the speech-organ, mouth, navel, and the secret region. "One each" is the intended meaning. "The secret region" refers to the genitals. || 4–5 ||

With the five verses beginning with "Red," the author describes the meditation on the Goddess and her retinue...

For the goddess Kurukullā <note>A red goddess associated with enchantment and a specific form of the mother goddess</note>, one should perform the fire sacrifice according to the rules. || 20 ||
> 
> One should perform the fire sacrifice <term>Homa</term> with flowers dipped in clarified butter <term>Ghee</term>, or with ghee alone. One should conclude the ritual as previously described; thus has the worship been declared to you. || 21 ||

---

**Commentary:** Regarding the names "Kāla" and "Akradanā" — these are two distinct goddesses mentioned previously. || 14-15 || In the phrase "intoxicated by greed," "Madā" (Intoxication) and "Unmattā" (Madness) are two separate names. || 16 || 

"Stationed in the directions" means at the gates. "At the sides" refers to the sides of the gates. First, one should worship at the sides of the four gates beginning with the West, and then in the corner directions such as the Northwest <note>Vāyu-koṇa</note>, proceeding in a clockwise direction. In all ritual enclosures <term>Āvaraṇas: the "layers" or circuits of a mandala</term>, one should worship starting from the front and moving clockwise. || 17 ||

With the four verses beginning with "Having prepared" and ending with "declared to you," the author instructs on the sequence of the daily worship of the Goddess. There, "the previously described form" means the meditation accompanied by the visualization of the Fire, Moon, and Sun. The "Crimson Ocean" <note>Śoṇābdhi</note> refers to the Sea of Red Nectar. || 18 || 

"There" means while she is seated upon the throne. "As before" refers to the use of the Triple-Section Mudrā <term>Tri-khaṇḍā-mudrā: a specific hand gesture used to invoke the deity</term> and other rituals. "Using their names inserted into the Seven-Syllabled Mantra of Illusion" means names joined within the seven syllables of the *Hṛllekhā* <note>The seed-syllable Hrīṃ</note>. The sequence for applying the mantras to the Crimson Ocean and other elements is the same. Unless a specific ritual sacrifice is mentioned elsewhere, one should offer the sacrifice everywhere using the primary विद्या <term>Vidyā: a female deity's mantra</term> of Kurukullā. "According to the rules" refers to those accepted in this tradition. || 20 || 

"As before" means concluding by uniting the divine light with one's own self. || 21 ||

# The Rules of Conduct for the Mastery of Mantras

### [The Ritual Disciplines]

->**The Verses**<-

One should undertake this practice in the Spring or Summer, beginning on the day of the Full Moon. During this time, the seeker should subsist on pure offerings <term>Havishya: ritually pure food, specifically unsalted boiled rice</term>, or live only on milk, or perhaps eat only fruits and roots. || 22 ||

Having bathed in fragrant waters, wearing red silk garments, and remaining pure; with the body smeared with camphor, sandalwood, and saffron <note>Original: Chandra-chandana-kāshmīra</note>, the seeker's entire form should appear crimson-red. || 23 ||

With both eyes adorned with collyrium <note>dark eye-salve</note> and the mouth reddened by betel leaves; keeping a fragment of camphor <note>Original: Indu-shakala - literally "a piece of the moon," referring to the cooling and aromatic properties of camphor</note> in the mouth, with a joyful heart and the senses under complete control. || 24 ||

Maintaining silence during the twilight rituals, having committed to the sequence of the practice; eating only at night the remains of what was offered to the sacred fire, one should recite the Mantra <term>Vidyā: specifically a feminine mantra or "Knowledge" goddess</term> with a focused mind. || 25 ||

One should recite the Mantra with constant splendor <insert>Variant reading: One should worship the Mantra</insert> and feed devotees who are eager for worship. For at least three days, the devoted seeker should provide sweet milk-rice <term>Pāyasa: a traditional ritual pudding</term>. || 26 ||

Having prostrated to the deities, worshipped them, and then ritually dismissed them daily during those days; the self-controlled practitioner should approach his Teacher <term>Guru</term> and prostrate before him repeatedly. || 27 ||

Having satisfied the Teacher with gifts of wealth, grain, and clothing, and having received his permission; one should begin the daily practice and worship the Teacher with deep devotion. || 28 ||

At the conclusion of the practice, having satisfied the Teacher with wealth and hymns of praise, the practitioner becomes successful. One should never practice stinginess regarding wealth, nor exhibit pride, hypocrisy, or untruthfulness— || 29 ||

Especially in the presence of the Teacher! Having thus recited the mantra 300,000 times <note>Original: Laksha-trayam</note>, one should then perform a fire-offering <term>Homa</term> with clarified butter (ghee) equal to one-tenth of the total count of the recitation <note>i.e., 30,000 offerings</note>. || 30 ||

The eleven and a half verses beginning with "In the Springtime" and ending with "the seeker" teach the general rules of conduct common to the mastery of all Mantras. Among these: **One who eats pure offerings** refers to one who eats only boiled rice made from husked grains without salt. || 22 || 23 || 24 ||

**Having committed to the sequence of the practice** means following the order of the yoga practice as per one's own vow. || 25 ||

**Those eager for worship** refers to those who are constantly dedicated to daily devotion. || 26 ||

**In those days** refers to the days of the preliminary ritual <term>Purashcharana: the intensive repetition of a mantra to "awaken" its power</term>. || 27 || 28 ||

**At the conclusion** means at the end of the preliminary ritual. **With hymns of praise** refers to five specific verses. **The Teacher** refers to the Guru. **Hypocrisy**— <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page</note>

# Chapter 12 | The Rules for Rituals, Eligibility, Obstacles, and Fire-Sacrifices

### [The Ritual Offerings]

->**The Verses**<-

With flowers of the Golden Shower tree <term>Āragvadha: Cassia fistula, known for its bright yellow cascades</term>, <insert>Variant: Or with flowers</insert> flowers born of the Bakula tree, and those from the Madhūka or Champaka trees, mixed together daily; || 31 ||

One who is devoted and firm should daily satisfy the deity with water scented with camphor, sandalwood, musk, and saffron. || 32 ||

Thus, the seeker who has mastered the mantra <note>Siddha-mantra: a practitioner for whom the mantra has become "alive" or effective through repetition</note> should perform the rituals for specific desires <term>Kāmya-prayoga: rituals performed to achieve a specific worldly or spiritual goal, as opposed to daily obligatory rites</term>. || 33 ||

One who is devoted to the Guru, performing <insert>Variant: having performed daily worship</insert> daily duties, joined with a firm resolve; firm-minded, repeating the mantra a thousand times, knowing the power of the mantra, and self-possessed—only such a person should perform rituals for desires, and no other, O Goddess! || 34 ||

If one performs them out of ignorance, delusion, or even fickleness, they will certainly encounter misfortune, a <insert>Variant: heap of</insert> suffering, and pain. || 35 ||

One should perform a fire-sacrifice <term>Homa: the act of offering substances into a consecrated fire</term> with red lotuses soaked in the "three sweets" <note>Madhura: typically a mixture of honey, ghee, and sugar</note>. Within one ritual cycle <term>Maṇḍala: a period of 40 or 41 days</term>, one attains great prosperity and a praiseworthy form. || 36 ||

With white water-lilies <term>Kalhāra</term> soaked in honey, starting from the full moon for <gloss>three</gloss> days; one should sacrifice daily with devotion, a thousand blossoming and auspicious flowers. || 37 ||

On those specific days, one should <gloss>certainly</gloss> feed <insert>Variant: the stated deities</insert> in the manner previously described. After the fire-sacrifice, one should recite the mantra as many times as the offerings <insert>Variant: as many as the offerings made</insert> were made. || 38 ||

### [The Commentary]

All that was said here regarding the preparatory rites <term>Purashcharana: the intensive preliminary stage of mantra practice</term> applies to the preparatory rites for all types of knowledge. || 32 || "Thus" means in the manner described. || 33 ||

From the phrase beginning "Devoted to the Guru" until the end of the first half of the verse ending "certainly" [Verse 35], these two verses teach the eligibility for the ritual even without the preparatory rites, and the negative consequences <term>Pratyavāya: the spiritual sin or "backlash" resulting from the incorrect or unauthorized performance of a ritual</term> of doing otherwise. In that context, "otherwise" means someone who does not possess these qualities. || 34 || 35 ||

From the verses beginning "With red [lotuses]" until the verse ending "would be," these twenty-seven verses [describe the results] of fire-sacrifices with various substances.

# Chapter 12 | The Rules for Rituals, Eligibility, Obstacles, and Fire-Sacrifices

### [Results of Specific Fire-Offerings]

->**The Verses**<-

By offering Champaka flowers <term>Champaka: Magnolia champaca, a fragrant orange-yellow flower</term> mixed with honey a thousand times, one certainly obtains one hundred gold coins <term>Nishka: an ancient denomination of gold currency</term> within a month, as described previously. || 39 ||

Likewise, by offering three thousand Trumpet-flowers <term>Pāṭala: Stereospermum chelonoides, a tree with fragrant, reddish blossoms</term> soaked in clarified butter <note>original: "ghṛta" or Ghee</note>, one obtains various garments throughout the months following the new moon. <insert>Variant: throughout the years</insert> || 40 ||

Within a month, one also obtains camphor, sandalwood, and other fragrant items, as well as other delightful objects for enjoyment and use. || 41 ||

On the seventh lunar days <term>Saptamī: the seventh day of either the waxing or waning moon</term>, one should offer a hundred grains of rice soaked in milk. By this, an abundance of rice will undoubtedly occur within six months. || 42 ||

By offering sesame seeds on that same day, one shall attain health for a year. Likewise, on one’s three birth-stars <note>original: "Sva-janma"; refers to the natal star and its repetitions in the lunar cycle</term>, one should offer <insert>Variant: among men</insert> Durvā grass <term>Durvā: Desmostachya bipinnata, a sacred grass used in rituals for longevity</term>. || 43 ||

Free from disease and possessing great enjoyments, such a person lives for a hundred years. Or, one may offer jaggery, honey, sesame, and Durvā grass during the three birth-stars. || 44 ||

Through this, one becomes a possessor of long life, heroism, beauty, merit, and treasures <insert>Variant: a share of glory</insert>. By offering clarified butter, milk-rice, and milk respectively on those three stars, || 45 ||

One becomes respected by kings and endowed with long life, health, and wealth. From a fire-sacrifice of bananas on the seventh lunar day, one who is restrained <note>original: "vṛtaḥ"; one who follows the ritual vows</note> attains good fortune. || 46 ||

---

->**The Commentary: The Mind’s Delight**<-

The author now instructs on how to attain various types of results. Regarding the ritual diagrams <note>original: "maṇḍalān"</note>, they are as described previously. || 39 ||

**"From that day forward"** means from the full moon day onwards. **"On those specific days"** refers to all the days of the ritual application. **"To those mentioned before"**—O Knower of Wisdom!—refers to the descriptions such as those consisting mostly of sweet juices. This applies to all ritual applications. The mention of **"so much"** and so forth is common to all fire-sacrifices. || 38-39 ||

**"Months starting from the new moon"** <note>original: "darśādi-māsān"</note> means the period from one new moon to the next. || 40-41 ||

**"On the seventh lunar days"**—the underlying reason for this timing should be understood from the mouth of the Guru. Since the eleventh chapter prescribes specific worship and fire-sacrifices for the Eternal Goddesses <note>Nityās: the fifteen aspects of the moon</note> on their respective lunar days, a special rule for the sixth days should also be performed here. || 42 ||

**"On that day"** means on the seventh lunar day. **"In the three birth-stars"** refers to one’s own natal star and its correlates.

# Chapter 12 | The Results of Fire-Offerings with Various Substances

### [Offerings for Healing and Subjugation]

->**The Verses**<-

With bundles of Durvā grass <term>Durvā: Desmostachya bipinnata, a sacred grass symbolizing longevity</term> the length of a span <note>original: "prādeśa-mātra"; the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the index finger, roughly 9 inches</note>, mixed with the "Three Sweets" <term>Trisvādu: A ritual mixture of honey, sugar, and clarified butter</term>, one should perform fire-offerings daily to cure the terrible disease of Complicated Fever <note>original: "sannipāta-jvara"; in Ayurvedic medicine, a severe fever resulting from the simultaneous aggravation of all three bodily humors</note>. || 47 ||

In cases of "Great Diseases" <term>Mahāroga: A category of eight severe chronic conditions, including epilepsy and leprosy</term>, one should perform daily offerings with Durvā grass, sesame seeds, and Heart-leaved Moonseed <term>Chinnodbhava: Tinospora cordifolia, a medicinal vine also known as Guduchi</term>. One may offer these three substances individually or combined with the Three Sweets. || 48 ||

Within six months or even a year, the person will be freed from disease and become happy. During those days, the practitioner should daily recite the Vidyā-mantra <term>Vidyā: A specific sacred feminine mantra used in this ritual</term> while touching water. || 49 ||

With that consecrated water, one should perform bathing and drinking a thousand times. For the sake of liberation from disease, one should even use that same water for cooking and other preparations. || 50 ||

One should grind the wood of the tree associated with the target's birth-star <term>Nakṣatra-vṛkṣa: Ancient Indian astrology assigns a specific tree species to each of the 27 lunar mansions</term>, along with cloves, mustard, and sesame. This should be mixed with dust gathered from the target’s footsteps <note>original: "sādhya-pādottha-rajas"</note>. || 51 ||

Making a doll <term>Puttalikā: A ritual effigy or "poppet" used to represent the person one wishes to influence</term> from these substances, and inscribing the person’s name upon its heart, one should cut the doll with sharp iron weapons as described previously and offer the pieces into the fire. || 52 ||

By doing this for seven days, or three, or even a single day, the target—even if they are far away or stubborn—will quickly come under one’s control. || 53 ||

Alternatively, one may bury such a doll in the earth within the center of the sacrificial fire-pit <term>Kuṇḍa: The consecrated hearth for fire-sacrifices</term>. Placing the fire above it, one should perform daily offerings while reciting the Vidyā-mantra. || 54 ||

---

### [Commentary and Notes]

This refers to the tenth and nineteenth lunar mansions <note>The 10th is Maghā and the 19th is Mūla</note>. Likewise, "a hundred" refers to the number of offerings. "Free from disease" <note>original: "arogaḥ"</note> means "without distress" or "unperturbed." Guḍūcī is another name for the Amṛtā plant <note>literally "the nectar-plant"</note>. These three substances, starting with Guḍūcī, should be offered in sequence during the time of the birth-ascendant <note>original: "janma-lagna"</note>. Alternatively, they are offered during the three stages of life: birth, maintenance, and the remainder. "In order" <note>original: "kramāt"</note> means according to the specified sequence. || 45 || 46 ||

"Bundles of Durvā" <note>original: "dūrvāñcikaiḥ"</note> refers to bunches of the sacred grass. "Mixed with the Three Sweets" means combined with the *Trimadhura* mixture <note>honey, ghee, and sugar</note>. || 47 ||

"Great Diseases" <note>original: "mahāroga"</note> refers to the eight major ailments, such as those caused by the wind humor <note>original: "vātādyo'ṣṭau"</note>. "Heart-leaved Moonseed" <note>original: "chinnodbhava"</note> refers to the medicinal Guḍūcī vines...

# Chapter 12 | The Results of Fire-Offerings with Various Substances

# Chapter 12 | Description of the Method for Constructing the Great Vajra and Other Yantras | 213

I shall now describe the Great Vajra, the Vajra, and other mystical diagrams <term>Yantra: A geometric diagram used in meditation or ritual as a symbolic representation of a deity or the universe</term> in their proper sequence, as well as their practical applications. Listen with a concentrated mind. || 63 ||

One should draw twenty lines from East to West and twenty lines from South to North. By doing so, three hundred and sixty-one squares <term>Koṣṭha: The individual cells or chambers within a ritual grid</term> are produced. || 64 ||

Among those, in each of the four corners, one should erase five squares. There will be forty remaining <note>This refers to the squares removed from the corners to begin shaping the outer boundary</note> so that the shape becomes like a thunderbolt <note>original: "vajrākāra"; the shape of the Vajra, a ritual weapon symbolizing both diamond-like hardness and the power of a lightning bolt</note>. || 65 ||

By erasing four squares in each of the cardinal directions to create a triangle shape, the remaining squares should number one hundred and sixty-five. || 66 ||

In these squares, one should write the letters of the Primary Wisdom-Mantra <term>Ādi-vidyā: The "First Knowledge," a foundational mantra associated with the Goddess</term> all around, starting from the East. As described before, these should be differentiated by various vowels according to the previously stated rule. || 67 ||

There are one hundred and forty-four of these letters. In the center of them, O Goddess! <note>original: "Ambike"; a title for the Divine Mother, to whom the text is addressed</note>, twenty-one squares remain. || 68 ||

---

...is weakened. || 61 || In the temple of the Goddess Chandika <note>original: "Caṇḍikā"; a fierce form of the Goddess</note> or of the Teacher, respectively, for a man or a woman. According to that procedure—the eighth zodiac sign, etc. || 62 ||

With the verses beginning with "The Great Vajra," and ending with "according to the required task," the text teaches the procedure for constructing the Great Vajra and other diagrams in eleven verses. There, as before, one uses the eleven repeating letters <note>original: "ekādaśāvṛttākṣarāṇi"</note> according to the previously mentioned method, following a clockwise inward movement. There are one hundred and seventy-six vowel-transformed variations of the Wisdom-Mantra letters, with six remaining letters among the remaining transformed characters. This includes the letters beginning with "Ca." The rest is easy to understand. Since the sequence of writing is obtained through oral tradition <note>original: "sampradāya-prāpyatvāt"</note>, this is the sequence for drawing here:

One should draw twenty vertical and twenty horizontal lines at equal intervals. When this is done, three hundred and sixty-one squares are produced. || 63-64 || Among them, in the four directions, excluding the four centermost squares: in the outer row, one should erase seventeen squares on each side around every corner. ### Chapter 12: On the Application and Results of the Great Vajra | 215

This is renowned as the **Great Vajra**, which is eternally undefeated. It is used in rituals for establishing pillars of victory and for the magical expulsion <note>original: "uccāṭana"; a tantric rite intended to drive an enemy away from a location</note> of foes. || 74 ||

It should also be employed for prosperity and peace <margin>(1) Variant: for protection, prosperity, and peace</margin> as well as for subduing enemies <margin>(2) Variant: for conflict</margin>. It is especially effective when establishing countries, kingdoms, cities, or villages. || 75 ||

In the event of terrifying portents <note>original: "utpāta"; natural disasters or ominous events like earthquakes or eclipses</note>, one should draw the diagram upon the ground using red chalk <term>Gairika: A red ochre or earthy hematite used in sacred drawings</term>. Having invoked the auspicious Goddess into its center, one should worship her daily. || 76 ||

At the three junctions of the day <note>Dawn, noon, and sunset</note>, one should perform the "waving of lights" ritual <term>Nīrājana: A purification and honorific rite involving the waving of lamps</term> according to the prescribed order. For specific desires, one should perform this ritual twice or even more as required. || 77 ||

If a King finds his city surrounded by an enemy army, he should draw this Great Vajra within a magnificent pavilion. || 78 ||

He should worship the "Sweetly-Smiling Goddess" <note>An epithet of the deity, likely Lalitā Tripurasundarī</note> in the center of the diagram using cinnabar <note>original: "darada"; red mercuric sulfide used as a pigment</note>, accompanied by dance, song, and music, particularly during the twilight hours. || 79 ||

By performing this as previously described for the specified number of days, the King shall become victorious—either through the destruction of his enemy, their flight, or their surrender. || 80 ||

Then, after erasing the diagram and placing a mark from it upon his forehead, the King should re-enter the city with his forces. Preceded by his spiritual teacher <term>Deśika: A guru or ritual specialist</term> and riding upon an elephant, he shall live for a long time in happiness. || 81 ||

Free from rivals, free from illness, possessing the six limbs of sovereignty <term>Ṣaḍ-aṅga: The six traditional components of a kingdom: the ruler, ministers, allies, treasury, territory, and army</term>, and of renowned majesty. Truly, who can describe the glory of this Vajra? || 82 ||

---

One should write eleven letters of the twenty-syllable wisdom-mantra: three each in the East and West, and two each in the South and North. || 63–73 ||

The nine verses beginning with "This is renowned as the Great Vajra" and ending with "who can describe" explain the specific ritual applications of the **Great Vajra Yantra** and its fruits. In that context, "according to the prescribed order" refers to the sequence taught by the Goddess Lalitā. || 74–79 ||

"As before" refers to the duration, such as a month or other specified time. Regarding the phrase "on an elephant," the implication is that the King should be seated upon it as he proceeds. || 80–81 ||

**[Commentary]**

...free from fear, and possessing the **Six Limbs**. These "Six Limbs" <term>Ṣaḍaṅga: The six constituents of a state</term> are known as: the **Minister** <gloss>amātya</gloss>, the **Kingdom** <gloss>rāṣṭra</gloss>, the **Fortress** <gloss>durga</gloss>, the **Treasury** <gloss>kośa</gloss>, the **Army** <gloss>bala</gloss>, and the **Ally** <gloss>suhṛt</gloss>. These are subordinate to the Sovereign. The rest is easy to understand. || 82 ||

Regarding the four verses beginning with "Now" (83) and ending with "one should write" (86), the author teaches the construction of another Vajra diagram. There, as before: in the ten corners of the Vajra-shape, within those squares, one should erase ten squares in each corner. In the remaining squares, and likewise in each direction, one should erase one square. This is the context for "one should draw triangles." Those [triangles] contain the elemental letters appropriate to the ritual act. 

Then, in the remaining twenty-seven squares, one should write the mantra letters—specifically twelve [pairs]. The "directions" are taken in pairs likewise, moving clockwise from the East. "In the belly of the Power" means in the middle of the *Hṛllekhā* <term>Hṛllekhā: The "Heart-streak," the sacred syllable HRĪṂ</term>. 

The order of drawing is as follows: having struck ten lines in each direction (East-West and North-South) at equal intervals, one erases seven squares in the outer row of each corner, two in the second row, and one in the third row. In this way, having erased ten squares on each side and four squares in the four directions, one creates the triangles. After writing the elemental letters in those triangles as before, one writes the mantra letters in pairs across the twenty-seven squares in six rotations. In the very central square, one should write the *Hṛllekhā* containing the name of the person for whom the ritual is performed <note>original: "sa-sādhyām"</note>. || 83 || 84 || 85 || 86 ||

# In the Tantrarāja Tantra, accompanied by the commentary named Manoramā

***

The author provides further direction. In the phrase "on the previously mentioned," he refers to the substrates such as gold and other materials. The meaning is as follows: The eleven syllables of the Vidyā <term>Vidyā: The specific mantra of the Goddess</term>—excluding the first and last syllables—become 176 in total when expanded through the vowels <note>original: "svara-prasāraṇāt"; a method of multiplying a mantra by combining its consonants with all Sanskrit vowels</note>.

Among these syllables, one first writes the first syllable in the middle of the lotus center <note>original: "karṇikā"</note>. Inside that syllable, one writes the second syllable. Below that, in the space for the hour-syllable, one writes the third syllable. On the eight petals outside, one writes eight syllables in a clockwise direction starting from the top. In this way, eleven syllables are placed. At the appropriate time, one should also write the specific hour-syllable belonging to the first of the sixteen segments of the day and night. This constitutes the **First Lotus**.

Next, taking the eleven syllables following the previous set, one writes them as before and adds the hour-syllable for the second segment of the day and night. This is the **Second Lotus**. Proceeding in this order, one creates the remaining fourteen lotuses. By worshipping the Goddess in each of these at their respective times, one attains their desires. By drawing these sixteen lotuses—one in each square of a sixteen-square grid <note>original: "maṇḍala"</note> made of gold or other materials—and worshipping them as described, the aforementioned spiritual success is achieved.

### Now Begins the Thirteenth Chapter

Now, regarding the eighth among the Sixteen Nityās <note>The Sixteen Nityās are eternal goddesses representing the phases of the lunar month</note> who was previously mentioned; hear her ritual procedure, O wise lady! It grants all desired fruits. || 1 ||

The extraction of her secret mantra <term>Vidyā: The specific mantra-form of a goddess</term> was performed previously; now I shall explain the sequence of ritual placement <term>Nyāsa: The practice of "placing" sacred sounds onto specific parts of the practitioner's body</term>, as well as the powers of her surrounding retinue <gloss>Avaraṇa-śakti</gloss>, her meditation form, and the method of her worship. || 2 ||

I shall speak of her practices, her applications with fire offerings <term>Homa: Ritual offerings made into a consecrated fire</term> and sacred diagrams <term>Yantra: Geometric mystical diagrams used in worship</term>, the ritual of instilling life <gloss>Prāṇapratiṣṭhā</gloss>, the secret knowledge itself, its specific procedures, and its results. || 3 ||

I shall describe these entirely and in sequence, O Great Goddess! By these mantras, one becomes famous in the world, becoming capable of both punishment and grace <note>original: "nigrahānugraha-kṣamaḥ"; the ability to restrain negative forces or bestow blessings</note>. || 4 ||

One should perform the "six-limbed" ritual <term>Ṣaḍaṅga: A ritual where mantras are assigned to the heart, head, tuft, armor, eyes, and weapons</term> as before, following the path previously described. With those same letters enclosed <note>original: "puṭitaiḥ"; a method of sandwiching a mantra between other sounds</note>, one should place them upon the five senses, starting with the ears<gloss>✱</gloss>. || 5 ||

Placing the sixth in the mind, one should perform the "pervasive" placement <gloss>Vyāpaka-nyāsa</gloss> with the secret mantra. The preparation of the offering-water <term>Arghya: A formal water offering to a deity</term> is designated as before; now hear of her female powers, O Parvati! || 6 ||

->**Now begins the Thirteenth Chapter.**<-

In the previous twelfth chapter, having taught the procedure for the seventh Nitya, the Great Diamond Goddess <gloss>Mahāvajreśvarī</gloss>, the author now teaches the procedure for the eighth, the Messenger of Shiva <gloss>Śivadūtī</gloss>. This is contained in the thirteenth chapter, which consists of one hundred verses starting with "Now, regarding the sixteen..." and ending with the completion of the procedures. 

Among these, with the four verses starting from "Now, regarding the sixteen..." and ending with "...capable," he outlines the contents of the chapter. There, "previously" refers to the third chapter. The rest is easy to understand. || 1 || 2 || 3 || 4 ||

With the two verses starting from "One should perform..." and ending with "...O Parvati," he teaches the method of ritual placement <gloss>Nyāsa</gloss> and the preparation of the offering-water <note>original: "arghyasādhanādikaṃ"</note>(1). In that context, "following the path described" means using the six long vowels. "With those same" refers to the specific seed-syllables *Hma-Khya*. Regarding "the five senses, starting with the ears"—this implies the sequence of hearing, skin, sight, taste, and smell. || 5 ||

Regarding the skin, it refers to the whole body; in the aforementioned places, one should perform the placement with each letter enclosed by *Hma-Khya*. || 6 ||

### In the 119th Chapter — Explanation of the Goddess's Retinue-Powers and the Method of Eternal Worship

Vihvalā, Karṣaṇī, Lolā, Nityā, and Madanamālinī;
Vinodā, Kautukā, Puṇyā, and Purāṇā—these are the goddesses dwelling in the square enclosure <note>original: "caturasra-gāḥ"</note>. || 7 ||

Vāgīśā <note>Mistress of Speech</note>, Varadā <note>Giver of Boons</note>, Viṣvavā, Vibhavā, Vighnakāriṇī <note>Obstacle-Maker</note>;
Vīrā <note>Heroic</note>, Vighnaharā <note>Obstacle-Remover</note>, and Vidyodyuktā—these are the eight powers of the sacred diagram <term>Yantra: A geometric diagram used as a tool for meditation and ritual</term>. || 8 ||

Sumukhī <note>Beautiful-Faced</note>, Sundarī <note>Beautiful One</note>, Sārā, Samarā, and Sarasvatī <note>Goddess of Learning</note>;
Samayā, Sarvagā, and Siddhedyuktā—these are the eight powers of the eight-pointed figure. || 9 ||

The Dākinīs and other goddesses <note>Specifically the group of internal yoginīs: Hākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, etc.</note> should be worshipped in the six-pointed figures, moving clockwise from the front. They possess the same form, color, and weapons as the Primal Goddess herself. || 10 ||

One should worship Śivā, Vāṇī, Dūrasiddhā, the one possessing the form of the syllable "Lyai" <gloss>Lyai-vigrahavatī</gloss>, Nādā, and Manomayī <note>Consisting of Mind</note> in the six petals all around. || 11 ||

One should worship the powers of Will, Knowledge, and Action <note>original: "Icchā-jñāna-kriyā-śaktī"</note> in the three corners. In the center, one should worship the eighth auspicious goddess <note>Śivā, referring here to the central deity Śivadūtī</note> surrounded by a circle of weapons <gloss>heti-vṛttām</gloss>. || 12 ||

O wise one! Hear now the meditation upon her, who is said to be the very essence of the universe; yet, for the sake of protecting her devotees, her supreme form has been specifically envisioned. || 13 ||

---

With the six verses beginning with "Vihvalā" and ending with "Śivā," the author teaches about the surrounding powers <term>Parivāra-śakti: The group of subordinate goddesses who make up the retinue of the primary deity</term> of the Goddess.

In that context, **Madanamālinī** refers to two distinct powers: Madanā and Mālinī.
**Dwelling in the square enclosure** means: at the sides of the two gates of the square, there are two on each side, making four; there are four in the four corners; and two in the North and South directions. Thus, ten reside in the square. This is the meaning. || 7 ||

**The eight powers of the instrument** <note>original: "yanvāṣṭa-śaktayaḥ"</note> are the powers located within the eight-part diagram. || 8–9 ||

By saying "from the front," it means that here, the Dākinīs and the others should be worshipped starting from the front and proceeding clockwise. Their positions are in the corners as explained previously in the definitions—thus, the sequence of worship is Hākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, and Dākinī. || 10 ||

**Śivā** and the others are the powers named after the second letter of the sacred mantra <term>Vidyā: A feminine mantra</term>. **Lyai-vigrahavatī** means having the form of the syllable "Lyai." || 11 ||

The **worship of the weapons** should be performed using their respective names, ending with the word "worship," proceeding clockwise from the Southeast <note>Agni-corner</note> to the Southwest <note>Nirṛti-corner</note>. || 12 ||

# In the Tantrarāja with the commentary named Manoramā

> The Goddess possesses a radiance equal to the midday sun in the summer season. She wears a crown of nine gems, has three eyes <gloss>✳</gloss> <note>original: "trīkṣaṇām"; variant: "tīkṣṇām" (sharp-eyed)</note>, and is dressed in red garments. || 14 ||
> 
> Her body is illuminated by the light reflecting from various ornaments. She has a gentle smile, eight arms, and is praised by the great sages. || 15 ||
> 
> In her left arms, she holds a noose, a shield, a mace, and a gem-studded cup. In her right arms, she holds a goad, a sword, an axe, and a lotus <gloss>†</gloss> <note>original: "kamalam"; variant: "kalhāram" (white lily)</note>. || 16 ||
> 
> She is intent on granting the desires of those devoted to her. Having meditated thus, one should worship the Goddess Dūtī <note>This refers to Śivadūtī, the "Messenger of Shiva"</note>, who destroys all wickedness <note>original: "durnīti-nāśinīm"</note>. || 17 ||
> 
> [To construct her mandala]: Two circles, two triangles outside of that, a six-petalled lotus, then a six-pointed figure, an eight-pointed figure, and similarly an eight-petalled lotus <gloss>(1)</gloss>. || 18 ||
> 
> In the square enclosure <term>Bhūpura: The "earth-city" or outermost square of a mandala</term> of Vahnivāsinī <note>One of the sixteen Nityā goddesses associated with fire</note>, having placed the auspicious Goddess Śivā in the center, one should invoke and worship those power-deities situated there according to the previously stated method. || 19 ||
> 
> Having chanted the mantra, performed the fire sacrifice, and offered salutations, one should then dissolve the deity back into one's own self. One should perform the practice according to the stated path with an alert mind. || 20 ||
> 
> O Goddess! Hear now the rules for the fire sacrifice for specific desires <term>Kāmya-homa: Rituals performed to achieve specific worldly or spiritual goals</term>, which grants the fulfillment of one's intentions. || 21 ||
>

---

With the five verses beginning with "The Goddess..." (13) and ending with "...wickedness" (17), the author teaches the method for the daily worship of the Goddess. In that context, the phrase "Hear the supreme form" from the previous section connects here. This form is common to all deities. Regarding the arms—one should visualize the noose, goad, etc., in the sequence of left and right, starting from the upper hands. A white lily <gloss>‡</gloss> is interpreted here as a small dagger <note>original: "asidhenu"</note>. She is called the "Destroyer of Wickedness" because she bestows perfect discernment <term>Viveka: The spiritual faculty of distinguishing the eternal from the temporary</term>. || 13–17 ||

With the three verses beginning with "Two circles" (18) and ending with "alert mind" (20), he teaches the mandala for daily worship, the conclusion of the ritual, and the extension of the instructions for the practice of the mantra <gloss>(2)</gloss>. Regarding that, in the square enclosure, one should make two squares, just like the worship mandala of the goddess Vahnivāsinī. The construction of the rest of the mandala...

### [ Chapter 13 ] Declaration of Specific Results from Specialized Offerings

->One may win over a beloved woman by making offerings in the fire of *guggulu* <note>A fragrant resin from the Commiphora wightii tree, often used in incense and traditional medicine</note> mixed with honey.<-

->By offering jaggery <note>unrefined cane sugar</note> combined with coconut fruit, one shall obtain the favor of Lakshmi <note>The goddess of wealth and prosperity</note>. || 22 ||<-

->Likewise, one may obtain prosperity through offerings of white lilies soaked in ghee <term>Ghee: Clarified butter used as a primary fuel and offering in Vedic and Tantric fire rituals</term>, or red water-lilies <note>original: "aruṇotpalaiḥ"</note> smeared with honey. Similarly, one should use Champaka flowers and blossoms of the Bakula tree smeared with *tri-madhu* <term>Tri-madhu: The "three sweets," typically a mixture of honey, sugar, and ghee</term>. || 23 ||<-

->By offering the blossoms of the Madhūka tree, one may obtain a maiden <note>This likely refers to success in finding a suitable bride</note>. By offering Punnāga flowers, one obtains fine garments; and by offering goat-derived ghee, one obtains whatever is desired. || 24 ||<-

->By offering buffalo-ghee, one obtains buffaloes; and by offering cow-ghee, one obtains cows. By offering gems along with ghee <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original variant: "hutairaktairatnai" (offered with red gems)</note>, the practitioner <term>Sādhaka: A disciplined practitioner of a spiritual or tantric path</term> obtains jewels. || 25 ||<-

->Having fashioned a small doll out of rice flour mixed with sugar, and having placed the name <note>The name of the person one wishes to influence</note> upon the region of its heart, one should cook it in a mixture of oil and ghee during the night. || 26 ||<-

->One should not eat <note>original: "anaśnan"</note> during the day, but at night, one should consume the doll while reciting the *vidyā* <term>Vidyā: A female mantra or sacred phonetic formula associated with a goddess</term>. By this seven-night practice <gloss>2</gloss> <note>original variant: "tāmajasram" (this constantly)</note>, a man, a woman, or even a king... || 27 ||<-

->...falls into servitude and surrenders their wealth, their life, and all else. Similarly, one should offer the red or white flowers of the *hayāri* <note>Literally "enemy of horses," a common name for the Karavīra or Oleander plant</note>. || 28 ||<-

->After twenty-one nights <note>Literally "three-seven nights"</note>, a person obtains great fortune. By offering goat meat smeared with the "three sweets" (*tri-madhu*), one shall obtain gold. || 29 ||<-

***

**Commentary by Śivānanda (Manoramā):**

The meanings of verses 18 and 19 are **easy to understand**. Regarding verse 20: just as was stated for the goddess Lalitā, the arrangement of letters and other details according to the specific World-Ages (*yugas*) should be followed as before.

With the ten verses beginning with "kāmya" [the desired results] and ending with "days," the author teaches the attainment of specific fruits from specific substances offered in the fire. In this context, the "red lotus" (*aruṇotpala*) is defined as before, meaning the red water-lily. The five substances mentioned before the Madhūka flower—starting with jaggery—are those which produce wealth (*lakṣmī*). || 21-23 ||

Regarding the term "from Punnāga"—the word "flowers" is understood. For the four substances beginning with Champaka and ending with Punnāga, one should apply the "three sweets" (*tri-madhu*). || 24 || The terms "buffalo-derived" and so on serve as adjectives for the ghee. || 25 ||

"Mixed with white" (*sita-saṃyutām*) means combined with sugar. The phrase "in oil and ghee" implies they are mixed together. || 26 || "Not eating" implies not eating other food. || 27 || "Hayāri flowers" refers specifically to Oleander blossoms (*karavīra*).

***
