# Chapter 14 | The Ritual of Suppression and the Kālī-Anuṣṭubh
### 246
->The Commentary known as the *Manoramā* (The Delighter of the Mind)<-

One should write the four seed-syllables <note>original: "bīja-catuṣkam"</note> which embody the nature of fire and wind. By these, enemies instantly abandon their own bodies. || 64 ||

The syllable *Rasa* joined with Fire, Earth, and the Self results in **Bhūm**. The syllable *Grāsa* joined with Fire, Earth, and the Self results in **Chūm**. The syllable *Prabhā* joined with Fire, Earth, and the Self results in **Vūm**. The syllable *Haṃsa* joined with Fire and the others results in **Hūm**. <note>These are technical tantric codes where "Fire" represents the sound 'R', "Earth" represents 'Ū', and "Self" represents the nasal 'M'.</note> || 66 ||

One should write them in rows, starting from the beginning of the "Lord’s Verse" <note>original: "īśvararcodi"</note>. In order, follow the sequence of the knowledge <term>vidyā: a female deity's mantra</term> of Kālī and the mantra of Yama <note>original: "manvam-asaṅkramam" or "manvañ-ca-saṅkramam" in variant readings</note>. || 67 ||

O Goddess, the Kālī-Anuṣṭubh <note>a 32-syllable mantra dedicated to the goddess Kālī</note> is in the form of the "All-Auspicious" <note>original: "Sarvatobhadra"</note> diagram. Listen, O Goddess, for I shall now describe the Yama-Anuṣṭubh. || 68 ||

Life <note>the sound 'K'</note> joined with Wind <note>the sound 'ā'</note> [Kā]; the Earth-goddess <note>the sound 'L'</note> joined with Fire <note>the sound 'au'</note> [Lau]; the Sky <note>the sound 'M'</note> joined with Wind <note>the sound 'ā'</note> [Mā]; and Fire <note>the sound 'R'</note>. These four, written in reverse, form the first foot of the mantra. || 69 ||

It is said that the first foot of this Kālī-Anuṣṭubh is formed by reading these four letters in reverse. Regarding the second foot: its first letter is the second letter of the first foot <note>Lau</note>. The second letter is the "Void" <note>the sound 'N'</note>. The third letter is the Sky joined with the Earth <note>the sound 'M' joined with 'O' resulting in 'Mo'</note>. The fourth is *Grāsa* <note>the sound 'Ch'</note>. This, in reverse, is the second foot. || 70 ||

The third foot is the eleventh letter, then the syllable *Go* joined with the "foot" <note>the sound 'V' with 'ā' resulting in 'Vā'</note>. Their reversal forms the third foot of the mantra. || 71 ||

---

Now, the commentator explains the result of these verses. **"In that"** refers to the specific ritual of suppression <note>original: "nigraha-prayogasya"</note>. || 62 ||

**"Within the Womb of Fire"**—this means inside the "belly" of the letter *Repha* <note>the sound 'R'</note> which is topped with a dot <note>bindu</note>. || 63 ||

**"Embodying fire and wind"**—this refers to the body of fire and wind both in terms of the written letters of the name and their inner power. **"By these"** refers to the four "syllable-fortresses" <note>original: "kūṭākṣaraiḥ"</note>. **"Body"** means the physical frame. || 64 ||

**"Rasa joined with Fire, Earth, and the Self"** results in **Bhūm**.
**"Grāsa joined with Fire, Earth, and the Self"** results in **Chūm**.
**"Prabhā joined with Fire, Earth, and the Self"** results in **Vūm**.
**"Haṃsa joined with Fire and the others"** results in **Hūm**. || 66–68 ||

**"Life joined with Wind"** results in **Kā**.
**"The Earth-goddess joined with Fire"** results in **Lau**.
**"The Sky joined with Wind"** results in **Mā**.
**"Fire"** results in the letter **Ra**.
**"The four in reverse order"**—this forms the first foot. || 69 ||

The meaning is as follows: by reading the four letters situated in the stated order in reverse, the foot of the Kālī-Vidyā-Anuṣṭubh is formed. **"The second"** refers to the second letter of the first foot of this mantra being the first letter of the second foot, which is **Lau**. **"Void"** refers to the letter **Na**, being the second letter. **"Sky and Earth"** results in **Mo**, the third letter. **"Grāsa"** results in...

# Chapter 14 | Description of the Results of the Mantras of Kālī and Yama
### 247

-> The fourth, the twelfth, the twentieth, and *rayo-bāla* (1) in reverse; <-
-> this fourth quarter is declared as the "All-Destroying" Wisdom. || 72 || <-
-> Pervasive, Kālī’s third syllable, joined with Wind and Water; <-
-> the Resonance—the first quarter in the rite of Yama is these in reverse. || 73 || <-
-> The second and fourth of these, along with Space, Earth, and the Resonance; <-
-> the second quarter of the mantra consists of these in reverse order. || 74 || <-

---

The letter *Ca* is the fourth syllable. This is the second in reverse order—meaning the second foot <term>pāda: one quarter of a verse</term> consists of the four syllables placed in the previously stated order but in reverse. || 70 || <note>The commentator is referring back to the previous verse's logic to explain the grid's construction.</note> "The third"—the third syllable of the first foot, the syllable *Mā*, becomes the first syllable of the third foot. "The eleventh"—the eleventh syllable of this *Anuṣṭubh* <note>a 32-syllable meter</note> is *Mo*, which is the second syllable [of this foot]. "Joined with the Cow-Walker" <note>original: "go-cara-anvitā"</note>—this refers to the syllable *De*, which is the third syllable. "The Speed" <note>original: "rayaḥ"</note>—the letter *Ta* is the fourth syllable. The third quarter is the reverse of these—meaning the third foot is the reading of these four syllables in reverse order. "Of the Mantra"—of the Wisdom <term>vidyā: a feminine mantra</term>. The word "Mantra" <note>original: "manu"</note> is a general term for both male and female sacred formulas. || 71 ||

"The fourth"—the letter *Va*, which is the fourth syllable of this Wisdom, is the first syllable of the fourth foot. "The twelfth"—the letter *Ca* is the second. "The twentieth"—the letter *Ta* is the third syllable. "The Speed"—the letter *Ta*. * "Because of its independence, the syllable 'Tva' is the fourth syllable, formed by the union of 'Aba' and 'Ambu' <note>technical codes for vowels and semi-vowels</note>." In reverse order—meaning the fourth foot is formed by reading these four syllables in reverse order. "This"—the one described thus. "All-Destroying"—the result of its ritual application is implied. In this way, the Kālī-Anuṣṭubh has been described in the form of an "All-Auspicious" <term>Sarvatobhadra: a 4x4 or 8x8 grid that reads the same from various directions</term> diagram, as before. || 72 ||

With the four verses starting with "Pervasive" and ending with "in Shiva," the author teaches the Yama-Anuṣṭubh in the form of a Sarvatobhadra diagram. In that context, "Pervasive" refers to the letter *Ya*, the first syllable. "Kālī’s third"—the third syllable of the Kālī-Anuṣṭubh, which is *Mā*, is the second syllable of this mantra. "Joined with Wind and Water"—the syllable *Vā* is the third syllable. "The Resonance" <note>original: "nāda"</note>—the letter *Tha* is the fourth syllable. "These in reverse"—the first foot is formed by reading these four syllables in reverse, as before. "In Yama"—in the diagram of Yama. || 73 || "The second and fourth of these"—the second and fourth syllables of this Yama-mantra become the first and second syllables of the second foot, which are *Mā* and *Tha*. "Space with Earth"—the syllable *So* is the third syllable. "The Resonance"—the letter *Tha* is the fourth syllable. By reversing these—reading these four syllables in reverse order as before...

### [ Chapter 14 ] Description of the application of the sixty-four-squared Restraining Diagram, etc.

## As before, O Goddess, with nine lines each way, create a grid of eight-by-eight squares.
## Within these, starting from the North-East <note>original: "isha"</note> and South-West <note>original: "rakshas"</note> directions, write the mantra of Kali; || 80 ||

## Then, having written the mantra of Yama and surrounding it with the two mentioned seed-syllables,
## one should place the diagram face-down on the ground. || 81 ||

## This diagram, O Supreme Lady, produces the same results as the previously described circles.
## Even where not explicitly stated, one should include the names of the targets within the center of the squares. || 82 ||

## Salt, pungent spices, urine <note>original: "mehambu"; see footnote 2 for variants</note>, soot from the house, and fire,
## combined with charcoal from a cremation ground and the sap of a Neem tree—this is declared to be "poison." || 83 ||

Having written the name [of the target] inside the center of the letter *Ra* <note>original: "repha"</note> which is marked with a nasal drop <term>bindu: a dot indicating a resonant nasal sound</term>, as before, one should write the four syllables *Bhrūṃ*, *Cūṃ*, *Vrūṃ*, and *Jhūṃ* in the four rows of squares in the prescribed order, moving from the inside out. If the person to be acted upon is a man, the Kali mantra <note>original: "Kali-Anustubh"</note> is placed inside and the Yama mantra is on the outside. If the target is a woman, the Yama mantra is inside and the Kali mantra is on the outside. 

Regarding the writing: one should write the Kali mantra starting from the North-East and South-West directions; similarly, write the Yama mantra. Then, write the other mantra continuously from the North-East to the South-West and back. Outside of that, write the letters *Pa* and *Ra* <note>original: "repha"</note> with nasal drops continuously from the North-East to the South-West, alternating between the inner and outer sections, and then apply it to the desired goal. This is also explained in the author's own commentary. If the target is a woman, one should bury the diagram beneath a shrine of the Teacher; if a man, bury it beneath a shrine of Kali. || 78 || <note>Note: The prose commentary here clarifies the application of verse 78 from the previous section.</note>

The three verses starting with "As before" and ending with "in the center of the squares" teach the Restraining Diagram <term>Nigraha-yantra: a mystical chart used for subduing or punishing an opponent</term> consisting of sixty-four squares, its application, and its specific results. The instruction to surround it with the Yama mantra applies when the target is a man. From this, the traditional meaning is understood: when the target is a woman, the Yama mantra is on the inside and the Kali mantra surrounds it on the outside. || 80 || 

"With the two seed-syllables"—this means one should surround it with the syllables *Ya* and *Ra* marked with nasal drops, as done previously. || 81 || 

The mention of "where not explicitly stated" refers to matters involving women. Here, after describing the famous and "unfailing restraint" <term>Amogha-nigraha</term> using the Kali and Yama mantras, the remedy is also provided through the construction of a diagram for the Graceful Knowledge <note>original: "Svarita-vidya"</note>. For this reason, the subduing power is described through the letters of the mantras. The order of the diagram's construction is as follows: having made sixty-four squares with nine lines as before, if the target is a man, write the Kali mantra inside and the Yama mantra outside from the North-East etc.; if a woman, the Yama mantra inside and the Kali mantra outside. Then, using the syllables *Ya* and *Ra* with nasal drops...

# In the Tantrarāja, accompanied by the commentary named Manoramā

## Having written the name of the target <note>original: "sādhya"</note> within the womb <term>jathara: the interior space of a written character</term> of the first letter of the mantra, one should then write the eight-syllabled *Phat* sound <note>original: "phaṭkāra"</note> in the eight divisions surrounding it. || 84 ||

## One should then surround that lotus, located in the pericarp <term>karṇikā: the central seed-head of the lotus</term>, with the seed-syllable of Illusion <note>original: "māyā," referring to the syllable Hrīṃ</note>. Outside of this, one should construct a pot-shaped border <note>original: "kumbha"</note> according to the prescribed rules for arranging letters. || 85 ||

## In the same manner, using the other nine letters of the mantra in sequence, one should create nine more diagrams. Now, hear the results of these ten! || 86 ||

## One attains universal protection, victory, the subjugation <term>vashya: the power to attract or control</term> of men, women, and kings, as well as immobilization <term>stambha: the ritual freezing of an opponent's actions</term>, wealth, fame, gold, and fine garments. || 87 ||

---

Following the previously stated order, one should wrap the diagram and place it face-down in the designated spots. This will produce the results mentioned before. || 82 ||

Through the verse beginning with "Salt," the text teaches the nature of the "poison" used for writing the restraining diagram. In that context: "pungent" <note>original: "uṣaṇa"</note> refers to alkaline earth or salt-crust; "body-water" <note>original: "mehāmbu"</note> refers to urine; "fire" <note>original: "agni"</note> refers to the Leadwort plant <term>Chitraka: Plumbago zeylanica, known for its burning, caustic properties</term>. Other details should be learned directly from the mouth of an initiated teacher. || 83 ||

Through the two verses beginning with "Mantra" and ending with "diagrams," the author teaches the method for the ten diagrams using the ten letters of the root mantra. In this context: "according to the prescribed rules for letters" means surrounding the diagram with a chain of the letter *Va* marked with nasal dots <term>bindu: a dot representing a resonant nasal sound</term>.

This is what is meant: Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, one writes the first "Heart-streak" syllable <note>original: "hṛllekhā," the seed-syllable Hrīṃ</note> of the mantra in the center of the pericarp. In its "womb" (the center of the character), one writes the syllable *Om* <note>original: "praṇava"</note>—which is the first part of the mantra—and within that, the name of the target. Then, one writes the remaining eight syllables of the mantra (excluding the "Heart-streak" and the "Phat" sound) in the eight petals, starting from the North-East and moving clockwise. One then surrounds this lotus with the second "Heart-streak" syllable. Outside this, as before, one should create a "pot" <note>original: "kumbha"</note> shape consisting of a chain of the letter *Ta* marked with nasal dots, with lotuses at the top and bottom. This is the first diagram.

In the same way, in the center of the pericarp of this very diagram, within the "Heart-streak" syllable, one should place the second letter of the mantra, each containing the name of the target. Following this, one should make nine diagrams with the letters placed in the petals as described. For the tenth diagram, one writes the syllable *Phat* along with the name inside the "Heart-streak" syllable, and places the remaining letters (excluding the syllable *Om*) in the petals. Thus, one should create ten diagrams. || 84–85 ||

Through the verse beginning with "Of the ten" and ending with "attains," the author teaches the ten specific, extraordinary results of these ten diagrams in order. The meaning there is easy to understand. || 86–87 ||

# Chapter 14: Instructions on the Eleven Diagrams and their Applications | 251

->The non-repeated letters [of the mantra] are placed at the end; then, through<-
->different vowel combinations, the total number of syllables is known to be one hundred and seventy-six. || 88 ||<-

->The fifth ensures the protection of the royal palace on all sides.<-

Through the four and a half verses beginning with "The non-repeated" and ending with "traditionally explained," the text teaches the eleven diagrams formed by the syllables of the root-mantra modified by vowels. In this context, "Shakti" refers to the Hṛllekhā <note>original: "hṛllekhā," the mantra syllable Hrīṃ</note>. || 88 || 89 || 90 || "In the remaining" means in the petals. "That" refers to the lotus. "With Illusion" means with the Hṛllekhā syllable. "Between the two circles" refers to the space between the two outer circular pathways of the lotus. The syntax implies: "One should surround the space between the circles with the Hṛllekhā syllable." "Outside" means at the very outermost edge. "The prescribed" refers to the drawing of a chain of the letter *Va* accompanied by nasal dots <note>original: "bindu"</note>, as previously described.

The meaning is as follows: Having drawn a sixteen-petaled lotus and placed two circles around it, and outside of that—as before—having drawn the "pot" <note>kumbha</note> shape consisting of a chain of *Va* characters with dots, and having placed a lotus both above and below it; one should then write the Hṛllekhā in the center of the lotus pericarp, containing the name of the target within it. On the sixteen petals, one should write the first sixteen syllables out of the total one hundred and seventy-six syllables (derived from the mantra's letters modified by vowels), proceeding clockwise from the top. Then, one should surround the space between the outer circles of the lotus with the Hṛllekhā. This constitutes the **First Diagram**. In the same way, one should write the other groups of sixteen syllables on the sixteen petals to create the remaining diagrams. Together with the one just described, there are eleven diagrams in total. || 91 ||

# Manoramā Commentary on the Tantrarāja | 252

The sixth [diagram] provides protection for ministers; the seventh protects the city. || 94 ||
The eighth provides protection for the home for everyone at all times,
against fears from snakes, thieves, malevolent planets, and likewise from enemies. || 95 ||
The ninth, O Goddess of the Devas, is a deliverer for all who are suffering from any disease,

leave him and instead destroy the sender <note>original: "prayoktāram," referring to the person who initiated the hostile magic</note> at that very moment, O Dear One!
In this way, these diagrams, when combined with the [target's] name, accomplish all tasks. || 99 ||
For the prosperity of all the Nityas <note>The fifteen or sixteen lunar goddesses central to this tradition</note>, at the very start of the morning,

Thus, the complete pervasion of the essence of life <term>Prāṇa-tattva: the fundamental principle of vital energy</term> has been well-described.
By contemplating this in the mind, that essence is assimilated into one's own self. || 101 ||

With the seven half-verses beginning with "Applications" and ending with "accomplishes all tasks," the author teaches the use of these diagrams. There—"Protector of the rod" <note>original: "daṇḍa-rakṣakaṃ"</note> means it protects the army. || 92-95 || 

"Combined with the ritual previously described" refers to the installation of life-force (*prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā*), consecration (*abhiṣeka*), wearing [the diagram], and worship. || 96 || 

Because the ritual application of the tenth and eleventh diagrams is the same, they are not mentioned separately. "Nearby" means near the person suffering from disease. "It" refers to the pot. || 97 || 

"Those" refers to the written letters of the mantra. || 98 || 

"Him" refers to the person suffering from disease. "The sender" refers to the one who performed black magic or malevolent rites. "Accomplishing all tasks through the name" means all these diagrams are made effective for any task by the skill of placing the letters of the target's name in the center.

With the verse beginning "For all," he explains the rule for the ritual offering (*bali*) at the start of the morning worship for all the Nitya goddesses. There—"For all" refers to the Nityas. "With the sixteen-syllable mantra" means the mantra mentioned at the end of the third chapter. || 99-100 ||

# Now begins the Fifteenth Chapter.

Now, among the sixteen Nityas <note>The Nityas are sixteen goddesses representing the phases of the moon in the Shrividya tradition</note>, listen to the ritual procedure for the tenth one who was mentioned, the wisdom-goddess <term>vidyā</term> known as Kulasundarī. || 1 ||

[I shall describe] Her meditation <term>dhyāna</term>, her internal absorption, her attendant powers <term>shaktis</term>, her worship, the method of attaining her mantra <term>sādhana</term>, her various forms, and the sacrifices that bestow the gift of speech. || 2 ||

She is of a deep red color, served by a host of powers who also share that red form. Her garments, ornaments, garlands, and ointments are all red. She has six lotus-like faces. || 3 ||

On every face, she has three eyes and a beautiful smile. She shines with a crown made of priceless gems and rubies. || 4 ||

She glitters with earrings, necklaces, armlets, waist-bands, and anklets. This auspicious goddess has a radiant chest adorned with clusters of red flowers. || 5 ||

She is the supreme embodiment of compassion and bliss, seated upon a red lotus throne. She possesses twelve arms and is the essence of all speech for all beings. || 6 ||

[In her hands, she holds] a rosary of coral, a lotus, a water-pot made of jewels, a vessel full of wealth <margin>original: "vasupūrṇāṃ"; a variant reading (1) suggests "filled with gems"</margin>, a drinking cup, a citron fruit, and the gesture of explanation <term>vyākhyāna-mudrā</term> <margin>A variant reading (2) combines the citron and explanation gesture</margin>. || 7 ||

"Her attainment" refers to the ritual mastery of the wisdom-mantra. "Of those" refers to both the wisdom-mantra and the deity herself. || 1–2 ||

# Chapter 15: The Sequence of Daily and Desired Worship, Meditation, and Ritual Placement.

[She is] holding in her right and left arms a book, a beautiful white lotus, a golden pen, a garland of gems, and a fine conch shell <margin>original: "kambuvaram"; a variant reading (1) suggests "a new arm"</margin>. || 8 ||

She is praised on all sides by gods, celestial musicians <term>Gandharvas</term>, half-human musicians <term>Kinnaras</term>, nature spirits <term>Yakshas</term>, fierce spirits <term>Rakshasas</term>, divine sages, perfected beings <term>Siddhas</term>, and wisdom-holders <term>Vidyadharas</term>. || 9 ||

One should meditate on her in this way and worship her daily for the attainment of speech, prosperity, and beauty. [One should visualize her as] white for the mastery of speech alone, and as Lakshmi <note>The goddess of fortune</note> with a golden luster [for wealth]. || 10 ||

[One should visualize her as] smoke-colored <margin>variant (2): "smoke-colored"</margin> to cause hatred in enemies, or for their death and restraint. One should remember her as blue for the purpose of "silencing" <note>mūkīkaraṇa: a tantric act to strike an opponent dumb or silent</note>, according to the specific goal desired. || 11 ||

With the three mantras mentioned, using the letters, one should perform the "six-limbed" rite <term>shad-anga</term> <note>A ritual where mantras are placed on six parts of the body: heart, head, crown, armor, eyes, and weapons</note>. This is done at the beginning, middle, and end of the worship and recitation <term>japa</term> sequence. || 12 ||

With each of those three seed-syllables <term>bījas</term> combined with long vowels, one should perform the ritual placement <term>nyāsa</term> of the hands, the limbs, and the faces as prescribed by the rules. || 13 ||

---

The commentary now explains the variations. Regarding the **six lotus faces**: these are the upper, East (front), South (right), North (left), West (back), and the lower face, which the author will explain himself in the section on the placement of the faces. || 3-5 ||

**The essence of all speech**: this means she is composed of all the languages and words of the Vedas. || 6 ||

**The gem-cup**: a drinking vessel made of jewels. **Citron**: the *mātuluṅga* fruit. || 7 ||

The connection is with the **right arms**. **Red lotus**: a red water-lily. Here, the arrangement of weapons/items should be imagined from the top downwards on both sides. || 8-10 ||

**For restraint**: meaning for the sake of afflictions like disease. **According to the specific desire**: in accordance with the particular ritual application being performed. || 11 ||

With the five verses beginning with "With the three [mantras]," he teaches the sequence of ritual placement <term>nyāsa</term>. 

Regarding the **beginning, middle, and end of the recitation and worship**: the "middle" refers to the halfway point of the intended number of mantra recitations. At that point, one should perform the placement and then recite the second half. This ritual placement in the middle of recitation is specific to this goddess, Kulasundarī; other times for ritual placement are common to all deities. **In order**: according to the prescribed sequence. || 12 ||

**Combined with long vowels**: regarding the first group <term>kūṭa</term> of the mantra, applying long vowels means—since that group consists of vowel sounds—reciting the six long vowels: *Ām, Īm, Ūm, Aim, Auṃ, Aḥ*. In this way, long vowels are applied to all the vowel-letters. The other two groups of the mantra follow the previous rules. Regarding the **hands, limbs, and faces**: the hands...

### Manoramā Commentary on the Tantrarāja Tantra

->[The practitioner should place the names of the faces] Above, East, South, North,<-
->and West, which is the other name [for the back direction] (1),<-
->situated between the words "Aiṃ" and "Salutation" (2), as the very self of those locations, in the proper order. || 14 ||<-

->This [is the first set]; the second is on the base, the crown, the heart, and the three eyes.<-
->The third is on the ears and chin; the fourth is on the nostrils and palate. || 15 ||<-

->The fifth is on the shoulders and navel, then on the two hands and two feet.<-
->One should perform this nine-fold placement using the primary syllables at the root, middle, and tip [of the limbs]. || 16 ||<-

The ritual for the two [hands and feet] is as before. As for the "faces," they are described in the following manner. || 13 || **Situated between Shuchi and Nati**—this refers to the names being placed in the middle of the seed-syllable <term>Aiṃ</term> <note>original: "shuchi"</note> and the word <term>Namaḥ</term> <note>original: "nati"; meaning "salutation" or "bowing"</note>. **By those**—meaning by the names of the faces. **In those selves**—meaning in the forms of those specific locations. Following the order of the six-limbed seed-syllables mentioned previously, one by one (or subtracting one by one), one should place them while saying: "Aiṃ, salutation to the Upward-facing One," on the upward face. The same applies to the others. The tradition teaches that one should perform the placement on the remaining five faces—East, South, North, West, and the Other—using the corresponding mantras in the specified order. At the time of worship, after the invocation <term>āvāhana</term>, one should worship the deity in her various faces with the first "peak" <term>kūṭa</term> <note>A 'peak' or cluster refers to a section of a long mantra; Kulasundarī’s mantra is divided into three such clusters</note> of six letters using those specific mantras.

The meaning is as follows: The mantra <term>vidyā</term> of the goddess Kulasundarī consists of three primary clusters. By adding the six long vowels to each of these, they are each made six-fold. Together, they form eighteen syllables. One should perform the "six-limbed" ritual placement and the "three-face" placement at the beginning of the worship and recitation <term>japa</term> using the first cluster of six syllables. In the middle of the rite, one should perform the same placements using the second cluster of six syllables. At the conclusion, one should perform the three placements using the third cluster of six syllables. || 14 ||

With the verse beginning **"The base..."**, the author teaches the sequence for the nine-fold ritual placement <term>nyāsa</term> using the three syllables of the root mantra. In this context, **one** means "one time." Similarly, "second" and so on refer to the number of repetitions. || 15 ||

**On the two hands and two feet**—this refers to both feet and both hands, totaling four limbs. In each of these, at the three points of the root, middle, and tip, one performs the placement for the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth times. Including the previous locations, the placement is performed nine-fold. This is the meaning: Here, in the nine locations from the base <note>the mūlādhāra at the base of the spine</note> onwards, which are arranged in groups of three <note>triangles</note>, one should perform the placement nine times at the designated spots using the three syllables of the mantra. The tradition holds that these placements should be performed as a "pervasive" <term>vyāpaka</term> rite <note>a ritual where the hands sweep over the entire body to distribute the mantra's power</note> at the beginning, middle, and end of the worship and recitation procedure. || 16 ||

<header>Chapter 15 | Instruction on the Retinue Powers, the Daily Worship Circle, and the Sequence of Worship</header>

## Speech, Sarasvati, Vani, Sanskrit, Prakrit, and the Supreme;
## She in the form of a Sword, She in the form of Mind, the Delightful One, Bliss, and Wonder (1). || 17 ||
## These eleven are proclaimed; one should worship them within the Nine Yonis.
## On the outer eight-petaled lotus, one should worship Brahmi and the other [Mother Goddesses]. || 18 ||
## In the square, one should worship the World Guardians in their "Power" forms:
## Indra, Agni, Yama, and the Rakshas, Varuna, Anila, and Soma. || 19 ||
## And Ishana—the rite follows the directions from the East, plus Above and Below.
## Worship them with names ending in the word "Power" as before, for the sake of all success. || 20 ||
## Having constructed two squares provided with doors at the East and West,
## one should create an eight-petaled lotus situated within two circles. || 21 ||
## From the divisions of four, three, five, and four parts, forming the Nine Yonis—
## having summoned Her there, one should worship Her properly as before. || 22 ||

With the four verses beginning with **"Speech"** and ending with **"for success,"** the author specifies the Retinue Powers <term>Parivāra-shaktis</term> <note>These are subsidiary goddesses that emanate from the central deity, representing different aspects of her power.</note> of the Goddess.

In that context: **Bliss and Wonder**—these are two distinct powers named Ananda and Kautuka. || 17 || **In the Nine Yonis**—this refers to the central diagram of nine triangles; one should worship the first goddess in the center yoni, and the tenth and eleventh goddesses in its three corners. || 18 || **In that way**—meaning in the manner that will be described. || 18 || **With names ending in "Power"**—this means they are worshipped as Indra-Shakti and so on, just as described previously. || 20 ||

With the four half-verses beginning with **"Having constructed two squares"** and ending with **"Her,"** the author teaches the construction of the Daily Worship Circle <term>Nitya-pūjā-cakra</term> and the sequence of worship. In that context: **From the divisions of four, three, five, and four parts**—this refers to the division of the diameter of the circle. The mention of "four" is stated independently [for each side]. 

The meaning is as follows: One should draw a central vertical line <term>Brahmasūtra</term> <note>Literally "The Thread of Brahma," the primary north-south axis of a sacred diagram.</note> representing the East-West axis within the diameter of the circle. One should divide this line into sixteen parts and make marks at the fourth, third, and fifth segments starting from the East. At these three marks, one should draw three horizontal lines extending to the edge of the circle. Starting from the intersection of the middle horizontal line with the southern and northern edges of the circle, one should strike two lines meeting at the western edge of the central axis. Then, starting from the intersection of the western horizontal line with the southern and northern edges of the circle, one should strike two lines meeting at the eastern edge of the central axis. Then, starting from the intersection of the eastern line with the southern and northern edges of the circle, one should strike a line toward the junction of the western line and the central axis...

# The Tantrarāja with the Commentary Named Manoramā

->Among the eleven, the final powers [are placed] on the sides of the middle triangle;<-

---

<gloss>+</gloss> After striking [the lines], one should wipe away the first-struck <term>Brahma-sūtra</term> <note>original: "brahmasūtra"; here referring to the central vertical axis line used as a guide in constructing mandalas, not the philosophical text.</note>. When this is done, a perfectly symmetrical nine-triangle circle <term>Navayoni-chakra</term> <note>A sacred geometric pattern consisting of nine intersecting triangles, representing the womb or source of creation.</note> is produced within the circle. Outside of that, having created an eight-petaled lotus, and outside of that, two squares provided with doors at the East and West, one should worship Her there in the stated sequence. || 21–22 || 

**Among the eleven**—this refers to the powers of Speech and the others previously mentioned. **The final powers** <gloss>*</gloss> refers to the tenth power named Bliss (*Ananda*) and the eleventh power named Wonder (*Kautuka*). **On the sides of the middle triangle**—these should be worshipped in the North and South corners of the central triangle. The worship of the first eight powers, beginning with "Speech" (*Bhasha*), occurs in the corners of the triangles surrounding the center, after the worship of the three primary powers in the central triangle. 

**The powers of the World Guardians**—this refers to the powers of the Infinite and Brahma. **At the two doors**—meaning in the East and West. This is what is meant: On the South side of the East door, one worships the power of Indra; on the North side, the power of the Infinite (*Ananta*). At the West door, on the South side, one worships the power of Varuna; on the North side, the power of Brahma. In the other directions, the guardians are worshipped in their respective quarters. || 23 || 

**This is the special procedure**—referring to the placement on the sides of the middle triangle, etc. Here, in the eight-petaled lotus and the nine triangles, one should worship in a clockwise direction starting from the front corner. In the square, however, one should worship in a clockwise direction starting from the East door according to the stated order. **General** means as previously described. || 24 || **Thus**—in the manner described.

The second half of the verse beginning with **In the morning** teaches the means for attaining knowledge. There, **attaining the Self through the Mantra** means that by drinking three mouthfuls of water consecrated with this <term>Kulasundarī-vidyā</term> <note>The specific mantra or "wisdom-form" of the goddess Kulasundarī.</note> alone, there will be a purification of the self that results in perfect knowledge. || 25 ||

The two verses (and a half) beginning with **Sandalwood** and ending with **attaining** prescribe the qualities of the practitioner and the aromatic substances used for the deity's worship. There, **deer-musk** refers to the secretions of the musk deer.

# Chapter 15: Description of the Rule of Qualities, Ritual Substances, and the Practice for Attaining Perfection in Speech

[258]

->With the body anointed, with a delighted heart, and maintaining silence,<-
->wearing colorful ornaments and clothes, and wearing a garland, one should chant the <term>Vidyā</term> <note>A "Vidyā" is a specific female deity's mantra, considered a form of secret knowledge.</note> at nightfall. || 27 ||<-
->One should worship the Auspicious One with these fragrances for the sake of attaining all goals,<-
->along with all the <term>Nityās</term> <note>The sixteen "Nityās" are goddesses representing the phases of the moon.</note> and the <term>Mātṛkā</term> <note>original: "mātṛkayā"; refers here to the Goddess as the personification of the Sanskrit alphabet.</note> in the morning. || 28 ||<-
->O Shiva! One should drink water with these formal petitions for the sake of attaining perfection in speech;<-
->it is accomplished through those other mantras and <term>Vidyās</term> as well. || 29 ||<-
->Having chanted three hundred thousand times as before, one should offer a tenth of that as a libation,<-
->and a fire-offering with the same amount using fragrant water and the "sweet nectar" [of honey and ghee]. || 30 ||<-
->With <term>Palāśa</term> flowers <note>The "Flame of the Forest" (Butea monosperma) flowers, prized for their bright orange color and sacred status.</note> that are fully blossomed, unblemished, and unbroken,<-
->the practitioner, having perfected the <term>Vidyā</term>, may then perform the rites for specific desired results. || 31 ||<-
->The variations in the results have been declared according to the different colors of the Goddess;<-
->listen, I shall speak of the variations in the nature of the <term>Vidyā</term> according to the rule. || 32 ||<-

---

**...with deer-musk** || 26 || <gloss>+</gloss> **With a delighted heart**—the implication is: through the feeling of identifying one's own self with the deity. **One should worship**—the word "and" [in the original] implies this. 
The phrase **at nightfall** is drawn into the meaning here. **With these fragrances**—referring to the ten types of substances like sandalwood. || 27 ||

With the two and a half verses starting with **With all...** and ending with **...is accomplished**, the author teaches the practice for attaining <term>Vāksiddhi</term> <note>original: "vāksiddhi"; the spiritual power where one's speech becomes perfectly eloquent or effectively manifests reality.</note> using all the Nityās, other <term>Vidyās</term>, and all mantras. In that context, **with all**—the implication is: with the sixteen [Nityās]. || 28 || 

**Vidyās**—the implication is: with others [not yet mentioned]. This is what is being said: At the conclusion of the morning twilight prayer, take water in the palm of the hand. Contemplate the <term>Mātṛkā-yantra</term> <note>A mystical diagram or internal visualization of the letters of the alphabet.</note> within that water. Recite the fifty letters of the alphabet from *A* to *Ha*, each ending with a nasalized *bindu* [m] sound, three times for each letter. Then, recite your chosen <term>Nitya</term> mantra or <term>Vidyā</term> three times. Thinking of that water as consisting of nectar, meditate on the **Sarasvatī-nāḍī** <note>original: "sarasvatīnāḍī"; a subtle energy channel associated with the goddess of wisdom, believed to flow to the tongue.</note> in the form of a candle flame, extending from the <term>Mūlādhāra</term> <note>The base energy center at the bottom of the spine.</note> to the tip of the tongue. Then, sip the water with the intention of making an internal fire-offering into that channel. By doing this every day in the morning, the four types of scholarship and knowledge of the Self will certainly be close at hand; this is the meaning of the tradition. || 29 ||

With the two verses starting with **As before...** and ending with **...the practitioner**, the author teaches the method of mastering the <term>Vidyā</term>. In that context, **as before**—means like the procedure for the goddess Lalitā. **The same amount**—means a tenth part of that [the total count of chants]. || 30 || **Unblemished**—meaning not spoiled by worms or insects. **Unbroken**—meaning they remain whole [still on their stalks]. || 31 ||

# In the *Tantrarāja* with the Commentary Named *Manoramā*

[260]

The mantra's nature is composed of the three Vedas, through the union of vowels and consonants (33).
I shall now explain, in order, how this mantra—which possesses an immeasurable self—is the cause of the entire universe,
which consists of both the name and the named, and how it is supreme and beyond measure.
Listen, O Wise One! to these descriptions of the expansive power of the ritual rules (34).

The *Sāmaveda* begins with the letter 'A', and the *Rigveda* likewise begins with that same letter.
The *Yajurveda* begins with the letter 'I'. From the union of these, the Pure One arises (35).
Listen, O Wise One, to how that syllable is produced, as taught in the sequence of what comes before and after.
One should first write them down and join them according to the rules of the Science of Language <note>Grammar or *Śabdaśāstra*.</note> (36).

Through the <term>Guṇa-Sandhi</term> <note>A rule of Sanskrit grammar where 'A' and 'I' combine to form 'E'.</note> of the *Rig* and *Yajur* Vedas, and then by applying
the <term>Vṛddhi-Sandhi</term> <note>A rule of Sanskrit grammar where 'A' and 'E' combine to form the stronger vowel 'Ai'.</note> to that result, the form of the Pure One <note>original: "śuci"; here referring to the vowel 'Ai'.</note> is produced (37).
By this process, the mantra is composed of the three Vedas through the union of cause and effect,
since all other things are produced from these initial and final letters (38).

---

With the three verses beginning with "Of the Goddess" and ending with "power," the author introduces the threefold power of the mantra.
In that context, "by the different colors of the Goddess" refers to the previously mentioned forms of the Goddess, such as "white for the sake of attaining perfection in speech" and so on (32). "Composed of the three Vedas" means it possesses the nature of the *Vedas*. "Of the mantra" <note>original: "vidyāyāḥ"</note> means of the Goddess Kulasundarī—this is the implied meaning. "Consisting of the name and the named" means consisting of both sound and meaning (33). "Supreme self-hood" means the state of being most excellent. "Immeasurability" means the state of not being limited by space, time, or form (34).

With the four verses beginning with "The Sāmaveda begins with A" and ending with "verily," the author teaches how the first cluster <note>original: "kūṭa"; a division or block of a long mantra.</note> of the mantra, which is related to speech, is composed of the three Vedas. Here, the meaning is as follows:
One should write the letter 'A', which is the beginning of the *Sāmaveda*; next to it, the letter 'A', which is the beginning of the *Rigveda*; and above both of them, the letter 'I', which is the beginning of the *Yajurveda*. By joining the first 'A' with the 'I', one produces the letter 'E' through <term>Guṇa-Sandhi</term>. Then, by joining that resulting 'E' with the other 'A' in the manner described, one produces the letter 'Ai' through <term>Vṛddhi-Sandhi</term>. In this way, because the letter 'Ai' is produced from the first letters of the three Vedas, and because all subsequent arrangements of letters are caused by these first letters (like a sprout from a seed), the letter 'Ai' is said to be "composed of the three Vedas" (35, 36, 37, 38).

### [15th Chapter] Explanation of the Threefold Nature of the Mantra

->The vital breath moving through the central path is the "Phonemic Mother" <term>Mātṛkā</term> <note>The set of letters in the Sanskrit alphabet, viewed as the creative forces of the universe.</note> beginning with consonants.<-
->Through the union of cause and effect, as described before, it takes the form of the Expressor <term>Vācaka</term> <note>The word or signifier.</note>. (39)<-
->Through the union of those letters and their subtle parts, they become the Expressed <term>Vācya</term> <note>The physical object or signified concept.</note>, starting with the five elements.<-
->Thus, the mantra is declared to be the "Soul of the Universe" because it embodies both the Word and the Object. (40)<-
->The Supreme Form <term>Parā-rūpa</term> is described in the third [section] as a triad, as stated in the twentieth verse.<-
->In this way, this Goddess is the embodiment of the universe; listen to the auspicious variations of her form. (41)<-
->The first form is "Pure" <note>original: "śuci"; referring to the vowel 'Ai'.</note> and has the nature of Speech. The second is said to be Fire.<-
->The third is the unity of the Dot <term>Bindu</term> and the Aspiration <term>Visarga</term>; it is the body of its own parts. (42)<-

In the two verses starting with "In the middle" and ending with "proclaimed" (39–40), the author explains the specific composition of the Mantra (Vidyā) and its threefold nature. He teaches that the Mantra is the unity of all words and all objects, which mutually pervade one another. 

The meaning is as follows: In the middle of the letters *Ka* and *La* found in the second syllable of the Mantra, the consonants exist as the "Phonemic Mother." Because the letter *Ka* is the source of the five elements and other things, the third section of the Mantra is described there. In that context, the consonants represent the "Knowable" <term>Jñeya</term> <note>The objects of the world.</note>, the vowels represent "Knowledge" <term>Jñāna</term> <note>The cognitive process.</note>, and the aspiration <note>The *Visarga*.</note> represents the "Knower" <term>Jñātṛ</term> <note>The conscious subject.</note>. 

Thus, this third section of the Mantra is shown to be the Soul of the Universe, consisting of this triad of Knower, Knowledge, and Known. Because it also contains the letter *Na*, which represents the element Earth, and by virtue of the word "and others," it encompasses the entire world of sounds (the Expressor) and the world of the five elements (the Expressed). Therefore, this entire phenomenal world is non-different from and pervaded by this Mantra. (39–40)

In the verse starting with "The Supreme Form" (41), after previously teaching how the first and second letters of the Mantra pervade reality, the author now explains the interpretation of the third letter. 

The meaning is as follows: This third section of the Mantra has the nature of the "Supreme Knowledge" <note>original: "para-vidyā".</note> taught in the scripture known as the *Trishikha* <note>Likely referring to the *Trishikha-Brahmana Upanishad* or a related Agamic text.</note>. <insert>As stated there, the consonants are the Knowable, the vowels are Knowledge, and the aspiration is the Knower. Thus, it is explained that this third section is the Soul of the Universe, consisting of this triad.</insert> In this way, through these three sections, the Mantra is established as being the soul of the entire universe in three different ways. Since this threefold nature is well-established, <note>text variant: "taccāttannokta" in the commentary manuscript.</note> nothing is unattainable for a practitioner who follows the true tradition. The phrase "variations of form" means: "Listen now to the different internal structures of this Mantra." (41)

In the three verses starting with "Pure" and ending with "Ambika," the author teaches the most secret doctrine called the "Mantra of the Sign" <term>Saṅketa-vidyā</term>, which is the root of the entire collection of the Goddess Tripurā’s mantras. In that context, "Pure" refers to the first form, which has the nature of Speech...

## [The Tantrarāja Tantra with the Commentary named Manoramā]

Through that seed-syllable, she is properly called the "Soul of the Universe." The third section, called the "Forest" <term>Vana</term>, is said to be joined with *Māyā* <note>In this context, the letter 'M' or the nasal Dot (Bindu).</note> or with its own [vowels]. (43)

This is the "Root of the Three Cities" <term>Vaipura-kanda</term> and is called the "Symbolic Code" <term>Saṅketa</term>. She consists of the triad of the Knower, Knowledge, and the Known, as well as the three aspects of defects, virtues, and brilliance. (44)

In her middle seed-syllable, by joining the "Nectar" <note>The letter 'La'.</note> and the "Breath" <note>The letter 'Ha'.</note>, she is the cause of the manifest world in the form of the Expressed and the Expressor. (45)

In the third [seed-syllable], through the union with the "Heart" <note>The letter 'Ha'.</note>, the nature of the Triad as the Soul of the Universe is revealed. From the "Swan" <term>Haṃsa</term> <note>A mantra representing the breath/soul.</note> residing in those heart-centers, she takes the form of all that is moving and stationary. (46)

O Supreme Goddess! Because of the combinations of one, two, or more consonants within these three [syllables], it is impossible to count the total number of Mantras <term>Vidyā</term>. (47)

---

The first part is called the "Origin of Speech" <term>Vāgbhava</term> and has the form of the twelve vowels. The second is "Fire"—this is the fourth vowel <note>The long vowel 'Ī'.</note>, which embodies the union of Shiva and Shakti and is the source of the Dot <term>Bindu</term> and the Aspiration <term>Visarga</term>, which are themselves the causes of all the letters of the alphabet. (42)

**"Through that seed-syllable"**—meaning, through the nature of that fourth vowel. **"She is the Soul of the Universe"**—this means that through the fourth vowel, which represents the union of Shiva and Shakti as previously explained, that Mantra is declared to be the Soul of the Universe. **"The third Forest"**—the third Mantra consists solely of the fourteen vowels. **"With Maya or its own"**—this means joined with either the Aspiration <term>Visarga</term> or the Dot <term>Bindu</term>. (43)

She is called the **"Root of the Three Cities"** and the **"Symbolic Code"** because this Mantra is like a root-bulb <term>Kanda</term> <note>A yogic term for the central point of the body's energy channels.</note>. It is the fundamental source of the countless masses of the "Three Cities" <term>Tripurā</term> Mantras produced by the combinations of one, two, or more consonants that will be described later in the three sections. **"The triad of Knower, Knowledge, and Known; defects, virtues, and brilliance"**—this means that she stands filling the entire universe in the form of the Knower, Knowledge, and the Known; in the form of the three humors—Wind, Bile, and Phlegm <note>The Ayurvedic Doshas: Vata, Pitta, and Kapha.</note>; and in the form of Fire, the Sun, and the Moon. (44)

Through the two verses beginning with **"In her"** and ending with **"stationary nature,"** the author teaches the pervasive nature of the Mantra. This involves the cessation of the letters *Ka* and *La* in the middle section, and the use of the letter *Sa* at the end. He explains the meditative realization of this pervasiveness through the union of the letters *Ha* and *Sa* in the three sections. In this context, **"In her"** refers to this Symbolic Code Mantra, and **"the cause"** is stated to show her absolute independence <term>Svātantrya</term>. (45)

**"The nature of the Triad as the Soul of the Universe"**—meaning the universal soul in the form of the Knower, Knowledge, and the Known. **"In those"**—referring to the three clusters of syllables <term>Kūṭa</term>. **"The nature of the moving and the stationary"**—the meaning is this: through the combination of the letters *Ha* and *Sa* in each of those three seed-syllables, the meditative realization of this Symbolic Code Mantra as the soul of all moving and unmoving things is expressed. (46)

# 15th Chapter: The Declaration of the Knowledge of the Jewels of the City of Triads

Since her glory is infinite, how could I describe her completely?
Yet, for the sake of protecting my devotees, I will speak of some aspects. || 48 ||
<note>original: "tathāpi bhaktasantrāṇahetoḥ kāñcana vachmi te" — The teacher Shiva addresses the Goddess, noting that while the variations are infinite, he will reveal the essential ones for the benefit of practitioners.</note>

She bestows longevity, prosperity, fame, enjoyment, beauty, and health.
She is the essence of knowledge regarding both this world and the next, and the granter of all perfections <term>Siddhi</term>. || 49 ||

From the union of the "Swan" <term>Haṃsa</term> <note>Representing the seed-syllable 'Ha'.</note> in the three parts of the *Kulasundarī* mantra in sequence,
The Great Wisdom <term>Mahāvidyā</term> named *Vijayā* <note>The Victorious One.</note> is formed, which is dedicated to the movement of the universe. || 50 ||

Through the union of the "Heart" <term>Hṛd</term> <note>Representing the seed-syllable 'Sa'.</note> to those sections,
The Wisdom named *Jīvā* <note>The Individual Soul or Life-Force.</note> arises, representing the consciousness of the universe.
By joining both [the 'Ha' and the 'Sa'] in those sections,
The body of both of us <note>Referring to the unified form of Shiva and Shakti.</note> is brought forth. || 51 ||

The Wisdom beginning with the "Heart" <note>the letter 'Sa'</note> is your form, O Goddess;
The mantra beginning with the "Swan" <note>the letter 'Ha'</note> is my form.
Through the combination of "Fire" <note>original: "dāha" — representing the letter 'Ra'.</note> with these,
She is known as *Viśvā*, the embodiment of the cosmos. || 52 ||

With the verse beginning with "One or two..." <note>Referring to verse 47 on the previous page.</note>, the text teaches the infinite nature of the Symbolic Wisdom <term>Saṅketa-vidyā</term> through the combination of one, two, or more consonants. The meaning is as follows: within the three sections <term>Khaṇḍa</term> of that Symbolic Wisdom, one might lack the second or third component in the first section, or the first and third in the second, or the first and second in the third. 

In any of these, or in both, or in all of them, using the twenty-five consonants from *Ka* to *Ma* <note>The five groups of five consonants that form the base of the Sanskrit alphabet.</note>, by applying them in or out of sequence in combinations of one, two, and so on, the number and nature of the resulting mantras are impossible for anyone to count or even describe. || 47 ||

Regarding the verses starting from "Since her glory is infinite..." to "Granter of perfections" (48-49), the author introduces the praise of the Wisdoms which are the "Jewels of the City of Triads" <term>Traipura-ratna</term>. 

In this context, "She" refers to the Symbolic Wisdom. "Her" refers to the infinite mantras arising from the combinations of one, two, or more consonants. "Some" refers to the primary ones. By stating she is "the essence of knowledge regarding both this world and the next," the author distinguishes these mantras from those belonging to inferior or incorrect systems. || 48 ||

From the verse starting with "From the Wisdom..." (50) until the end of the six verses <note>Ending at verse 55, though only 50-52 are fully present here.</note>, the nature of the eleven Wisdoms is taught, concluding with the total count of these "Jewels of Tripura." 

The meaning is this: By adding the letter "Ha" <note>The "Swan".</note> above each of the three sections of the *Kulasundarī* mantra, the Wisdom named *Vijayā* is formed. Because she provides knowledge of both worldly and spiritual realms, she is the "Protectress of All." || 50 || 

In those same sections, by removing the letter "Ha" and adding the letter "Sa" <note>The "Heart".</note> instead, the Wisdom named *Jīvā* is formed, which embodies the universal consciousness. || 51 || 

In those sections, by adding "Sa" before "Ha," the mantra called *Manva* is formed; and by adding "Ha" before "Sa," the Wisdom called *Vidyā* is formed. In these three...

# Manoramā: A Commentary on the King of Tantras

> When each section is encased by the syllable of Power <term>Shakti</term>, she becomes the Wisdom known as the *Universal Enchanter* <term>Viśvavimohinī</term>. However, when she is encased by the syllables of Illusion <term>Māyā</term> combined with the elements of air and nectar, she is called the *Fullness of Nectar* <term>Vipurāmṛtā</term>. || 53 ||
> <note>original: "śakti-puṭitā... māyābhyāṃ puṭitā" — "Encasing" (puṭitā) refers to the practice of placing a specific seed-syllable both before and after a mantra or its sections to amplify its power.</note>
>
> If the mantra begins with the syllable of Illusion, it is called the *Enchantress* <term>Mohinī</term>. If that syllable is placed in the middle, she is considered the *Agitator* <term>Kṣobhiṇī</term>. || 54 ||
>
> If placed at the end, she is known as the *Moistener* <term>Kledinī</term>. If the mantra starts with the letter 'A' <note>The first vowel, representing the source.</note>, she is called the *Great Elevation* <term>Mahodayā</term>. These are the thirteen methods known as the *Jewels of the City of Triads* <term>Tripurā-ratna</term>. || 55 ||
>
> From the variations in the order of these thirteen arise seventy-eight different forms of Wisdom. Their complete rituals have been explained to you in the *Ocean of a Hundred Thousand* <term>Lakṣasāgara</term>. || 56 ||
> <note>The "Lakṣasāgara" is a referenced scripture, likely a larger or earlier version of this tradition containing exhaustive ritual details.</note>
>
> There exists a certain Wisdom called the *Bringer of Prosperity* <term>Sampatkarī</term>, whose glory is beyond thought. I shall speak of her to you, O Queen of Gods, for the attainment of all that the practitioner desires. || 57 ||

In the first of the mantra-clusters, by joining the letters 'Ha' and 'Sa' below and between other consonants, the *Universal Essence* <term>Viśvamayī</term> and *Universal Form* <term>Viśvarūpā</term> Wisdoms are formed. || 52 || <note>This commentary note refers back to the construction of the previous verse.</note> 

In the standard sequence, one should encase the three sections of the *Beautiful One of the Clan* <term>Kulasundarī</term> individually with two instances of the "Heart-Line" <term>Hṛllekhā</term> <note>The seed-syllable "Hrīṃ".</note>. This creates the *Universal Enchanter* <term>Viśvavimohinī</term> Wisdom. || 53 || 

Furthermore, by encasing that same mantra with two "Heart-Line" syllables in a specific way, the Wisdom named *Fullness of Nectar* <term>Vipurāmṛtā</term> is created. || 54 || 

Due to the realization of Truth and the attainment of all gains, her form is one of complete nourishment. By removing the first cluster <term>kūṭa</term> of that *Kulasundarī* mantra and placing the "Heart-Line" there instead, the Wisdom named *Enchantress* <term>Mohinī</term> is formed. Similarly, by removing the middle section and placing the "Heart-Line" there, the Wisdom named *Agitator* <term>Kṣobhiṇī</term> arises. Likewise, by placing the "Heart-Line" in the position of the final section, the Wisdom named *Moistener* <term>Kledinī</term> is formed. Furthermore, by removing the first section of that *Kulasundarī* mantra and placing the letter 'A' there, the Wisdom called *Great Elevation* <term>Mahodayā</term> is created. 

Thus, the symbolic Wisdom called the *Bulb of the City of Triads* <term>Tripurā-kandā</term>, together with the aforementioned *Kulasundarī* Wisdoms and the forms starting from *Vijayā* and ending with *Mahodayā*, comprise eleven Wisdoms. Combined, these thirteen Wisdoms are declared to be the *Jewels of the City of Triads* <term>Tripurā-ratna</term>. || 55 ||

Regarding the verse beginning with "Of these" <note>Verse 56</note>: by applying the methods of regular order, reverse order, and mixed order mentioned in the twenty-fifth chapter to each of these thirteen Wisdoms, six variations arise for each. This results in seventy-eight total Wisdoms. The teacher explains that the expanded ritual procedures for these are taught in the scripture titled *The Ocean of a Hundred Thousand* <term>Lakṣasāgara</term>. || 56 ||

With the eleven verses beginning with "The Bringer of Prosperity" and ending with "one should elevate," the text introduces and then teaches the *Bringer of Prosperity* <term>Sampatkarī</term> Wisdom—so named because her name matches her function—along with instructions for her meditation and ritual application, as well as the order of worship for the previously mentioned seventy-eight Wisdoms. There, through the southern union of breath, essence, and wind...

### Chapter 15 ] Statement on the Method, Ritual, and Worship of the Wisdom of the Perfect Boon

The first section is said to be composed of Life <note>original: "prāṇa" — code for the letter 'L'</note>, the chest <note>original: "urasā" — code for the long vowel 'Ā'</note>, the wind <note>original: "marut" — code for the vowel 'I'</note>, and fire <note>original: "vahni" — code for the nasal dot or bindu</note>. The second section, O Pārvatī, consists of the air <note>original: "vāta" — the letter 'A'</note>, and the two "moving ones" <note>original: "carasva" — code for the vowel 'E' and the bindu</note>. || 58 ||

The third section, O Supreme Goddess, is made of the swan <note>original: "haṃsa" — the letter 'H'</note>, the heart <note>original: "hṛd" — the letter 'S'</note>, the gift <note>original: "dana" — the vowel 'AU'</note>, and the illusion <note>original: "māyā" — here referring to the visarga or breath-release ':'</note>. Thus, this Wisdom consists of three syllables. Now its ritual method is described. || 59 ||

Using the third seed-syllable <note>The 'Hsauḥ' syllable</note> combined in sequence with the long vowels, one should perform the ritual placement <term>nyāsa</term> on the hands and limbs as described before. Then, one should meditate upon Her as follows: || 60 ||

Her body, garments, and ornaments have the brilliant hue of a pomegranate flower. She has four arms, three eyes, and a face characterized by a gracious, gentle smile. || 61 ||

She is being bathed in a rain of jewels. She is seated in the auspicious *svastika* posture <note>A cross-legged sitting position used in meditation</note> within a triangle located in the center of an eight-petalled lotus. She is the very temple of compassion and bliss. || 62 ||

In Her hands, she holds a rosary of red coral, a gemstone cup filled with jewels, a book, and the gesture of granting boons <term>varada-mudrā</term>. She is the source of all auspiciousness. || 63 ||

She resides upon the "Noble Seat" <term>kulasana</term>, which is constructed of three sets of sixteen letters starting from 'A' and ending with 'S'. In the center of the letters from 'Ha' to 'Kṣa', she is united with Her Wisdom-mantra. || 64 ||

---

The first cluster <term>kūṭa</term> is composed of the letters L, Ā, I, and the dot (bindu). In this instance, the standard rules of phonetic blending <note>original: "guṇa-sandhi"</note> between 'Ā' and 'I' are not applied <note>Meaning it is pronounced 'Lā-īṃ' rather than 'Leṃ'</note>. The second cluster consists of the letters A, E, and the dot. Here too, the rules of phonetic growth <note>original: "vṛddhi-sandhi"</note> are not applied. || 57-58 ||

The third cluster consists of the letters H, S, AU, and the breath-release (visarga). "Supreme Goddess" is the address used for the Deity. || 59 ||

"On the hands and limbs" refers to the ritual placements <term>karāṅga-nyāsa</term>. The meaning is that one should perform this using the third seed-syllable combined with the long vowels and the dot. "In this way" refers to the method about to be described. || 60-61 ||

"Seated in the *svastika*" means staying in the specific yogic posture of that name. The word "temple" <note>original: "mandirām"</note> is used to express her sovereignty—it means she is the dwelling place of all grace. || 62 ||

The items held in the hands should be visualized in sequence from the upper right hand to the lower left hand. || 63 ||

"Constructed of three sets of sixteen...": This refers to the three lines forming a triangle, beginning with the letters A, Ha, and Tha, and ending with the breath-release, Ta, and Sa. Within this, the Supreme Power <term>Shakti</term> resides, whose form is the expansion of the meaning of all sounds and words starting from the remaining consonants. In the mantras of the Goddess <term>Shakti-mantras</term>, this "Supreme Extraction" is the traditional meaning. The "Noble Seat" <term>kulasana</term> is the name for this specific diagram or triangle. "United with her Wisdom"...

# In the Tantrarāja, accompanied by the commentary named Manoramā

> Having invoked Her, and after performing the water offering and the declaration of intent as before, one should worship Her in the proper sequence. In the center and in the corners of the triangle, one should worship Rati, Prīti, and Manobhava <note>original: "manobhavān"; these are the deities of Desire: Attachment, Pleasure, and the Mind-Born Cupid</note>. || 65 ||
> Moving to the left <note>original: "savyagāḥ"</note> starting from the front, one should likewise worship the Mothers in the eight-petaled lotus. In the outer square, one should worship the World Guardians <note>original: "lokapālān"</note> and their Powers <term>shaktis</term> as previously described. || 66 ||
> This method <term>vidhāna</term> for the seventy-eight Wisdoms has been correctly declared. One should also perform the two offerings <term>bali</term> and the fire sacrifice <term>homa</term> by elevating them as before. || 67 ||
> Using four parts [of juice], one-fourth part [of root], and an equal part [of milk], combined with ghee: one should boil the juice of Brahmi <note>original: "brāhmī-rasa"</note>, Vacha <note>original: "vacā"</note>, and milk with the ghee for three days. || 68 ||

---

— ...accompanied by that Wisdom. This is an attribute of the "Seat of the Kula" <note>the ritual foundation</note>. || 64 || The intent and water offering are as described before. || 65 ||
**Moving to the left** — this means in a counter-clockwise direction <note>original: "vāmāvarta-krameṇa"</note>. **Likewise** — means starting from the front and moving counter-clockwise. **The eight Mothers** — these are the goddesses starting with Brāhmī, as described previously. **Powers** — this means those who take the form of power and are situated in the directions starting with the East. || 66 || **For the seventy-eight** — the word "Wisdoms" <note>original: "vidyānām"</note> is implied. The meaning is that this is the specific ritual method for the seventy-eight types of Wisdom mantras. **The two offerings** — this refers to those given at the beginning and the end. **Fire sacrifice** — the daily fire ritual as described before. The point being made is this: during the worship and other rites, one should provide the two offerings using the sixteen-syllable mantra at the start and the seven-syllable mantra of the goddess Kurukullā at the end in the prescribed order, and then perform the fire sacrifice according to the daily worship sequence. **Other** — refers to the arrangement of the seven syllables at the beginning and end of the mantras.
The sequence for constructing the daily worship diagram <term>cakra</term> for these goddesses is as follows: having drawn two perfect squares equipped with eastern and western gates, and having drawn an eight-petaled lotus inside that, and having drawn a triangle <note>original: "yoni"</note> with three equal lines according to the measurement in the pericarp of that lotus, one should worship the specified Powers in the stated order. || 67 ||

With the two verses starting with **"Using four parts"** and ending with **"the poet,"** the text teaches the method for producing "Brahmi-Ghee" <note>original: "brāhmī-ghṛta"</note> and the ritual application of that ghee to grant the power of speech <term>vāk-siddhi</term> to one who is mute. In this context, the identities of **Brahmi** <note>the herb Bacopa monnieri</note> and **Vacha** <note>the herb Acorus calamus</note> should be learned from the mouth of a Guru. **Clarified butter** — means ghee. The meaning is this: 
1. Take a quantity of Brahmi juice equal to four times the amount of ghee to be prepared.
2. Take a quantity of Vacha equal to one-fourth the amount of ghee.
3. Take a quantity of milk equal to the amount of ghee.
Having combined these four in the specified proportions, one should cook them over a gentle fire for three days. Then, having refined it and poured it into a clean ghee-pot, during the cold season, one should fashion a "Diagram of the Mothers" <term>mātṛkā-yantra</term> <note>a diagram containing the letters of the Sanskrit alphabet</note> on a silver plate. After performing the ritual of "Establishing Life" <term>prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā</term> into that diagram, one should submerge the diagram into this ghee. While touching the ghee with a blade of Kusha, Durva, or Darbha grass, one should recite the Mother-mantra with the nasal dot <term>bindu</term> ten thousand times...

### [ Chapter 15 ] Concerning the worship of the two deities for each day

With great care, one should daily lick the medicinal ghee in the morning while reciting the Wisdom of the Mother <note>original: "mātṛkā-vidyā"; the mantra associated with the Sanskrit alphabet</note> ten thousand times, along with the sacred diagram <term>yantra</term>. After one year, even a mute person will become a poet. || 69 ||

Shiva, Ambikā, Kumāra, Vidhi <note>original: "vidhiḥ"; a name for Brahma the Creator</note>, Viṣṇu, Ramā <note>original: "ramā"; the goddess Lakshmī</note>, Kubera, Āra <note>original: "āra"; the planet Mars</note>, the Moon, the Sun, Jupiter, Venus <note>original: "sita"</note>, and Saturn <note>original: "saura"</note>. || 70 ||

These are the Lords of the Days. On their respective days, one should worship them using the Wisdom associated with that day, combined with the seven-syllable formula of their name. One should also perform libations <term>tarpaṇa</term> and fire sacrifices <term>homa</term>. || 71 ||

Using ash produced from medicinal plants and empowered with mantras, one should perform the ritual placement <term>nyāsa</term> of the Mothers and touch the mantra <note>The text suggests touching specific points on the body while reciting the mantra</note> in the shape of a jewel. <note>original: "ratnākṛte"</note> || 72 ||

One should perform this rite especially for kings and those who are suffering. By this, they will become happy again, along with their families, for as long as they live. || 73 ||

---

Having recited the mantra, and afterwards having recited the previously mentioned Wisdom ten thousand times, one should store the medicine safely in a certain place. One should worship it at the three junctions of the day <note>dawn, noon, and dusk</note> using the Mother Wisdom. Every morning, after reciting the Mother Wisdom over it three times, one should lick a measure of three *nishkas* <note>a historical unit of weight, roughly 12-15 grams</note> of that ghee. From this, the stated result will be achieved after one year. || 68-69 ||

With the two verses starting with **Shiva** and ending with **fire sacrifice**, the author teaches the two deities for each of the seven days starting with Sunday, their worship, and its purpose. In this context, **Ramā** refers to Lakshmī. **Āra** refers to Mars. The terms **Sita** and **Saura** are used independently here, meaning Venus and Saturn respectively. || 70 ||

**On those** — this refers to the seven days starting with Sunday. **Them** — refers to the Lords of the Days, who are of two types <note>The planet and its corresponding deity</note>. **Using the Wisdom of that day** — refers to the specific *Nityā* Wisdom <term>vidyā</term> belonging to that day. **Combined with the seven-syllable formula of their name** — this means using the specific name of the deity ending with a seven-syllable mantra. **Should sacrifice** — means performing the fire offering. The result is that one’s desires will be fulfilled.

The meaning is as follows: on the seven days starting with Sunday, one should worship the two types of Lords mentioned for each day in the prescribed order. By using the specific *Nityā* Wisdom of that day ending in the seven-syllable name-mantra, and by performing worship, libations, and fire sacrifice in the appropriate sacred circle <term>maṇḍala</term>, one achieves the desired success. || 71 ||

With the two verses starting with **medicinal plants** and ending with **as long as they live**, the author explains a protective rite. Using the ash from medicinal plants associated with the letters of the alphabet, and after performing the drawing of the Mother-diagram and the infusion of life-force <term>prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā</term>, one empowers it with the Wisdom. By touching the locations of the Mother-letters <note>ritual points on the body</note> at the two twilights <note>sunrise and sunset</note>, protection from all calamities is granted to everyone. || 72-73 ||

With the four verses starting with "When severe" and ending with "on the earth," the author teaches how to cross over calamities through the worship of the nine planets <note>original: "navagraha-pūjā"</note>. In that context—"thus"—refers to the method that will be described in the twenty-eighth chapter. "In the circle of nine chambers" means in those respective diagrams. || 74 ||

With the verse beginning with "In the center," the author reminds us of the directional placement of the planets to be described hereafter, in order of their auspicious or inauspicious nature. "Them"—the nine planets. "By those"—referring to the nine name-mantras found in the middle of the "seven-syllable hair" formulas of the Daily Goddesses of the days, as previously described. || 75 ||

The gist of what is said is this: One should prepare a grid of nine equal chambers <term>koṣṭha</term> using four lines drawn east-to-west and four north-to-south. In these, one should arrange the planetary circles <term>maṇḍala</term> as will be described in the twenty-eighth chapter. By worshipping there with the nine name-mantras—which are derived from the middle of the seven-syllable "hairs" of the Daily Goddesses—and by performing libations, fire sacrifices, and giving gifts of gold and other items to the experts of this science, one is released from all calamities and diseases and becomes happy. || 77 ||

With the eight verses starting with "Tell me" and ending with "one should place," the author teaches the ritual placement of the "Mother" letters <note>original: "mātṛkā-nyāsa"</note>, including the six-limbed placement <term>ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa</term>. In that context: "that diagram" refers to the diagram of the Mother letters <term>mātṛkā-yantra</term>. "The two" refers to the ritual placement <term>nyāsa</term> and the diagram <term>yantra</term>. "Today" means in this specific chapter. "In that chapter" refers to the chapter dedicated to the Mother letters. "The whole" refers to the remaining details. || 78 ||

With one verse and three quarters starting with "With the short" and ending with "in this way," the meaning is as follows: Among the vowels, there are four "sixth" letters, namely: ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ. Excluding those, the remaining twelve—a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, e...

<meta>This page continues the instructions for Mātṛkā-nyāsa, the ritual installation of the Sanskrit alphabet into the practitioner's body. ### 15th Chapter: Description of the Construction of the Mother-Letter Yantra. 269

Among the vowels, four are said to be the middle ones, having the forms of *ṣa*, *ga*, and *ḍha*. <note>The Sanskrit here describes specific phonetic shapes or groupings used for the ritual "limbs" of the mantra.</note> Having performed the placement on the hands and limbs in this way, one then places the letters from *A* to *Kṣa*— || 80 ||

On the forehead, the circumference of the face, the eyes, ears, nose, and cheeks; on the lips, teeth, head, and tongue—one should place the vowels individually. || 81 ||

On the roots, middle joints, and tips of the hands and feet, one should place the four groups <note>vargas: the consonant clusters of the Sanskrit alphabet</note>; and the fifth group should be placed on the sides and the back. || 82 ||

Placing them on the navel and the heart, one should then place the "pervasive" letters <note>the semi-vowels and sibilants</note> in the ten bodily elements <term>dhātus: the fundamental tissues of the body</term>—those that go into the skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen. || 83 ||

As well as in the life-breath, the energy, and the self, one should place them thus with a composed mind. Touching the heart, one should meditate on those letters and place them within the bodily elements. || 84 ||

Alternatively: [place them] in the heart, the two shoulders, the lower back, and the armpits. One should also place them below the heart, in the feet, the belly, and the face. || 85 ||

---

With the six syllables of "Oñca," and the six long vowels—*Ā*, *Ī*, *Ū*, *Ai*, *Au*, *Aḥ*—each with a nasal point <note>bindu</note>, one should join the groups of consonants <note>the ka, ca, ṭa, ta, and pa groups</note> and the ten-letter group starting with *Ya*. Following the stated order, and adding the ritual suffixes <note>such as "namaḥ" or "svāhā"</note> at the end, one should perform the placement on the hands and limbs <term>karāṅganyāsa: a ritual practice of touching parts of the hand and body to "install" the power of a mantra</term>. || 79–80 ||

With the five verses beginning with "From A to Kṣa" and ending with "one should place," the author teaches the sequence for the ritual placement of the "Mother" letters <note>Mātṛkā-nyāsa</note> on the body, starting from the feet. In that context, "at the roots and middle joints": for the arms, the "roots" are the shoulders and the "middle joints" are the elbows. The "middle joints" [further down] refers to the wrists and the bases of the fingers. For the feet, the words "root" and "middle" refer to the hips and the knees. There, "the two middle joints" refers to the joints between the forefeet and the toes. "The fifth group" refers to the remaining consonants. || 81–82 ||

"Pervasive"—this refers to the letters *Ya* through *Kṣa*. These are called pervasive because they are the internal essence of the bodily elements <note>dhātus</note>. || 83 || "In the life-breath, energy, and self"—these are also considered "elements" in this context. "Of them"—this refers to the elements; the grammar here indicates placing the letters *into* the elements. || 84 ||

"Alternatively"—this marks a different tradition or method. In this second option, while touching from the heart down to the tips of the feet... <note>The text here describes a sweeping ritual motion</note>... one places the letter *Sa* by moving the hand from the heart to the ends of the arms, and the letter *Ha* by moving from the heart to the tips of the feet. || 85 ||

---

(1) A variant reading for "below the heart and at the tips of the feet" is found in the So. manuscript. <span style="margin-left: 2em;">* A variant reading for "lower back" is found in the Ti. manuscript.</span>

This process is intended to spiritualize the body, equating phonemes with biological and subtle-energy systems.</summary>
