---

With the verse beginning with "Pramodā," the teacher points out eight names. Regarding the name "Saratipriyā," the letter 'S' is used as before. "Kalādakṣā" is one name. The other names are easy to understand. [53] <note>The commentator is referencing names from the preceding section to ensure the practitioner correctly identifies each spirit.</note>

With the two verses beginning with "Thus" and ending with "one's desires," he concludes the previous section and teaches the ritual knowledge for the perfection of the Yakṣiṇīs. In that context, "of them" refers to the Yakṣiṇīs. "In order" means according to the method to be described. "Enveloped by those two seed-syllables" means enclosed by the two seed-syllables at the beginning and the end of the root-ritual-knowledge. [54]

The phrase "with the six groups and their own names" connects to the next verse. "Flowing Eternal Intoxication" <note>Variant: nityamadramavadradami</note> is the mantra arrangement. By saying these are "at the beginning and end of the root-ritual-knowledge," he indicates that these six syllables, which describe the nature [of the deity] <margin>(4) Variant: "Possessing the nature of the middle of the root ritual knowledge"</margin> and are joined with the two enveloping seed-syllables, are common to all Yakṣiṇī ritual knowledges. "By their declared names" means that the distinction between the mantras—starting with **Vicitrā**—arises from using the names themselves, attached to the end of the six-syllable formulas. [55]

With the four verses starting with "of them" and ending with "others," he teaches the syllable count for each of the ritual knowledges. There, "of them" refers to the Yakṣiṇīs. "The last" refers to the twenty-sixth. [56]

"Four"—meaning four ritual knowledges. "Fifteen"—meaning they consist of fifteen syllables. [57]

The phrase "and the twenty-first" connects to "twelve syllables." Thus, there are six twelve-syllable ritual knowledges in total. "Likewise, those joined with fourteen"—meaning just like the twelve-syllable ones...

Regarding the arrangement: the phrase is "Always flow with passion" (*mada-nitya-drave*). The "names" refer to the sixty-four names starting with Vibhrama and others. "In the second case" means using the accusative case endings. These are "encased" or prefixed by the six syllables of the **Mūlavidyā** <term>Mūlavidyā: the 'Root Knowledge' or primary mantra of the main deity</term>. These six syllables are common to all the mantras; the mantras differ only by the specific names used. The sequence for assembling the mantra is as follows: Two seed-syllables of the Root Knowledge, then the six syllables [of the Root Knowledge], then the respective name in the accusative case, then the word "Give" (*dehi*), and finally the same two seed-syllables in reverse order (*viloma*). # Discussion of the Names and Syllables of the Servant Spirits
## 17th Chapter, Page 309

->Twenty-five **mantras** <note>sacred chants</note> are said to have sixteen syllables;<-
->Likewise, four have seventeen syllables, following a non-linear order. [71]<-
->The fourteen final letters of the "Knowledge-Syllables" are surrounded<-
->By the vowels, resulting in a total count of two hundred and twenty-four. [72]<-
->With these, there are seven **yantras** <term>Yantra: a geometric diagram used as an instrument for meditation and ritual worship</term> in which one should worship in order,<-
->The deities throughout the seven days of the week, starting with Sunday, with devotion. [73]<-

---

Regarding those **mantras** <note>original: "manunām"</note> [from verse 68]: Among them, nine mantras are declared to have fourteen syllables—the connection here is that within the previously mentioned set, nine specifically consist of fourteen syllables. These are the 3rd, 6th, 11th, 16th, 19th, 52nd, 57th, 60th, and 62nd spirits in the list. Twenty-six mantras have fifteen syllables—these are the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th, 9th, 10th, 14th, 15th, 17th, 18th, 20th, 30th, 22nd, 34th, 36th, 40th, 44th, 50th, 51st, 55th, 56th, 58th, 59th, 63rd, and 64th. [70] There are twenty-five mantras of sixteen syllables—these are the 7th, 8th, 12th, 13th, 20th, 21st, 23rd, 29th, 27th, 21st, 38th, 39th, 40th, 41st, 40th, 46th, 47th, 48th, 49th, 53rd, and 54th. There are four seventeen-syllable mantras—these are the 33rd, 25th, 27th, and 40th. "In a non-linear order" means following the sequence just described. The rest is easy to understand. Here, the mantra for the "Attainment of Illusion" <note>Māyā-siddhi</note> was not explicitly mentioned because it is contained within the "Servant" category according to the Supreme Tradition <note>Mukhyāgama</note>. Therefore, by substituting the word "Illusion" <note>Māyā</note> in place of the word "All-groups" <note>Sarvagaṇa</note>, that mantra becomes fourteen syllables long. In this way, 111 fundamental mantras, distinguished by their individual forms, are correctly shown. [71]

Through the twenty-four verses beginning with "With the Knowledge-syllables" and ending with "measuring a man's height," the author teaches the seven **yantras** (the locations for practice), the methods of proof for each, and their results, for the purpose of mastering the 111 previously mentioned "Success-mantras" <note>Siddhi-mantras</note> via the vowels modified by the seven days of the week. In that context, "with vowels" <note>sasvaraiḥ</note> means graced by the sixteen vowels as described before. "Two hundred and twenty-four" means the number 224 <note>14 letters multiplied by 16 vowels</note>. [72] "With these" refers to those letters. "In those" refers to the **yantras**. "Declared" refers to the ten kinds of attainments <note>Siddhis</note> mentioned previously. "In the seven days starting with the Sun" means on each day of the week, starting with Sunday, one should worship all the "Deities of Attainment" <note>Siddhi-devatās</note> <gloss>(2) One manuscript reads: "Deities of the Lunar Day" (Tithi-devatā)</gloss> in each of the seven **yantras** during their respective rituals.

---

# Tantrarāja with the Manoramā Commentary
## 17th Chapter, Page 310

> One should write the name of the spirit ending in the seventh case, followed by "give me what I desire."
> In the center of the diagram, within the Syllable of Illusion <note>original: "māyāstham", referring to the seed-syllable Hrīṃ</note>, one should worship the **Siddhis** <term>Siddhis: supernatural powers or perfections attained through yoga or ritual</term>. [74]
>
> Having fashioned a "nine-womb" <note>original: "navayoni", a geometric pattern of nine interlocking triangles</note> within two circles, one should draw an eight-angled figure on the outside.
> Beyond that, one should correctly draw a pair consisting of a sixteen-petaled lotus and a "ground-lotus" <note>a square base</note> according to the rules. [75]
>
> Writing upon these in sequence, one should transcribe twenty-two letters.
> These go on the petals and the corners, and again within the two middle circles. [76]
>
> One should write the mother-letters <note>the Sanskrit alphabet</note> starting with the **A-Ka-Tha** groups in the inner sequence.
> In the intervals between the corners, one should write the letters *Ha*, *La*, and *Kṣa* in order. [77]
>
> Moving clockwise from the top, there are seven **yantras** created this way.
> They are for the **Siddhis**, the **Yakshinis** <note>nature spirits or semi-divine beings</note>, and the **Chetakas** <note>servant spirits</note> individually. [78]
>
> There is a specific variation for the **Chetakas**: an eight-petaled lotus is placed in the center.
> Their rituals and results are as previously stated. [79]

---

The meaning of the text is "one should worship." [Regarding verse 74]: **Ending in the seventh** — this means using the seventh grammatical case ending <note>original: "saptamī-vibhaktyantām"; usually the locative case, though in ritual use it often dictates a specific phonetic transformation of the name</note>. **Within Illusion** — this means situated inside the heart of the syllable *Hrīṃ*. The instruction to write "give me what I desire" connects to the previous passage. **Your** — this refers to the interior of the "Illusion" syllable. **Siddhis** — these are the deities governing all perfections. [74]

**On the outside** — this means outside of the two circles. **Beyond** — this means outside of the eight-angled figure. **Sixteen-petaled** — this refers to a lotus with sixteen petals. **According to the rules** — this means drawing them according to the correct proportions. [75]

**On those** — this refers to the petals. The mention of "corners" connects to the subsequent text. **Within the two middle circles** — this means the two paths (circles) located outside the sixteen petals, which are themselves outside the eight-angled figure, which is outside the "nine-womb" center. [76]

**Starting with A-Ka-Tha** — this refers to the forty-eight letters of the alphabet arranged in three groups of sixteen: the first sixteen starting with *A*, the next sixteen starting with *Ka*, and the final sixteen starting with *Tha*. **Of that** — this refers to the pair of squares written on the outside. **The letters Ha, La, and Kṣa in the corner intervals** — this means writing these three specific letters in the four corner intervals of the "ground-lotus" pair in the order described. [77]

**Clockwise from the top** — the remaining letters should follow this direction. **Seven yantras** — the word "exist" is implied here. **By those** — referring to those specific diagrams. **Individually** — this implies that the ritual procedures for each one are distinct. [78]

**An eight-petaled lotus in the middle** — this means placing an eight-petaled lotus in the space where the "nine-womb" pattern would otherwise be. [79] This also includes the pericarp <note>the center of the lotus</note>.

# Tantrarāja with the Manoramā Commentary
## 17th Chapter, Page 311

->Listen to the ritual applications, O Goddess! By succeeding in these, one becomes equal to me on this earth,<-
->worshipped by all the worlds, everywhere and at all times. [80]<-
->At the foot of a banyan tree in the forest, on a mountain peak, in caves,<-
->in the middle of a garden, in a wilderness, or at the foot of a Mother-Tree— [81]<-
->as well as in a forest on a riverbank—one should master these Yakshinis in groups of three.<-
->One should chant 100,000 repetitions for each individual syllable according to the stated procedure. [82]<-

---

There are nine locations. These belong to the spirits, from Vijayā to the last of the servant spirits <term>Chetakas: minor spirits or "servants" invoked for specific tasks</term>. "By which" refers to the ritual applications.

"Equal to me" means the Supreme Lord <note>The speaker is Shiva, addressing the Goddess Parvati</note>. By these nine verses <note>starting from verse 74 on the previous page</note>, the following is explained:

Having fashioned two concentric circles with a one-inch gap between them, divided into inner and outer sections according to the desired measurement, one should create a "nine-womb" pattern <term>Navayoni: a sacred geometry consisting of nine interlocking triangles</term> in the center according to the previously stated rules. Outside of that, one should create an eight-angled figure <note>an octagon</note> by using two overlapping squares.

Outside of that, one should draw two more circles with a one-inch gap. Beyond those, one should fashion sixteen petals and two more outer circles. Outside of these, one should draw two squares <note>the *Bhūpura* or outer walls of the mandala</note>, divided into inner and outer sections.

In the very center womb of the diagram, one should write: "Grant me this success in this turn" within the seed-syllable *Hrīṃ* <note>original: "hṛllekhāyāṃ", the "Heart-Scribe" syllable</note>, along with one's own name and the syllable *Grīṃ* <note>original: "vārākhyāṃ", referring to the letter *Ra* combined with *Ga* and *Ī*</note>. Within the intervals, one should write "Grant success."

Outside of this, moving clockwise starting from the top, one should write thirty-two letters in the following manner: eight letters in the corners, eight in the eight-angled figure, and sixteen in the sixteen petals. These letters are drawn from the root-mantra's transformed vowels <note>the *Svaravikṛta*</note>, which number 124 in total.

In the gaps between the circles, the inscriptions are as follows:
1. In the gap surrounding the inner "nine-womb" pattern, write the sixteen vowels from **A** to **Aḥ**.
2. In the gap surrounding the middle eight-angled figure, write the sixteen consonants from **Ka** to **Ta**.
3. In the gap surrounding the sixteen petals, write the sixteen letters from **Ya** to **Sa**.
4. In the four outer corners of the squares, write the two letters **Ha** and **La** in each corner interval.

This constitutes the **first Yantra**. For the remaining six **yantras**, one should write the subsequent sets of thirty-two letters from the mantra mentioned before. Having thus created seven **yantras** <term>Yantra: a mystical geometric diagram used for meditation or ritual</term>, one should employ them in the stated order on the seven days of the week, starting with Sunday.

"At the foot of a Mother-Tree"—the eight "Mother-Trees" were previously described in the section concerning the primary *Nityā* deities and the rituals for desired fruits; thus, there are eight such locations. "In a forest on a riverbank" refers to a forest situated by a river. In this way, a total of twelve locations are possible. "In groups of three"—this means that in each of the twelve locations, there are three individual **Yakshinis** <term>Yakshini: a class of semi-divine female nature spirits</term>.

### [Chapter 17] Description of the Signs of Perfection of the Sixteen Nityas
#### Page 313

These servant spirits <term>Chetakas: minor spirits or "messengers" invoked to perform tasks</term> arrive at midnight, appearing extremely terrifying. They may attempt to shake or disturb the practitioner; however, if he remains unmoved, they will then appear directly before him. [91]

Visible to the eyes, they will ask at night, "What is your desire? I shall do it." Each one, having been addressed, replies "So be it," and says, "Do not let me go." [92]

One should worship them daily with chants and offerings; then, when they are remembered <note>The text implies a mental summons after the initial mastery is achieved</note>, they arrive and accomplish the desired message or goal. [93]

They bring about the defeat of enemies in battle and strike down harmful people; they provide requested objects and wealth both day and night. [94]

They will surely bring desired women in an instant, and they can immobilize <term>Stambhana: the magical power of paralyzing or freezing an opponent or object</term> a rutting elephant, a horse, or a man. [95]

When perfection <term>Siddhi: spiritual or supernatural attainment</term> of the Sixteen Nityas <term>Shodasha Nitya: the sixteen eternal goddesses of the lunar cycle in the Shri Vidya tradition</term> is achieved, one is honored or assisted by:
Divine Sages <term>Devarshis</term>, Ancestors <term>Pitris</term>, and Spirits <term>Rakshasas</term>;
by Ghosts <term>Pisachas</term>, Serpent-beings <term>Uragas</term>, and Perfected Beings <term>Siddhas</term>;
by Celestial Musicians <term>Kinnaras</term> and groups of Nymphs <term>Apsaras</term>; [96]

By the Wind Deities <term>Maruts</term>, the Elemental Gods <term>Vasus</term>, the Seven Sages <term>Saptarishis</term>, and the Nature Spirits <term>Yakshas</term> and Titans <term>Danavas</term>;
by the eleven types of Storm Gods <term>Rudras</term>, the Celestial Beings <term>Sadhyas</term>, and the nine Planets <term>Grahas</term>. [97]

---

**Commentary (Manoramā)**

Regarding the "days of practice" <note>original: "sādhana-dineṣu"</note>, this applies to all general practices. [98] The phrase "day and night" means at all times. "Of all" refers to those previously mentioned, such as Vijayā and others, ending with Māyā—the eight mentioned and the others as well. [80] "Him" <note>original: "amum"</note> refers to the practitioner (<term>Sādhaka</term>). "Before him" means in front of the practitioner. [91]

"Each" <note>original: "pratyekam"</note> means every single servant spirit. This connects to the word "should say." "They" refers to the servant spirits. The remainder of the verse beginning with "So be it" represents the words of the practitioner's prayer. [92]

"Daily" <note>original: "nityaśaḥ"</note> means following the mentioned order after the perfection of each specific servant spirit. "When remembered" <note>original: "smṛte"</note> refers to the servant spirits. "Desired goal" is understood to be the practitioner's. [93]

The section beginning with "Of enemies" describes the method of accomplishing the desired goals. This is what is meant: among the servant spirits, one should master each specific spirit that one favors, following the prescribed order. The use of plural forms here is a tradition indicating that these rules for practice apply to all servant spirits collectively. This also applies to the procedures for mastering Māyā, Vijayā, and others of similar status. [94-95]

The five verses beginning with "Nityā..." and ending with "would become..." describe the signs of attaining perfection in the Sixteen Nityas...

### [Chapter 17] The Fruits of Mastery and the Conclusion of the Tongue-Essence

# In the Tantraraja with the Commentary named Manorama

By the twelve Suns <term>Adityas: the solar deities representing the twelve months of the year</term>, by the Guardians of the World <term>Lokapalas: the deities presiding over the cardinal directions</term>, and by other various deities; by kings and by women, as well as by other men and even by animals— [98]

He is worshipped at all times, having become a dwelling place of the happiness desired by the perfected ones. He is joyful in heart, eloquent and generous, compassionate, pleasant of face, and forgiving. [99]

He is full of heart <note>meaning he is entirely content and lacks nothing</note>, eternally blissful, and remains unattached to the fruits of his actions. He is wealthy, an enjoyer of life, free from hatred toward others, and becomes the very ground of love for the two of us <note>original: "avayoh"; referring to the divine couple Shiva and Shakti who are the speakers of the Tantra</note>. [100]

The pervasiveness of the Essence of the Tongue <term>Jihva-tattva: the mystical reality associated with speech, taste, and the mantra-power of this specific stage of practice</term> has thus been properly described. By contemplating this in the heart, that reality is made one's own. [101]

->Thus concludes the seventeenth chapter in the Shrikadimata of the Sixteen Nitya Tantras, fully considered. [17]<-

[99] "Full of heart" because he is independent of anything further to be known. "Independent" or "unattached" refers to worldly matters such as wealth. "Free from hatred toward others" is the word-analysis; it means he is averse to performing acts of hatred toward others. "For the two of us" means for Shiva and Shakti. [100]

# Chapter 18

> Now, O wise one, listen to the ritual procedure of the thirteenth among the sixteen Eternal Goddesses <term>Nityas: a group of sixteen goddesses representing the lunar days</term>, whose mantra <term>Vidya</term> was previously revealed to you. [1]
>
> I shall speak of her auxiliary parts <term>Angas</term>, the ritual placement of letters <term>Akshara-nyasa</term>, her meditation and worship with the attendant powers <term>Shaktis</term>, and the use of her weapons which grant victory. [2]
>
> Using the consonants of the mantra joined with the long vowels, one should create four [limbs]. With the remaining two vowels, one makes the final two, thus performing the six-limbed rite on the hands and the body <term>Karanga-nyasa: a ritual where sounds are "placed" on fingers and body parts to sanctify them</term>. [3]
>
> These letters, combined with the nasal point <term>Bindu: the dot representing the resonance of divine consciousness</term>, should be placed in sequence on the organs of sense—starting with the ears—and on the mind. The rest is performed as previously described. [4]

->Now, the Eighteenth Chapter.<-

In the previous seventeenth chapter, the procedure for the twelfth Nitya, Nilapataka <note>literally "Blue Banner"</note>, was taught. Following that, the procedure for the thirteenth Nitya, Vijaya <note>meaning "Victory"</note>, is taught in this eighteenth chapter, which begins with the verse "Now, regarding the sixteen..." and consists of one hundred verses. The first two verses, beginning with "Now, regarding the sixteen..." and ending with "granting victory," define the scope of the chapter. In this context, the "Thirteenth" refers to Vijaya Nitya. "Previously" refers to the Third Chapter where her mantra was first mentioned. [1] "Meditation and worship" <note>original: dhyānarce</note> is a dual compound meaning both the internal contemplation and the external ritual. "The application of her weapons" refers to the specific weapons she holds and the methods of using them in ritual or magic. [2]

The two verses starting with "the consonants of the mantra" and ending with "as before" teach the procedure for the placement <term>Nyasa</term> of the letters of the foundational mantra onto the hands, the six limbs, and the sense organs. Specifically, the verse "with the consonants of the mantra... one should perform the six-limbed rite" explains the following: by using the first four long-vowel versions of the mantra's consonant joined with the nasal point—namely **Jhām**, **Jhīm**, **Jhūm**, and **Jhaim**—one should perform the ritual placement on the heart, head, crest <note>the top of the head/tuft of hair</note>, and the "armor" <note>the torso</note>. Then, using the remaining two forms, **Jhaum** and **Jhaḥ**, one performs the placement for the eyes and the "weapon" <note>an outward gesture of protection</note>. In this way, the six-limbed rite should be performed following the placement on the hands. [3] "In the sense organs, starting with the ears" refers to the ears, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose. In that ritual, the placement on the skin is considered "pervasive" <note>covering the entire surface of the body</note>. "The rest" refers to the pervasive placement using the entire mantra, just as was described in earlier chapters.

***

<note>(1) A variant manuscript reading for verse 2 suggests "meditation among the women" (dhyānaṃ veśyāsu) instead of "meditation and worship" (dhyānarce).</note>

<summary>This page introduces Chapter 18, focusing on the ritual of Vijaya Nitya, the thirteenth lunar goddess, specifically detailing the phonetic ritual placements (Nyasa) of her mantra onto the practitioner's body and sense organs.</summary>
<keywords>Vijaya Nitya, Nyasa, ritual placement, seed syllables, Jhām, sense organs, Tantraraja Tantra, Manorama commentary</keywords>

--- Page 370 ---
<meta>This page continues the Eighteenth Chapter of the Tantraraja, detailing the visualization (Dhyana) and ritual placement (Nyasa) for the Goddess Vijaya Nitya. It follows the initial description of her six-limbed rite and the placement of her mantra syllables on the sense organs.</meta>

> She has five faces and ten arms, with three eyes on every face. She is adorned with a crescent moon placed upon her brilliant crown. [5]
> 
> She is decorated with all types of ornaments and shines in yellow garments. Her bodily luster is like the orb of the rising sun, and she possesses a pure, gentle smile. [6]
> 
> In her left arms, she holds a conch, a noose, a shield, a bow, and a white water-lily. In her right hands, she bears a discus, a goad, a sword, an arrow, and a citron fruit <note>original: "matulungaka"</note>. [7]
> 
> She appears terrifying in specific ritual applications <term>Prayoga: rituals performed for a specific goal, like victory or protection</term>, yet she is exceedingly gentle in daily meditative worship <term>Upasana: the practice of sitting near the divine through devotion</term>. She is seated upon a lion. [8]
> 
> She is surrounded on all sides by Shaktis <term>Shaktis: female personifications of the Goddess's own powers</term> who are mounted upon tigers. She remains in a comfortable seated posture <term>Sukhasana: a relaxed, cross-legged ritual pose</term> during battle-worship and other ritual applications. [9]
> 
> During her worship, the attendant Shaktis are also seated in the comfortable posture. They all possess divine forms, faces, hands, and weapons identical to her own. [10]

---

The phrase "by the previously mentioned method" implies the following: One should take the six syllables of the Root Mantra <term>Mula-vidya</term>—namely, *Bhaṃ, Maṃ, Raṃ, Yaṃ, Auṃ,* and *Ūṃ*—joined with the nasal point <term>Bindu</term>, and place them in sequence on the six locations: the five sense organs (starting with the ears) and the mind. In the three pairs of sense organs (ears, eyes, nostrils), one syllable is placed on each side of the pair. After this, one should perform the "pervasive placement" <term>Vyapaka-nyasa: a ritual gesture where the hands pass over the entire body to envelop it in the mantra</term> using the complete form of the Mantra. [4]

Through the six verses beginning with "She has five faces" and ending with "also," the text teaches the daily worship meditation and the ritual application meditation for the Goddess and her retinue. In this context, the arrangement of her five faces is the same as that described for the Goddess Nilapataka <note>The twelfth Nitya, "The Blue Banner," described in the previous chapter</note>. The description of her ten arms is also similar. The weapons in her arms should be understood as being held from the top-left downward and from the top-right downward respectively. [5, 6, 7]

The term "in ritual application" refers to rituals for victory in battle and the like. "In worship" refers to her daily service. "Seated upon a lion" means she is mounted on a lion. [8] "In battle-worship" means worship performed specifically for the sake of victory in war. Having visualized her as terrifying and mounted on a lion—surrounded by Shaktis who resemble her but are mounted on tigers—one should worship her for the sake of victory in war. "In others" refers to rituals such as subjugation <term>Vashya: the ritual power to attract or influence others</term>. [9] "In worship" refers to the daily ritual. The word "also" in the tenth verse is used in a distributive sense, meaning "all" the Shaktis. The essence of what is said is this: for rituals like subjugation and for daily meditative worship, one should meditate on the Goddess and her retinue as being seated in the comfortable, relaxed posture. [10]

<meta>This page continues the Eighteenth Chapter of the Tantraraja, moving from the meditative visualization of the Goddess Vijaya Nitya to the geometric construction of her ritual space (Mandala) and the theological relationship between the fifteen lunar deities and the supreme sixteenth goddess, Lalita.</meta>

### Chapter 18 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Instruction on the sequence for constructing the Mandala for the Daily Worship of the Goddess. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 317

Having drawn two squares adorned with four gates,
and provided with eight petals, one should worship there as before. || 11 ||

Inside that, having made an eight-sided figure <term>Octagon</term> between two circles;
and inside that, likewise, a lotus with sixteen petals. || 12 ||

Likewise, having made an eight-petaled lotus and invoking her there,
one should worship her properly with her respective Powers <term>Shaktis: the personified energies of the Goddess</term> and ritual offerings. || 13 ||

One should perform the daily fire offering <term>Homa: a ritual where offerings are cast into a consecrated fire</term> with cooked rice and clarified butter <note>original: "ajya"</note>, or with sesame and grains.
One should also offer two sacrificial portions <term>Bali: food offerings placed on the ground for spirits or deities</term> and then conclude the worship. || 14 ||

The fifteen Eternal Goddesses <term>Nityas: deities representing the fifteen days of the waxing and waning moon</term>, apart from Lalita, are the mistresses of the lunar days.
She [Lalita] is considered to consist of them, joined with the beautiful crescent moon on her crown. || 15 ||

One should worship them using names placed within the seven-syllabled Maya-mantra.
The Powers residing in those enclosures <term>Avarana: the 'veils' or concentric layers of a sacred diagram</term> possess the same form and power as her. || 16 ||

---

With these fifteen verses beginning with “Having drawn two squares” and ending with “easy,” the teacher instructs on: the sequence of constructing the *Mandala* <term>Mandala: a sacred geometric diagram used for centering and worship</term> for the daily worship of the Goddess; the ritual method for the daily worship within its four enclosures; the esoteric meaning of the fifteen *Nityas* who wear the digit of the moon; Lalita’s own way of wearing that digit; and the names of the enclosure-powers.

In that context, “as before” means the *Nitya* is in the square (implying the daily worship ritual). || 11 ||

“Inside that” means inside the square. || 12 ||

“There” means in the diagram <term>Chakra</term>. “Likewise” means in the manner to be described.

The sequence for constructing the daily worship *Mandala* is as follows:
Having drawn two squares, an inner and an outer according to measurement, each provided with two “branches” <note>gateposts</note> and four gates; inside that, having drawn two circles that may or may not touch the square lines; inside that, having made an eight-sided figure as before; inside that, a sixteen-petaled lotus; and inside that, having constructed an eight-petaled lotus <note>The question mark appears in the original printed text</note> (?); in the pericarp <term>Karnika: the central seed-pod or heart of the lotus</term> of that, having invoked the Goddess with her retinue, one should worship. || 13 ||

“Or” indicates an alternative choice in materials. “Two sacrificial offerings” are to be done as before. || 14 ||

This involves the contemplation of the three lights, etc. “She consists of them” means that Lalita is of the form of the imperishable sixteenth digit of the moon.

By this verse, the following is explained: The fifteen lunar days are the fifteen forms of the moon's digits, characterized by waxing and waning, and they are distinct from one another. However, they are all permeated by the sixteenth digit <term>Shodashi</term> which is the underlying cause of all the other digits.

<note>Footnote 1: The original manuscript reads "Mistresses who are the soul of the Nityas" (nityātmikāśvarāḥ).</note>

# Chapter 18: On the Rites of Preliminary Perfection and Other Procedures

> ...the captivating [Manohara], the auspicious [Mangala], she who is overflowing with passion [Madotsikta], the wise [Manasvini],
> the proud [Manini], the sweet [Madhura], the illusory [Maya], and she who has the aforementioned form of the enchantress [Mohini]. || 24 ||
>
> In this way, through worship, ritual repetition, meditation, and fire-offerings, the self-controlled practitioner who constantly serves the Goddess becomes happy in every way. || 25 ||
>
> Following the previously mentioned sequence, the self-controlled one should recite one hundred thousand repetitions for every letter of the <term>Vidya: the sacred mantra of the goddess</term>. After performing the fire-offering with red lotuses, he attains the state where the mantra is perfected. || 26 ||
>
> The practitioner should then perform the ritual applications according to the rules for the fire-offering diagram, through recitation, libations, and worship as prescribed. || 27 ||
>
> With lotuses and water-lilies—both red and white—and fragrant blue lilies, as well as the fragrant <term>Shephalika: the night-flowering jasmine, Nyctanthes arbor-tristis</term>, smeared with the <term>Trimadhua: "three sweets," a mixture of honey, ghee, and sugar</term> according to the rules. || 28 ||
>
> From the fire-offering, he should perform the rites on the seven days of the week with the seven mentioned flowers; or on the two specified days within that <term>Mandala: a sacred geometric diagram</term>. || 29 ||

***

[The commentary states:] Inside the sixteen-petaled lotus are the Powers [Shaktis]—Manohara and the others who are described in the verse following this one. <note>Refers to the list in Verse 24</note> || 23 ||

**Their forms are as described before** <note>meaning they share the physical attributes and ornaments of the primary deity</note>. The sequence of worship for these surrounding deities is by entering from the outside toward the interior. || 24 ||

**In this way**—meaning according to the form previously described. || 25 ||

Through the two verses beginning with "According to the previous..." and ending with "...as prescribed," the author teaches the rules for <term>Purascharana: the preliminary ritual of "empowering" a mantra through massive repetition</term> and the eligibility to perform ritual applications only for one who has completed this preparation. In that context, **"according to the previously mentioned sequence"** refers to the sequence described in the chapter on <term>Nilapataka: the Blue-Banner Nitya Goddess</term>. By this, it is meant that one should separate and count the vowels, consonants, and nasal points [bindus] within the root-mantra, and then perform a hundred thousand repetitions [Japa] for each of those letters. The number of letters in this specific mantra is seven <note>Implying a total of 700,000 repetitions</note>. The rest of the text is easy to understand. || 26–27 ||

Through the three half-verses starting with **"With lotuses..."** and ending with **"certainly,"** the author teaches the sequence for the fire-offerings and worship with the seven flowers on the seven days of the week, which leads to the mentioned "Success in Victory." In this regard, the phrase **"red and white"** applies to both the lotuses [Kamala] and the water-lilies [Kairava]. This means: red lotuses, white lotuses, red lilies, and white lilies. These are to be smeared with the "three sweets" [honey, ghee, and sugar] during the fire-offering. || 28 ||

In the word **"From the fire-offering" [homat]**, the fifth case ending is used to imply the completion of an action <note>grammatical note: the 'lyab-lopa' construction</note>. It means "after having performed the fire-offering." **On the seven days** refers to the days starting with Sunday. **With the seven mentioned**—the word "flowers" is implied. **On the two specified days**—the phrase "in the chapter of <term>Kulasundari: one of the sixteen Nitya goddesses</term>" is implied. **Within that Mandala**—these Mandalas are also described there, and should be examined in the twenty-eighth chapter. This is what is being said.

**[The Commentary states:]**
The result occurs—by using the seven flowers mentioned: the red lotus, white lotus, red water-lily, white water-lily, fragrant blue lily, and the fragrant <term>Shephalika: the night-flowering jasmine</term> (here referred to by names like <term>Karnikara</term> and others). By worshiping the "Lord of the Door" <note>original: "varesha", the planetary deity ruling that specific day</note> in his <term>Mandala: sacred ritual circle</term> on the seven days of the week starting with Sunday, and offering them into the fire with the <term>Mula-vidya: the primary mantra of the Goddess</term>, the stated results are achieved. (This refers to the previous verse 28).

**In battle** refers to the seven subjects to be discussed. **In single combat** is as mentioned before. **In both types of gambling** refers to gambling with living beings <note>such as cockfighting or animal racing</note> and inanimate objects <note>such as dice or board games</note>. || 30 || **In all** means in other types of disputes or lawsuits as well.

With the two verses beginning with **"By offering flowers of the Chaturangula"** and ending with **"certainly,"** the author teaches the method for paralyzing enemies. This is done by performing fire-offerings over the seven days of the week with the <term>Aragvadha: Indian Laburnum</term> and the other seven flowers. There, **Chaturangula** refers to the Laburnum tree. || 31 || **Nameru** refers to the flowers of the <term>Suraparna: the "divine leaf" tree</term>. **Rajavriksha** refers to the flowers of the Laburnum. || 32 ||

**As before** means preceded by the worship of the Lord of the Day. **On the seven days** refers to the week starting with Sunday. **With the seven** refers to the flowers starting with Karnikara. Here, the Laburnum is mentioned twice to indicate its use both as a general requirement and as a specific offering for certain days. **In the matters mentioned** refers to single combat and the rest. The gist of this is: through the fire-offering of these seven flowers over the seven days, preceded by the worship of the Lord of the Day at the respective ritual door, and using the Laburnum flowers, the stated results are achieved. || 33 ||

With the twenty-one verses starting with **"Of the enemy"** and ending with **"doubt,"** the author describes the rituals using specific substances on particular lunar days and weekdays...

->From the sixth day to the tenth, one should use goat ghee; || 51 ||<-
->by offering the previously mentioned grains without their husks,<-
->one attains the same result mentioned before.<-
->Beyond that, until the fifteenth day, one should offer all the grains with two types of sesame; || 52 ||<-
->along with white rice and milk pudding, all soaked in sheep ghee.<-
->From such an offering, one attains the result of victory as described. || 53 ||<-
->In the same way, using fire produced from the wood of a star-associated tree,<-
->by offering the various parts of those trees soaked in honey,<-
->the attainment of that result certainly occurs; of this, there is no doubt. || 54 ||<-

The phrase <note>original: "krishna-go-ghritaih"</note> **with ghee from a black cow** and **from that day** refers to the practice within the ritual circle <term>Mandala: a sacred consecrated space or diagram</term> as explained previously. The **results** mentioned are the results of **victory**. This is the meaning of the phrase **as stated in the described form** || 48 ||. The word **victory** is mentioned here in connection with what preceded it. The word **from the fire-offering** connects to both what comes before and after. This implies that victory is declared through these seven types of offerings in the manner described. Furthermore, the text says: **Listen to the victory to be described next, which comes from offerings made on specific lunar days and under specific stars.** || 49 ||

**On those lunar days** refers to the five days starting from the <term>Pratipat: the first day of the lunar fortnight</term> up to the fifth. One should **attain**—the word "victory" is implied here. Similarly, for the five days starting from the sixth to the tenth || 51 ||, the **previously mentioned** substances are the five grains like rice and so on. **Without husks** means the outer skin or chaff has been removed. The **previously mentioned result** is the result of victory. **Beyond that, until the fifteenth** means the group of five lunar days starting from the eleventh and ending on the fifteenth. **With all** refers to using all five grains (rice, etc.) on the eleventh day.

Regarding the **two types of sesame**: these are the black and white varieties. On the twelfth day, one should offer black sesame; on the thirteenth, white sesame || 52 ||. **White food** refers to plain cooked rice; these are offered on the fourteenth day. **Milk puddings** <note>original: "payasa" — a ritual sweet rice porridge</note> are offered on the fifteenth. **Soaked** means the five grains and other substances are drenched in the specified fats. **On those lunar days**, the **result described** is, again, the result of victory || 53 ||.

**In fire produced from a star-associated tree** refers to the fire kindled from the wood of trees corresponding to specific <term>Nakshatras: the 27 lunar mansions or star signs of Indian astronomy</term>, such as the Poison Tree and others. **By those various parts** means using the twigs <term>Samidh: sacrificial fuel-sticks</term> of those specific trees. **Honey** refers to the product of bees. **From the fire-offering** means performing this daily. **Attainment of that** refers to the attainment of victory. The summary of this teaching is: for each of the twenty-seven stars starting with Ashvini, if one performs a fire-offering using the wood of the tree assigned to that star, soaked in honey, one will surely attain the corresponding results. || 54 ||

---

<note>(1) A variant reading in the primary manuscript suggests "with two types of offerings" instead of "with two types of sesame."</note>

<header>In the Tantraraja along with the commentary named Manorama</header>

->In the sacred mantra, one should join the five letters with the vowels as before;<-
->listen, O Dear One, to the Yantras made of that eighty-lettered mantra. || 55 ||<-
->By drawing ten lines horizontally and ten lines vertically,<-
->there shall be eighty-one squares; in them, one should write the letters in order. || 56 ||<-
->Having placed the name in the middle square according to the previously stated rule,<-
->and having made the ends of the lines into tridents, one should invoke and worship her. || 57 ||<-
->One should attend to the primary mantra, perform the daily recitation, and worship;<-
->by worshipping the sequence of the mantra in that Yantra, one obtains the result. || 58 ||<-

With the four verses starting with **In the mantra** <note>original: "vidyāyām"</note> and ending with **obtains the result** <note>original: "prāpnuyāt"</note>, the author teaches the attainment of victory through the worship of a grid-diagram <term>Yantra: a geometric diagram used in meditation and ritual</term> composed of eighty letters generated from the five root-mantra consonants modified by vowels. 

In that context, **as before** <note>original: "prāgvat"</note> means those letters which are not repeated. The **five** letters are the consonants **Jha, Ma, Ra, Ya, and Au** which will be described later. The vowel **U** and the nasal drop <term>Bindu: the dot representing the manifestation of consciousness</term> are not included here because they would be redundant as vowels. 

**With the vowels** means with the sixteen vowels. **In that way** means according to the previously stated order. This order consists of joining each of the five consonants with each of the sixteen vowels <note>5 consonants x 16 vowels = 80 syllables</note>. **By those** refers to those letters. **The Yantras** are those which will be described. || 55 ||

**By drawing ten lines** implies they should be equally spaced. **In them** refers to the squares <term>Kosthas: the individual cells within the grid</term>. **Those** refers to the syllables of the mantra, eighty in number. **In order** means starting from the front and proceeding in a clockwise, inward-moving direction. || 56 ||

**In the middle square** refers to the eighty-first cell. **The name** refers to the names of the practitioner <note>Sadhaka</note>, the object to be achieved <note>Saadhya</note>, and the action to be performed <note>Karma</note>. **By the previously stated rule** means writing from top to bottom and middle to end. **The ends of the lines** are forty in number <note>20 lines have two ends each</note>. **In this** refers to the Yantra. **Her** refers to the Goddess **Vijaya Nitya**. || 57 ||

**One should attend** means through worship and recitation <term>Japa: the meditative repetition of a mantra</term>. **Daily** refers to one's own daily ritual sequence. **The sequence of the mantra** means for the purpose of the specific ritual application of the mantra's sequence. **In this** means that in this Yantra, one should worship the daily sequence and the mantra-sequence for the ritual application. **One should worship** according to the prescribed manner. **The result** is the fruit of victory.

The procedure for constructing the Yantra is as follows: After drawing ten equally spaced lines horizontally and ten vertically, eighty-one squares are produced. Starting from the middle square of the bottom-most row, one should write the eighty syllables of the root-mantra (modified by vowels) in a clockwise, inward-spiraling motion. In the one remaining square in the center, one should write the names of the practitioner and others according to the prescribed writing order. One should slightly extend the forty ends of the twenty lines of the Yantra outward and turn each into a trident <term>Trishula: the three-pronged spear of Shiva</term>. 

One should then invoke the Goddess **Vijaya Nitya** into that Yantra, set aside the usual daily worship circle <term>Mandala</term>, and worship one's own daily sequence there. Within that, one should also worship the mantra-sequence for the specific ritual application. By doing so, the perfection of the result of victory is attained. || 58 ||

<header>In the 18th Chapter ] The description of the Lotus Diagram consecration and its results.</header>

By drawing four lines—east to west and south to north—O Supreme Goddess, nine squares are formed here. || 59 ||

In each of these squares, one should draw lotuses with eight petals. In the pericarp <term>Karnika: the central seed-pod or heart of a lotus</term> of the middle lotus, one should write... || 60 ||

The mantra containing the name <note>The name of the practitioner or the person for whom the ritual is performed</note>, and outside that, in the eight petals, one should write the first eight letters with a dot <term>Bindu: a nasalizing dot representing the concentration of power</term>. Outside of that... || 61 ||

In the pericarp, one name, and likewise eight in the eight petals. Having written in this way in all eight surrounding lotuses, one should encircle it with the letters of the alphabet <term>Matrka: the "Mother" letters of the Sanskrit alphabet, considered the building blocks of the universe</term>. || 62 ||

One should write these letters in both reverse and direct order, combined with the *Maya* <note>original: "māyā", referring here to the transformative syllable HRIM</note> and the *Bindu*. In the two squares outside the front of the Yantra, one should write as follows... || 63 ||

Having prepared it thus on a space of two cubits <term>Hasta: a measurement of length from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</term>, one should place the ritual pot <term>Kumbha: a water vessel used for consecration</term>, and fill it with water containing herbs and other substances as before. || 64 ||

---

With the fifteen half-verses beginning with **By drawing east-west** <note>original: "prāgityādibhiḥ"</note> and ending with **abundant**, the author teaches the Lotus Diagram situated in nine squares. Through its consecration <term>Abhisheka: a ritual bathing or sprinkling of water to empower a person or object</term> and worship, one attains results such as victory. In that context, **by drawing four lines** implies they are equally spaced. **Here** refers to the place where the lines are drawn. || 59 ||

**In those** means in the nine squares; **in those** lotuses, in all nine. || 60 ||

**Containing the name** <note>original: "nāmagarbhā"</note>... <insert>The name of the practitioner is written in the belly of the letter **Bha**, the name of the target in the part of the letter **Ra**, and the intended action in the space between them.</insert> **That mantra** refers to the modified form. **Outside that** means outside the pericarp. **In those** refers to the eighty modified letters of the mantra. **Eight** letters are written with the **Bindu**. **Outside that** refers to the lotuses situated outside the central lotus. || 61 ||

**One** refers to the letter following the previously written eight. **Outside** means outside the pericarp. **Eight** means the eight letters following the one written in the pericarp. **In the eight** petals. **Thus** refers to the described characteristics. **In the eight** means in the lotuses located in the squares surrounding the center, including the middle square of the bottom row. || 62 ||

**Maya** refers to the *Visarjaniya* <term>Visarjaniya: a phonetic sound in Sanskrit (represented by two dots) symbolizing the outward breath or manifestation</term>. **In the two squares** refers to the two pathways between the two squares. That is the place for the alphabet letters. **Outside** refers to being outside the two squares. This connects with the instruction to write at the "front" of this Yantra. || 63 ||

**In the measure of two cubits** <note>original: "hasta-yugma-māne"</note>—it is understood that this applies to the nine-square grid. It means one should make the nine-square grid two cubits in size.

-> Having worshipped the mantra <term>Vidya: a female deity in the form of a sacred sound-syllable</term> and chanted it ten thousand times, <-
-> one should perform the consecration with those waters according to the rules; then, being freed from all afflictions, one becomes happy. || 65 || <-
-> Victory shall be achieved everywhere, even in the seven situations previously mentioned, <-
-> whenever distress arises from the nine planets, from enemies, or from any other source. || 66 || <-
-> In the effort of battle, or when seeking fame and prosperity, <-
-> or for the attainment of a son or any desired object, one should perform this on the three birth-days <note>The "three births" refers to the three specific astrological days in a month: one's birth star (Janma-nakshatra) and its two recurring counterparts in the 27-day lunar cycle</note>. || 67 || <-
-> Having inscribed this diagram <term>Yantra: a mystical geometric design used in worship</term> with red chalk on an altar, and there <-
-> having invoked and worshipped the Goddess, one should likewise chant the mantra ten thousand times. || 68 || <-

***

**"That"**—refers to the ritual pot, implying one for each pericarp <term>Karnika: the central seed-pod or heart of a lotus</term>. **"As before"**—referring to the decoration with fruits, sprouts, and similar items. || 64 || **"Having worshipped"**—meaning according to the daily ritual sequence. **"The mantra"**—the unmodified form of the sacred chant. Because it contains letters beyond the count of ten thousand <note>The commentator is clarifying the relationship between the letter-count and the number of repetitions</note>. **"With those"**—refers to the waters. **"Then"**—meaning after the consecration ceremony. || 65 || **"In the seven mentioned"**—this refers to the seven types of conflict, such as duels and so on, mentioned previously in the thirtieth verse of another chapter. || 66 || **"Fame and prosperity"**—these are the two specific desires mentioned. **"On the three birth-days"**—as explained previously. **"One should perform"**—the word "consecration" is to be supplied here to complete the sense.

The meaning of these nine verses is as follows: In a space measuring two cubits <term>Hasta: roughly 18 inches, the length from the elbow to the fingertips</term> in the directions of East, West, South, and North, one should draw four lines at equal intervals to create nine squares. In these, one should draw nine lotuses, each endowed with eight petals. 

In the center of the pericarp of the lotus located in the middle square, one should write the unmodified mantra containing the name <note>The name of the practitioner is inserted into the center of the mantra</note> as before. Then, one should write the first eight letters of the root-mantra (modified by vowels) in the eight petals, starting from the front and moving clockwise, with one letter accompanied by a dot <term>Bindu: a nasalizing mark representing concentrated power</term> in each petal. 

Outside of this, in the eight surrounding squares starting from the center of the bottom row and moving clockwise, one should write the letters succeeding the previously written eight in the pericarp of each lotus. In their respective eight petals, one should write the eight letters succeeding those, starting from the front and moving clockwise. In this way, having created a nine-square diagram containing nine lotuses using eighty letters, one should draw two squares around the outside with a one-inch space between them. 

In the inner path between these two squares, one should write the letters of the alphabet in reverse order <note>original: "viloma"</note> including the aspiration <note>original: "visarga", the ':' sound in Sanskrit</note>. In the outer path, one should write the same alphabet in the natural order <note>original: "anuloma"</note> with the nasalizing dots. Outside the entire diagram, at the front, one should write the two letters of the word for "Fortune" <note>original: "lakṣmī"</note>. 

In the center of each of the nine pericarps of these lotuses, one should place a ritual pot <term>Kumbha: a water vessel</term> and fill them with water decocted with the herbs associated with the letters of the mantra. Having worshipped them as before according to the daily rite, and having placed fruits and sprouts upon them, one should invoke the Goddess there. By worshipping and chanting according to the daily rite and performing the consecration on the three birth-days, the mentioned results will be achieved. || 67 ||

<header>Chapter 18 ] Description of the Arts of Diagrams and Related Matters</header>

Having inscribed the diagram on a board made of **Sacred Fig** <note>original: "Aśvattha"; Ficus religiosa</note> wood using **red sandalwood**,
And having perfected it through the ritual of repetition and worship, one should place it in empty houses. || 81 ||

Or in a particular region; there, stable **Prosperity** <note>original: "Śrī"; the Goddess of fortune and beauty</note> increases daily.
Ghosts, demons, malevolent spirits, and vampires will certainly not frequent that place. || 82 ||

However, by inscribing this according to the rule on a board of **Flame-of-the-Forest** <note>original: "Palāśa"; Butea monosperma</note> wood,
And establishing it anywhere, that place becomes an auspicious dwelling for the learned. || 83 ||

By the aforementioned establishment, a capital city becomes firmly stable.
By inscribing it on **Banyan** <note>original: "Vaṭa"</note> wood and burying it, a town becomes permanent. || 84 ||

By performing this on **Cluster Fig** <note>original: "Udumbara"</note> wood and establishing it, very quickly indeed,
The place becomes a sanctuary for those seeking refuge; of this there is no doubt. || 85 ||

From the space between the corner-triangles of the **Diamond** <term>Vajra</term>, one should draw a small trident.
One should write the letters of **Fire** and **Air** <note>original: "dāha-vyāpta"; technical terms for the seed-syllables 'Ra' and 'Ya'</note> combined with the **dot of the void** <note>original: "kha-saṃyukta"; referring to the Anusvāra or 'm' sound</note> between the two outer points of that trident. || 86 ||

Having established the **Mace-Bearer** <note>original: "Gadin"; an aspect of a deity or a protector spirit</note> there through the repetition of the sacred mantra and other rites,
And by reciting the mantra while concentrating on the forehead, the spirit will enter the mace and speak. || 87 ||

---

**[Commentary]**

Writing the **Alphabet** <term>Mātṛkā</term> in reverse order with the *visarga* <note>the 'ḥ' aspiration</note> as before, and then the same in forward order with the *bindu* <note>the 'ṃ' nasalization</note>, through the process of moving from inside to outside—by this diagram alone, without needing any other means, one attains all fruits such as victory through its ritual application. || 79 ||

*In the things mentioned*—refers to the *Lodhra* wood and others mentioned in the eighth chapter. *Also in the seven*—in this chapter, this refers to the seven contexts such as hand-to-hand combat mentioned in the thirtieth verse. || 80 ||

*Diagram*—the diamond-shaped one. *With red sandalwood*—as described previously. *In a region*—the word "empty" is understood here. *There*—meaning in the house or the region. || 82 ||

*This*—the diamond-shaped diagram. *Anywhere*—the word "field" or "land" is understood. *From the aforementioned establishment, a capital*—meaning the land where it is established. *A town*—the region where it is established. || 84 ||

*Place*—the location occupied by the diagram. || 85 ||

*From the space between the corner-triangles of the Diamond*—this means from the middle space between the triangles located in the four directions. *Associated with Fire and Air*—the letters *Ra* and *Ya*. *The void*—refers to the dot (*bindu*). *Between the two outer points*—on the points or "horns" on either side of the central line of the trident located in the space between the triangles.

This is what is being said: Having made a trident in the middle space of the triangles located in the directions of the previously described Diamond, and having written the letters *Ra* and *Ya* (which are the essences of Fire and Wind) with the dot on the two points of that trident, one should perform the ritual application described hereafter. || 86 ||

*There*—in the Diamond marked with the trident. *Him*— <note>The commentary here begins to explain the possession or communication ritual involving the spirit in the mace.</note>

<summary>This page describes the magical utility of the Diamond Diagram (Vajra-yantra) when inscribed on different types of wood, such as Sacred Fig for prosperity and Banyan for urban stability. It also introduces a specialized ritual involving a trident-marked Diamond used for a form of divination where a spirit is said to speak through a ritual mace.</summary>

<header>Tantrarāja with the Commentary named Manoramā</header>

Regarding the ritual for causing possession or its removal:
Planetary spirits, ghosts, demons, and others who have possessed a person surely depart by the power of this diagram. || 88 ||

At that very moment, the possessed becomes like a servant under the practitioner's control. Having inscribed this diagram, worshipped it, one should establish it in a specific location. || 89 ||

If placed in the palace of a king, **consumption** <note>original: "Rājayakṣmā"; literally the "King of Diseases," historically identified with pulmonary tuberculosis or chronic wasting diseases</note> will undoubtedly leave that place. In the stables of elephants or mounts, one should prepare nine such diagrams. || 90 ||

Having established them in those nine locations—in the four directions, the four intermediate points, and the center—one should worship them daily. Because of the diagram's power, diseases and **malevolent sorcery** <note>original: "Kṛtyā"; personified magical spells or entities sent by an enemy to cause harm</note> sent by others || 91 ||

Are not even able to look at the protected person. Having inscribed the diagram with **camphor, sandalwood, and saffron** <note>original: "candra-candana-kāśmīraiḥ"</note> on a fresh cloth, || 92 ||

And having worshipped it and empowered it with the recitation of the **sacred mantra** <term>vidyā</term>, one should spread the cloth and have the patient lie upon it. A person suffering from **burning fever** <note>original: "dāhajvara"</note> is quickly liberated from that fever. || 93 ||

This should also be done for the removal of other ailments. This diagram is also proclaimed for the use of kings in **battles** <note>original: "samara"</note>. || 94 ||

One should inscribe it upon the **kettledrums** <note>original: "niśāna"</note>, the **war-drums** <note>original: "paṭaha"</note>, and other musical instruments. Then, using **vermilion** <note>original: "darada"; cinnabar</note>, one should invoke and worship the Goddess **Victory** <note>original: "Vijayā"</note> within the center of the diagram. || 95 ||

Seeking to attain victory, one should march while striking those drums simultaneously. The **enemy army** <note>original: "pratyarthi-senā"</note>, upon hearing that sound, flees in terror. || 96 ||

Agitated by fear, they flee to the ten directions and never return to attack. This diagram is also prepared for use during **gambling matches involving living beings** <note>original: "sajīva-dyūta"; likely referring to animal racing or cockfighting common in historical courts</note>. || 97 ||

The sick person. || 97 || Specifically, the disease. || 88 || The diagram—without the trident. || 89 || **The land** <note>original: "kṣmā"</note>—the earth or ground. || 90 || **Nine**—referring to the required locations. In nine places. || 91 || By its power. **With camphor, sandalwood, and saffron**—meaning these substances are mixed together. || 92 || "One suffering from burning fever"—this connects to the instruction "one should lay them down." He—the sick person. || 93 || For the removal of that—meaning the removal of the disease. This—the form of the diagram. || 94 || 95 || **Striking**—beating the drums to produce sound. "By that sound"—referring to the sound produced by the striking...

<page-num>331</page-num>
<header>Chapter 18 ] Description of Ritual Prerequisites and Procedures</header>

Having carved the diagram into a small pellet, one should bind it to the neck <note>The commentary specifies this could be the neck of a bird like a rooster, or the practitioner's own neck as an amulet</note> and then employ it. Merely by the sight of this, enemies flee in the ten directions. || 98 ||

One desiring victory achieves it everywhere through this diagram. There is nothing impossible to achieve with this **Vajra-yantra** <note>original: "vañca-yantreṇa"; likely a scribal variant or error for Vajra-yantra, the "Diamond" or "Lightning" diagram mentioned previously</note>, O Parvati! || 99 ||

One should meditate on the enemy's mouth containing the diagram or the **sacred mantra** <term>vidyā</term>, visualizing it as having a glowing red form. At that very moment, through the power of that meditation, the enemy becomes as submissive as a servant. || 100 ||

Thus, the glories of the Eternal Goddess of Victory have been described to you. This is the all-pervading nature of the **Eye-principle** <term>Netra-tattva</term>. By drawing this principle into the consciousness, one makes that essential reality one’s very own. || 101 ||

->Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, fully examined, in the<-
->*Kadimata* section of the *Tantra of the Sixteen Eternals*. || 18 ||<-

---

<margin>Notes on verses 96-100</margin>
Regarding the phrase "to the neck" in verse 98: this refers to the neck of a rooster or similar creature used in the rite. Regarding "achieves victory" in verse 99: it is implied that the person wearing or carrying the diagram is the one who succeeds. Regarding "the mantra" in verse 100: this refers to the root-mantra of the Goddess, used as an alternative to the diagram. "Having a red form" is a description of the diagram itself; when visualized this way, the enemy becomes the subject of the ritual. "Through that power" refers to the specific power generated by meditation as described. || 100 ||
